### Cross-Language Programs

Aura 0.8.0 is the first release of the plan to bring Aura to Rust speed on
the 30
[cross-language programs](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura/blob/main/benchmarks/cross_language/README.md),
complete programs written in Aura, Python, and Rust that do the same work.
Its first phase removed the costs that made some of them quadratic or boxed
every value. On a shared Linux x86-64 container with 4 vCPUs, at `abd8fef`:

| Measure | Aura 0.7.1 | Aura 0.8.0 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| All 30 programs, wall time | 227 s | 147 s |
| Median Aura / Rust, wall time | 35x | 16x |
| Median Aura / Python 3.13, wall time | 3.9x | 2.7x |
| Programs faster than Python | 4 | 9 |
| All 30 programs, instructions at the check size | 14,793M | 9,323M |

Twenty-nine programs got faster. `task_pool` went from 1.5 to 2.8 seconds
while it runs 39% fewer instructions: its workers finish each job so
quickly that they find their queue empty three times as often, and each
wait sleeps and wakes a thread. The largest remaining cost is copying a
class instance or an enum payload into a new box when a program reads it
from a list, a field, or a `match`. The benchmark README has the table for
each program, and the
[operation probes](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura/blob/main/benchmarks/operation_probes/README.md)
give the cost of single operations next to Rust.

The plan's second phase keeps classes, records, tuples, enums, and unions
in typed layouts, lends them instead of copying them on reads, and takes
ownership bookkeeping off the boxes. On the same kind of container, at the
end of that phase:

| Measure | End of phase 1 | End of phase 2 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| All 30 programs, wall time | 147 s | 48.5 s |
| Median Aura / Rust, wall time | 16x | 8.2x |
| Median Aura / Python 3.13, wall time | 2.7x | 0.71x |
| Programs faster than Python | 9 | 19 |
| All 30 programs, instructions at the check size | 9,323M | 3,442M |

Its final targets are 1.5x Rust for compute programs, 2x for string and
data-structure programs, and 1.25x for I/O-bound ones. Only `hashing`
(1.5x) meets its target; `bytecode_vm` (1.7x) and `image_filters` (2.0x)
are close, and `sql_engine` (98x), `spreadsheet` (19x), and
`regex_match` (15x) are furthest. What is left is mostly call frames and
runtime calls on every function call, reads of elements of nested
lists, which stay boxed, and strings, dicts, and JSON, which the third
phase covers. Wall times on the container vary by up to a quarter from
run to run, so the per-step sections below give instruction counts.

Aura 0.9.0 ships phases 2, 3, and 4. The third phase reads strings in
place, keeps short text inline, builds an f-string as one text, probes a
dictionary once, and parses and writes JSON without a second tree. The
fourth makes calls cheaper, reads socket lines a chunk at a time, parses
HTTP on the calling task, and hands queue values over without boxes. On
the same kind of container, median of five runs:

| Measure | Aura 0.8.0 | End of phase 3 | Aura 0.9.0 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| All 30 programs, wall time | 147 s | 27.9 s | 23.5 s |
| Median Aura / Rust, wall time | 16x | 4.8x | 4.6x |
| Median Aura / Python 3.13, wall time | 2.7x | 0.51x | 0.53x |
| Programs faster than Python | 9 | 20 | 22 |

`http_api` (1.0x), `kv_server` (1.2x), `hashing`, `bytecode_vm`,
and `image_filters` (1.4x) are closest to Rust. `task_pool` is 2.4x with
four workers and 1.4x with one: tasks stay on the worker they start on,
so pipeline stages on different workers pass each value between cores.
`sql_engine` (22x), `binary_trees` (10x), and `regex_match` (10x) are
furthest; they spend most of their time allocating boxes for strings,
enums, and class instances, which the next phase takes out of boxes.

Aura 0.10.0 ships phase 5. It shares payload-free variants, skips repeated
type tags, makes text from a byte slice without the slice, reads instance
fields and element views in place, and allocates small blocks from
per-thread lists and chunks, and passes values a function only reads
where they lie instead of copying them (Repeated Type Tags through
Borrowed Reads below give each step). Both compilers measured in the same
two passes on 30 October 2026, median of ten runs:

| Measure | Aura 0.9.0 | Aura 0.10.0 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| All 30 programs, wall time | 26.1 s | 20.9 s |
| Median Aura / Rust, wall time | 4.6x | 3.9x |
| Median Aura / Python 3.13, wall time | 0.50x | 0.40x |
| Programs faster than Python | 22 | 25 |
| Programs above 8x Rust | 4 | 1 |

The phase's own targets, a median of 3x Rust and no program above 8x, are
not met. `regex_match` is 8.6x: its matcher builds and compares small enum
values for each step. `sql_engine` went from 21.8x to 5.9x, `graph_paths`
from 10.5x to 3.8x, and `binary_trees` from 9.2x to 3.7x.

Aura 0.11.0 works on the programs still slower than Python. File calls
hand off to the blocking-I/O pool for less, a read-only `match
d.lookup(key)` finds the entry once, `json.parse` builds the tree in one
pass, list elements passed to a borrowing function are lent, and
one-character `replace`, `count`, and `split` patterns scan with
`memchr`. Both compilers measured in the same two passes on 31 October
2026, median of ten runs:

| Measure | Aura 0.10.0 | Aura 0.11.0 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| All 30 programs, wall time | 17.9 s | 16.4 s |
| Median Aura / Rust, wall time | 3.9x | 3.7x |
| Median Aura / Python 3.13, wall time | 0.41x | 0.40x |
| Programs faster than Python | 25 | 25 |
| Programs above 8x Rust | 0 | 0 |

The container ran faster than on 30 October, so 0.10.0 measures 17.9
seconds here instead of 20.9 and `regex_match` 7.4x instead of 8.6x.
`file_io` went from 2.4x to 1.5x Rust (1.2 times Python's time), `docdb`
ran 26% faster, `json_roundtrip` 21%, and `template_render` 18%. Aura
is still slower than Python on `csv_aggregate`, `docdb`, `file_io`,
`json_roundtrip`, and `template_render`.

### Per-Call Attribution

Eleven symbol-preserving xctrace recordings on the foundations host attribute
recovered Fibonacci samples as follows. They measure `aa52bfc` and earlier,
before calls used static frame descriptors.

| Category | Share of recovered samples |
| --- | ---: |
| Call-frame push/pop and metadata validation | 49.29% |
| Other runtime work | 37.38% |
| Scalar argument and result moves | 6.28% |

The
[boundary note](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura/blob/main/architecture_docs/15-backend-boundary.md#per-call-cost-attribution)
has all eight categories and the sample exclusions.

### Call Frame Cost

Each generated function has one static frame descriptor. It holds the
function name, source path, and position. The runtime validates the
descriptor's text on the function's first call. Each call then records one
pointer and the current task's state comes from a cached pointer. A call
that does not hand a view back to its caller stores nothing else.

Callgrind counts the instructions of the whole `fib(30)` process:

| Build | Instructions | Per recursive call |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `aa52bfc` | 1,917,708,454 | about 1,150 |
| Static frame descriptors | 568,735,408 | about 340 |

On the shared Linux container, 15 alternating GO to DONE runs give a
`fib(30)` median of 129.3 ms at `aa52bfc` and 34.7 ms with descriptors. The
Rust reference takes about 4 ms. Creating and joining 10,000 tasks is
unchanged at about 446 ms.

### Loop Element Reads

A shared `for` loop over a local list reads each element in place when the
element is a `str`, `list`, `dict`, or `set` and the body uses it only in
these ways:

- as a side of `==` or `!=`
- as the receiver of `len()`
- as the receiver of `get(key)`, for a `dict` element

Any other use, such as passing the element to a function, storing it, or
capturing it in a lambda, makes the loop copy each element as before.

```aura
def count_matches(names: list[str], wanted: str) -> int64:
    mut hits = 0
    for name in names:
        if name == wanted:
            hits += 1
    return hits

def main():
    print(count_matches(["ada", "bo", "ada"], "ada"))
```

On the shared Linux container, 11 alternating whole-process runs give these
medians. Before is `aa52bfc`.

| Program | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `string_list_scan` | 115.0 ms | 32.8 ms |
| `record_field_reads` | 149.9 ms | 122.9 ms |
| `dict_build_get` | 298.2 ms | 283.4 ms |
| `set_insert_contains` | 33.6 ms | 33.0 ms |
| `int_list_sum` | 44.7 ms | 45.6 ms |

`record_field_reads` still spends most of its time looking up the key and
matching the `json.Value` it finds.

### List Reads

Native code reads a list's length and its `int64`, `float64`, and `bool`
elements inline. Each read checks the index once against the length. A
list that another task can reach, an index out of range, or an integer
too large for `int64` goes through the runtime, which reports the same
error as before. Appending one of those scalars to a list stores it
without a box.

Callgrind counts the instructions of each whole process. Before is the
loop element reads above.

| Program | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `int_list_sum` | 444,958,513 | 106,060,271 |
| `string_list_scan` | 363,824,369 | 365,899,833 |
| `record_field_reads` | 1,137,789,339 | 1,154,420,211 |
| `dict_build_get` | 2,998,211,951 | 3,049,793,892 |
| `set_insert_contains` | 347,380,497 | 349,860,346 |

`int_list_sum` went from a median of 47.3 ms to 23.9 ms over 11
alternating runs, about 10 times the Rust reference. The other programs
run up to 1.7% more instructions. Each boxed value keeps its list's
element address and length, and every write to a box updates them.

A shared `for` loop over a list or a span reads each element with no
bounds check and advances its index with no overflow check. The loop
already compares the index with the length, and the list cannot change
length while the loop borrows it. `int_list_sum` runs 78,654,607
instructions instead of 106,060,271.

An `Array` with one dimension, indexed by one `int64`, is read inline the
same way, with one bounds check. A loop that reads each of 100,000
`float64` elements by index, 20 times, runs 63,478,022 instructions
instead of 3,445,483,320, and takes about 10.8 ms instead of 367 ms. An
`Array` with more dimensions reads through the runtime.

A list whose elements all have one fixed-width scalar type stores them
unboxed. [Unboxed Scalar Lists](#unboxed-scalar-lists) gives the details.

### Integer Array Kernels

The `int32` and `int64` Array operators, their `wrapping_` and
`saturating_` forms, and `sum()` run on machine integers in blocks of 256
elements. Checked mode computes a whole block, then scans a block that
overflowed for its first failing element. So `AU4002` names the same flat
index as an element-by-element loop. `sum()` adds a block at once when its
largest value cannot push the running sum out of range. Otherwise it adds
that block element by element and reports the first prefix that overflows.

Each program below repeats one operation 100 times on one-million-element
arrays. Each time is the fastest whole-process run on Linux x86-64, of three
runs before and five after. Times include building the inputs, about 45 ms.

| Operation | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `int64` `left + right` | 3,724 ms | 138 ms |
| `int32` `sum()` | 3,974 ms | 47 ms |
| `int64` `sum()` | 4,080 ms | 100 ms |
| `int32` `wrapping_mul` | 2,935 ms | 58 ms |
| `int32` `max()`, unchanged | 68 ms | 52 ms |

### Unboxed Scalar Lists

A list whose elements all have one fixed-width scalar type stores the
scalars themselves. The types are `int8`, `int16`, `int32`, `int64`,
`uint8`, `uint16`, `uint32`, `uint64`, `float32`, `float64`, and `bool`.
Each integer element takes its own width, from 1 to 8 bytes. Each
`float32` element takes 4 bytes, each `float64` 8, and each `bool` 1. A
boxed element takes 112 bytes. Any
other list stores boxed values, and so does a list that mixes two integer
types, such as `int32` and `int64` values in an `int32 | int64` list.

The storage follows the elements. Adding a value of another type, such as
a `str` to an `int64 | str` list, moves the list to boxed storage. An empty
list takes the form of its first element. A program cannot tell which form
a list uses: printing, equality, hashing, copies, and errors behave the
same. A `list[float32]` prints its elements with `float32` digits, as
`print` prints a `float32` value, so `[0.1]` rather than
`[0.10000000149011612]`.

Native code reads the length and the elements of an unboxed list in place,
and appends, writes, and pops elements in place. `pop()` with no index
returns the last element without a box. A list that another task can reach
goes through the runtime.

On the shared Linux container, 11 alternating whole-process runs give these
medians. Before reads lists as the List Reads section describes, with boxed
elements.

| Program | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `int_list_sum` | 21.0 ms | 9.5 ms |
| `string_list_scan` | 32.5 ms | 31.6 ms |
| `record_field_reads` | 122.0 ms | 122.5 ms |
| `dict_build_get` | 326.3 ms | 316.5 ms |
| `set_insert_contains` | 40.8 ms | 41.7 ms |

`int_list_sum` runs about 4.1 times the Rust reference. Callgrind counts
73,209,689 instructions instead of 78,657,685, so most of the gain comes
from the smaller list fitting in the processor cache. The other programs
run within 1% of their previous instruction counts.

### Strings, Keys, And Membership Without Boxes

Native code builds an f-string in one string. The first literal starts it,
and each later part appends in place. A number or `bool` part is copied
when the f-string evaluates it and rendered as it appends, because rendering
it runs no `Display` code. An `int64` part appends without a box.

A literal `str` key, as in `doc.get("age")` on a `dict[str, V]`, is looked
up where it lies in the program image. An `int64` needle, as in `j in seen`
on a `set[int64]`, is tested without a box. A `for` loop that lends each
element of a list checks the index against the length once, so the loan
begins without a second check. Native code also skips a type tag that
repeats the tag the same value received earlier in the block.

On the shared Linux container, 11 alternating whole-process runs give these
medians.

| Program | Before | After | Instructions before | Instructions after |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `int_list_sum` | 11.6 ms | 10.8 ms | 73,209,658 | 73,212,011 |
| `string_list_scan` | 35.7 ms | 14.1 ms | 370,041,432 | 150,970,171 |
| `record_field_reads` | 127.3 ms | 84.4 ms | 1,173,189,605 | 692,557,847 |
| `dict_build_get` | 322.4 ms | 89.3 ms | 3,080,859,389 | 939,551,832 |
| `set_insert_contains` | 39.6 ms | 18.0 ms | 351,223,140 | 148,691,758 |

`record_field_reads` still copies each `Lookup` payload and each enum name,
and every box passes through the task's ownership ledger.

### Plain Record Lists

A plain record is a class whose fields are all `int32`, `int64`, `uint64`,
`float32`, `float64`, or `bool` values, or other plain records. It holds no
`str`, collection, handle, or union. Native code keeps a list of plain
records as the records' fields side by side in the list's storage, the way
a Rust `Vec` of a `Copy` struct does. Reading `points[i].x` loads the field
from the list, and `points.append(p)` and `points[i] = p` store the fields
there. Moving a record into or out of a box, as passing it where any value
is accepted does, takes one runtime call, and so does reading a record
field of a class instance that holds a handle.

The storage follows the elements, as for the scalar lists above. A program
cannot tell which form a list uses: printing, equality, hashing, copies,
and errors behave the same.

Callgrind instruction counts on the shared Linux container, cross-language
suite at the check size:

| Program | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `bytecode_vm` | 48.9M | 6.9M |
| `graph_paths` | 561.5M | 80.4M |
| `raytracer` | 464.1M | 94.0M |

Reading a `float64` field of a record from a `list` costs about 23
instructions instead of about 4,900.

### Lent List Elements

Reading an element of a list of class instances, enums, lists, dicts, or
other values that need a box used to copy the element into a new box.
Native code now lends the element instead when the local that receives it
is only read: the program reads its fields, calls methods that only read
it, or matches it. Each element of a `for` loop that reads its fields is
such a read, and so is `len(items[i].name)`. A read whose value is kept,
changed, or passed to a function still copies.

The list keeps each element it lends in a box of its own. A list moves to
that form once native code has copied out as many elements as an eighth of
its length, so a list that is read only a few times is never converted.
`str` elements keep the copying read, which their list view already makes
cheap.

A lent element keeps the value it had when it was read. Before the program
changes, frees, or passes on the list while it still reads the element,
the element is copied, as every read used to be. A list that a closure, a
task, or a mutable borrow can reach is never lent from, and a list that
another task can reach, or that shares its storage with a copy, is read
through the runtime first.

Callgrind instruction counts on the shared Linux container, cross-language
suite at the check size:

| Program | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `interpreter` | 368.8M | 238.3M |
| `mini_browser` | 1,392.1M | 1,153.8M |
| `sort_records` | 75.2M | 67.1M |
| `sql_engine` | 2,809.7M | 2,616.8M |

The other programs change by less than 2%. The largest increase is
`order_book`, at 1.1%.

### Class Fields In Place

A class instance that native code builds keeps its fields in one block in
the class's native layout, as a Rust struct does. Scalar fields and fields
that hold other classes sit in the block, and each `str`, collection,
enum, union, or runtime object field is a pointer to a box of its own.
Reading `self.count` loads the field from the block and writing it stores
it there, about five instructions each, where the instance used to keep a
map from field names to values and every read copied the field into a new
box. An operation on a field, such as `self.items.append(x)` or
`self.seen.add(k)`, works on the field's box where it lies, and a class
literal builds the block with one runtime call.

Generic classes and classes whose fields hold the class itself, such as a
linked list node, keep the map, and so do instances `aura run` and the
runtime build, such as those `json` decoding returns. A program cannot
tell which form an instance uses: printing, equality, hashing, copies,
and errors behave the same. An instance another task can reach is read
through the runtime.

Callgrind instruction counts on the shared Linux container, cross-language
suite at the check size:

| Program | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `order_book` | 114.9M | 19.3M |
| `regex_match` | 1,940.6M | 366.6M |
| `bank_ledger` | 41.7M | 19.3M |
| `raytracer` | 78.1M | 38.4M |
| `spreadsheet` | 54.4M | 33.4M |
| `lru_cache` | 426.1M | 276.0M |
| `sort_records` | 67.1M | 46.9M |
| `mini_browser` | 1,153.8M | 819.5M |
| `sql_engine` | 2,616.8M | 1,936.2M |

No other program grows by more than 2.6%.

### List Element Fields In Place

`counters[i].count += 1` changes the field where it lies. Native code
checks the list's form and the position once, then the element's class,
and reads and writes the field in the element's block. An operation on a
field of an element or on an element itself, such as
`items[i].tags.append(t)` or `rows[i].append(v)`, works on that box where
it lies. A list of scalars is changed in its storage the same way. Each
write costs about 28 instructions, where it used to walk the element path
through the runtime for about 6,800.

This works for a list in a local or in a field of a class instance kept in
its layout, with one position selected, as in `self.levels[p].append(v)`.
A nested selection, such as `grid[i][j] += 1`, and an element of a `dict`
still take the runtime walk. A class instance appended to a list keeps its
box in the list, so a list built by appends is ready from the first pass.
A list of `Value`s moves its elements into boxes of their own once loans
have missed as many times as an eighth of its length.

A list and its copy share their storage until either changes, so native
code changes an element in place only while the list's storage is its
own. After `copy()`, the next change goes through the runtime, which
copies the storage first, and the copy keeps the old elements.

Callgrind instruction counts on the shared Linux container, cross-language
suite at the check size:

| Program | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `pubsub_broker` | 146.8M | 124.4M |
| `order_book` | 18.9M | 16.2M |
| `binary_trees` | 16.7M | 15.0M |
| `spreadsheet` | 33.2M | 31.1M |
| `mini_browser` | 773.1M | 739.5M |
| `sql_engine` | 1,808.4M | 1,758.2M |

No other program grows by more than 0.4%, apart from `task_pool`, whose
count moves with thread scheduling.

### Nested Reads And New Lists

A read of an element of a list held in a field, such as
`self.asks[level][head].qty` in a method, borrows the element where the
list keeps it, as a read from a local list does. The borrow lasts until
the method changes or frees that field, or uses a loan that may reach it;
the element is copied there first.

A new list with a known element type, `[]` or `list[int64]()`, is built
by one runtime call that also gives it its type, and it starts in the
storage of its element type, so the first `append` of an `int64` runs in
native code. A list, dict, or set appended to a list of lists, dicts, or
sets keeps its own box in the list, so a list of lists built by appends is
ready for element loans from the first pass.

Callgrind instruction counts on the shared Linux container, cross-language
suite at the check size:

| Program | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `order_book` | 16.2M | 11.8M |
| `regex_match` | 355.1M | 294.6M |
| `file_io` | 27.4M | 22.9M |
| `lzw_compress` | 5.2M | 4.7M |
| `kv_server` | 82.6M | 75.4M |
| `astar_pathfinding` | 16.2M | 14.8M |

No program grows by more than 0.6%. `http_api` and `task_pool` move by a
few percent between runs of one build.

### Enum Payloads In Place

A variant of an enum the program defines keeps its payloads in one block
in the enum's native layout, as a Rust enum does. Scalar payloads sit in
the block, and each other payload, a recursive one included, is a pointer
to a box of its own. A `case` compares the variant's index instead of its
name, a scalar binding loads the payload from the block, and any other
binding shares the payload's box. Matching a recursive enum, such as a
tree, used to copy the subtree under each node it visited, and now copies
nothing. Building a variant takes one runtime call.

Variants that `aura run`, JSON decoding, or the runtime build keep their
payloads as values, and so do the compiler's own enums, such as `Result`,
and the library's, such as `json.Value`. A program cannot tell which form
a variant uses: printing, equality, hashing, copies, and errors behave the
same. A variant another task can reach is read through the runtime.

A value read out of a local that only plain assignments write, a
parameter that only named calls fill, or the result of a function that
returns only through `return` already carries its static type, so native
code no longer tags it again when it is assigned or passed on.

Callgrind instruction counts on the shared Linux container, cross-language
suite at the check size:

| Program | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `binary_trees` | 15.1M | 4.7M |
| `interpreter` | 231.8M | 101.2M |
| `spreadsheet` | 29.3M | 26.3M |
| `lzw_compress` | 4.6M | 4.3M |
| `order_book` | 11.6M | 11.2M |

No other program grows by more than 2.2%, apart from `kv_server`, whose
count moves by a few percent between runs of one build.

### Unions And Result Values

A union value shares its type with every other value of that union, so
building, matching, and dropping one no longer copies and frees the type.
The `str | None`, `int64 | None`, and `(str, str) | None` results of text,
I/O, and `json` helpers, such as `strip_prefix`, `read_line`, `find`,
`split_once`, and `as_int`, come ready-made instead of being built by the
general union code on each call. When native code reads such a result
into a `match own`, it moves the payload out of the box, and the box is
reused when nothing else holds it, where it used to copy the string
twice.

A `Result` that native code builds keeps its payloads in its enum layout,
as program-defined enums do, and `try` tests and reads it in place. A
`Result` that a runtime helper returns is read through the runtime, as
before.

Callgrind instruction counts on the shared Linux container, cross-language
suite at the check size:

| Program | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `kv_server` | 85.1M | 51.9M |
| `pubsub_broker` | 133.4M | 85.3M |
| `bank_ledger` | 18.4M | 13.6M |
| `http_api` | 31.6M | 25.7M |
| `docdb` | 79.1M | 66.0M |
| `mini_browser` | 707.8M | 595.6M |
| `spreadsheet` | 26.3M | 25.1M |

No other program grows by more than 1.1%.

### Shared Arguments Stay With The Caller

A shared parameter cannot be rebound or changed while its call runs, so
a function that only direct calls reach reads its shared arguments, and
a shared `self`, where the caller holds them. The caller takes no new
reference for the call and the callee releases nothing when it returns.
A callee that keeps such a value, by storing it or passing it to an
`own` parameter, takes its own reference then. Functions reached through
a function value, a task, a closure, a cleanup, a `From` conversion, or
a method picked at run time, and functions that return a view, keep
taking a reference to each argument; so do arguments of types the
compiler copies freely, such as a `Queue` handle.

Across the 30 cross-language programs at the check size, generated code
retains values 34% less often. Callgrind instruction counts on the shared
Linux container:

| Program | Retains before | Retains after | Instructions before | Instructions after |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `sql_engine` | 156,514 | 71,207 | 1,705.4M | 1,413.8M |
| `lru_cache` | 23,005 | 18,005 | 51.4M | 42.8M |
| `spreadsheet` | 7,916 | 4,021 | 25.1M | 22.4M |
| `json_roundtrip` | 55,702 | 49,660 | 644.2M | 576.5M |
| `template_render` | 7,120 | 4,620 | 34.1M | 32.5M |
| `interpreter` | 339,335 | 226,756 | 101.5M | 98.0M |
| `mini_browser` | 83,879 | 38,941 | 595.6M | 584.0M |
| `raytracer` | 12,612 | 1,850 | 37.0M | 36.5M |

No other program grows by more than 0.3%.

### Mutable Arguments Move Into The Call

A `mut` parameter hands its value back to the caller when the call
returns. When a direct call passes a whole local, or a `mut` parameter of
the calling function, to a `mut` parameter or a `mut self` receiver, the
value moves into the call and the write-back puts it back, so the call
takes no new reference and the write-back drops none. A call through a
function value, a method picked at run time, and a value that a `with`
block cleans up keep taking a reference.

Retains across the 30 cross-language programs at the check size, with
the change above and this one together:

| Program | Retains before | Retains after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `regex_match` | 249,932 | 221 |
| `nbody` | 7,011 | 0 |
| `raytracer` | 12,612 | 0 |
| `lru_cache` | 23,005 | 2,452 |
| `mini_browser` | 83,879 | 15,153 |
| `sql_engine` | 156,514 | 34,867 |
| `graph_paths` | 25,226 | 13,450 |
| All 30 programs | 1,062,951 | 400,936 |

A retain is an inline count update, so instruction counts move less:
`regex_match` runs 1.9% fewer instructions than with shared arguments
alone, and no program runs more.

### Collection Writes Change The Collection In Place

A write to a collection held by a local or a `mut` parameter, such as
`swap`, `append`, `remove`, `extend`, `sort`, a `dict` or `set` write,
or an `Array` `set`, changes the collection where it is. The local keeps
holding the same collection, so nothing is stored back into it after
the write. A `mut` parameter still hands the change to its caller.

### Payload Bindings Hold The Variant's Box

A variant keeps a payload that is not a scalar in a box of its own. A
match arm's binding for such a payload, such as `left` in
`case Expr.Binary(op, left, right)`, holds that box without a reference
of its own when the arm only reads the binding, calls its methods, or
passes it to a shared parameter. The scrutinee keeps the box while the
binding is in use, since the language does not let it change before the
binding's last read. If the scrutinee is handed to code that may keep or
drop it while the binding is still to be read, the binding takes its own
reference first. A binding that is copied whole takes a reference as
before, and a payload the pattern ignores with `_` is not read at all.

| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `interpreter` | 212,087 | 23,005 | 97.6M | 86.8M |
| `binary_trees` | 8,632 | 0 | 4.6M | 4.2M |
| `bank_ledger` | 3,575 | 1,156 | 13.5M | 13.2M |
| `json_roundtrip` | 46,640 | 28,086 | 574.9M | 574.2M |
| `sql_engine` | 26,017 | 13,422 | 1,412.9M | 1,412.2M |
| All 30 programs | 326,693 | 87,876 | | |

### Math Built-ins Compute In Words

`abs`, `min`, `max`, `sqrt`, and `round` compute in machine words in a
native build when each argument is a number local or a number literal.
`min` and `max` compare the two values and keep the first when they are
equal, `abs` negates a negative integer or clears a float's sign, and
`sqrt` and `round` of a float call small runtime routines that take and
return words. The results are the ones the runtime gives: `abs` of the
smallest `int8`, `int16`, `int32`, or `int64` still stops the program,
and `round` of a float that does not fit `int64` still does. The
runtime routines that check or replace a value inside a collection for
an element loan no longer allocate a result either.

| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `image_filters` | 31,101 | 33 | 18.4M | 1.3M |
| `nbody` | 20,092 | 52 | 14.4M | 7.3M |
| `raytracer` | 38,758 | 4,109 | 36.6M | 24.0M |
| `astar_pathfinding` | 8,782 | 34 | 13.3M | 8.9M |
| `spreadsheet` | 15,766 | 8,858 | 22.2M | 18.5M |
| `sql_engine` | 683,934 | 552,398 | 1,412.2M | 1,375.5M |
| All 30 programs | 1,886,045 | 1,523,899 | | |

### Lookup Keys, Callbacks, And Union Strings Take No Reference

A dictionary lookup such as `match table.lookup(key)` reads its key where
it lies, without a reference of its own, when the key is a parameter or
a local that nothing rebinds, moves, or changes while the lookup's
element is in use. A key that may change in that time is still copied
first, so the lookup keeps the key it started with. An `int`, `float`,
or `bool` that `get` finds is read straight out of the dictionary.

A plain function named as the callback of a list's `sort(key=...)`,
`map`, or `filter` is called directly, as a call written to it would be,
so each element is lent to it. A lambda, or a function value held in a
local, is still called as a value.

A `str` bound from a narrowed union, such as `digits` in
`case str as digits`, holds the string the union keeps while the arm
only reads it: passes it to `parse_int64`, calls its methods, or joins it
with `+`.

| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `json_roundtrip` | 28,086 | 0 | 566.6M | 568.0M |
| `interpreter` | 23,005 | 8,245 | 83.2M | 82.9M |
| `sql_engine` | 13,422 | 5,946 | 1,375.5M | 1,377.5M |
| `docdb` | 6,104 | 40 | 64.6M | 64.6M |
| `csv_aggregate` | 5,548 | 0 | 65.1M | 65.0M |
| `word_freq` | 2,935 | 1,000 | 53.0M | 53.0M |
| `lru_cache` | 2,447 | 0 | 42.2M | 42.2M |
| `bank_ledger` | 1,156 | 0 | 13.2M | 13.2M |
| `sort_records` | 1,000 | 0 | 41.3M | 41.3M |
| `kv_server` | 563 | 4 | 54.6M | 54.8M |
| All 30 programs | 87,876 | 16,507 | | |

Native code already took and dropped these references inline, so
instruction counts hardly move: no program changes by more than 0.4%
apart from `file_io`, which varies run to run with its file system.
Retains across the 30 programs are 98.4% below the 1,062,951 they were
before the change in Shared Arguments Stay With The Caller.

### Values Cross Tasks And Queues As They Are

A `copy class` value, such as a `Point` of two numbers, lives in machine
words in native code. When it has to be boxed, for example to go into a
`Queue[Point]`, to be a task's result, or to be the payload of a
`QueueReceive.Item`, the box holds the record's bytes in the class's
layout, and the code that takes the record back out reads those bytes
where they lie. Before, the box held a copy of each field converted to a
runtime value, and taking the record out converted each field back.

A list literal of numbers, `bool` values, or `copy class` values, such
as `[1, 2, 3]` or `[Point(x=1, y=2), Point(x=3, y=4)]`, builds its list
from the elements' bits. Before, each element was boxed and then stored
in the list.

| Program | Instructions before | Instructions after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 6,000 records and enums through queues, 400 tasks | 165.1M | 122.3M |
| 300 calls that build lists of records with literals | 3.9M | 1.3M |
| `graph_paths` | 73.2M | 68.6M |
| `raytracer` | 24.1M | 22.3M |
| `mini_browser` | 561.9M | 548.9M |
| `sql_engine` | 1,377.5M | 1,371.2M |

The first two rows are probe programs; the others are among the 30
cross-language programs, and no other one of them changes by more than
0.5%.

A value that a task start moves into the task, such as a record or a
list built for the call, `group.start(sum_order, make_order(i), 3)`, or
a local passed for the last time, now goes to the task as it is when
nothing else holds it. The task reads it in place, with inline list and
field reads and no lock. A value that the starting task still holds,
such as a local it reads again after the start, is still shared, and
both tasks lock it on each access. A probe that starts 2,000 tasks, each
summing a record with 50 points or a list of 100 numbers moved into it,
runs 99.8M instructions instead of 489.2M.

A module constant that is not a plain number, such as
`WORDS: list[str] = ["alpha", "beta"]` or a `dict` constant, is built
once, the first time the program needs it, and then frozen: every task
reads it in place, with inline list reads and no lock or reference
count. Before, each read looked the constant up by name, took a
reference, and gave the value its type again, and a constant read from
two tasks was shared and locked. A constant still cannot change: code
that wants to change one copies it first, as before. A probe that reads
list and `dict` constants in loops, in the main task and in two worker
tasks, runs 14.2M instructions instead of 47.8M.

### Values Stay In Their Layouts

Native code keeps classes, records, tuples, and enums in typed layouts,
and converts one to a runtime value only where the runtime needs one:
printing it, a host call, or FFI. The runtime stats line counts these as
`conversions`. Three places still converted on every use:

- An enum or union field of a class, such as `value: Value` in
  `class Condition`, was kept in the field's bytes, so every read built
  a runtime value from them and every write converted back. Such a field
  is now kept in a box of its own, which a read or write moves as native
  code holds the enum. A class field and a `copy class` field stay in
  place, where native code reads their numbers directly.
- `match own` of an enum variant took each payload out as a runtime
  value and boxed it again. It now moves the payload's box.
- `pop()` of a list of `copy class` records built a runtime value and
  converted it back to the record's fields. It now reads the record where
  it lay.

Two costs of the same kind went too. An append that reaches the runtime,
such as one to a new empty list or a full one, built a runtime value for
each number and stored it through the generic path; it now stores the
number's bits. And a box passed to a `mut` parameter, or moved into a
call, was given its static type again when the call handed it back,
which compares types; a box whose type nothing can have changed keeps
its type.

| Program | Instructions before | Instructions after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `nbody` | 7.3M | 4.9M |
| `astar_pathfinding` | 9.0M | 7.4M |
| `graph_paths` | 68.8M | 58.8M |
| `interpreter` | 83.6M | 73.6M |
| `regex_match` | 286.9M | 254.2M |
| `sql_engine` | 1,377.7M | 1,307.5M |

No other of the 30 cross-language programs changes by more than 3%, and
29 of them convert no value at all. `mini_browser` converts 20 times a
run, when it stores a class held in place in a field.

### Strings Keep Short Text In Place

A `str` value records whether every byte is ASCII. On ASCII text, `len()`
is the byte count and `text[a:b]` takes bytes `a` to `b`, so neither
decodes a character. A string of at most 29 bytes, such as a word, a CSV
field, a token, or a short slice, keeps its bytes inside the value, so
making, copying, and freeing it allocates nothing. A longer string keeps
its bytes on the heap.

A read-only element view passed to a function that only reads the
parameter, such as `view row = self.rows[slot]` passed to
`matches(row, conditions)`, gives the function the element where the
list keeps it instead of a copy. A selection inside the view, such as
`row[i]`, reads from the same element. A list that keeps its elements as
plain values moves them into boxes of their own once such reads miss
often enough, as a list of lists or instances already did; a list of
enum values, dicts, or sets now does too.

| Program | Instructions before | Instructions after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `sql_engine` | 1,307.5M | 779.5M |
| `mini_browser` | 545.1M | 458.2M |
| `json_roundtrip` | 569.6M | 523.9M |
| `word_freq` | 52.5M | 42.3M |
| `csv_aggregate` | 63.8M | 53.2M |
| `template_render` | 31.7M | 25.6M |
| `spreadsheet` | 17.6M | 15.2M |

### Calls With `mut` Arguments Stay In Generated Code

A call that passes a `mut` argument, such as `self.unlink(slot)` inside a
`mut self` method, used to hand the runtime a list of write-through sinks
first, which made the runtime push and pop the call's frame. A sink only
exists inside a `with` block or for a parameter whose caller had one, so
the call now checks for one and hands nothing over when there is none.

An `int64` value updated through `match mut counts.lookup(key)` is found
once, when the update begins, and each read and write goes to the entry
where the dict keeps it. A dict shared with another thread, or a missing
key, takes the runtime path as before.

| Program | Instructions before | Instructions after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `raytracer` | 21.7M | 6.6M |
| `hashing` | 12.4M | 3.9M |
| `interpreter` | 66.4M | 33.8M |
| `graph_paths` | 55.1M | 34.2M |
| `lru_cache` | 38.6M | 24.7M |
| `csv_aggregate` | 53.2M | 40.9M |
| `word_freq` | 42.3M | 35.4M |

### String Operations Read In Place

`a + b` on two strings builds the result once at its final size, without
copying either operand first. `starts_with`, `ends_with`, `contains`, and
`replace` read their arguments where they lie, and a literal argument,
such as `word.ends_with(",")`, needs no box at all. `replace` copies text
that does not contain the pattern as it is. A copy of a `list[str]`
element, such as `words[i].clone()`, reads the element where the list
keeps it and copies it once. `split_whitespace()`, `lines()`,
`to_lower()`, `to_upper()`, and string literals keep a result of at most
29 bytes inside the value, as other short strings already were.

| Program | Instructions before | Instructions after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `word_freq` | 35.3M | 26.2M |
| `sort_records` | 35.2M | 30.0M |
| `template_render` | 24.9M | 21.6M |
| `http_api` | 28.5M | 24.9M |
| `text_diff` | 8.3M | 7.3M |
| `csv_aggregate` | 40.9M | 36.5M |
| `markdown_render` | 6.2M | 5.6M |

### f-Strings Build One Text

An f-string builds its text in one buffer. A `str` part is appended from
where it lies, and an `int64` part, with or without a format spec such as
`{cents % 100:02}`, is written from its value without a box. `replace`
with two literal arguments, as in `text.replace("<", "&lt;")`, reads them
where the program keeps them, and a list literal of `str` literals, such
as `["let", "value", "return"]`, adds each element without a box of its
own.

| Program | Instructions before | Instructions after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `template_render` | 21.6M | 15.2M |
| `text_diff` | 7.3M | 5.5M |
| `spreadsheet` | 12.9M | 11.3M |
| `sort_records` | 30.0M | 26.5M |
| `csv_aggregate` | 36.5M | 33.0M |
| `markdown_render` | 5.6M | 5.1M |

### Dictionary Lookups Probe Once

`match mut counts.lookup(key)` with a `Found` arm that changes an `int64`
value finds the entry once: the test for the key and the update of its
value share the same probe. `counts[key] = 1` on a `dict` whose values
are `int64` stores the value without a box.

| Program | Instructions before | Instructions after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `lru_cache` | 24.5M | 22.7M |
| `interpreter` | 33.3M | 31.0M |
| `lzw_compress` | 3.6M | 3.3M |
| `bank_ledger` | 10.9M | 10.2M |
| `word_freq` | 26.2M | 25.2M |

### JSON Parses And Writes Without A Second Tree

`json.parse` builds the `json.Value` itself as it reads the text, and
`json.dumps` writes the text straight from the value. A copy of a
`json.Value`, such as a field read passed to a function, shares the
storage of the lists and dicts inside it until one side changes them.

| Program | Instructions before | Instructions after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `json_roundtrip` | 491.8M | 365.0M |
| `pubsub_broker` | 67.3M | 58.5M |
| `docdb` | 35.6M | 32.1M |
| `http_api` | 28.1M | 26.3M |

### Calls Keep Their Frame Records For Less

Each Aura call records its function on the task's frame stack, so a trap
can report where it happened. Generated code pushes and pops that record
with one check each, and LLVM can keep the stack's length in a register
across the record's store. A program large enough to compile in parallel
units inlines a small function called only from its own unit, as a small
program does. A call of a small `int64` function costs 12 instructions
instead of 37.

### Socket Lines Are Read A Chunk At A Time

`read_line` on a `net` TCP or Unix stream reads up to 4 KB per system call
and keeps whatever follows the line for the stream's next read, so
`read_bytes`, `read_exact`, and `read_all` see the same bytes in the same
order. When a read comes back short, the socket had nothing more, and the
next `read_line` waits for readiness before reading. A socket stays
registered with the runtime's poller between waits, so each wait re-arms
it with one call. A request and reply over loopback costs a send, a
receive, and one poller call on each side.

### HTTP Stays On The Calling Task

An HTTP request or response is parsed, decoded, and rendered on the task
that reads or writes it. These steps are iterative and use little stack,
so they no longer go to the protocol-step service, which keeps its
larger stacks for TLS and WebSocket work. A connect to a literal socket
address starts nonblocking and waits on the reactor, and only a host name
still resolves and connects on the blocking-I/O pool. Over loopback, an
HTTP request and its response make no thread hand-offs.

### Queue Hand-Offs

A `for` loop over a queue, and a `match` on `queue.get()` that tests only
`QueueReceive.Item`, receive the item itself: no `QueueReceive` value is
built, tagged, or matched. A `put` whose result is not used builds no
`Result`. A task registers with each queue it uses once.

While several tasks take values from one queue, each receive that leaves
values behind yields, so they take the values in turn. Once one task has
made the last 32 receives from a queue alone, it yields every 32 receives
instead, so a pipeline stage drains its queue without a task switch per
value.

A worker with nothing to run spins for up to 50 microseconds before it
blocks in its poller, unless one of its tasks waits on a descriptor. A
hand-off from a task on another worker usually lands within that time,
and a sender wakes a worker with a system call only when the worker is
blocked. Tasks stay on the worker they start on, so a queue pipeline whose
stages run on different workers still pays for moving each value between
cores: `task_pool` runs in about 0.31 s with `AURA_WORKERS=1` and about
0.54 s with four workers.

### Repeated Type Tags

A value whose static type names a generic, such as `list[int64]` or
`Option[str]`, gets a runtime type tag when it reaches code that reads the
tag. Each box remembers the tag it was last given through a tag cell in
generated code, so a repeated tag is one load and compare instead of a
runtime call. A write that may change the value's shape, such as a push
or an element store, clears the remembered tag, and the next tag looks
again. Methods reached only by direct calls take `self` without a tag,
as functions do. `regex_match` runs 9.9% fewer instructions and
`interpreter` 13.7% fewer. The remembered tag adds 8 bytes to a box, and
alignment adds 8 more, so a box takes 208 bytes.

### Text From Bytes

`str.from_bytes(bytes[a:b])` checks the slice's bounds as the slice
would, then reads the bytes where the list keeps them, so no slice is
copied into a new list. When the result is matched with an `Err` arm
that binds nothing, as in

```aura
def text_of(data: list[uint8], start: int64, end: int64) -> str:
    match own str.from_bytes(data[start:end]):
        case Result.Ok(text):
            return text
        case Result.Err(_):
            return ""
```

native code keeps only the text, or nothing for bytes that are not
UTF-8, and builds no `Result`. A tokenizer that cuts each token out of a
byte list this way runs 55% fewer instructions. `sql_engine` runs 26.7%
fewer and `mini_browser` 8.4% fewer.

A match on `parse_int32`, `parse_int64`, or `parse_float64` whose `Err`
arm binds nothing keeps only the number in the same way, and builds no
error text for input that does not parse. `csv_aggregate`, which parses
three numbers per row, runs 6.6% fewer instructions.

### Variants Without Payloads

A variant with no payloads, such as `Tree.Leaf`, is built once per
program as a frozen box that every thread shares. Building it again
returns that box, and a payload, field, or list element holds it as it
is, so a tree whose leaves are `Tree.Leaf` allocates only its inner
nodes. A new variant's box also starts with its type's tag, so the first
function that takes it does not tag it.

A program that builds and drops a tree of thousands of nodes reuses the
same memory for the next tree (see Small Allocations below).
`binary_trees` at depth 14 runs in about 3.8x Rust's time, down from
8.7x.

### Field Reads In Place

A comparison, an `in` test, or a length test reads a `str`, list, set,
or dict field of an instance where it lies, without copying the field,
when the instance is kept in its typed layout. The test gives back a
`bool` or a number and keeps nothing it read, so the field stays the
instance's for the whole test:

```aura
class Rule:
    tag: str
    class_name: str

def applies(rule: Rule, tag: str, classes: list[str]) -> bool:
    if rule.tag != "" and rule.tag != tag:
        return false
    return rule.class_name == "" or rule.class_name in classes
```

A field passed to a function or stored somewhere else is still copied.
`mini_browser`, which runs a test like `applies` for every rule and
node, runs 16.9% fewer instructions.

### Element Views

Native code reaches an element through its list without a runtime walk
of the path in more cases:

```aura
class Node:
    tag: str
    children: list[int64]

copy class Arc:
    target: int64
    weight: int64

def weigh(nodes: list[Node], index: int64, adjacency: mut list[list[Arc]]) -> int64:
    view node = nodes[index]
    mut total = 0
    if node.tag == "p":
        total += 1
    for child in node.children:
        adjacency[child].append(Arc(target=index, weight=total))
    return total
```

The fields of a read-only `view` of a class element, such as `node.tag`
and `node.children`, are read in the element's box. An append to an
element of a list of lists, such as `adjacency[child].append(...)`,
changes the element where the outer list keeps it; before, the element
was copied, which copied its storage, changed, and stored back. A `str`
element of a list field, such as `template.texts[i]`, is checked and
copied out of the field's box. `graph_paths`, which builds its adjacency
lists this way, runs 47% fewer instructions.

### Small Allocations

Programs allocate through the runtime's own allocator. Each thread keeps
the blocks of up to 1 KiB it frees on a list for each 16-byte size, and
takes the last one freed when it needs a block of that size; a thread
with no freed block cuts one from a 64 KiB chunk it holds. Either way a
small block costs a few instructions. A thread that frees many more
blocks of a size than it makes, or that ends, hands them to a list other
threads take from, so a program holds no more small blocks than it had in
use at once. Small blocks are not handed back to the operating system
while the program runs. Blocks over 1 KiB go to the system allocator.

Time spent allocating falls from up to 35% of a program's instructions
to under 3% in 29 of the 30 benchmark programs. `sql_engine` runs in 24%
less time and `graph_paths` in 27% less.

### Borrowed Reads

Native code passes a value a function only reads where it lies, instead
of copying it. A box field such as `condition.value` goes to a call as it
is when every argument of the call goes to a parameter the callee
borrows, or is a scalar, and none is written back. A `match` on an
element of a `view`, such as `match row[k]` for `view row = rows[slot]`,
tests the variant and reads the payload in the element's box. A read of
an element, such as `totals[p][i]` in `max(totals[p][i], x)`, takes no
copy of `totals[p]` when the same function also writes `totals[p][i]`, so
that write stays in generated code too. `sql_engine` runs 25% fewer
instructions and in about 60% less time at its bench size, and
`graph_paths` runs 20% fewer instructions.

### File Calls

In a native build, every file-system call, `fs.exists` included, runs
on the blocking-I/O pool, never on the worker thread that runs Aura
tasks, so a slow disk or a network file system holds up only the task
that made the call. Closing a file opened for writing, and writing out
buffered bytes before another call, run there too.

The hand-off is cheap when calls come one after another. A pool worker
that finishes a job checks the queue for 50 microseconds before it
sleeps, and a new job wakes one sleeping worker, not all of them. The
calling task checks for its result for 50 microseconds before it parks,
and runs its worker's other ready tasks between checks. On a RAM disk, a
`fs.write_string` or `fs.read_to_string` call takes about 8 microseconds
instead of 38, as in Python, and `file_io` runs in about 0.45 s instead
of 0.76 s (Python 0.45 s).

### Read-Only Lookups

When the `Found` arm of `match d.lookup(key)` only reads the value, or
passes it to functions, a native build finds the entry once. One probe
both tests for the key and copies the value out, where before the
program tested for the key, probed again, and then walked from the
dictionary to the value to copy it. This holds for a dictionary in a
local variable and for one in a class field, with `str` or `int64` keys.

| Program | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `docdb` | 1.88 s | 1.49 s |
| `json_roundtrip` | 0.88 s | 0.69 s |

### JSON Scalar Reads

`json.as_int`, `json.as_float`, and `json.as_bool` return a `T | None`
that native code keeps in words, not in a box. One runtime call checks
the variant and writes the number or flag into those words, where it used
to pass the value through an argument buffer and build a boxed result for
native code to take apart. In `docdb`, whose field readers call
`json.as_int` and `json.as_bool` on every document, this removes about 8%
of the instructions.

### JSON Parsing In One Pass

`json.parse` first reads the source in a single pass that builds the
tree as it goes and checks the nesting and size limits on the way. A key
or string with no escapes is copied straight from the source into its
`str`. Anything this pass does not take as plainly valid JSON, such as a
syntax error or a source past a limit, goes to the full parser, which
ranks and reports the error as before, so results and error messages do
not change. Parsing the `json_roundtrip` payload 50 times takes about
0.24 s instead of 0.30 s, and the whole program about 0.59 s instead of
0.67 s.

### Loop Elements Lent To Calls

When a loop passes each element of a list to a function that only
borrows that parameter, as in `for item in items: total += size(item)`,
a native build hands the function the element the list already holds
instead of a fresh copy, and has nothing to free after the call. This
already held for element reads that a `match` or a field read used in
place; it now holds for borrowed call arguments too. A call that could
change the list first gives the loop its own copy, as before.

### One-Character Patterns

`text.replace("&", "&amp;")` and `text.count("&")` scan for the single
byte directly. A longer pattern still builds a substring searcher, which
costs more to set up than a short string takes to scan. An HTML escape
written as five chained `replace` calls, as in `template_render`, now
runs about 15% faster. `line.split(",")` scans for the comma the same
way, so `csv_aggregate`, which splits every line, runs about 7% fewer
instructions.

### Type Checks on New Lists

Native code skips the runtime type check on a value that already has the
type it is given. A new empty list such as `mut states: list[int64] = []`
now counts as having its type from the start, and appending an `int64` to a
`list[int64]` keeps it. A loop that builds a fresh list for each step and
passes it on, as `regex_match` does for every byte, no longer pays a
runtime type check for each pass.

## Performance Direction

Performance work will address task creation and scheduling, native loop and
call-boundary optimization, allocation and copying, and numeric kernels. It
will keep ownership, checked arithmetic, deterministic reductions, and
MIR/direct parity. The Array kernels run Rust runtime code. Replacing the
native emitter alone does not solve these gaps.

## Representation

These measurements count allocations with the runtime's own counters, not a
host allocator. On both backends, the runtime counts every union payload box,
closure environment, opaque runtime box, and callable overflow allocation. A
process run with `AURA_RUNTIME_STATS=1` prints the totals on standard error
when its program ends.

The same line reports how often the direct backend retains, releases, and
copies a boxed value, as `retains`, `releases`, and `clones`, and how many
of its boxes it freed, as `freed_boxes`, and how many values it built
from a class, record, tuple, enum, or union kept in its typed layout, or
wrote into one, as `conversions`. The direct runtime counts these only
when the report is requested. The interpreter reports zero for them.
A native program prints the line after its module constants are gone, so a
program that freed everything it allocated reports as many `freed_boxes`
as `opaque_boxes`. The cleanup tests in `crates/aura/tests/cleanup_leaks.rs`
check this for programs that finish, stop at a failed check deep in their
calls, and fail or cancel tasks that hold values.

`benchmarks/representation` holds the programs.
`scripts/bench-representation.py` records the counters, the direct binary's
size, and wall time, with commit provenance. The table shows the counters,
which are deterministic for these programs. They were measured at `a8aac70a`
and archived with a checksum manifest in
[work/2026-09-20-representation-measurements](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura/blob/main/work/2026-09-20-representation-measurements).

| Program | Interpreter | Direct backend |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `union_scalar_local` (one million `int64 \| None` injections and tag tests) | 2,000,000 union boxes | 0 union boxes |
| `union_class_field` (one hundred thousand `Point \| None` class fields) | 100,000 union boxes | 0 union boxes |
| `union_string_local` (one hundred thousand `str \| None` injections and matches) | 100,000 union boxes | 0 union boxes |
| `callable_pack_inline` (one hundred thousand one-capture packings) | 100,000 environments | 0 environments |
| `callable_pack_overflow` (one hundred thousand four-capture packings) | 100,000 environments | 0 environments, 100,000 overflow blocks |
| `callable_move` (one packing moved one hundred thousand times) | 1 environment | 0 environments |

**Unions.** On the direct backend, every concrete union is one tagged value in
registers and locals. A runtime-object member rides along as an owned handle
word. Injections allocate no union box. The interpreter's box counts are
reference numbers for its `Value` model, not an ABI claim.

**Callables.** On the direct backend, a callable value is four words.

- Captures that fit in three words live in the value.
- A wider environment takes one checked block, counted as a callable overflow
  allocation.
- Packing, calling, and moving allocate no closure environment.
- The direct backend boxes a callable only where it leaves generated code: a
  container, a task start, a runtime helper, or a generic frame. The
  closure-environment counter reports these boxes.

Design record:
[first-class callables and binding contracts](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura/blob/main/architecture_docs/decisions/0058-first-class-callables-and-binding-contracts.md)

## Executable Size

A native executable contains the Aura runtime code its program can reach.
A program that never uses TLS, WebSocket, TOML, or JSON does not carry their
libraries. The counts below are exact bytes from release builds that
include unboxed scalar lists. The size gate records them as its baselines.

| Executable | Linux x86-64 | macOS arm64 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Native hello world | 973,016 | 961,496 |
| Reference agent (`tool_runner`) | 1,915,000 | 1,792,816 |
| JSON example | 1,506,456 | 1,431,448 |
| TLS example | 3,303,264 | 2,860,000 |
| WebSocket example | 3,608,752 | 3,137,448 |

On Linux x86-64, the `aura` compiler is about 66 MB stripped, because it
links LLVM statically. The runtime archive `libaura_runtime.a` is about
63 MB. User executables link the runtime archive. It contains no compiler
code, and the size gate checks that no user program links LLVM.

The JSON example is `examples/json/dynamic_values.au`. The TLS example is
`examples/io/unix_tls_roundtrip.au`, and the WebSocket example is
`examples/io/websocket_roundtrip.au`. Each links only the libraries it uses:

| Executable | Links | Does not link |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hello world | runtime core | `serde_json`, `toml`, `http`, `httparse` |
| Reference agent, JSON example | runtime core, `serde_json` | `toml` |
| TLS example | runtime core, `rustls`, `ring` | `serde_json`, `http`, `httparse` |
| WebSocket example | runtime core, `rustls`, `ring`, `tungstenite`, `http`, `httparse`, `url` | `serde_json` |

Hello world still holds about 11 KB of `rustls`, `ring`, and `tungstenite`
cleanup code. The runtime's value type can hold a TLS or WebSocket
connection, so the code that drops one stays reachable.

The compiler profile uses level 3, fat LTO, one codegen unit, and no debug
data, and strips compiler symbols. It keeps unwinding and Aura diagnostic
metadata. User executables use unused-section removal and debug and
local-symbol stripping. Each generated function has its own object section,
so the linker drops runtime code no function calls.

Hello world and the reference agent ran with Cargo unavailable. Hello world
matched its single-print output. The agent matched every byte of its
package's pinned stdout.

[Linux size provenance](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura/blob/main/work/2026-10-17-batch-5-step-6/executable-sizes-linux.json)
records the commit, commands, toolchain, linker, source identities, and
executable SHA-256 hashes. The macOS counts come from the `native-binaries`
CI job on the same tree. That job builds every subject in
`benchmarks/native_binaries/contents.json` on both platforms. It fails when
a library appears in a program that should not link it, or when hello world
or another subject grows more than 10% over its recorded size.

### Foundations Size Comparison

This comparison is from the foundations session and predates the Array kernel
rewrite. The older tag has no equivalent `tool_runner` package, so the table
claims no before-size reduction for the reference agent.

| Executable | Before: v0.3.3-preview, Cargo default | After: Cargo default | After: tuned release | Reduction from before |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `aura` compiler | 15,424,032 | 15,866,008 | 10,897,392 | 29.35% |
| Native hello world | 23,646,792 | 1,702,088 | 1,586,968 | 93.29% |
| Retrying-network-worker example | 23,715,816 | 4,049,240 | 3,666,600 | 84.54% |

The after-default control sets the documented release values through
`CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_*` in a separate target directory. It keeps Cranelift
speed and the user-executable link and strip steps. The before ref is
`v0.3.3-preview` (`d3cc6b96104dd597687a98e9624f800a0cb3cf1e`). The
[original size evidence](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura/blob/main/work/2026-09-07-pre-batch-1-executable-sizes.json)
keeps the exact earlier commits, hashes, and commands.

Both size sessions use:

- Mac14,9 / Apple M2 Pro, arm64 macOS 26.5.2
- Rust 1.95.0 (`59807616e`, LLVM 22.1.2)
- Apple clang 21.0.0 (`clang-2100.1.1.101`)

### Reproducing The Size Table

Reproduce the hello world, reference agent, and compiler sizes from a clean
checkout of the desired ref:

```bash
python3 scripts/bench-binary-size.py \
  --after-ref "$(git rev-parse HEAD)" --after-only \
  --output /tmp/aura-executable-sizes.json
```

Measure every subject and check its contents against a local release build:

```bash
cargo build --release -p aura
python3 scripts/check-native-binaries.py
```

Add `--attribute` to print the symbol bytes for each library.

To collect the before, default, and tuned profile comparison, omit
`--after-only` and pass `--before-ref v0.3.3-preview`. The script records that
the older reference-agent subject is absent. It never substitutes a different
program. The hello input is identical single-print source. It is staged
outside old source trees that predate its maintained path.

### Cargo 1.95 Default-Profile Check

The
[pinned Cargo reference](https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/blob/rust-1.95.0/src/doc/src/reference/profiles.md)
lists `strip = "none"` in the release defaults, not `debuginfo`. Under the
session's conditional decision, the size column, source JSON, and size script
are kept without remeasurement.

The column sets `strip=none` explicitly. It is not an experiment with the
setting omitted. When the option is omitted and no compiled package needs
debug information, Cargo's
[deferred strip implementation](https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/blob/rust-1.95.0/src/cargo/core/profiles.rs)
can strip pre-existing debug information automatically. That difference limits
how far the column works as a default-profile control.

The
[reference check](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura/blob/main/work/2026-09-07-foundations-measurements/approved/cargo-default-strip-recheck.json)
records Cargo's exact version, the reference URL and source hash, the relevant
lines, and this decision.

## Source: docs/manual/process.md

# Process Module

The `process` module runs child processes. By default it uses no shell. A command is an explicit `list[str]` argument vector, or argv. So `["/bin/echo", "hello world"]` runs one executable with one argument. Aura does not split strings or expand shell syntax.

```aura
import process
```

Pick the entry point by what the parent needs:

- `process.run(...)` starts a child, waits for it, and collects its output.
- `process.start(...)` returns a live child handle, for pipes or a long-running child.
- `process.supervisor()` owns a named set of children, with restarts and lifecycle events.

## Stdio Configuration

| API | Signature | Contract |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `process.inherit` | `inherit() -> process.Stdio` | Connects the child stream to the parent's stream. |
| `process.null` | `null() -> process.Stdio` | Connects the child stream to the null device. |
| `process.pipe` | `pipe() -> process.Stdio` | Creates a pipe that the parent can capture or use through `process.Pipe`. |

`process.Stdio` variants:

| Variant | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `process.Stdio.Inherit` | Use the parent's stream. |
| `process.Stdio.Null` | Discard output, or give EOF as input. |
| `process.Stdio.Pipe` | Create a pipe. |

In normal code, use the functions `process.pipe()`, `process.null()`, and `process.inherit()` rather than the variants.

The functions are also capture-free function values. For example, `factory: def() -> process.Stdio = process.pipe` followed by `factory()` gives the same result as the qualified direct call.

## process.run

Signature: `process.run(command: list[str], cwd: str | None = None, env: dict[str, str] = {}, stdin: process.Stdio = process.null(), stdout: process.Stdio = process.pipe(), stderr: process.Stdio = process.pipe(), timeout: Duration = ..., group: bool = false) -> Result[process.Completed, process.Error]`

`process.run(...)` starts a child, waits for it, and returns a `process.Completed` value. By default, stdin is null and stdout and stderr are captured.

Omitting `timeout` means no caller deadline. The runtime marks the absence internally, and no `Duration` value stands for it. An explicit negative timeout is invalid. It does not mean unlimited.

```aura fragment
def run_echo() -> Result[None, process.Error]:
    command = ["/bin/echo", "aura"]
    completed = try process.run(command, stdout=process.pipe(), stderr=process.pipe(), timeout=1s)

    try completed.check()
    print(completed.stdout().trim())
    return Result.Ok(None)
```

The `env` dictionary adds to the inherited host environment. An entry with the same name as an inherited variable replaces it.

Aura never invokes a shell for `run` or `start`. Only streams configured with `process.pipe()` are captured. Each captured stream is capped at 64 MiB.

Set `group=true` when the child may spawn descendants. On maintained Unix hosts, the parent then cleans up the whole process group.

Like other builtin module functions, `process.run` is a capture-free first-class function value:

- A direct alias such as `runner = process.run` keeps the parameter names and defaults. So `try runner(command)` still uses null stdin, captured stdout and stderr, and no caller deadline.
- Storing the value behind a structural function annotation, a class field, or a mutable collection drops those call-site extras. Every call then needs every positional argument.

## process.start

Signature: `process.start(command: list[str], cwd: str | None = None, env: dict[str, str] = {}, stdin: process.Stdio = process.null(), stdout: process.Stdio = process.inherit(), stderr: process.Stdio = process.inherit(), group: bool = false) -> Result[process.Child, process.Error]`

`process.start(...)` returns a live `process.Child`. The defaults suit interactive use: stdout and stderr inherit the parent's streams unless you ask for pipes.

```aura fragment
def start_cat() -> Result[process.Child, process.Error]:
    command = ["/bin/cat"]
    child = try process.start(command, stdin=process.pipe(), stdout=process.pipe(), stderr=process.pipe(), group=true)
    return Result.Ok(child)
```

The caller must wait for, kill, terminate, or close the child.

## process.Child

| API | Signature | Contract |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `stdin` | `stdin() -> process.Pipe \| None` | Returns the child's stdin pipe if the child started with `stdin=process.pipe()`. Otherwise returns `None`. |
| `stdout` | `stdout() -> process.Pipe \| None` | Returns the child's stdout pipe if the child started with `stdout=process.pipe()`. Otherwise returns `None`. |
| `stderr` | `stderr() -> process.Pipe \| None` | Returns the child's stderr pipe if the child started with `stderr=process.pipe()`. Otherwise returns `None`. |
| `wait` | `wait(timeout: Duration = ...) -> process.Wait` | Waits for exit. Returns an exit, timeout, cancellation, or failure outcome. |
| `wait_or_none` | `wait_or_none(timeout: Duration = ...) -> Result[process.ExitStatus \| None, process.Error]` | Returns `Ok(status)` on exit and `Ok(None)` on timeout. Returns `Err(...)` for cancellation or a wait failure. |
| `wait_ok` | `wait_ok(timeout: Duration = ...) -> Result[process.ExitStatus, process.Error]` | Returns the exit status only for a successful exit. A non-zero status or a wait failure becomes `process.Error`. |
| `kill` | `kill() -> Result[None, process.Error]` | Kills the child at once. With `group=true`, targets the process group on maintained Unix hosts. |
| `terminate` | `terminate() -> Result[None, process.Error]` | Asks the child to terminate gracefully. With `group=true`, targets the process group on maintained Unix hosts. |
| `close` | `close() -> None` | Closes the child resource. Terminates the child if it is still running. |

`process.Wait` variants:

| Variant | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `Exited(status: own process.ExitStatus)` | The child exited or was signaled. |
| `TimedOut` | The wait timeout expired. |
| `Cancelled` | Cancellation interrupted the wait. |
| `Failed(error: own process.Error)` | Waiting failed. |

`process.ExitStatus` variants:

| Variant | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `Exited(code: own int32)` | The process exited with a numeric code. |
| `Signaled(signal: own int32)` | A signal terminated the process. Only on platforms that expose signal status. |

## process.Pipe

| API | Signature | Contract |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `read_all` | `read_all() -> Result[str, process.Error]` | Reads the remaining strict UTF-8 text until EOF. Capped at 64 MiB. Use the byte APIs for arbitrary output. |
| `read_line` | `read_line(timeout: Duration = ...) -> Result[str \| None, process.Error]` | Reads one strict UTF-8 line without its trailing LF or CRLF. Returns `Ok(None)` only at EOF, or an error. |
| `read_bytes` | `read_bytes(max_bytes: int32, timeout: Duration = ...) -> Result[list[uint8] \| None, process.Error]` | Reads up to `max_bytes` raw bytes. Returns `Ok(None)` only at EOF. `max_bytes` must be in `1..=67108864`. |
| `write_all` | `write_all(text: str, timeout: Duration = ...) -> Result[None, process.Error]` | Writes all the text. |
| `write_bytes` | `write_bytes(bytes: list[uint8], timeout: Duration = ...) -> Result[None, process.Error]` | Writes all the bytes. |
| `flush` | `flush() -> Result[None, process.Error]` | Flushes buffered pipe output. |
| `close` | `close() -> None` | Closes the pipe handle. |

Timeouts and cancellation are errors, never `Ok(None)`:

- An expired pipe deadline returns `Err(process.Error.TimedOut)`.
- Cancellation returns `Err(process.Error.Cancelled)`.
- `read_bytes(0, ...)` and requests above 64 MiB return `process.Error.Io(io.Error.InvalidInput)`.

Close a child's stdin pipe when the child expects EOF:

```aura fragment
def close_stdin(child: process.Child) -> Result[None, process.Error]:
    match own child.stdin():
        case process.Pipe as pipe:
            try pipe.write_all("hello\n")
            pipe.close()
        case None:
            pass
    return Result.Ok(None)
```

The accessor returns an owned `process.Pipe | None`. `match own` moves the pipe out of that result, so the arm holds an owned resource that it can write, flush, and close. A bare `match` binds only a shared view of the pipe. The checker rejects a write, flush, or close through that view with `AU3003` and suggests `match own`.

## process.Completed

`process.run(...)` returns a `process.Completed`.

| API | Signature | Contract |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `status` | `status() -> process.ExitStatus` | Returns the captured exit status. |
| `success` | `success() -> bool` | Returns `true` when the status is exit code `0`. |
| `stdout` | `stdout() -> str` | Returns captured stdout decoded as strict UTF-8. Invalid UTF-8 raises a runtime diagnostic. Use `stdout_bytes` for untrusted output. |
| `stdout_bytes` | `stdout_bytes() -> list[uint8]` | Returns captured stdout as raw bytes. |
| `stderr` | `stderr() -> str` | Returns captured stderr decoded as strict UTF-8. Invalid UTF-8 raises a runtime diagnostic. Use `stderr_bytes` for untrusted output. |
| `stderr_bytes` | `stderr_bytes() -> list[uint8]` | Returns captured stderr as raw bytes. |
| `check` | `check() -> Result[None, process.Error]` | Returns `Ok(None)` for a successful exit status. Otherwise returns `Err(...)`. |

Use `check` when a failed command should stop the current `Result`-returning function:

```aura fragment
def must_succeed() -> Result[None, process.Error]:
    completed = try process.run(["/bin/false"], timeout=1s)
    try completed.check()
    return Result.Ok(None)
```

Use the byte methods for tools that may emit binary or non-UTF-8 output.

## process.supervisor

```aura fragment
process.supervisor() -> process.Supervisor
```

A supervisor is a resource that owns named child process specs and emits lifecycle events. Bind it with `with` where you can:

```aura fragment
def wait_for_worker() -> Result[process.SupervisorWait, process.Error]:
    with supervisor = process.supervisor():
        try supervisor.start(name="worker", command=["/bin/sleep", "1"])
        return Result.Ok(supervisor.wait(timeout=2s))
```

## process.Supervisor

| API | Signature | Contract |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `start` | `start(name: own str, command: own list[str], cwd: own (str \| None) = ..., env: own dict[str, str] = ..., stdin: own process.Stdio = ..., stdout: own process.Stdio = ..., stderr: own process.Stdio = ..., restart: own process.RestartPolicy = ..., backoff: own Duration = ..., max_restarts: own int32 = ..., group: own bool = ...) -> Result[None, process.Error]` | Starts a named child under supervision. Keeps the owned configuration it needs for restarts. Each name must be unique within the supervisor. |
| `wait` | `wait(timeout: Duration = ...) -> process.SupervisorWait` | Waits for the next supervisor event, a timeout, or cancellation. |
| `wait_or_none` | `wait_or_none(timeout: Duration = ...) -> Result[process.SupervisorEvent \| None, process.Error]` | Returns `Ok(event)`, or `Ok(None)` on timeout. Returns `Err(...)` on cancellation or a wait failure. |
| `stop` | `stop() -> Result[None, process.Error]` | Stops every supervised child and clears the supervisor. |
| `is_empty` | `is_empty() -> bool` | Returns `true` when no services are running or waiting to restart. |
| `close` | `close() -> None` | Closes the supervisor and stops all the children it manages. |

Runtime defaults for `Supervisor.start(...)`:

| Parameter | Default |
| --- | --- |
| `cwd` | `None` |
| `env` | empty dictionary |
| `stdin` | `process.null()` |
| `stdout` | `process.inherit()` |
| `stderr` | `process.inherit()` |
| `restart` | `process.RestartPolicy.OnFailure` |
| `backoff` | `100ms` |
| `max_restarts` | unlimited when omitted. `-1` is also accepted as unlimited. |
| `group` | `true` |

When restart is enabled, `backoff` must be at least `10ms`.

`process.RestartPolicy` variants:

| Variant | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `Never` | Do not restart. |
| `OnFailure` | Restart only when the child exits unsuccessfully. |
| `Always` | Restart after every exit, while the restart limit allows. |

`process.SupervisorEvent` variants:

| Variant | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `Exited(name: own str, status: own process.ExitStatus, restart_count: own int32)` | A child exited and was not restarted. |
| `Restarted(name: own str, status: own process.ExitStatus, restart_count: own int32)` | A child exited and a replacement started. |
| `Failed(name: own str, error: own process.Error, restart_count: own int32)` | A child failed to start or restart. |

`process.SupervisorWait` variants:

| Variant | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `Event(event: own process.SupervisorEvent)` | A supervisor event is available. |
| `TimedOut` | No event arrived before the timeout. |
| `Cancelled` | Cancellation interrupted the wait. |

An invalid timer passed to `Supervisor.wait` cannot come back as a `process.Error`, because `wait` returns `process.SupervisorWait`. It maps to exactly this value:

`process.SupervisorWait.Event(process.SupervisorEvent.Failed("<supervisor>", process.Error.Io(io.Error.InvalidInput), 0))`

The synthetic name is `<supervisor>` and the synthetic restart count is zero. `wait_or_none` has an error carrier in its return type, so the same invalid timer returns `Result.Err(process.Error.Io(io.Error.InvalidInput))` instead.

## process.Error

| Variant | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `NoCommand` | The command list was empty. |
| `TimedOut` | A process operation timed out. |
| `Cancelled` | Cancellation interrupted the operation. |
| `Io(error: own io.Error)` | The operation failed with an I/O error. |
| `Spawn(message: own str)` | The child could not be spawned. |
| `Other(message: own str)` | A process failure that no other variant covers. |

## Cleanup Rules

Child, pipe, and supervisor values are resources. Use `with` for supervisors. Call `close()` on children and pipes when their ownership is not scoped.

`close()` on a child terminates it if it is still running. With `group=true`, cleanup targets the process group on maintained Unix hosts.

When `process.run` times out, or its Aura task is cancelled, the runtime terminates the child and waits for cleanup. With `group=true`, it does this to the process group on maintained Unix hosts. As with all host I/O, cancellation cannot undo side effects that the child already performed.

## Grammar

The process module adds no grammar. A command is an ordinary `list[str]` expression passed to an ordinary call. Aura does not parse shell syntax, split a command string, expand variables, interpret redirections, or build pipelines. Named arguments, `Duration` literals, `Result`, `T | None` unions, `try`, `match`, and `with` use their general grammar.

A parameter shown with `= ...` takes the builtin default documented on this page. The ellipsis is reference notation, not a source expression. Process and standard-I/O variants use ordinary qualified enum construction and pattern syntax.

For `process.run`, an omitted timeout is marked internally, not by a sentinel `Duration`. An explicit zero is a real, immediate deadline. An explicit negative value is invalid input.

## Typing Rules

The function and method signatures above are normative.

- Commands are `list[str]`.
- Environment overlays are `dict[str, str]`.
- Working directories are `str | None`. `None` inherits the parent's directory.
- Timeout parameters are `Duration`.

Fallible start, run, pipe, and control operations use `process.Error`. The wait APIs return an enum, a `T | None`, or a `Result` by design, as their tables show.

`process.Child`, `process.Pipe`, and `process.Supervisor` are non-copy resources. These operations need a mutable receiver place: kill, terminate, pipe write, flush, and close, and supervisor start, stop, and close.

`Supervisor.start` consumes every configuration argument marked `own`, because the supervisor keeps that configuration for possible restarts.
