- `architecture_docs/decisions/0019-duration-conversion-and-timer-policy.md`: Duration rounding, rendering, and invalid host-timer policy.
- `architecture_docs/decisions/0026-minimal-tuples.md`: structural tuple types and tuple equality.
- `architecture_docs/decisions/0033-structural-transfer-and-task-results.md`: Transfer classification and conditional `Task[T]` copies.

## Source: docs/book/index.md

# The Aura Programming Language

This is a book about Aura, a compiled programming language that reads like
Python. You write indented blocks, `def`, `class`, f-strings, and
`for name in names`, much as you would in a Python file. The difference is
what happens before your program runs: the compiler checks the type of every
value, checks who owns each piece of data and who is only borrowing it, and
checks that every failure your code can meet is handled somewhere. Then it
either runs the program straight away or compiles it to a native executable
with no runtime to install alongside it.

The book follows Aura 0.11, a technical preview. Most of the language is in
place and stable enough to learn from, and the places where it is still
moving are called out where we meet them.

## Who this book is for

We assume you already program in some language. Most readers come from
Python, and the book leans on that: when Aura does something the way Python
does, we say so and move on, and when it does something differently, we stop
and explain why. If your background is JavaScript, Go, Java, or C, you will
still be at home, because nothing here depends on knowing Python's corners.

We do not assume you have used Rust or thought about ownership before. That
idea gets its own chapter, and we build up to it slowly, with programs that
break and compiler messages that we read together.

## How to read this book

The chapters are meant to be read in order. Early chapters introduce an idea
briefly so that we can write a working program, and a later chapter comes back
to explain it properly. Chapter 2, for example, builds a word counter that
uses ownership and pattern matching before either has been explained. That is
on purpose: it is easier to understand a rule once you have run into it.

Some chapters teach concepts, and some are projects. The project chapters
(2, 12, and 19) build a complete tool from an empty directory, one step at a
time. If you like to learn by building, you can read them first and dip back
into the concept chapters when something puzzles you.

The first half of the book is about the language itself. After installing
Aura in Chapter 1 and writing the word counter in Chapter 2, we go through
the building blocks every program uses in Chapter 3, and then spend Chapter 4
on ownership, the idea the rest of the book leans on. Chapters 5 and 6 cover
the two ways to define your own types, classes and enums, and Chapter 7 shows
how to split a growing program into modules and packages. Chapter 8 tours
the collections, Chapter 9 covers error handling, Chapter 10 covers generics,
traits, and conversions, and Chapter 11 covers testing. Chapter 12 puts all of
that to work in a log analyzer.

The second half is about programs that deal with the world outside their own
memory. Chapter 13 covers closures and decorators, Chapter 14 covers resources
and cleanup with `with`, and Chapter 15 covers structured concurrency.
Chapter 16 reads and writes files, runs other programs, talks to the network,
and handles JSON. Chapter 17 takes a program from `aura run` to a shipped
binary that you can debug and measure, and Chapter 18 calls into C. Chapter 19
brings most of the book together in a supervised job runner. The appendices
at the end are for looking things up: keywords, operators, a guide for Python
developers, the tools, and the diagnostics you will meet most often.

You will see a lot of code that does not compile. When the obvious first
attempt at something is wrong, we write the obvious first attempt, show what
the compiler says about it, and then fix it. The error messages are part of
the lesson. Learning to read them is most of what it takes to get comfortable
with a new compiler.

This book teaches. It does not try to list every method or every rule. When
you want the complete contract for something, the
[Aura Manual](/manual/) is the reference, and the book links to the right
page of it whenever we simplify.

## Every example is compiled

Each Aura code block in this book is checked by the repository's continuous
integration on every change. A block that should compile is run through
`aura check` and must pass. A block that we show as an error is marked with
the diagnostic code it should produce, and CI fails if the compiler stops
reporting exactly that code. Short pieces of code shown out of context are
marked as fragments, and CI checks that they really are incomplete. The
output shown after a `$` prompt was produced by running the command, not
written by hand.

That means the book cannot quietly drift away from the compiler. If you find
an example that behaves differently on your machine, check `aura --version`
first, and then please report it, because it is a bug either in the book or
in Aura.

## Getting started

To follow along you need the `aura` command. The
[installation guide](/install/) has instructions for macOS, Linux, and
Windows through WSL, and [Chapter 1](/book/ch01-00-getting-started) walks
through the same steps with a little more explanation. The source for Aura
and for this book lives at
[github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura), in the
`docs/book/` directory.

When you are ready, start with the [Foreword](/book/foreword), or go straight
to [Getting started](/book/ch01-00-getting-started).

## Source: docs/book/foreword.md

# Foreword

Most people who write Python for a living have a story about the bug that
only showed up in production. Maybe a function was handed `None` on a path
nobody tested, or one part of the program was still reading a list while
another part emptied it, or a network call failed, raised an exception
nobody caught, and took a long-running worker down with it at three in the
morning. None of these are exotic. They are what happens when a language lets
you write code quickly and then asks you to find out at run time whether the
pieces fit.

The usual answer is to move to a language with a stricter compiler, and the
usual price is that the code stops looking like the problem. You trade
`for line in lines:` for pages of declarations, and the program that used to
fit on a screen now needs a build system and an hour of reading before a new
colleague can change it. Aura is an attempt to avoid that trade. It keeps the
part of Python that people love, which is code that reads close to how you
would explain it out loud, and it adds a compiler that checks the things
Python leaves to luck.

## What the compiler checks

The first thing Aura checks is types. Every value has a type the compiler
knows before the program runs, and nothing converts implicitly. An `int32`
does not quietly turn into an `int64`, a string does not become a boolean in
an `if`, and an integer that overflows stops the program with a message
instead of wrapping around to a negative number. Most of the time you do not
write the types yourself, because the compiler works them out from the
values, but they are always there and always checked.

The second thing is ownership. Aura has no garbage collector. Every value has
one owner, and when the owner goes away, the value is cleaned up at that
moment, not at some later point when a collector gets round to it. A function
signature says what the function does with each argument: whether it only
reads it, changes it in place, or takes it over. The compiler holds both sides
of every call to that promise. This is what lets Aura free memory, close
files, and shut down network connections at a predictable point without you
having to remember to, and it is what stops one part of a program from
changing data that another part is still using.

The third thing is failure. An operation that can fail in a way the caller
should care about, such as reading a file, parsing a number, or waiting on a
network peer, returns a value that says so in its type. You cannot reach the
number inside a parse result without saying what happens when the text was not
a number. The compiler will not let a failure path go unhandled by accident.
Some failures, like an index past the end of a list, are bugs rather than
conditions to recover from, and those stop the task with a clear diagnostic
pointing at the line.

## What you get for it

Because the compiler knows every type and every owner, it can produce fast
native code. `aura run` gives you the quick edit-and-run loop of a scripting
language, and `aura build` turns the same source into a standalone executable
that runs on a machine where Aura is not installed.

Concurrency is structured. Tasks start inside a task group, and leaving the
group's block waits for every task in it. Aura has no way to spawn a task that
floats free of the code that started it, and the compiler checks that the
data you hand to a task is safe to hand over. The result is concurrent code
you can read top to bottom.

None of this is free. You will write `mut` when a binding changes. You will
meet errors about moved values in your first week, and some of them will feel
fussy until the reason behind them clicks. We think the trade is worth it, and
this book tries to show you why, one real error at a time.

## About this book

The book is written in the style of *The Rust Programming Language*, which
taught a generation of programmers a language with an unusual compiler by
sitting beside them and reading its messages together. We have tried to do
the same for Aura. Each chapter builds working programs, and when something
does not compile, we show you exactly what the compiler said and explain what
it noticed.

Aura is young. The version this book describes is a technical preview, and
some things you would expect from a mature language are still missing. Where
that matters, the book says so plainly and shows the workaround. We hope you
enjoy learning it, and that the programs you write with it keep working long
after you have stopped looking at them.

## Source: docs/book/ch01-00-getting-started.md

# Getting started

Before we can write any Aura, we need the tool that understands it. Aura ships
as one command, `aura`, which checks, runs, builds, tests, and formats your
code, and also powers the editor support. In this chapter we install it and
write our first few programs. By the end you will have `aura` on your path,
you will have run a program three different ways, and you will have a package
with its own tests that you can open in an editor.

We will install Aura on macOS, Linux, or Windows through WSL. Then we will
write the traditional program that prints `Hello, world!`, first as a
one-line script and then with an explicit `main` function, and turn it into a
native executable. Finally we will use `aura new` to create a package, which
is how most real Aura code is organized, and meet `aura check` and
`aura test`, the two commands you will run more than any others.

If you have used Python, most of this chapter will feel familiar. The one new
idea is the build step: the same `aura` tool that runs your program can also
compile it to a standalone binary. We will see both, and why you might want
each.

## Source: docs/book/ch01-01-installation.md

# Installation

The first step is to install `aura`. Aura ships as a single command-line tool
together with a small native runtime that it links into the programs you
build. There is no separate interpreter, package manager, or language server
to install: the one `aura` binary does all of those jobs.

Aura 0.11 is a technical preview, and the set of platforms it ships for is
small. Release archives exist for these hosts:

| Platform | Release archive |
| --- | --- |
| macOS 15 on Apple silicon | `aarch64-apple-darwin` |
| macOS 15 on Intel | `x86_64-apple-darwin` |
| Ubuntu 24.04 or another glibc-based Linux, x86-64 | `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` |
| Windows 11, x86-64 | the Linux archive, inside WSL 2 |

There is no native Windows build, no Linux ARM64 build, and no build for
musl-based distributions such as Alpine. If your machine is not in the table,
you can still build Aura from source, which we cover at the end of this
section, but you are outside the set of hosts the project tests on.

## Installing with the install script

On macOS and Linux, one command downloads the right archive for your machine
and installs it:

```console
$ curl -fsSL https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/install.sh | sh
```

The script looks at `uname` to pick the archive, downloads it along with the
release's `SHA256SUMS` file, and refuses to install anything if the checksum
does not match. If everything checks out, it installs under `~/.local`:

```text
~/.local/
├── bin/aura
├── lib/aura/
│   ├── libaura_runtime.a
│   └── native-link-args.json
└── share/aura/
    ├── examples/
    ├── README.md
    └── LICENSE
```

`bin/aura` is the tool itself. The files under `lib/aura` are the runtime
that `aura build` links into native executables, and `aura` finds them
relative to its own location, so keep the layout as it is. If you would
rather install somewhere other than `~/.local`, set `AURA_INSTALL_PREFIX`
when you run the script:

```console
$ AURA_INSTALL_PREFIX="$HOME/tools/aura" \
    sh -c "$(curl -fsSL https://johnolafenwa.github.io/Aura/install.sh)"
```

The script needs `curl`, `tar`, and a SHA-256 tool. macOS has all three
already. On Ubuntu, install them with
`sudo apt install -y curl ca-certificates tar coreutils` if they are missing;
`coreutils` provides the `sha256sum` command the script uses.

### Putting `aura` on your path

The installer puts the binary in `~/.local/bin`, and your shell needs to look
there. Many Linux setups already include that directory in `PATH`. If yours
does not, the installer prints the line to add. On Linux with bash, add it to
`~/.profile`:

```console
$ echo 'export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.profile
$ export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
```

On macOS, where the default shell is zsh, use `~/.zshrc` instead:

```console
$ echo 'export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.zshrc
$ source ~/.zshrc
```

The first line makes the change permanent for new terminals, and the second
applies it to the terminal you have open now.

### Windows with WSL 2

Aura does not run natively on Windows. On a Windows 11 machine, you install
Ubuntu under the Windows Subsystem for Linux and use the Linux release inside
it. From an administrator PowerShell, install Ubuntu 24.04:

```console
> wsl --install -d Ubuntu-24.04
```

Restart if Windows asks you to, launch **Ubuntu 24.04 LTS** from the Start
menu, and create a Linux user when it prompts you. From then on, run every
command in this book in the Ubuntu terminal, not in PowerShell. Follow the
Linux steps above inside Ubuntu, and keep your projects under your Linux home
directory (for example `~/projects`) rather than under `/mnt/c`, so that file
permissions and other filesystem behavior match what Linux tools expect.

The [Windows with WSL guide](/install/windows-wsl) covers checking that you
are on WSL 2 rather than WSL 1, and connecting VS Code to the Ubuntu side.

## Checking the installation

Open a new terminal and ask `aura` for its version:

```console
$ aura --version
```

A release build prints a line that starts with `aura 0.11.0-preview`,
followed by the source commit it was built from in parentheses. If you built
Aura yourself, the line starts with `aura 0.11.0-dev` instead. Either way, if
you see a version, you are ready to go. `aura help` lists every command the
tool understands; we will meet the important ones over the next two sections.

If the shell says `aura: command not found`, check that the binary exists with
`ls -l ~/.local/bin/aura`, and then check that `~/.local/bin` is in your
`PATH`. That is almost always the problem.

## Installing a C toolchain for native builds

`aura` can run your programs as soon as it is installed. It can also compile
them to native executables with `aura build`, and for that last step it
needs your system's C compiler and linker, because it hands the final link to
them. If you only want to run programs for now, you can skip this and come
back later.

On macOS, install Apple's command-line tools:

```console
$ xcode-select --install
```

On Ubuntu, including Ubuntu under WSL, install `build-essential`:

```console
$ sudo apt install -y build-essential
```

You can check the result with `xcode-select -p` on macOS or `cc --version` on
Linux. We will build our first native binary in the next section.

## Updating

To move to a newer release, run:

```console
$ aura upgrade
```

`aura upgrade` downloads the current installer, verifies the release
checksums the same way a fresh install does, and replaces both the compiler
and its runtime in the place they are already installed. If you used a custom
prefix, set `AURA_INSTALL_PREFIX` again when you upgrade.

## Building from source

If you want to work on Aura itself, or your platform has no release archive,
you can build it from a checkout. You need three things: Rust through
[rustup](https://rustup.rs) (the repository's `rust-toolchain.toml` pins the
exact version), a host C compiler, and the static libraries of LLVM 22, which
Aura uses to generate native code. The repository includes a script that
fetches LLVM for you:

```console
$ git clone https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura.git
$ cd Aura
$ scripts/install-llvm.sh
$ export LLVM_SYS_221_PREFIX="$HOME/.cache/aura/llvm/22.1.2"
$ cargo build --release -p aura
$ export PATH="$PWD/target/release:$PATH"
```

On Linux, the LLVM script also needs the `libzstd-dev` and `libxml2-dev`
packages. On macOS it installs Homebrew's `llvm@22`, and it prints the
`LLVM_SYS_221_PREFIX` value to export, which is different from the Linux path
above.

## Editor support

You can write Aura in any text editor, but you will have a better time with
one that shows the compiler's errors as you type. The **Aura Programming
Language** extension for VS Code (and for editors that use Open VSX, such as
VSCodium) provides highlighting, diagnostics, completion, hover, and
go-to-definition. All of the language knowledge comes from `aura` itself,
through the `aura lsp` command, so the editor and the command line always
agree. We set it up at the end of
[Hello, packages](/book/ch01-03-hello-packages), once we have a project to
open.

## Getting help

The [installation guides](/install/) have a page per platform with
troubleshooting notes. The [Aura Manual](/manual/) is the reference for the
language and the tools, and the
[repository](https://github.com/johnolafenwa/Aura) is the place to report a
problem. With `aura` installed, let's write a program.

## Source: docs/book/ch01-02-hello-world.md

# Hello, world

Now that `aura` is installed, it's time for the program every language book
starts with: one that prints `Hello, world!` to the screen. We will write it
twice, once as a script and once with a `main` function, and then compile it
to a native executable so that you can see both ways Aura runs code.

## Making a directory

Aura does not care where your code lives, but it helps to keep the examples
from this book together. Make a `projects` directory in your home directory
and a directory for this program inside it:

```console
$ mkdir -p ~/projects/hello_world
$ cd ~/projects/hello_world
```

If you are on Windows, run these commands in the Ubuntu terminal of WSL, as
described in the [previous section](/book/ch01-01-installation).

## Writing and running a script

Create a file called `hello.au` and put one line in it:

*Filename: hello.au*

```aura
print("Hello, world!")
```

<span class="caption">Listing 1-1: A program that prints `Hello, world!`</span>

Aura source files end in `.au`. If a file name has more than one word, the
convention is to separate the words with underscores, as in
`hello_world.au`.

Save the file and run it with `aura run`:

```console
$ aura run hello.au
Hello, world!
```

That's the whole program. If you see `Hello, world!`, you have written and run
your first Aura program. If you don't, go back to
[Checking the installation](/book/ch01-01-installation#checking-the-installation)
and make sure `aura --version` works.

A file like Listing 1-1, with statements written directly at the top level,
is a *script*. Aura runs it from the top to the bottom and then exits, the
same way Python runs a `.py` file. Scripts are a good fit for quick
experiments and small tools, and you will see many short examples in this
book written as scripts for that reason.

`print` writes its argument to standard output, followed by a newline. The
argument here is a string literal. Aura strings can use double quotes or
single quotes, `"Hello, world!"` or `'Hello, world!'`, and the two mean exactly
the same thing. Unlike Python, Aura does not need a `#!` line or an
`if __name__ == "__main__":` check: what is at the top level is what runs.

## Adding a `main` function

Scripts are convenient, but most programs want an explicit starting point.
Change `hello.au` so that it defines a function called `main`:

*Filename: hello.au*

```aura
def main():
    print("Hello, world!")
```

<span class="caption">Listing 1-2: The same program, with a `main` function</span>

Run it again, and the output is the same:

```console
$ aura run hello.au
Hello, world!
```

When a file defines `main`, Aura calls it to start the program. The first line
declares a function named `main` that takes no parameters: `def`, the name,
an empty parameter list in parentheses, and a colon. The body of the function
is the indented block below it. As in Python, indentation is how Aura knows
which lines belong to the function, and the convention is four spaces per
level.

A file has to choose one style. It can have top-level statements, or it can
have a `main` function, but not both. Let's see what happens if we try to mix
them. Make a new file, `mixed.au`:

```aura check-fail:AU2999
print("starting up")

def main():
    print("Hello, world!")
```

```console
$ aura run mixed.au
error[AU2999]: files cannot mix top-level statements, including declarations, with an explicit `main` function
 --> mixed.au:3:1
  |
3 | def main():
  | ^
```

This is our first compiler error, so let's read it carefully. The first line
starts with `error` and a code in square brackets, `AU2999`. Every Aura
diagnostic has a code like this, and the codes are stable, so you can search
for one in the [Manual](/manual/diagnostics) or in your editor's help. After
the code comes the message: the file mixes top-level statements with a
`main` function. The second line, starting with `-->`, gives the file, line,
and column where the compiler noticed the problem, here line 3, column 1. The
lines after that show the source with a caret (`^`) under the place it is
pointing at.

The rule exists because "where does this program start?" should have exactly
one answer. If a file had both, you would have to know whether the top-level
`print` runs before `main`, after it, or not at all. Aura avoids the question.
The error also tells you something else: the compiler checked the whole file
before it ran any of it. Nothing was printed, not even `starting up`. A
program with an error like this never starts. Delete `mixed.au` before moving
on.

Despite the "including declarations" in the message, other `def` functions
and constants such as `LIMIT = 10` are fine next to `main`, and we will write
plenty of files like that. It is statements that *do* something at the top
level, like this `print` call, that clash with it.

## Exit codes

`main` can also report how the program went. Every process returns an exit
code to whatever started it, and by convention `0` means success and anything
else means some kind of failure. Shell scripts, CI systems, and process
supervisors all look at that number. In Aura, `main` returns it:

*Filename: status.au*

```aura
def main() -> int32:
    print("something went wrong")
    return 2
```

<span class="caption">Listing 1-3: A `main` function that returns an exit code</span>

The `-> int32` after the parameter list is the function's return type. It
says `main` returns a 32-bit signed integer, which is what operating systems
use for exit codes. `return 2` hands back the value. Run the program and then
ask the shell for the exit code of the last command with `echo $?`:

```console
$ aura run status.au
something went wrong
$ echo $?
2
```

`main` must take no parameters, and it must return either `int32` or nothing
at all. A `main` with no `->` returns `None`, Aura's value for "nothing", and
the program exits with `0` when it finishes normally. Trying to return some
other type, such as `int64`, is an error, because the operating system has no
way to receive a 64-bit exit code.

## Checking without running

You will often want to know whether a program is correct without running it.
`aura check` does everything `aura run` does up to the point of execution: it
reads the file, checks the syntax, works out the type of every expression,
and checks the ownership rules, but it does not run anything.

```console
$ aura check status.au
ok
```

On a correct program it prints `ok`. On a program with a mistake, it prints
the same diagnostics `aura run` would. Let's leave out a closing parenthesis
to see one:

*Filename: broken.au*

```aura check-fail:AU1001
def main():
    print("Hello, world!"
```

```console
$ aura check broken.au
error[AU1001]: unclosed delimiter `(`; expected `)` before end of file
 --> broken.au:3:1
  = related broken.au:2:10: opening delimiter `(` is here
```

The primary location is line 3, column 1, the end of the file, because that is
where the compiler finally gave up waiting for the `)`. A message that points
at the end of the file is not much help on its own, so the diagnostic adds a
`related` line that points back at the `(` on line 2 that was never closed.
Many Aura diagnostics have related lines like this, and they are often the
part that tells you where to look. Add the `)` back, and `aura check` is happy
again.

`aura check` is fast, and it is the command you will run most while you
write code. Editors run the same check on every keystroke, which we will set
up in the [next section](/book/ch01-03-hello-packages).

## Compiling a native executable

So far, `aura run` has done all the work. It checks the program, translates
it into an internal form called MIR (Aura's mid-level intermediate
representation), and executes that directly. There is no separate compile
step to wait for, which is what you want while you are writing and testing.

When you want to give a program to someone else, or run it without `aura`,
you compile it instead. `aura build` turns the source into a native
executable for your machine:

```console
$ aura build -o hello hello.au
aura: built `hello` with direct backend
$ ./hello
Hello, world!
```

`-o hello` names the output file. The result is an ordinary executable, as if
you had compiled a C program: it does not need `hello.au` any more, it does
not need `aura` to be installed, and you can copy it to another machine with
the same operating system and processor and run it there. The phrase
"direct backend" in the message refers to the part of the compiler that
generates machine code directly through LLVM.

This is the step that needs the C toolchain from the
[installation section](/book/ch01-01-installation#installing-a-c-toolchain-for-native-builds).
Aura generates the machine code itself, but it uses the system linker to
produce the final file. If `aura build` reports a linker problem, check that
`cc --version` (Linux) or `xcode-select -p` (macOS) works.

The exit code of a native binary comes from `main` in the same way:

```console
$ aura build -o status status.au
aura: built `status` with direct backend
$ ./status
something went wrong
$ echo $?
2
```

A native binary also keeps the file, line, and column information it needs to
report runtime errors, so a failure in a built program points at the same
source line that `aura run` would.

## `aura run` or `aura build`?

Both commands run the same checks, and a program that passes them behaves the
same way under either one. The difference is when the work happens. Use
`aura run` while you are developing, because it starts executing straight
away. Use `aura build` when you want the speed of native code, or a single
file you can ship. We will come back to what goes into a native binary, and
how to choose between the two, in
[Chapter 17](/book/ch17-00-shipping).

Writing one file at a time is fine for small programs. Real projects have
several files, tests, and maybe dependencies on other code, and for that Aura
has packages. Let's make one.

## Source: docs/book/ch01-03-hello-packages.md

# Hello, packages

A single `.au` file is enough for a small program, but most code grows past
one file. It picks up helper modules, tests, and eventually dependencies on
other people's code. Aura's answer to all of that is the *package*: a
directory with a manifest called `Aura.toml` and a fixed layout that the
`aura` commands understand. Let's create one, split our greeting into a
module of its own, write tests for it, and set up an editor to work on it.

## Creating a package with `aura new`

Go back to your `projects` directory and ask `aura` to create a new package
called `greeter`:

```console
$ cd ~/projects
$ aura new greeter
created `greeter`
$ cd greeter
```

`aura new` makes a directory with four files in it:

```text
greeter/
├── .gitignore
├── Aura.toml
├── src/
│   └── main.au
└── tests/
    └── smoke.au
```

It refuses to overwrite a directory that already exists, so you can't run it
by accident over code you care about.

Open `Aura.toml` first:

*Filename: Aura.toml*

```toml
[package]
name = "greeter"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2026"
```

<span class="caption">Listing 1-4: The manifest `aura new` generates</span>

This file is in [TOML](https://toml.io), a simple configuration format.
`[package]` starts a section, and the three lines under it describe the
package. All three are required. `name` is how other packages will refer to
this one, so it must look like an Aura identifier: letters, digits, and
underscores, not starting with a digit. That means `word_count` is a valid
name and `word-count` is not. `version` is the package's own version number.
`edition` selects which edition of the language the package is written in.
There is only one edition so far, `"2026"`, but the field exists so that a
future edition can change the language without breaking packages written for
this one. When a package depends on others, they are listed in a
`[dependencies]` section below this one;
[Chapter 7](/book/ch07-00-modules-and-packages) covers that.

The generated `.gitignore` holds one line, `target/`, which is where we will
put build output. Now look at the program:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
def main() -> int32:
    print("Hello from Aura")
    return 0
```

<span class="caption">Listing 1-5: The `src/main.au` that `aura new` generates</span>

It is the same shape as the `main` we wrote by hand in the last section. All
of a package's source code lives under `src/`, and `src/main.au` is the
conventional entry point. Run it by naming the file, the same as before:

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
Hello from Aura
```

The difference from a loose file is invisible here, but it matters as soon as
there is more than one file. Because `src/main.au` is inside a package,
`aura` finds the `Aura.toml` above it, treats `src/` as the root for imports,
and can resolve modules and dependencies by name.

## Splitting code into a module

Let's give the greeting a home of its own. Every file under `src/` is a
module, named after its path without the `.au`. Create `src/greeting.au`:

*Filename: src/greeting.au*

```aura
def greet(name: str) -> str:
    return f"Hello, {name}!"
```

This defines a function, `greet`, that takes one parameter called `name` of
type `str` (a string) and returns a `str`. The body uses an *f-string*, which
works as it does in Python: the `f` before the opening quote means that
anything inside `{` and `}` is evaluated and its value is placed into the
string. We will look at functions properly in
[Chapter 3](/book/ch03-03-functions).

Now replace `src/main.au` so that it uses the new function:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura fragment
from greeting import greet

def main() -> int32:
    print(greet("world"))
    return 0
```

<span class="caption">Listing 1-6: Importing `greet` from the `greeting` module</span>

`from greeting import greet` reads the same as it would in Python: from the
module `greeting`, bring in the name `greet`. Let's check the program:

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2999]: item `greet` is private in module `greeting`
 --> src/main.au:1:22
  |
1 | from greeting import greet
  |                      ^
```

The compiler found the module and found `greet` in it, and then refused to
let us use it. In Aura, every top-level name is private to its module unless
you say otherwise. Python has a convention that names starting with an
underscore are private, but nothing enforces it. Aura makes the default the
safe one, so that the only names other modules can depend on are the ones you
chose to offer. That matters more as a program grows, because anything that
is public is something you have promised not to break.

To offer `greet`, mark it `public`:

*Filename: src/greeting.au*

```aura
public def greet(name: str) -> str:
    return f"Hello, {name}!"
```

<span class="caption">Listing 1-7: Making `greet` public</span>

Now the check passes and the program runs:

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
ok
$ aura run src/main.au
Hello, world!
```

## Testing with `aura test`

`aura new` also made a `tests/` directory with one file in it, `smoke.au`,
which contains a `main` that returns `0`. It is there so that `aura test` has
something to run from the very first minute:

```console
$ aura test
ok tests/smoke.au
1 passed; 0 failed
```

With no arguments, `aura test` looks for `.au` files under `tests/` and runs
the tests it finds in each one. A file like `smoke.au` with no test functions
counts as a single test, which passes if its `main` returns `0`. More often,
a test file contains functions whose names start with `test_`, and each of
those is its own test. Let's write some for `greet`. Create
`tests/greeting_test.au`:

*Filename: tests/greeting_test.au*

```aura fragment
from greeting import greet

def test_greets_by_name():
    assert greet("Ada") == "Hello, Ada!"

def test_keeps_full_name():
    assert greet("Grace Hopper") == "Hello, Grace Hopper"
```

<span class="caption">Listing 1-8: Two tests for `greet`, one of them wrong</span>

Test files in a package can import the package's modules in the same way
`src/main.au` does. Each test calls `greet` and uses `assert` to state what
the result should be. `assert` takes a condition, and if the condition is
false, the test fails at that line. We have made a deliberate mistake in the
second test: the expected string is missing its `!`. Run the tests:

```console
$ aura test
ok tests/greeting_test.au::test_greets_by_name
FAILED tests/greeting_test.au::test_keeps_full_name
error[AU4001]: assertion failed
 --> tests/greeting_test.au:7:5
  |
7 |     assert greet("Grace Hopper") == "Hello, Grace Hopper"
  |     ^
  = note: left = Hello, Grace Hopper!
  = note: right = Hello, Grace Hopper
  = note: Aura call chain (innermost first): test_keeps_full_name at 6:1
ok tests/smoke.au
2 passed; 1 failed
```

Each test is reported by its file and function name. The failing one shows
the same kind of diagnostic as a compiler error, but this one happened while
the program ran: the assertion on line 7 was false. Because the condition
compared two values with `==`, `aura` shows both sides, the `left` value that
`greet` returned and the `right` value we expected, and the difference jumps
out. The last note is the *call chain*, the list of functions that were
running when the failure happened, innermost first. Here there is only one,
the test itself.

Fix the expected string by adding the `!`, and run the tests again:

```console
$ aura test
ok tests/greeting_test.au::test_greets_by_name
ok tests/greeting_test.au::test_keeps_full_name
ok tests/smoke.au
3 passed; 0 failed
```

When you only want to run some of the tests, `-k` picks the ones whose names
contain a piece of text:

```console
$ aura test -k full
ok tests/greeting_test.au::test_keeps_full_name
1 passed; 0 failed
```

`aura test` exits with a non-zero status when any test fails, so a CI job can
run it directly. [Chapter 11](/book/ch11-00-testing) covers testing in depth,
including setup and teardown functions and parameterized tests.

## Formatting with `aura fmt`

Aura comes with a formatter, so that code written by different people looks
the same and nobody has to argue about it in review. `aura fmt --check`
reports the files it would change without touching them:

```console
$ aura fmt --check .
would format `./src/main.au`
would format `./tests/greeting_test.au`
```

and `aura fmt` with no arguments rewrites every `.au` file under the current
directory in place:

```console
$ aura fmt
$ cat src/main.au
from greeting import greet

def main() -> int32:
    print(greet("world"))
    return 0
```

The formatter wants two blank lines between top-level declarations, the same
rule as Python's PEP 8. The listings in this book use one blank line to save
space, so `aura fmt` will always find something to change in code copied from
the book. That's fine; the two layouts mean the same program.

## Building the package

`aura build` works on a package's entry point in the same way it works on a
loose file. The generated `.gitignore` ignores `target/`, which makes it a
good place for build output:

```console
$ aura build -o target/greeter src/main.au
aura: built `target/greeter` with direct backend
$ ./target/greeter
Hello, world!
```

`aura build` creates the `target` directory if it does not exist.

## Setting up an editor

Now that you have a project, open it in an editor. The VS Code extension is
called **Aura Programming Language**, from the publisher **JohnOlafenwa**.
Install it from the Extensions view, or from a terminal:

```console
$ code --install-extension JohnOlafenwa.vscode-aura-lang
```

Editors that use the Open VSX registry, such as VSCodium, have the same
extension; with VSCodium, use `codium --install-extension` with the same name.
On Windows, open the project from the Ubuntu terminal with `code .` and
install the extension into the **WSL: Ubuntu** window, so that the extension
runs on the same side as `aura`.

The extension has very little logic of its own. It starts `aura lsp`, a
long-running mode of the same `aura` tool, and asks it about the files you
are editing. That means diagnostics, completions, hover information, and
go-to-definition all come from the real compiler, and your editor can never
disagree with `aura check`. The extension finds `aura` on your `PATH`; if
VS Code was started from somewhere that cannot see it, set
`AURA_LSP_AURA_PATH` to the full path of the binary before launching the
editor.

To check that everything is connected, open `src/greeting.au`. The language
mode in the bottom-right corner of the window should read **Aura**. Hover over
`greet` and you should see its signature. Then delete the closing `"` of the
f-string: within a moment, the editor should underline the line with the same
kind of `AU` diagnostic you have seen on the command line. Put the quote back
before you move on. The [VS Code guide](/install/vscode) has troubleshooting
steps if any of this does not work. VS Code's Format Document command runs
the same formatter as `aura fmt`.

## Summary

You have installed `aura`, and you have run a program as a script, with a
`main` function, and as a native binary. You have read compiler errors and
a test failure, created a package with `aura new`, split it into modules, and
tested it with `aura test`. These are the commands you will use throughout
the book:

- `aura run file.au` checks a program and runs it.
- `aura check file.au` checks it without running it.
- `aura build -o output file.au` compiles a native executable.
- `aura new name` creates a package.
- `aura test` runs the tests under `tests/`.
- `aura fmt` formats your code.

It's time to write something more substantial. In the next chapter we build a
program that reads text from standard input and counts the words in it, and
along the way we meet most of the ideas the rest of the book explains.

## Source: docs/book/ch02-00-word-counter.md

# Programming a word counter

Let's jump into Aura by writing a real program together. We will build a
small command-line tool that reads text from standard input, counts how often
each word appears, and prints the most common ones. By the end, you will be
able to feed it any text file and get back something like this:

```console
$ aura run src/main.au < poem.txt
    6 the
    4 rain
    3 it
    3 falls
    3 on
```

Tools like this are the bread and butter of the command line. They read from
standard input, so you can pipe another program's output into them, and they
write plain text to standard output, so you can pipe their output onward.

Along the way we will meet a lot of Aura at once: bindings and `mut`,
`match` and the `Result` type, loops, dictionaries and lists, f-strings, and
the first hints of ownership. We won't explain everything fully here. The
goal of this chapter is to write a working program and to see what the
compiler says when we get something wrong; the chapters after it go back
over each idea in detail. If something feels unexplained, keep going, and
trust that it will come back.

## Setting up a new project

We'll make a package for the tool, as we did in
[Chapter 1](/book/ch01-03-hello-packages). Go to your `projects` directory
and run `aura new`:

```console
$ aura new word_count
created `word_count`
$ cd word_count
```

The package name uses an underscore rather than a hyphen, because a package
name must be a valid Aura identifier. Run the generated program to make sure
everything is in place:

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
Hello from Aura
```

We also need some text to count. Save this as `poem.txt` in the `word_count`
directory, next to `Aura.toml`:

*Filename: poem.txt*

```text
The rain, the rain! It falls on the plain.
It falls on the hills, and it falls on the lane.
"Rain," said the girl. "Rain again."
```

It is short, so we can check the counts by eye, and it has capital letters
and punctuation, which will cause us trouble in a useful way.

## Reading a line of input

The first job is to read text. Aura's functions for standard input and output
live in a module called `io`, and the one we want is `io.read_line`, which
reads one line. Replace the contents of `src/main.au` with Listing 2-1.

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura check-fail:AU2013
import io

def main() -> int32:
    match io.read_line():
        case Result.Ok(str as line):
            print(f"read: {line}")
        case Result.Err(error):
            print(f"could not read input: {error}")
    return 0
```

<span class="caption">Listing 2-1: A first attempt at reading one line from standard input</span>

There's a lot in these few lines. `import io` makes the `io` module available
in this file, so that we can call `io.read_line()`. The rest is a `match`
statement, which looks at a value and picks one of several `case` branches
depending on its shape. Before we go through it, let's see what the compiler
thinks:

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU2013]: non-exhaustive match over `Result`: missing `Ok(None)`
 --> src/main.au:4:5
  |
4 |     match io.read_line():
  |     ^
```

The program didn't run. The compiler says our `match` is *non-exhaustive*:
there is a possible value that none of our cases handles, and it even names
the missing one, `Ok(None)`. To see where that comes from, we need to know
what `io.read_line` returns. Its type is:

```text
Result[str | None, io.Error]
```

Reading input can fail. The input might not be valid text, or the operating
system might report an error. Many languages handle this with exceptions,
which means the possibility of failure is invisible at the call site: nothing
about `line = input()` in Python tells you it can raise `EOFError`. Aura puts
the possibility in the return type instead. A `Result` is either
`Result.Ok(value)`, holding the successful value, or `Result.Err(error)`,
holding a description of what went wrong. Here the error is an `io.Error`.

The successful value has its own twist. Its type is `str | None`, which means
"either a `str` or `None`". `io.read_line` returns `Ok` with a string for each
line it reads, and `Ok(None)` when it reaches the end of the input and there
are no more lines. So there are three outcomes, not two: a line, the end of
the input, and an error. Our `match` handled the first and the last, and the
compiler noticed that we forgot the middle one.

This check is one of the things that makes Aura programs hold up well. If we
had been allowed to run Listing 2-1, it would have worked when we tested it
with a line of text, and then done something unpredictable the first time
someone ran it on an empty file. Because `match` must be exhaustive, the
question "what happens at end of input?" has to be answered before the
program can run at all.

Add the missing case, as in Listing 2-2.

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
import io

def main() -> int32:
    match io.read_line():
        case Result.Ok(str as line):
            print(f"read: {line}")
        case Result.Ok(None):
            print("no input")
        case Result.Err(error):
            print(f"could not read input: {error}")
    return 0
```

<span class="caption">Listing 2-2: Handling a line, the end of input, and an error</span>

Each `case` is a *pattern*. `Result.Ok(str as line)` matches an `Ok` whose
contents are a `str`, and binds that string to the name `line` so the body
can use it. `Result.Ok(None)` matches an `Ok` holding `None`. And
`Result.Err(error)` matches any error and binds it to `error`. The body of
each case uses an f-string to build its message, like the ones we saw in
Chapter 1. Patterns can do a good deal more than this, and
[Chapter 6](/book/ch06-00-enums-and-match) covers `match` in full;
[Chapter 9](/book/ch09-00-error-handling) does the same for `Result`.

Now let's run it. Piping text into a program with `echo` is a quick way to
give it a line of input:

```console
$ echo "the quick brown fox" | aura run src/main.au
read: the quick brown fox
```

The shell's `<` operator sends a file to standard input instead. With
`/dev/null`, which is always empty, we get the end-of-input case straight
away:

```console
$ aura run src/main.au < /dev/null
no input
$ aura run src/main.au < poem.txt
read: The rain, the rain! It falls on the plain.
```

With `poem.txt`, the program read the first line and stopped, because we only
asked for one. Notice that the line has no newline character at the end:
`io.read_line` removes the line ending for us. It does not trim anything else,
so leading and trailing spaces are kept.

We can even trigger the error case, by sending bytes that are not valid UTF-8
text. `printf` with `\xe9` produces a byte that is a lone accented `é` in an
old encoding, but is not allowed on its own in UTF-8:

```console
$ printf 'caf\xe9\n' | aura run src/main.au
could not read input: io.Error.InvalidData
```

Aura strings are always valid UTF-8, so input that isn't becomes an error
rather than a string with garbage in it.

If you run the program with no redirection at all, it waits for you to type a
line. Type something and press Enter, or press Ctrl-D on an empty line to
send end-of-input.

## Reading until the end of the input

We want every line, not only the first. Let's put the `match` in a loop that
keeps going until the end of the input. To check that it works before we
count any words, we'll count lines first. Change `src/main.au` to Listing
2-3.

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura check-fail:AU3003
import io

def main() -> int32:
    lines = 0
    while true:
        match io.read_line():
            case Result.Ok(str as line):
                lines += 1
            case Result.Ok(None):
                break
            case Result.Err(error):
                print(f"could not read input: {error}")
                return 1
    print(f"lines: {lines}")
    return 0
```

<span class="caption">Listing 2-3: Counting lines until the end of input</span>

`while true:` loops forever, and the `break` in the `Ok(None)` case gets us
out when the input runs out. If reading fails, we print a message and
`return 1` from `main`, which ends the program with a non-zero exit code to
tell the shell that something went wrong. The line count lives in a binding
called `lines`, which starts at `0` and goes up by one for every line. Let's
try it:

```console
$ aura run src/main.au < poem.txt
error[AU3003]: cannot assign to immutable binding `lines`; declare it with `mut` to rebind it
 --> src/main.au:8:17
  |
8 |                 lines += 1
  |                 ^
```

This is the error that almost every newcomer to Aura meets first, so it's
good to get it out of the way. In Aura, a binding created with `name = value`
is *immutable*: once it has a value, it keeps that value. `lines += 1` tries
to change it, and the compiler stops us. The message also says exactly how to
fix it: declare the binding with `mut`.

Why make immutability the default? Because most bindings in a program never
change, and when you read code, knowing which ones *can* change is valuable.
If a binding is not marked `mut`, you know that its value at the bottom of a
function is the value it was given at the top, without reading every line in
between. The `mut` marks are the places to look when you want to know what
changes. [Chapter 3](/book/ch03-01-bindings-and-mutability) has more on this.

Change the line that creates the binding to:

```aura fragment
    mut lines = 0
```

and run the program again:

```console
$ aura run src/main.au < poem.txt
lines: 3
```

Three lines, which is right. It also handles input whose last line has no
newline, and empty input:

```console
$ printf 'one\ntwo' | aura run src/main.au
lines: 2
$ printf '' | aura run src/main.au
lines: 0
```

## Counting words

Now for the real work. For each line, we need to split it into words and
keep a tally of how many times we have seen each word. A *dictionary* is the
natural fit: a `dict` maps keys to values, so we can map each word to its
count. Listing 2-4 is our first attempt.

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura check-fail:AU3002
import io

def main() -> int32:
    mut counts: dict[str, int64] = {}
    while true:
        match io.read_line():
            case Result.Ok(str as line):
                for word in line.split_whitespace():
                    if word in counts:
                        counts[word] += 1
                    else:
                        counts[word] = 1
            case Result.Ok(None):
                break
            case Result.Err(error):
                print(f"could not read input: {error}")
                return 1
    print(counts)
    return 0
```

<span class="caption">Listing 2-4: A first attempt at counting words in a dictionary</span>

The line `mut counts: dict[str, int64] = {}` creates an empty dictionary.
This time we wrote the type ourselves, after the colon: a `dict` whose keys
are `str` and whose values are `int64`, Aura's standard 64-bit integer. We
have to, because `{}` on its own says nothing about what will go in it. When
we wrote `lines = 0`, Aura could tell from the `0` that `lines` was an
integer; with an empty dictionary there is nothing to go on. The binding is
`mut` because we will add entries to it.

Inside the loop, `line.split_whitespace()` splits the line at runs of spaces
and tabs, and gives us a list of the pieces. The `for` loop visits each one.
If the word is already a key in the dictionary (`word in counts`), we add one
to its count; otherwise we store it with a count of `1`. At the end we print
the whole dictionary. Let's run it:

```console
$ aura run src/main.au < poem.txt
error[AU3002]: cannot move borrowed value `word`
 --> src/main.au:10:32
   |
10 |                         counts[word] += 1
   |                                ^
  = related src/main.au:8:21: value is borrowed here
  = help: take `word` as `own str` when ownership is required, or call `.clone()` to consume an independent copy
  = fix: replace src/main.au:10:36-10:36 with `.clone()`
```

This error is our first meeting with *ownership*, the idea at the heart of
Aura, and it deserves a careful read. The message says we tried to *move* a
*borrowed* value, `word`. The primary location is the `word` inside
`counts[word]` on line 10. The `related` line points at line 8, column 21,
which is the `word` in `for word in line.split_whitespace()`, and says that
is where the value is borrowed.

Here is what the compiler sees. In Aura, every value has exactly one owner,
and the owner is responsible for cleaning the value up when it is no longer
needed. The list that `split_whitespace()` returns owns its strings. When a
`for` loop walks over a list, it doesn't take the strings out of it; it
*borrows* each one in turn, which means `word` lets us look at a string that
still belongs to the list. That's fine for reading, and `word in counts` only
reads.

Storing a key in a dictionary is different. Once the dictionary has the
string, the dictionary has to own it, because it will keep it long after this
loop iteration is over. But we only borrowed `word`. If Aura let the
dictionary take it, the list and the dictionary would both think they owned
the same string, and when the list was cleaned up at the end of the loop, the
dictionary would be left holding a string that no longer existed. Languages
with a garbage collector, like Python, avoid this by keeping every value alive
as long as anything can reach it. Aura has no garbage collector, so it tracks
owners instead, and it checks that tracking before the program runs.

The `help` line offers two ways out. We could call `.clone()` to make an
independent copy of the string for the dictionary to own; the `fix` line even
gives the exact edit, as a line and column range and the text to insert there.
That would work.
But our counter has another problem we haven't seen yet: `The` and `the`
would be counted as different words. The usual fix for that is to convert
every word to lowercase, and `to_lower()` returns a brand-new string, which
means a string that we own. One change solves both problems. Update the loop
as in Listing 2-5.

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
import io

def main() -> int32:
    mut counts: dict[str, int64] = {}
    while true:
        match io.read_line():
            case Result.Ok(str as line):
                for raw in line.split_whitespace():
                    word = raw.to_lower()
                    if word in counts:
                        counts[word] += 1
                    else:
                        counts[word] = 1
            case Result.Ok(None):
                break
            case Result.Err(error):
                print(f"could not read input: {error}")
                return 1
    print(counts)
    return 0
```

<span class="caption">Listing 2-5: Lowercasing each word gives the dictionary a string it can own</span>

The loop now borrows each piece as `raw`, and `word = raw.to_lower()` makes a
new lowercase string owned by the binding `word`. When we store it with
`counts[word] = 1`, ownership moves from `word` to the dictionary. That's
allowed, because `word` was ours to give. Run it:

```console
$ aura run src/main.au < poem.txt
{the: 6, rain,: 1, rain!: 1, it: 3, falls: 3, on: 3, plain.: 1, hills,: 1, and: 1, lane.: 1, "rain,": 1, said: 1, girl.: 1, "rain: 1, again.": 1}
```

It works, and `The` and `the` are now counted together: six of them. The
dictionary prints its entries in the order the keys were first added, which
is the order Aura dictionaries always keep. (Printing shows strings without
quotes, which is why the keys look bare.)

The output also shows our next problem. `rain,`, `rain!`, `"rain,`, and
`"rain` are all counted as different words, because the punctuation is still
attached. We'll come back to that. First, let's turn this dump into a
readable report.

Ownership is the subject of all of
[Chapter 4](/book/ch04-00-understanding-ownership). For now, the thing to
take away is that the compiler knows, at every line, who owns each value and
who is only borrowing it, and it will tell you when those two get mixed up.

## Sorting and printing the top words

We want the most common words first, and only the top few. A dictionary isn't
sorted by its values, so we'll copy its entries into a list and sort that.
Replace the `print(counts)` line and add a constant at the top of the file,
as in Listing 2-6.

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
import io

TOP: int64 = 5

def main() -> int32:
    mut counts: dict[str, int64] = {}
    while true:
        match io.read_line():
            case Result.Ok(str as line):
                for raw in line.split_whitespace():
                    word = raw.to_lower()
                    if word in counts:
                        counts[word] += 1
                    else:
                        counts[word] = 1
            case Result.Ok(None):
                break
            case Result.Err(error):
                print(f"could not read input: {error}")
                return 1

    mut entries = counts.items()
    entries.sort(key=lambda entry: entry[1], reverse=true)
    for word, count in entries[:TOP]:
        print(f"{count:>5} {word}")
    return 0
```

<span class="caption">Listing 2-6: Sorting the entries by count and printing the top five</span>

`TOP: int64 = 5` is a binding at the top level of the file, outside any
function. A top-level binding is a *module constant*: it can't be changed,
and every function in the file can read it. Writing its name in capitals is a
habit from Python that makes constants stand out.

`counts.items()` returns a new list of the dictionary's entries. Each entry is
a *tuple*, a fixed-size group of values written in parentheses: here
`(word, count)`, of type `(str, int64)`. We sort that list in place with
`entries.sort(...)`, and because sorting changes the list, `entries` is `mut`.

The two arguments to `sort` are passed by name, as you can in Python. `key`
says what to sort by. Its value is a *lambda*, a small unnamed function
written inline: `lambda entry: entry[1]` takes an entry and returns its
second element, the count. (`entry[0]` would be the word.) `reverse=true`
sorts from largest to smallest. Note that `true` is lowercase in Aura.

The `for` loop then unpacks each tuple into two bindings, `word` and `count`,
the same way Python does. `entries[:TOP]` is a *slice*, the first `TOP`
entries of the list. Finally, `{count:>5}` in the f-string formats the count
right-aligned in a field five characters wide, so the words line up. The
format specifications after the `:` work much like Python's.

Let's see the report:

```console
$ aura run src/main.au < poem.txt
    6 the
    3 it
    3 falls
    3 on
    1 rain,
```

That looks like a word counter. `it`, `falls`, and `on` all have three, and
they come out in the order they first appeared in the poem, because Aura's
sort is *stable*: entries that compare equal keep their original order.

Let's try a different input, a famous line with fewer distinct words:

```console
$ echo "to be or not to be" | aura run src/main.au
error[AU4003]: slice end `5` is outside `0..=4`
 --> src/main.au:24:32
   |
24 |     for word, count in entries[:TOP]:
   |                                ^
  = note: Aura call chain (innermost first): main at 5:1
```

This time the program passed every compile-time check and started running.
The error happened at run time, on line 24, and stopped the program. Aura
calls this kind of failure a *trap*, and
[Chapter 9](/book/ch09-01-traps) has the full story. The message is precise: we asked for a
slice ending at position `5`, but the list only has four entries
(`to`, `be`, `or`, `not`), so valid end positions run from `0` to `4`. The
note gives the call chain, the functions that were running when it happened;
here it was `main`, defined at line 5.

If you know Python, this may be a surprise, because Python quietly shortens a
slice that runs past the end of a list. Aura does not, on purpose. A slice
that runs off the end is often a sign that the code's idea of the data is
wrong, and quietly returning fewer items hides that until something further
along goes wrong in a more confusing way. Aura would rather stop at the line
that made the bad assumption. The compiler could not catch this one before
running, because the length of `entries` depends on the input, so it is
checked at the moment the slice happens.

Here, though, "fewer than five words" is a perfectly normal situation, so the
code should handle it. The fix is to slice to whichever is smaller, `TOP` or
the length of the list. Aura has a `min` builtin, as Python does. Replace the
last loop with this:

```aura fragment
    shown = min(TOP, entries.len())
    for word, count in entries[:shown]:
        print(f"{count:>5} {word}")
```

`entries.len()` is the number of entries, and `min` returns the smaller of its
arguments. Now the short input works:

```console
$ echo "to be or not to be" | aura run src/main.au
    2 to
    2 be
    1 or
    1 not
```

## Cleaning up punctuation

The last problem is the punctuation stuck to the words. We'll write a
function, `clean`, that strips punctuation characters from the start and end
of a word and lowercases what's left. While we are at it, we'll move the
counting loop into a function of its own, so that `main` reads as a summary
of what the program does. Listing 2-7 is the finished program.

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
import io

TOP: int64 = 5

def clean(word: str) -> str:
    """Lowercase `word` and strip punctuation from both ends."""
    punctuation = ".,;:!?\"'()"
    mut start: int64 = 0
    mut stop = word.len()
    while start < stop and word[start:start + 1] in punctuation:
        start += 1
    while stop > start and word[stop - 1:stop] in punctuation:
        stop -= 1
    return word[start:stop].to_lower()

def count_words(line: str, counts: mut dict[str, int64]):
    for raw in line.split_whitespace():
        word = clean(raw)
        if word == "":
            continue
        if word in counts:
            counts[word] += 1
        else:
            counts[word] = 1

def main() -> int32:
    mut counts: dict[str, int64] = {}
    while true:
        match io.read_line():
            case Result.Ok(str as line):
                count_words(line, counts)
            case Result.Ok(None):
                break
            case Result.Err(error):
                print(f"could not read input: {error}")
                return 1

    mut entries = counts.items()
    entries.sort(key=lambda entry: entry[1], reverse=true)
    shown = min(TOP, entries.len())
    for word, count in entries[:shown]:
        print(f"{count:>5} {word}")
    return 0
```

<span class="caption">Listing 2-7: The finished word counter</span>

Let's start with `clean`. Its signature, `def clean(word: str) -> str`, says
it takes a string called `word` and returns a string. Every parameter in Aura
has a type written after it, and so does the return value, after the `->`.
Aura could work out the types of local bindings for us, but at the boundary
of a function it wants them spelled out, so that you can tell what a function
accepts by reading one line. The triple-quoted string on the first line of the
body is a *docstring*, as in Python; your editor shows it when you hover over
a call to `clean`.

The body walks two positions inward from the ends of the word. `start` begins
at `0` and `stop` at `word.len()`, the number of characters. The first
`while` loop moves `start` forward as long as the character at that position
is punctuation. `word[start:start + 1]` is a slice of the string containing
only that one character, and `in punctuation` asks whether that character
appears in our string of punctuation marks. Inside that string, `\"` is an
escaped double quote, so the string contains `"` along with `'`. The second
loop does the same from the other end. The `start < stop` and `stop > start`
conditions stop the loops from crossing, which matters for a "word" made
entirely of punctuation, such as `--` or `...`. Finally, we slice out the
middle and lowercase it.

We wrote `mut start: int64 = 0` with a type, while `mut stop = word.len()`
needed none. The two mean the same kind of thing; `int64` is what `0` would
have been anyway. Writing it here only makes the two loop positions look
alike. Both are `mut`, because the loops change them.

Now `count_words`. Look at its second parameter:
`counts: mut dict[str, int64]`. The `mut` in a parameter's type means the
function is allowed to change the caller's dictionary. When `main` calls
`count_words(line, counts)`, it lends its dictionary to the function, the
function adds to it, and when the call returns, `main` has the updated
dictionary back. Without `mut`, the compiler would reject the
`counts[word] += 1` lines, because a plain parameter can only be read. The
first parameter, `line: str`, is plain: `count_words` only reads the line.
This is how Aura function signatures tell you what a function will do to each
argument, and it's covered in
[Chapter 4](/book/ch04-00-understanding-ownership).

Notice that the call site doesn't change: there's no special marker on
`counts` in `count_words(line, counts)`. The function's signature decides
what kind of access it gets.

Inside `count_words`, a word that was nothing but punctuation is now an empty
string, and `continue` skips it and moves on to the next one. And because
`clean` returns a new string, `word` is owned, and storing it in `counts` is
allowed for the same reason as before.

Let's run the finished program:

```console
$ aura run src/main.au < poem.txt
    6 the
    4 rain
    3 it
    3 falls
    3 on
$ echo "to be or not to be" | aura run src/main.au
    2 to
    2 be
    1 or
    1 not
$ echo '...' | aura run src/main.au
```

`rain` is now counted four times, as it should be, and input with no real
words prints nothing at all.

## Building the tool

A word counter is the kind of program you want to keep around, so let's
compile it:

```console
$ aura build -o target/word_count src/main.au
aura: built `target/word_count` with direct backend
$ ./target/word_count < poem.txt
    6 the
    4 rain
    3 it
    3 falls
    3 on
```

The binary works anywhere a pipe does. Here it reads two copies of the poem,
one after the other, from `cat`:

```console
$ cat poem.txt poem.txt | ./target/word_count
   12 the
    8 rain
    6 it
    6 falls
    6 on
```

If you want to experiment further, here are some ideas to try. Each uses
only what we have seen in this chapter:

- Change `TOP` and see how the output changes.
- Skip very short words, such as those with fewer than three characters.
- Print the total number of words, and the number of distinct words, before
  the list.

## Summary

That was a lot of ground for one program. We used `io.read_line` to read
input, and saw that it returns a `Result` whose type spells out every outcome,
including the end of the input. We used `match` to handle each case, and the
compiler made sure we did not forget one. We met immutable bindings and `mut`,
dictionaries, lists, tuples, lambdas, slices, and f-strings. And we ran into
three different kinds of error: a non-exhaustive `match`, an assignment to an
immutable binding, and a borrowed value that we tried to store, all caught
before the program ran, plus a slice past the end of a list that was caught
the moment it happened.

The rest of the book takes those ideas one at a time. The next chapter starts
with the building blocks that almost every program uses: bindings, the basic
data types, functions, comments, and control flow.

## Source: docs/book/ch03-00-common-concepts.md

# Common programming concepts

The word counter in the last chapter used a lot of Aura without stopping to
explain it. This chapter slows down and goes through the pieces that nearly
every program is built from: bindings, the basic data types, functions,
comments, and control flow. None of these ideas is unique to Aura, and if you
know Python, much of the syntax will look familiar. What is worth your time
is the set of places where Aura's rules differ, and the reasons it chose
them.

Three themes run through the chapter. The first is that Aura is explicit
about change: bindings are immutable unless you mark them `mut`, so you can
see at a glance which values move under you. The second is that Aura is
explicit about types: it works out most of them for you, but it never turns
one type into another behind your back, not even an `int32` into an `int64`.
The third is that the compiler checks the whole program before any of it
runs, so the mistakes this chapter shows you are ones you find at your desk,
not in production.

The examples are small and mostly self-contained, so you can paste each one
into a file and run it with `aura run`. We'll come back to a small
temperature-conversion program in several sections, ending with a function
that prints a conversion table using everything the chapter covers.

The [Aura Manual](/manual/) has the complete rules for everything here. Its
[Types](/manual/types), [Functions](/manual/functions), and
[Statements](/manual/statements) pages are the ones to keep nearby.

## Source: docs/book/ch03-01-bindings-and-mutability.md

# Bindings and mutability

A program needs somewhere to keep the values it is working with. In Aura you
give a value a name by writing `name = value`, exactly as you would in Python.
We call that a *binding*: the name is bound to the value. There is no `let`,
`var`, or other keyword in front of it.

To follow along with this chapter, make a scratch package with
`aura new concepts`, and put each example in its `src/main.au`. Then run it
with `aura run src/main.au`.

## Bindings are immutable by default

Here is a small program that binds a name, prints it, and then tries to give
it a new value:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura check-fail:AU3003
def main():
    x = 5
    print(f"x is {x}")
    x = 6
    print(f"x is {x}")
```

<span class="caption">Listing 3-1: Trying to assign a second value to an immutable binding</span>

In Python this prints two lines. In Aura it doesn't run at all:

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU3003]: cannot assign to immutable binding `x`; declare it with `mut` to rebind it
 --> src/main.au:4:5
  |
4 |     x = 6
  |     ^
```

You saw this error in the word counter, and you will see it again, so it's
worth reading closely once. The compiler points at line 4, where we assign
`6` to `x`. It says `x` is an *immutable binding*: when a binding is created
with plain `name = value`, it keeps that value for as long as it exists. The
message also tells us the fix: if we want to change `x` later, we have to say
so when we create it, with `mut`.

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
def main():
    mut x = 5
    print(f"x is {x}")
    x = 6
    print(f"x is {x}")
```

<span class="caption">Listing 3-2: A mutable binding can be assigned again</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
x is 5
x is 6
```

`mut` goes in front of the binding the first time it appears. After that,
`x = 6` and the compound forms such as `x += 1` work as you would expect.
Aura has the usual compound assignments: `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `//=`, `%=`, and
`**=`, plus `/=` for floating-point numbers.

Why make immutability the default? When you read a function, most of the
bindings in it are set once and never touched again. In a language where any
name can be reassigned at any point, you can't know that without reading
every line between where a value is set and where it is used. In Aura, a
binding without `mut` is a promise that its value never changes, and the
compiler holds you to it. That makes code easier to read, and it makes it
safer to change: if you rearrange a function and accidentally reassign
something that other code relies on, the compiler tells you. The bindings that
do change carry a `mut` that says so, which is exactly where you want your
attention to go when something behaves unexpectedly.

The cost is a few extra `mut` keywords, and the error above the first few
times you forget one. Most people find that it fades quickly, and that the
`mut` marks end up being useful information.

## `mut` covers changes inside a value too

`mut` isn't only about pointing a name at a new value. It also controls
whether you may change the value the binding holds. A list is a good example:

```aura check-fail:AU3003
def main():
    guests = ["Ada", "Grace"]
    guests.append("Linus")
    print(guests)
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU3003]: method `append` requires a mutable receiver
 --> src/main.au:3:12
  |
3 |     guests.append("Linus")
  |            ^
  = help: declare the receiver place with `mut` before calling a mutating method
```

`append` changes the list it is called on, which the message calls the
*receiver*. Because `guests` is immutable, its list can't be changed either.
The `help` line says what to do, and with `mut guests = ["Ada", "Grace"]` the
program prints `[Ada, Grace, Linus]`.

This is a real difference from Python, where nothing is fixed by default:
any name can be rebound, and any list can be changed through any name that
refers to it. In Python you can pass a list to a function and
have no idea, from the call, whether it comes back changed. In Aura an
immutable binding means the whole value is frozen, contents and all. When you
need a value that changes, you say so once, and anyone reading the code can
see it. Functions follow the same idea through their parameters, as the
`counts: mut dict[str, int64]` parameter in the word counter showed. We'll
look at that properly in
[Chapter 4](/book/ch04-00-understanding-ownership).

## A binding keeps its type

Aura works out the type of a binding from the value you give it. `x = 5`
makes `x` an `int64`, Aura's default integer type, and `name = "Ada"` makes
`name` a `str`. That type is fixed for the life of the binding, even when the
binding is `mut`:

```aura check-fail:AU2002
def main():
    mut attempts = 0
    attempts = "three"
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU2002]: cannot assign value of type `str` to `attempts` of type `int64`
 --> src/main.au:3:5
  |
3 |     attempts = "three"
  |     ^
```

`mut` lets you replace the value, but the new value has to be the same type
as the old one. This is where Aura differs from Python most visibly. A Python
name can hold an integer on one line and a string on the next, and code
further down has to cope with either. Aura decides each binding's type once,
which is what lets it check every use of that binding before the program
runs.

Some languages let you reuse a name for a new binding in the same scope, which
is called *shadowing*. Aura doesn't. Writing `x = ...` a second time in the
same block always means assignment to the existing `x`, which is why
Listing 3-1 was an error rather than a new binding. If you need a value of a
different type, give it a different name, such as `attempts_text`.

## Writing the type yourself

You can write a binding's type after its name, separated by a colon:

```aura
def main():
    count: int64 = 3
    ratio: float64 = 0.25
    mut names: list[str] = []
    names.append("Ada")
    print(names)
```

Most of the time you don't need to. The type of `count` would have been
`int64` anyway. There are two situations where you do. The first is when the
value doesn't say enough. An empty list literal `[]` could be a list of
anything, so the compiler needs to be told what will go in it:

```aura check-fail:AU2002
def main():
    empty = []
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU2002]: empty list literals require an expected `list[T]` type annotation in the bootstrap compiler
 --> src/main.au:2:13
  |
2 |     empty = []
  |             ^
```

`names: list[str] = []` above is the fix, and the same goes for an empty
dictionary, as in `counts: dict[str, int64] = {}` from Chapter 2. (The
"bootstrap compiler" in the message is how the current preview compiler
refers to itself.)

The second is when you want a type other than the default. `count: int32 = 3`
makes `count` a 32-bit integer instead of a 64-bit one. We'll see in the
[next section](/book/ch03-02-data-types) why that choice sticks, and why
Aura won't mix the two.

Every binding needs a value when it is created. There is no way to declare a
name now and give it a value later, which means there is no such thing in Aura
as reading a binding that was never set.

## Blocks and scope

A binding exists from the line that creates it to the end of the block it was
created in. A block is an indented body: a function body, or the body of an
`if`, `else`, `while`, or `for`. Here is a pattern that is common in Python:

```aura check-fail:AU2001
def main():
    raining = true
    if raining:
        advice = "take an umbrella"
    else:
        advice = "leave it at home"
    print(advice)
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU2001]: unknown name `advice`
 --> src/main.au:7:11
  |
7 |     print(advice)
  |           ^
```

In Python, a name assigned inside an `if` is visible after it, as long as the
branch that set it actually ran. In Aura each branch is its own block, and the
two `advice` bindings end when their blocks end. By line 7 neither exists, so
the compiler reports an unknown name.

Aura scopes bindings to blocks because the alternative needs a run-time check
that can fail. If one branch of an `if` forgot to set `advice`, Python would
only find out when that branch ran and the `print` raised a `NameError`. Aura
wants every name to be known to exist wherever it is used, at compile time,
and tying bindings to blocks is the simplest rule that makes that possible.
Block scope also matters for cleanup, which we'll see in
[Chapter 4](/book/ch04-00-understanding-ownership): when a block ends, the
values it owned are cleaned up right there.

There are two good ways to write this. When each branch only chooses a
value, use a *conditional expression*, which has the same syntax as
Python's:

```aura
def main():
    raining = true
    advice = "take an umbrella" if raining else "leave it at home"
    print(advice)
```

When the branches need to do more work, create a `mut` binding with a
default before the `if`, and assign to it inside:

```aura
def main():
    raining = false
    mut advice = "leave it at home"
    if raining:
        advice = "take an umbrella"
    print(advice)
```

Because `advice` belongs to the function's block, it is still alive at the
`print`.

## Module constants

Bindings don't have to be inside a function. A binding at the top level of a
file, next to your `def`s, is a *module constant*:

```aura
FREEZING_F = 32.0

def main():
    print(FREEZING_F)
```

Every function in the module can read it. As the name says, it can't be
changed, not even from inside a function:

```aura check-fail:AU3003
FREEZING_F = 32.0

def main():
    FREEZING_F = 0.0
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU3003]: module constant `FREEZING_F` is immutable
 --> src/main.au:4:5
  |
```
