Shared borrows can overlap freely, since nobody is changing anything. Mutable
access has one more rule: while a value is borrowed mutably, nothing else may
reach it at the same time, not even for reading. Here is a function that
appends every element of one list onto another, called with the same list for
both:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura check-fail:AU3002
def merge(into: mut list[int64], source: list[int64]):
    for value in source:
        into.append(value)

def main():
    mut scores = [10, 20, 30]
    merge(scores, scores)
    print(scores)
```

<span class="caption">Listing 4-10: Passing one list as both a mutable and a shared argument</span>

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU3002]: argument for parameter `source` in function `merge` overlaps mutable borrow for parameter `into`; mutable borrows must be exclusive
 --> src/main.au:7:19
  |
7 |     merge(scores, scores)
  |                   ^
  = related src/main.au:7:11: mutable borrow for parameter `into` begins here
  = help: pass non-overlapping places; shared accesses may overlap, but mutable access must remain exclusive
```

Read the two locations together. The `related` line says that a mutable
borrow for `into` begins at column 11, the first `scores`. The arrow points
at column 19, the second `scores`, which tries to share the same list as
`source` while that mutable borrow is still live.

Think about what `merge` would do with one list behind both names. It loops
over `source` and appends each element to `into`. Every append makes `source`
longer, so the loop never reaches its end. Python shows exactly this
behavior. If you write

```python
scores = [10, 20, 30]
for value in scores:
    scores.append(value)
```

the loop runs until the program runs out of memory. Aura refuses the same
loop written directly, for the same reason:

```aura check-fail:AU3002
def main():
    mut scores = [10, 20, 30]
    for value in scores:
        scores.append(value)
    print(scores)
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU3002]: cannot mutate `scores` while `scores` is borrowed for iteration
 --> src/main.au:4:16
  |
4 |         scores.append(value)
  |                ^
  = related src/main.au:3:18: `scores` is borrowed for this loop here
  = help: perform owner mutation after the loop; use `for item in mut scores:` when mutating elements through the loop binding
```

A `for` loop borrows the list it walks over for the whole loop, and the
append in the body tries to change it while that borrow is live. The help
line gives the two usual fixes: collect the new values somewhere else and add
them after the loop, or, if what you wanted was to change each element, use
`for ... in mut`, which we'll see shortly.

Infinite loops are the friendly outcome. In a language without a garbage
collector, growing a list can move its storage to a bigger block of memory,
and anything still pointing into the old block is now pointing at freed
memory. C++ programmers know this as *iterator invalidation*. The exclusivity
rule rules out the whole family of bugs at once: if a value can change, only
one piece of code can be looking at it. The same rule is what later lets Aura
run tasks in parallel without data races, which we'll come back to in
[Chapter 15](/book/ch15-00-concurrency).

## Borrowed fields stay where they are

Shared access lets a function read a value's fields, but not take them away.
Here is a function that tries to return a user's name from a borrowed
`User`:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura check-fail:AU3002
class User:
    name: str
    age: int64

def name_of(user: User) -> str:
    return user.name

def main():
    user = User(name="Ada", age=36)
    print(name_of(user))
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU3002]: cannot move non-copy field `name` out of borrowed value `user`
 --> src/main.au:6:17
  |
6 |     return user.name
  |                 ^
  = related src/main.au:5:13: `user` is borrowed here
  = help: take `user` as `own User` when the field should be moved, or call `.clone()` on the field to return an independent value
  = fix: replace src/main.au:6:21-6:21 with `.clone()`
```

Returning a value from a function moves it to the caller, as we saw with
`make_roster`. But `name_of` doesn't own `user.name`. The caller does, and it
expects to get its `User` back intact when the call ends. Returning the field
would move the string out of someone else's value.

The help line lists the two honest options, and they mean different things.
Cloning the field returns a new string and leaves the caller's `User`
untouched. Taking `own User` consumes the whole user and moves the name out of
it, which is the right shape for a function that converts one value into
another. Here are both in one program:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
class Player:
    name: str
    score: int64

def name_of(user: Player) -> str:
    return user.name.clone()

def into_name(user: own Player) -> str:
    return user.name

def main():
    player = Player(name="Ada", score=90)
    print(name_of(player))
    print(player.score)
    print(into_name(player))
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
Ada
90
Ada
```

After `into_name(player)`, `player` is gone. Fields that are copy values,
like `score`, are never a problem: returning `user.score` from a shared borrow
returns a copy.

## Receivers follow the same rules

Methods take their instance through a *receiver*, the `self` at the front of
the parameter list, and it comes in the same three forms. Bare `self` is
shared access, `mut self` is mutable access, and `own self` takes ownership.
Here is a small scoreboard class that uses all three:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
class Scoreboard:
    scores: list[int64]

    def best(self) -> int64:
        mut top: int64 = 0
        for value in self.scores:
            if value > top:
                top = value
        return top

    def record(mut self, value: int64):
        self.scores.append(value)

    def curve(mut self, points: int64):
        for value in mut self.scores:
            value += points

    def into_scores(own self) -> list[int64]:
        return self.scores

def main():
    mut board = Scoreboard(scores=[70, 85])
    board.record(92)
    print(board.best())
    board.curve(5)
    scores = board.into_scores()
    print(scores)
```

<span class="caption">Listing 4-11: A class whose methods read, change, and consume the instance</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
92
[75, 90, 97]
```

`best` only reads, so it takes `self`. `record` and `curve` change the list,
so they take `mut self`, and the instance has to live in a mutable place:
drop the `mut` from `mut board` and the call to `record` fails the same way
`add_bonus` did, with an error that points at `.record`:

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU3003]: method `record` requires a mutable receiver
 --> src/main.au:23:11
   |
23 |     board.record(92)
   |           ^
  = help: declare the receiver place with `mut` before calling a mutating method
```

`into_scores` takes `own self`, so calling it consumes `board`. If we add a
`print(board.best())` at the end of `main`, the compiler points at both the
use and the call that moved it:

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU3001]: use of moved value `board`
 --> src/main.au:28:11
   |
28 |     print(board.best())
   |           ^
  = related src/main.au:26:14: value moved here
  = help: pass shared access when ownership is not needed, or transfer this non-cloneable value only once
```

The help mentions that `Scoreboard` is non-cloneable. Classes don't get a
copy method automatically, so the only way forward is to call `into_scores`
last. We'll spend more time on receivers in
[Chapter 5](/book/ch05-00-classes).

## Changing elements in a loop

`curve` uses a loop form we haven't seen yet. A plain `for value in scores`
borrows the list and gives you each element with shared access, so you can't
assign to `value`:

```aura check-fail:AU3003
def main():
    scores = [10, 20, 30]
    for value in scores:
        value += 1
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU3003]: cannot assign to immutable binding `value`; declare it with `mut` to rebind it
 --> src/main.au:4:9
  |
4 |         value += 1
  |         ^
```

In Python this loop would run and do nothing visible, since `value += 1`
rebinds the loop variable and leaves the list alone. Aura offers the version
you probably meant. Writing `mut` before the list makes each `value` a
mutable view of the element itself, so assignments land in the list. And
writing `own` before the list consumes it, handing you each element as an
owned value:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
def main():
    mut scores = [10, 20, 30]
    for value in mut scores:
        value *= 2
    print(scores)
    for value in own scores:
        print(value)
```

<span class="caption">Listing 4-12: `for ... in mut` changes elements in place; `for ... in own` consumes the list</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
[20, 40, 60]
20
40
60
```

The `mut` loop needs a mutable list, for the same reason a `mut` parameter
does. After the `own` loop, `scores` has moved into the loop and can't be
used again. Notice where the keyword goes. On a parameter it sits in the type,
as in `values: mut list[int64]`, because a parameter has a type position. A
loop has no type to annotate, so the keyword goes in front of the thing being
iterated.

## Choosing an access mode

When you write a function, ask what it does with each argument, and pick the
weakest access that does the job:

1. If it only reads, use a bare type. This is the common case, and it leaves
   the caller free to keep using the value.
2. If it changes the caller's value in place, use `mut`. The caller will need
   a `mut` binding, which makes the change visible at both ends.
3. If it keeps the value (storing it in a list or a field, returning it, or
   taking it apart), use `own`. The caller gives it up, or passes a copy.

Python lets every function do all three to everything it's given. Aura asks
you to write down which one you mean, and in return every signature tells the
reader, and the compiler, what happens to the arguments. The
[Manual](/manual/ownership-and-borrowing) has the complete rules, including
views, returned views, and borrowed pattern matching.

There is one situation we keep running into, where we really do want a
second, independent value: two owners, each free to change its own. In the
next section we'll look at copies and slices, and at what they cost.

## Source: docs/book/ch04-03-copies-and-slices.md

# Copies and slices

Borrowing covers most of what functions need, but sometimes you really do
want two independent values. You want to keep yesterday's scores while you
change today's, or keep a name in a list and also store it in a record. For
those cases Aura makes copies, and it makes them only when you ask. Asking
takes a different spelling for different types, and every copy has a cost
that grows with the value, so both are worth knowing before you reach for
one.

Let's start with an error that looks like it should not be one. We have a
list of names, and we want the first:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura check-fail:AU3005
def main():
    names = ["Ada", "Grace", "Margaret"]
    first = names[0]
    print(first)
```

<span class="caption">Listing 4-13: Binding a list element to a new name</span>

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU3005]: cannot implicitly copy `str` out of a list index; use `view value = items[index]` for shared access, `items[index].clone()` for an explicit cloned owner, or `pop(index)` or `set(index, value)` to transfer ownership
 --> src/main.au:3:13
  |
3 |     first = names[0]
  |             ^
```

In Python, `first = names[0]` makes `first` a second name for the string in
the list, and that's that. In Aura, `first = ...` creates a new owner, and the
string already has one: the list. The compiler won't quietly duplicate the
string, and it won't quietly pull it out of the list either, because either
choice would surprise someone. So it lists the options and asks you to pick
one:

- `view value = items[index]` gives you shared access to the element where it
  sits, without copying it or taking it out.
- `items[index].clone()` makes a new string with its own owner.
- `pop(index)` or `set(index, value)` takes the element out of the list and
  gives you ownership of it, leaving the list one element shorter or holding
  a replacement.

Here are the first two side by side:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
def main():
    names = ["Ada", "Grace", "Margaret"]
    first = names[0].clone()
    view also_first = names[0]
    print(first)
    print(also_first.len())
    print(names)
```

<span class="caption">Listing 4-14: Cloning an element, and viewing one in place</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
Ada
3
[Ada, Grace, Margaret]
```

`first` is a new string, owned by `main`, which we could change, store, or
return without affecting the list. `also_first` is a *view*: another name for
the string inside the list, with shared access. A view costs nothing to make,
and the compiler makes sure the list doesn't change underneath it while the
view is in use. If all you need is to read the element, a view is the better
choice. Most of the time you won't even need the `view` keyword, because
using `names[0]` directly as an argument, as in `print(names[0])`, lends the
element for that one call. The [Manual](/manual/ownership-and-borrowing) has
the full rules for views, including `view mut` for changing an element in
place.

## Making copies with `.copy()` and `.clone()`

When you need a second owner, the operation that makes one depends on the
type. Lists, dictionaries, and sets have `.copy()`. Strings have `.clone()`.
The two spellings come from the compiler itself, and its diagnostics always
suggest the right one for the type in front of them. If you mix them up, it
tells you:

```aura check-fail:AU2999
def main():
    name = "Ada"
    other = name.copy()
    print(other)
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2999]: unsupported method call `copy` on `str`
 --> src/main.au:3:18
  |
3 |     other = name.copy()
  |                  ^
```

A copy of a collection is fully independent. It gets its own storage, and
every element is copied or cloned into it, so changing one list never shows
up in the other:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
def main():
    mut today = [70, 85, 92]
    yesterday = today.copy()
    today.append(64)
    print(today)
    print(yesterday)
```

<span class="caption">Listing 4-15: A copied list does not see changes to the original</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
[70, 85, 92, 64]
[70, 85, 92]
```

If you have used Python's `list.copy()`, notice the difference. Python's copy
is *shallow*: the new list holds the same element objects as the old one, so
a list of lists or a list of objects still shares its contents, and you reach
for `copy.deepcopy` when that bites. Aura's copy goes all the way down. A list
of class instances copies each instance and each of their fields:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
class Player:
    name: str
    score: int64

def main():
    team = [Player(name="Ada", score=90), Player(name="Grace", score=88)]
    mut backup = team.copy()
    backup[0].score = 10
    print(team[0].score)
    print(backup[0].score)
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
90
10
```

The two lists can't share anything, because each element can only have one
owner. A shallow copy would give every player two owners, which is exactly
what ownership rules out.

Your own classes don't come with a copy method. When you want one, write it,
copying each field the way its type expects:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
class Player:
    name: str
    score: int64

    def copy(self) -> Player:
        return Player(name=self.name.clone(), score=self.score)

def main():
    ada = Player(name="Ada", score=90)
    mut twin = ada.copy()
    twin.score = 95
    print(ada)
    print(twin)
```

<span class="caption">Listing 4-16: A hand-written `copy` method on a class</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
Player(name=Ada, score=90)
Player(name=Ada, score=95)
```

`self.name.clone()` makes a new string, and `self.score` copies because it is
an `int64`. Printing a class instance shows its fields by name. (The fields
come out in alphabetical order, which is the default rendering for a class.
[Chapter 5](/book/ch05-00-classes) shows how to choose your own.)

### Some values can't be copied

A few types refuse to be copied at all. A random number generator,
`random.Rng`, is the standard example: two generators with the same internal
state would produce the same "random" numbers, which is a classic source of
subtle bugs in simulations and tests. So `Rng` has no copy, and neither does
anything that contains one:

```aura check-fail:AU3007
import random

def main():
    gens = [random.Rng(seed=1)]
    more = gens.copy()
    print(more.len())
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU3007]: cannot use `list.copy` because `list[random.Rng]` contains non-cloneable `random.Rng` state
 --> src/main.au:5:17
  |
5 |     more = gens.copy()
  |                 ^
  = help: move or remove the value so it has one owner, or construct an independent generator with an explicit seed
```

The help line is the design in one sentence: if you need a second generator,
make a new one with its own seed, so that the program says plainly where each
stream of numbers comes from.

## Slices are copies too

A *slice* picks out a range of a list or a string with `start:end`, the same
syntax Python uses. In Aura a slice is always a fresh owned value. It copies
the selected elements into new storage, and it never refers back to the
original:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
def main():
    names = ["Ada", "Grace", "Margaret"]
    mut rest = names[1:]
    rest.append("Katherine")
    print(rest)
    print(names)
    word = "ownership"
    print(word[0:3])
    print("A🎉Z"[1:2])
```

<span class="caption">Listing 4-17: List and string slices produce new owned values</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
[Grace, Margaret, Katherine]
[Ada, Grace, Margaret]
own
🎉
```

`rest` started as a copy of the last two names, and appending to it left
`names` unchanged. The string slices work the same way: `word[0:3]` is a new
three-character string. String positions count Unicode characters, not bytes,
which is why `"A🎉Z"[1:2]` gives the whole emoji rather than a piece of its
UTF-8 encoding. We'll come back to how strings are stored in
[Chapter 8](/book/ch08-00-collections).

This matches Python, where `names[1:]` also builds a new list. One Python
habit doesn't carry over, though. Python lets you assign to a slice to
replace part of a list in place. Since an Aura slice is a separate value,
assigning to one would change nothing, so the compiler refuses:

```aura check-fail:AU2005
def main():
    names = ["Ada", "Grace", "Margaret"]
    names[1:] = ["Grace"]
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2005]: slice assignment is unavailable because slices are owned copies; mutate the source by index or build a new value
 --> src/main.au:3:12
  |
3 |     names[1:] = ["Grace"]
  |            ^
```

Since a slice copies its elements, slicing a list of `random.Rng` values is
rejected with the same `AU3007` error as `.copy()`.

## What copying costs

Every `.copy()`, `.clone()`, and slice allocates new memory and copies into
it, so the cost grows with the size of the value. Copying a list of ten
numbers is nothing. Copying a list of a million strings means a million
allocations. That is why Aura never copies an owned value on its own: every
copy appears in the source as a method call or a slice, where you can see it
and decide whether it is worth it.

Python makes the opposite trade. Assignment never copies, so it is always
cheap, but two names can share a value without either of them knowing, and
the cost shows up later as reference counting on every assignment and as
bugs where a change in one place appears in another.

A few habits keep copying under control in Aura:

1. Borrow first. A shared or `mut` parameter costs nothing, and it is what
   most functions want.
2. Copy close to the reason. When you do clone, do it at the line where you
   need the second owner, so a reader can see why it is there.
3. Move when you are finished. If the caller doesn't need a value after the
   call, an `own` parameter hands it over without any copying at all.

Copy values such as integers, floats, and `bool` are the exception. They are
copied on every assignment, because copying them is as cheap as reading them,
and there is no separate memory behind them to share.

## Summary

Ownership is how Aura manages memory and resources without a garbage
collector. Each value has one owner, assigning or passing an owned value moves
it unless the function only borrows it, and the value is cleaned up at the
end of its owner's scope. The compiler checks all of this before the program
runs, and its errors name both the place you used a value and the place it
moved. You can now read a signature and know what a function does with each
argument: a bare type borrows for reading, `mut` borrows for changing, and
`own` takes the value over. You also know when to reach for `.copy()`,
`.clone()`, a slice, or a view, and what each one costs.

These rules are going to show up everywhere from here on. In the next
chapter we'll use them to build our own types with classes, where fields,
constructors, and the three kinds of `self` all follow the patterns you've
learned here.

## Source: docs/book/ch05-00-classes.md

# Using classes to structure data

A program that tracks a book you're reading needs a few facts about it: a
title, an author, a page count, and how far you've got. You can keep those in
four separate bindings, and for a dozen lines that works. Once there are
several books, or functions that need all four facts at once, loose bindings
start to drift apart. Nothing in the code says that `pages` and `pages_read`
describe the same book, and nothing stops a function from being handed the
page count of one book and the progress of another.

A *class* gives a group of related values a name and a shape. In this chapter
we'll declare classes, build instances of them, and read and change their
fields. Then we'll write a small reading-tracker program twice: once with
loose values and once with a class, so you can see what the class buys.
Finally we'll move the functions that work on a book into the class itself as
*methods*, and look at how the three kinds of `self` say what each method does
to its instance.

If you have written Python classes, much of this will look familiar, from
`__init__` to `@property`. Two things will be new. Every field has a declared
type, and every method says, in its first parameter, whether it reads the
instance, changes it, or consumes it, using the ownership rules from
[Chapter 4](/book/ch04-00-understanding-ownership). And Aura classes have no
inheritance. We'll talk about why, and what to use instead, at the end of the
chapter.

## Source: docs/book/ch05-01-defining-classes.md

# Defining and building classes

A class declaration lists the fields every instance has, with a type for each.
Here is a class for a book:

```aura
class Book:
    title: str
    author: str
    pages: int64
```

<span class="caption">Listing 5-1: A `Book` class with three fields</span>

The declaration starts with `class` and the class name, by convention in
`CamelCase`. The indented body holds one line per field: a name, a colon, and
a type. The order of the fields matters in one place, positional construction,
which we'll get to in a moment.

Compare this with a Python class, where fields usually appear for the first
time as assignments inside `__init__`. A Python object can grow new
attributes at any point, and nothing stops two `Book` objects from having
different sets of them. An Aura class is a fixed shape. Every `Book` has
exactly these three fields with exactly these types, and the compiler checks
every construction and every field access against that shape.

## Creating instances

To make a `Book`, call the class name with a value for each field:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
class Book:
    title: str
    author: str
    pages: int64

def main():
    book = Book(title="Dune", author="Frank Herbert", pages=412)
    print(book.title)
    print(book.pages)
    print(book)
    other = Book("Emma", "Jane Austen", pages=474)
    print(other.author)
```

<span class="caption">Listing 5-2: Building two books and reading their fields</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
Dune
412
Book(author=Frank Herbert, pages=412, title=Dune)
Jane Austen
```

The first call names every field. The second passes `title` and `author` by
position, in the order the class declares them, and then names `pages`. You
can mix the two styles as long as the positional arguments come first. Named
arguments are easier to read when a class has more than two or three fields,
and they keep working if someone reorders the declaration later, so we'll use
them most of the time.

You read a field with a dot, as in `book.title`. Printing a whole instance
shows the class name and each field with its value. The fields appear in
alphabetical order, not declaration order. That rendering is meant for
debugging; in [Methods](/book/ch05-03-methods) we'll see how to give a class
its own.

The compiler checks each construction against the declaration. Leave a field
out and it names the one that's missing:

```aura check-fail:AU2999
class Book:
    title: str
    author: str
    pages: int64

def main():
    book = Book(title="Dune", author="Frank Herbert")
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2999]: class constructor `Book` is missing required field `pages`
 --> src/main.au:7:12
  |
7 |     book = Book(title="Dune", author="Frank Herbert")
  |            ^
```

And a field the class doesn't have is an error too, pointing at the argument
that doesn't belong:

```aura check-fail:AU2999
class Book:
    title: str
    author: str
    pages: int64

def main():
    book = Book(title="Dune", author="Frank Herbert", pages=412, year=1965)
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2999]: class `Book` has no field named `year`
 --> src/main.au:7:66
  |
7 |     book = Book(title="Dune", author="Frank Herbert", pages=412, year=1965)
  |                                                                  ^
```

In Python both mistakes would show up later, if at all: a missing attribute
as an `AttributeError` the first time some code reads it, and a misspelled
one as a new attribute that nothing ever reads. Aura reports them at the
line that built the instance.

## Default values

A field can have a default, written after its type. Fields with defaults can
be left out of the constructor call:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
class Book:
    title: str
    pages: int64
    tags: list[str] = []

def main():
    mut dune = Book(title="Dune", pages=412)
    emma = Book(title="Emma", pages=474)
    dune.tags.append("science fiction")
    print(dune.tags)
    print(emma.tags)
```

<span class="caption">Listing 5-3: Each instance gets its own fresh default list</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
[science fiction]
[]
```

If you've been bitten by Python's mutable default arguments, look at the
output again. Aura evaluates a default expression afresh for every
construction that leaves the field out, so `dune` and `emma` each get their
own empty list, and appending to one leaves the other alone. Under ownership
there is no other sensible choice: one list can't have two owners, so two
books can't share a default list.

## Changing fields

Assigning to a field changes the instance, and the instance has to be in a
mutable binding for that, the same way a list does before you can append to it:

```aura check-fail:AU3003
class Book:
    title: str
    pages: int64
    pages_read: int64 = 0

def main():
    book = Book(title="Dune", pages=412)
    book.pages_read = 50
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU3003]: cannot assign through immutable place `book.pages_read`
 --> src/main.au:8:5
  |
8 |     book.pages_read = 50
  |     ^
```

Mutability belongs to the binding, and the fields inherit it. A `mut` binding
lets you change any field, and an immutable one lets you change none. There
is no way to mark one field read-only and another writable. Declaring the
binding `mut` fixes the error:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
class Book:
    title: str
    pages: int64
    pages_read: int64 = 0

def main():
    mut book = Book(title="Dune", pages=412)
    book.pages_read = 50
    book.pages_read += 25
    print(book.pages_read)
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
75
```

## Classes are owned values

A class instance is an owned value, so everything from
[Chapter 4](/book/ch04-00-understanding-ownership) applies to it. Assigning
it moves it. Passing it to an `own` parameter moves it. Putting it into a list
moves it too:

```aura check-fail:AU3001
class Book:
    title: str
    pages: int64

def main():
    book = Book(title="Dune", pages=412)
    shelf = [book]
    print(book.title)
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU3001]: use of moved value `book`
 --> src/main.au:8:11
  |
8 |     print(book.title)
  |           ^
  = related src/main.au:7:14: value moved here
  = help: pass shared access when ownership is not needed, or transfer this non-cloneable value only once
```

The list literal `[book]` on line 7 took ownership of the book. From then on
the book lives in `shelf`, and we'd reach it as `shelf[0]`. The construction
call itself works the same way: every field argument is an owned position, so
`Book(title=name, pages=412)` moves the string in `name` into the new book.

### Copy classes

Some classes are as small and simple as a number. For those you can write
`copy class`, and the instances copy on assignment the way integers do:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
copy class Rating:
    stars: int64
    out_of: int64

def main():
    first = Rating(stars=4, out_of=5)
    mut second = first
    second.stars = 5
    print(first.stars)
    print(second.stars)
```

<span class="caption">Listing 5-4: A copy class duplicates on assignment</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
4
5
```

`second = first` made a copy, so changing `second` left `first` at four
stars. A copy class may only contain copy values. Give `Rating` a `str` field
and the compiler stops you, because a string can't be duplicated for free:

```aura check-fail:AU2002
copy class Rating:
    stars: int64
    comment: str
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2002]: field `comment` on `copy class Rating` must be a copy type, found `str`
 --> src/main.au:3:5
  |
3 |     comment: str
  |     ^
```

Use `copy class` when copying is part of what the type means: a point, a
color, a rating, a pair of numbers. Don't use it to get out of an ownership
error. If a class holds strings or lists, it is an owned value, and the
ownership rules are doing their job.

## Initializers

Sometimes the constructor shouldn't take the fields one for one. Perhaps a
field is always computed, or an argument needs checking first. For those
cases a class can declare `__init__`, as in Python:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
class Book:
    title: str
    pages: int64
    pages_read: int64

    def __init__(self, title: own str, pages: int64):
        self.title = title
        if pages < 1:
            self.pages = 1
        else:
            self.pages = pages
        self.pages_read = 0

def main():
    book = Book("Dune", 412)
    blank = Book("Notebook", 0)
    print(book)
    print(blank.pages)
```

<span class="caption">Listing 5-5: An initializer that computes and checks fields</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
Book(pages=412, pages_read=0, title=Dune)
1
```

Once a class has `__init__`, calling the class calls the initializer. Its
parameters replace the field list, so `Book("Dune", 412)` passes a title and a
page count, and `Book(title="Dune", pages=412, pages_read=10)` is now an
error that says the class expects two arguments. Inside the body, `self` is
the instance being built, and the job of the body is to give every field a
value.

The compiler checks that it does, on every path. Delete the last line,
`self.pages_read = 0`, and you get:

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU3012]: initializer falls through without initializing `pages_read`
 --> src/main.au:6:5
  |
6 |     def __init__(self, title: own str, pages: int64):
  |     ^
  = help: assign every field without a declaration default on every path through `__init__`
```

The `if` sets `pages` on both branches, so that field is fine. `pages_read`
is set on no path at all. Python would let this through, and the first read
of `book.pages_read` would raise an `AttributeError` far from the cause. In
Aura, an instance with an unset field can't exist.

Notice the `own` on `title`. The initializer stores the string in a field,
which keeps it, so it needs ownership. If we write `title: str` instead, the
compiler catches the assignment that tries to keep a borrowed value:

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU3002]: parameter `title` is borrowed; declare it as `own str` to take ownership, or clone the value before consuming it
 --> src/main.au:7:22
  |
7 |         self.title = title
  |                      ^
  = related src/main.au:6:24: parameter `title` is borrowed here
  = help: declare the parameter as `own str` when the function should consume it, or call `.clone()` to consume an independent copy
  = fix: replace src/main.au:7:27-7:27 with `.clone()`
```

That is the "pick the weakest access that does the job" rule from the last
chapter, applied to a constructor. Storing is keeping, and keeping needs
`own`.

An initializer has no return value and can't fail. When building an
instance can go wrong, for example when a page count comes from user input,
write a function on the class that returns a `Result` instead. We'll see
functions on the class in [Methods](/book/ch05-03-methods) and `Result` in
[Chapter 9](/book/ch09-00-error-handling). The
[Manual](/manual/classes) has the complete construction rules, including
evaluation order and visibility across modules.

With classes in hand, let's put them to work in a small program and see what
they change.

## Source: docs/book/ch05-02-example-program.md

# An example program using classes

To see what a class changes, let's write a small program the long way first.
We want a reading tracker: given how many pages a book has and how many we've
read, it tells us how far through we are. We'll start with separate bindings,
move to a tuple, and end with a class, looking at what each version makes
easy and what it leaves to chance.

Make a new project for it:

```console
$ aura new reading
created `reading`
```

All the listings in this section replace the contents of
`reading/src/main.au`, and we run them from inside the `reading` directory.

## Starting with loose bindings

The first version keeps the two numbers in their own bindings and passes both
to a function:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
def percent_read(pages: int64, pages_read: int64) -> float64:
    return pages_read.to_float() / pages.to_float() * 100.0

def main():
    pages = 412
    pages_read = 103
    print(f"You have read {percent_read(pages, pages_read):.1f}% of the book.")
```

<span class="caption">Listing 5-6: Computing progress from two separate bindings</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
You have read 25.0% of the book.
```

`percent_read` converts both counts to `float64` with `.to_float()`,
because Aura never converts between integer and float types for you, and `/`
isn't defined on two `int64` values at all (that was the `AU2003` error in
[Data types](/book/ch03-02-data-types)). A percentage is a ratio, so the
rounding `.to_float()` allows is fine here. The `:.1f` in the f-string prints
the result with one decimal place, as it would in Python.

The program works, but look at the signature: `percent_read(pages: int64,
pages_read: int64)`. Both parameters have the same type, so nothing stops us
from passing them in the wrong order. Swap them in the call and see:

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
You have read 400.0% of the book.
```

The compiler had no reason to object. As far as it knows, any two `int64`
values will do. The connection between `pages` and `pages_read` (that they
describe the same book, and which is which) exists only in our heads and in
the parameter names.

## Grouping with a tuple

A tuple lets us carry the two numbers as one value:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
def percent_read(progress: (int64, int64)) -> float64:
    return progress[1].to_float() / progress[0].to_float() * 100.0

def main():
    dune = (412, 103)
    print(f"You have read {percent_read(dune):.1f}% of the book.")
```

<span class="caption">Listing 5-7: Passing the counts together as a tuple</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
You have read 25.0% of the book.
```

This is better in one way. The function now takes a single argument, so the
two numbers travel together and can't be mixed up with another book's. But
it's worse in another. Inside the function, `progress[1]` and `progress[0]`
say nothing about what they mean. We had to remember that the page count
comes first, and anyone who builds a tuple as `(103, 412)` gets the 400% bug
back. Tuples are fine for a pair that is obvious from context, like a point's
`(x, y)`, or for returning two values from a function. They are a poor home
for data whose parts have different meanings.

## Naming the parts with a class

A class gives each part a name and keeps the parts together:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
class Book:
    title: str
    pages: int64
    pages_read: int64 = 0

def percent_read(book: Book) -> float64:
    return book.pages_read.to_float() / book.pages.to_float() * 100.0

def main():
    dune = Book(title="Dune", pages=412, pages_read=103)
    print(f"You have read {percent_read(dune):.1f}% of {dune.title}.")
```

<span class="caption">Listing 5-8: A `Book` class keeps the counts together and named</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
You have read 25.0% of Dune.
```

Now the function body reads as what it computes, `book.pages_read` over
`book.pages`. The construction call names every field, so the 400% mistake
would mean writing `pages=103, pages_read=412`, which is hard to do by
accident. And because the type has a name, a function that takes a `Book`
can't be handed some other pair of numbers. We also gained a place to put the
title, which the earlier versions had no room for.

`percent_read` takes `book: Book` with no prefix, so it borrows the book with
shared access, which is all it needs. After the call, `main` still owns
`dune` and can read `dune.title` in the same f-string.

## A shelf of books

One book isn't much of a tracker. Let's keep several in a list, add a
function that records some reading, and print a report:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
class Book:
    title: str
    pages: int64
    pages_read: int64 = 0

def percent_read(book: Book) -> float64:
    return book.pages_read.to_float() / book.pages.to_float() * 100.0

def read_pages(book: mut Book, count: int64):
    book.pages_read += count
    if book.pages_read > book.pages:
        book.pages_read = book.pages

def main():
    mut shelf = [
        Book(title="Dune", pages=412, pages_read=103),
        Book(title="Emma", pages=474),
        Book(title="Beloved", pages=324, pages_read=300),
    ]
    read_pages(shelf[1], 50)
    read_pages(shelf[2], 50)
    for book in shelf:
        print(f"{book.title:<10} {percent_read(book):>5.1f}%")
```

<span class="caption">Listing 5-9: Tracking a shelf of books</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
Dune        25.0%
Emma        10.5%
Beloved    100.0%
```

`read_pages` changes the book it's given, so its parameter is `mut Book`.
The call `read_pages(shelf[1], 50)` lends the second element of the list to
the function for the length of the call, and the change lands in the list.
That only works because `shelf` is a `mut` binding. `Emma` used the default
`pages_read` of 0, so after fifty pages it's at 10.5%. `Beloved` would have
gone past its last page, and the clamp in `read_pages` stopped it at 324.

The format specifications line the report up: `:<10` pads the title on the
right to ten characters, and `:>5.1f` right-aligns the percentage in five.

Now let's list the books we've finished. A first attempt collects the titles
into a new list:

```aura fragment
def finished(books: list[Book]) -> list[str]:
    mut titles = list[str]()
    for book in books:
        if book.pages_read == book.pages:
            titles.append(book.title)
    return titles
```

When we add this function to Listing 5-9, after `read_pages`, and print
`finished(shelf)` at the end of `main`, the compiler objects:

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU3002]: cannot move non-copy field `title` out of borrowed value `book`
 --> src/main.au:18:32
   |
18 |             titles.append(book.title)
   |                                ^
  = related src/main.au:16:9: `book` is borrowed here
  = help: take `book` as `own Book` when the field should be moved, or call `.clone()` on the field to return an independent value
  = fix: replace src/main.au:18:37-18:37 with `.clone()`
```

This is the borrowed-field rule from
[Chapter 4](/book/ch04-02-shared-and-mutable-access) showing up in a real
program. `append` takes ownership of what it stores, and the loop only has
shared access to each `book`, so it can't give the book's title away. The
books still need their titles: the report prints them. So the right fix is
the clone the `fix` line suggests, which puts a new copy of each title in the
result. Here is the whole program with `finished` added:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
class Book:
    title: str
    pages: int64
    pages_read: int64 = 0

def percent_read(book: Book) -> float64:
    return book.pages_read.to_float() / book.pages.to_float() * 100.0

def read_pages(book: mut Book, count: int64):
    book.pages_read += count
    if book.pages_read > book.pages:
        book.pages_read = book.pages

def finished(books: list[Book]) -> list[str]:
    mut titles = list[str]()
    for book in books:
        if book.pages_read == book.pages:
            titles.append(book.title.clone())
    return titles

def main():
    mut shelf = [
        Book(title="Dune", pages=412, pages_read=103),
        Book(title="Emma", pages=474),
        Book(title="Beloved", pages=324, pages_read=300),
    ]
    read_pages(shelf[1], 50)
    read_pages(shelf[2], 50)
    for book in shelf:
        print(f"{book.title:<10} {percent_read(book):>5.1f}%")
    print(f"Finished: {finished(shelf)}")
```

<span class="caption">Listing 5-10: The tracker with a list of finished titles</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
Dune        25.0%
Emma        10.5%
Beloved    100.0%
Finished: [Beloved]
```

Look at the three function signatures together. `percent_read(book: Book)`
reads a book. `read_pages(book: mut Book, count: int64)` changes one.
`finished(books: list[Book])` reads a whole shelf and returns new data. You
can tell what each function does to its arguments without reading a line of
its body, and the compiler holds each one to what it says.

All three functions are about books, though, and nothing in the code ties
them to the `Book` class except their parameter types. In the next section
we'll move them into the class as methods.

## Source: docs/book/ch05-03-methods.md

# Methods

A *method* is a function declared inside a class body. It is called on an
instance with a dot, as in `dune.read(50)`, and its first parameter is a
*receiver* that names that instance. You've seen receivers briefly in
[Chapter 4](/book/ch04-02-shared-and-mutable-access). Here we'll
turn the reading tracker's free functions into methods and look at each form
of receiver in turn.

## Defining methods

Here are `percent_read` and `read_pages` from the last section, moved into
`Book`, along with a new `is_finished`:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
class Book:
    title: str
    pages: int64
    pages_read: int64 = 0

    def percent_read(self) -> float64:
        return self.pages_read.to_float() / self.pages.to_float() * 100.0

    def is_finished(self) -> bool:
        return self.pages_read == self.pages

    def read(mut self, count: int64):
        self.pages_read += count
        if self.pages_read > self.pages:
            self.pages_read = self.pages

def main():
    mut dune = Book(title="Dune", pages=412)
    dune.read(103)
    print(f"{dune.title}: {dune.percent_read():.1f}%")
    dune.read(1000)
    print(dune.is_finished())
```

<span class="caption">Listing 5-11: `Book` with its first methods</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
Dune: 25.0%
true
```

Each method's body is the free function's body with `book` renamed to
`self`. What changed is the first parameter. `percent_read(book: Book)`
became `percent_read(self)`, and `read_pages(book: mut Book, count: int64)`
became `read(mut self, count: int64)`. The receiver has no type annotation,
because it is always the class the method is declared in.

Calls changed too. `dune.read(103)` passes `dune` as the receiver and `103`
as `count`. As with parameters, the call site doesn't say what kind of
access the method gets. That comes from the receiver in the declaration.

Methods buy us two things over free functions. Everything you can do with a
`Book` now lives in one place, so a reader looking for it knows where to
look. And the names get shorter: `read` is enough, because `dune.read(...)`
already says what is being read.

## The three receivers

The receiver works exactly like the parameter forms from Chapter 4. Bare
`self` is shared access, `mut self` is mutable access, and `own self` takes
ownership.

### `self` reads

`percent_read` and `is_finished` only look at the fields, so they take bare
`self`. The caller keeps its book, and the method can't change it. Try to
write a mutating method with bare `self` and the compiler points at the
first write:

```aura check-fail:AU3003
class Book:
    title: str
    pages: int64
    pages_read: int64 = 0

    def read(self, count: int64):
        self.pages_read += count
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU3003]: cannot mutate through shared receiver `self`; declare the receiver as `mut self`
 --> src/main.au:7:9
  |
7 |         self.pages_read += count
  |         ^
  = related src/main.au:6:5: shared receiver `self` is declared here
  = help: declare the receiver as `mut self` when the method mutates through `self`
```

Python has no equivalent check. Any method can assign to any attribute of
`self`, so "does this method change the object?" is a question you answer by
reading the body. In Aura it's answered by the signature. That turns out to
matter most when you're reading someone else's class: every method with bare
`self` is safe to call without wondering what it does to your instance.

### `mut self` changes

`read` takes `mut self`, so it can assign to the fields. The instance must be
in a mutable place to call it, which is why `main` declared `mut dune`. As
we saw with `Scoreboard` in Chapter 4, calling a `mut self` method on an
immutable binding fails with "method `read` requires a mutable receiver".

### `own self` consumes

A method that takes `own self` takes the whole instance. After the call, the
caller doesn't have it anymore. That's the right shape for a method that
turns an instance into something else. Here is the simplest example, a
method that gives up the book and keeps only its title:

```aura check-fail:AU3001
class Book:
    title: str
    pages: int64

    def into_title(own self) -> str:
        return self.title

def main():
    dune = Book(title="Dune", pages=412)
    title = dune.into_title()
    print(title)
    print(dune.pages)
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU3001]: use of moved value `dune`
 --> src/main.au:12:11
   |
12 |     print(dune.pages)
   |           ^
  = related src/main.au:10:13: value moved here
  = help: pass shared access when ownership is not needed, or transfer this non-cloneable value only once
```

`into_title` can return `self.title` without cloning it because it owns
`self`: moving a field out of a value you own is allowed. A bare-`self`
method trying the same thing would get the "cannot move non-copy field out
of borrowed value" error from the previous section. The `into_` prefix is a
common convention for consuming methods, so a reader knows to expect the
instance to be gone afterwards.

A more realistic use is building a new value from an old one. When we
finish a book, we might want to turn it into a review that owns the book and
a rating:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
copy class Rating:
    stars: int64

class Book:
    title: str
    pages: int64
    pages_read: int64 = 0

    def into_review(own self, stars: int64) -> Review:
        return Review(book=self, rating=Rating(stars=stars))

class Review:
    book: Book
    rating: Rating

impl Display for Book:
    def display(self) -> str:
        return f"{self.title} ({self.pages_read}/{self.pages})"

def main():
    dune = Book(title="Dune", pages=412, pages_read=412)
    print(dune)
    review = dune.into_review(5)
    print(f"{review.book}: {review.rating.stars} stars")
```

<span class="caption">Listing 5-12: A consuming method that moves the book into a review</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
Dune (412/412)
Dune (412/412): 5 stars
```

`into_review` moves `self` into the new `Review`, so after the call the book
lives inside `review`, and `review.book` is how we reach it. There is still
one book, with one owner. (The `impl Display` block controls how a `Book`
prints. We'll come to it at the end of this section.)

### Choosing a receiver

Choose a receiver the same way you choose a parameter's access: the weakest
one that does the job. Start with `self`. Use `mut self` when the method
changes fields. Use `own self` only when the method keeps or dismantles the
instance.

One mistake is worth knowing about, because it looks reasonable to Python
eyes. Writing the receiver with a type annotation, as in `self: Book`, does
not make a receiver:

```aura check-fail:AU3004
class Book:
    title: str
    pages: int64

    def describe(self: Book) -> str:
        return self.title
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU3004]: `self: Type` is not a method receiver; use `self` for shared access, `own self` to consume, or `mut self` to mutate
 --> src/main.au:5:18
  |
5 |     def describe(self: Book) -> str:
  |                  ^
```

## Associated functions

A function in a class body with no receiver at all is an *associated
function*. You call it on the class, not on an instance. Associated
functions are how Aura does what Python does with `@classmethod` and
alternative constructors:

```aura
class Book:
    title: str
    pages: int64
    pages_read: int64 = 0

    def unread(title: own str, pages: int64) -> Book:
        return Book(title=title, pages=pages)

    def started(title: own str, pages: int64, pages_read: int64) -> Book:
        return Book(title=title, pages=pages, pages_read=pages_read)

def main():
    emma = Book.unread("Emma", 474)
    dune = Book.started("Dune", 412, 103)
    print(emma.pages_read)
    print(dune.pages_read)
```

A class can have as many of these as it needs, each with a name that says
what kind of instance it builds. Since an initializer can't fail, an
associated function is also the place for construction that can: one that
returns a `Result` and builds the instance only when its input is valid.
[Chapter 9](/book/ch09-00-error-handling) shows that pattern.

## Properties

Some values are computed from the fields but read like a field. Python marks
those with `@property`, and so does Aura:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
class Book:
    title: str
    pages: int64
    pages_read: int64 = 0

    def started(title: own str, pages: int64, pages_read: int64) -> Book:
        return Book(title=title, pages=pages, pages_read=pages_read)

    @property
    def pages_left(self) -> int64:
        return self.pages - self.pages_read

def main():
    dune = Book.started("Dune", 412, 103)
    print(f"{dune.pages_left} pages to go in {dune.title}")
```

<span class="caption">Listing 5-13: A read-only computed property</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
309 pages to go in Dune
```

`dune.pages_left` has no parentheses. Each read calls the getter once and
gives back a fresh value. A property getter must take bare `self` and no
other parameters, since reading a property shouldn't change anything.

A property is read-only. Python lets you add a setter with
`@pages_left.setter`. Aura has no setters, and assigning to a property is an
error:

```aura check-fail:AU2045
class Book:
    title: str
    pages: int64
    pages_read: int64 = 0

    @property
    def pages_left(self) -> int64:
        return self.pages - self.pages_read

def main():
    mut dune = Book(title="Dune", pages=412)
    dune.pages_left = 0
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2045]: property `pages_left` is read-only and cannot be assigned
 --> src/main.au:12:5
   |
12 |     dune.pages_left = 0
   |     ^
  = help: a property computes a fresh value on each read; bind it to a local to change the copy
```

The reasoning is the same as for receivers. Assignment to a field is visibly
a change to the instance, and the compiler checks that the instance is
mutable. A setter would hide an arbitrary method call behind something that
looks like a field write. If changing a value takes logic, write a `mut self`
method with a name that says what it does, such as `read`.

## Choosing how an instance prints

So far, printing a `Book` has shown the default rendering:
`Book(pages=412, pages_read=0, title=Dune)`. Python lets a class choose its
own text with `__str__`. Aura uses an `impl Display` block, which you saw in
Listing 5-12:

```aura fragment
impl Display for Book:
    def display(self) -> str:
        return f"{self.title} ({self.pages_read}/{self.pages})"
```

The block sits next to the class, not inside it, and defines one method,
`display`, which takes bare `self` and returns a `str`. Once it exists,
`print(book)`, `str(book)`, and `f"{book}"` all use it, and so does printing
a list that contains books. `Display` is a *trait*, a named set of methods a
type can promise to provide. Traits get a chapter of their own,
[Chapter 10](/book/ch10-00-generics-traits-conversions), but this one is
useful enough to reach for now.

## There is no inheritance

If you try to write a subclass the Python way, the parser stops at the
parenthesis:

```aura check-fail:AU1101
class Animal:
    name: str

class Dog(Animal):
    breed: str
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU1101]: expected Colon, found LParen
 --> src/main.au:4:10
  |
4 | class Dog(Animal):
  |          ^
```

Aura classes cannot inherit from other classes. This is a deliberate choice.
Inheritance mixes two things: sharing data (a `Dog` has every field an
`Animal` has) and sharing behavior (a `Dog` can be used where an `Animal` is
expected). In Python both come from one line, along with method resolution
order, `super()` chains, and subclasses that override a method the base class
relied on.

Aura gives you the two pieces separately. To share data, put one class inside
another as a field, as `Review` holds a `Book` in Listing 5-12. To share
behavior, declare a trait and implement it for each type that should have
it, as `Display` does for printing. Composition makes ownership plain: a
`Review` owns its `Book`, and you reach it through `review.book`. Traits let
a function accept any type that provides certain methods without those types
being related.

## Putting it together

Here is the reading tracker rewritten with methods, a factory, a property,
and a `Display` implementation that does the report formatting:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
class Book:
    title: str
    pages: int64
    pages_read: int64 = 0

    def unread(title: own str, pages: int64) -> Book:
        return Book(title=title, pages=pages)

    def percent_read(self) -> float64:
        return self.pages_read.to_float() / self.pages.to_float() * 100.0

    def is_finished(self) -> bool:
        return self.pages_read == self.pages

    @property
    def pages_left(self) -> int64:
        return self.pages - self.pages_read

    def read(mut self, count: int64):
        self.pages_read += count
        if self.pages_read > self.pages:
            self.pages_read = self.pages

impl Display for Book:
    def display(self) -> str:
        return f"{self.title:<10} {self.percent_read():>5.1f}%"

def main():
    mut shelf = [
        Book(title="Dune", pages=412, pages_read=103),
        Book.unread("Emma", 474),
        Book(title="Beloved", pages=324, pages_read=300),
    ]
    shelf[1].read(50)
    shelf[2].read(50)
    mut total_left: int64 = 0
    for book in shelf:
        print(book)
        total_left += book.pages_left
    print(f"{total_left} pages to go")
    for book in shelf:
        if book.is_finished():
            print(f"Finished: {book.title}")
```

<span class="caption">Listing 5-14: The reading tracker built around a `Book` class</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
Dune        25.0%
Emma        10.5%
Beloved    100.0%
733 pages to go
Finished: Beloved
```

`shelf[1].read(50)` calls a `mut self` method on a list element, and the
change lands in the list, as it did when we passed `shelf[1]` to
`read_pages`. The second loop no longer builds a list of finished titles, so
it no longer needs to clone them: it reads each title in place. The
[Manual](/manual/classes) has the full rules for methods, properties, and
initializers.

## Summary

Classes let you give a group of values a name and a fixed shape, and the
compiler checks every construction and field access against it. You can
build instances by field name or position, give fields defaults that are
fresh for every instance, compute fields in `__init__`, and add associated
functions for other ways of building one. Methods put a type's behavior next
to its data, and their receivers say what each one does to the instance:
`self` reads, `mut self` changes, and `own self` consumes. Properties give
read-only computed values, `impl Display` controls printing, and composition
and traits take the place of inheritance.

Every field of a class is present at once: a book always has a title, a page
count, and a position. Plenty of data isn't like that. A command is either
"add" or "remove", never both, and a lookup either found something or didn't.
In the next chapter we'll model data like that with enums, and take it apart
with `match`.

## Source: docs/book/ch06-00-enums-and-match.md

# Enums and pattern matching

A class describes data where every part is present at once. A book always has
a title, a page count, and a position. A lot of data has a different shape.
A book on your shelf is unread, in progress, or finished: exactly one of the
three, never two. A command typed into our reading tracker is "read some
pages of this book" or "list the shelf" or "quit", and each kind carries
different information. A search finds a result or finds nothing.

Python programs usually model these with strings (`status = "reading"`), with
a class full of attributes that are sometimes `None`, or with a family of
subclasses. Each of those leaves room for values that make no sense, such as
a misspelled status, or a "list" command that somehow has a page count, and
the program finds out only when it runs into one.

Aura's answer is the *enum*: a type whose value is exactly one of a fixed set
of named *variants*, each carrying its own data. Paired with it is `match`,
which takes an enum apart, runs the code for whichever variant is there, and
is checked by the compiler to handle every variant. In this chapter we'll
define enums for a book's status and for the tracker's commands, write
`match` expressions over them (including a small recursive one that
evaluates arithmetic), and then look at `T | None`, the type Aura uses for a
value that might be missing.

By the end you'll be able to model "one of several things" so that the
nonsense cases can't be written down, and handle each case in a way the
compiler checks for completeness. Enums show up everywhere in Aura,
including in its error handling, so the patterns here will come back in
[Chapter 9](/book/ch09-00-error-handling).

## Source: docs/book/ch06-01-defining-an-enum.md

# Defining an enum

Let's give each book in the tracker a status. The quick way is a string
field, `status: str`, holding `"to-read"`, `"reading"`, or `"finished"`. That
works until someone writes `"Reading"` or `"finshed"`. The compiler sees a
`str` either way, and the mistake waits for whatever code compares
`status == "finished"` and quietly gets `false`.

An enum lists the possibilities once, as part of the type:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
enum Status:
    ToRead
    Reading
    Finished

def main():
    status = Status.Reading
    print(status)
    other = status
    print(status == other)
```

<span class="caption">Listing 6-1: An enum with three variants</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
Status.Reading
true
```

The declaration starts with `enum` and the type's name, and the indented
body lists the *variants*, one per line, in `CamelCase`. A `Status` value is
always exactly one of them. You name a variant through its enum, as in
`Status.Reading`, so variants from different enums never collide. Printing a
variant shows that same qualified name.

Now a typo is a compile error. `Status.Finshed` isn't a variant of `Status`,
and the compiler says so on the line where it appears, instead of the
program carrying a bad string around until something trips over it. And as
we'll see in the next section, a `match` over a `Status` has to say what to
do with each of the three variants, so adding a fourth later shows you every
place that needs updating.

Notice also that `other = status` didn't move `status`: we compared the two
afterwards. An enum whose variants carry no data, or only copy values, is a
copy value itself. It is as cheap to duplicate as an integer.

## Variants that carry data

A status is only a label. A command for the tracker needs more. "Read" needs
a book title and a page count, "finish" needs a title, and "list" and "quit"
need nothing at all. Each variant of an enum can carry its own *payload*:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
enum Command:
    Read(title: str, pages: int64)
    Finish(str)
    List
    Quit

def main():
    first = Command.Read(title="Dune", pages=50)
    second = Command.Finish("Dune")
    third = Command.List
    print(first)
    print(second)
    print(third)
```

<span class="caption">Listing 6-2: A `Command` enum whose variants carry different data</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
Command.Read(Dune, 50)
Command.Finish(Dune)
Command.List
```

There are three variant shapes here. `Read` has named payloads, written like
fields, `title: str` and `pages: int64`. `Finish` has one positional payload,
written as only its type. `List` and `Quit` have no payload, and you write
them without parentheses, both in the declaration and when you use them.
A payload variant is built by calling it like a function, with named or
positional arguments to match its declaration. Use names when a variant
has more than one payload: `Command.Read(title="Dune", pages=50)` can't be
misread the way `Command.Read("Dune", 50)` might be once the variant grows a
third field.

The payload slots are owned, the same as constructor fields on a class.
`Command.Finish(title)` moves the string in `title` into the command. And
because `Command` has variants that hold a `str`, the whole enum is an owned
value, so assignment moves it:

```aura check-fail:AU3001
enum Command:
    Read(title: str, pages: int64)
    Finish(str)
    List
    Quit

def main():
    first = Command.Read(title="Dune", pages=50)
    copied = first
    print(first)
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU3001]: use of moved value `first`
 --> src/main.au:10:11
   |
10 |     print(first)
   |           ^
  = related src/main.au:9:14: value moved here
  = help: pass shared access when ownership is not needed, or transfer this non-cloneable value only once
```

The compiler decides this from the declaration, not from the variant you
happen to hold. Even `Command.List`, which carries nothing, is a `Command`,
and `Command` is an owned type because some of its variants own strings.

## Why not a class?

You could try to model commands with a class instead:

```aura
class CommandRecord:
    kind: str
    title: str = ""
    pages: int64 = 0
```

Every `CommandRecord` has all three fields, whatever its `kind`, so the type
happily represents a "quit" command with a title, a "read" command with no
title, and a `kind` of `"raed"`. Every function that receives a
`CommandRecord` has to check for those cases or hope they never happen. This
is the shape of a lot of Python code, where a class has a handful of
attributes that are `None` except in some situations, and the knowledge of
which situations lives in comments.

The enum version can't express any of those. A `Command.Quit` has no title
because the variant has no payload. A `Command.Read` always has both a title
and a page count, because you can't construct it without them. The rule of
thumb is short: use a class when every field is present at once, and an enum
when exactly one of several shapes is present. Often you'll use both, a class
that holds an enum field, such as a `Book` with a `status: Status`.

## Recursive enums

A variant's payload can be the enum itself. That lets an enum describe
nested structure, like an arithmetic expression where each operand is
another expression:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
enum Expr:
    Number(int64)
    Add(Expr, Expr)
    Multiply(Expr, Expr)

def main():
    expr = Expr.Add(Expr.Number(2), Expr.Multiply(Expr.Number(3), Expr.Number(4)))
    print(expr)
```

<span class="caption">Listing 6-3: An enum for arithmetic expressions, with variants that contain other expressions</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
Expr.Add(Expr.Number(2), Expr.Multiply(Expr.Number(3), Expr.Number(4)))
```

This value is the expression `2 + 3 * 4`, already grouped: an `Add` whose
right-hand side is a `Multiply`. Each `Expr` owns its sub-expressions, so the
whole tree has one owner, `expr`, and is released as one when `expr` goes out
of scope. In the next section we'll write a function that walks this tree and
computes 14.

Classes are stricter about recursion. A class field whose type contains the
class itself has to be marked `indirect`, which tells the compiler to store
that field out of line so the class has a fixed size:

```aura check-fail:AU2999
class Chapter:
    title: str
    next: Chapter | None = None
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2999]: recursive field `next` on class `Chapter` requires `indirect`
 --> src/main.au:3:5
  |
3 |     next: Chapter | None = None
  |     ^
```

Writing `next: indirect Chapter | None = None` fixes it. Enum payloads, as
Listing 6-3 shows, can refer to their own enum without the marker. The
[Manual](/manual/enums-and-match) has the complete rules for declaring
enums, including generic enums such as `Result[T, E]`.

An enum on its own only holds data. To do anything with a `Command` or an
`Expr`, we need to find out which variant we have and get at its payload.
That is the job of `match`.

## Source: docs/book/ch06-02-match.md

# The `match` control flow construct

`match` compares a value against a series of *patterns* and runs the code
for the first one that fits. If you've used Python 3.10's `match` statement,
the shape will look familiar. The difference that matters is that Aura checks
your patterns at compile time: a `match` over an enum must handle every
variant, or the program doesn't compile.

Let's start with the `Status` enum from the previous section and turn each
variant into a label:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
enum Status:
    ToRead
    Reading
    Finished

def label(status: Status) -> str:
    match status:
        case Status.ToRead:
            return "on the pile"
        case Status.Reading:
            return "in progress"
        case Status.Finished:
            return "done"

def short(status: Status) -> str:
    return match status:
        case ToRead: "-"
        case Reading: "~"
        case Finished: "x"

def main():
    for status in [Status.ToRead, Status.Reading, Status.Finished]:
        print(f"{short(status)} {label(status)}")
```

<span class="caption">Listing 6-4: Two ways to match on a `Status`</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
- on the pile
~ in progress
x done
```

The value after `match` is the *scrutinee*, here `status`. Each `case` line
holds a pattern followed by a colon. Aura evaluates the scrutinee once, tries
the patterns from top to bottom, and runs the body of the first one that
matches. No other arm runs.

`label` uses the *statement* form. Each arm has an indented block of
statements, the same as an `if` branch, and here each block returns.
`short` uses the *expression* form: `return match status:` makes the whole
`match` produce a value, and each arm is a single expression. When the arms
are short, you can put the expression on the same line as the pattern. Every
arm of a `match` expression has to produce the same type.

`short` also leaves the enum name off its patterns, writing `ToRead` instead
of `Status.ToRead`. That works whenever the compiler already knows the
scrutinee's type, as it does here from the parameter. The qualified form
always works and is clearer when there's any doubt.

## Matches are exhaustive

Let's forget an arm:

```aura check-fail:AU2999
enum Status:
    ToRead
    Reading
    Finished

def label(status: Status) -> str:
    match status:
        case Status.ToRead:
            return "on the pile"
        case Status.Reading:
            return "in progress"
```

<span class="caption">Listing 6-5: A `match` that doesn't cover `Status.Finished`</span>

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2999]: non-exhaustive match over `Status`: missing `Finished`
 --> src/main.au:7:5
  |
7 |     match status:
  |     ^
```

The compiler names the variant we left out. This check is what makes enums
worth the trouble. In Python, an `if`/`elif` chain over status strings that
forgets `"finished"` falls off the end and returns `None`, and a Python
`match` with a missing case does nothing at all. Both fail silently, at run
time, on whichever input you didn't test. In Aura the gap is a compile error.
Better still, when you add a variant to an enum later, every `match` that
doesn't handle it stops compiling, and the error list is a to-do list of the
places that need thought.

When you really do want to treat the remaining variants the same way, end the
`match` with `case _:`. The `_` pattern matches anything and binds nothing:

```aura fragment
match status:
    case Status.Finished:
        print("done")
    case _:
        print("not done yet")
```

Use `_` deliberately. It also matches variants that don't exist yet, so a
`match` that ends in `_` won't warn you when the enum grows.

## Binding payloads

Patterns can do more than name a variant. When a variant carries data, the
pattern can bind that data to names for the arm to use. Here is a function
that describes each `Command`:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
enum Command:
    Read(title: str, pages: int64)
    Finish(str)
    List
    Quit

def describe(command: Command) -> str:
    return match command:
        case Command.Read(title, pages) if pages >= 100:
            f"a long session: {pages} pages of {title}"
        case Command.Read(title, pages):
            f"read {pages} pages of {title}"
        case Command.Finish(title):
            f"finish {title}"
        case Command.List | Command.Quit:
            "no book needed"

def main():
    commands = [
        Command.Read(title="Dune", pages=40),
        Command.Read(title="Emma", pages=120),
        Command.Finish("Beloved"),
        Command.List,
        Command.Quit,
    ]
    for command in commands:
        print(describe(command))
```

<span class="caption">Listing 6-6: Binding payloads, a guard, and an or-pattern</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
read 40 pages of Dune
a long session: 120 pages of Emma
finish Beloved
no book needed
no book needed
```

In `case Command.Read(title, pages):`, the names `title` and `pages` aren't
values to compare against. They're new bindings that receive the payload,
in the order the variant declares it, and they exist only inside that arm.
`Command.Finish(title)` binds the one string a `Finish` carries. The payload
names you use in a pattern don't have to match the names in the declaration,
but matching them keeps the code easy to follow.

Listing 6-6 also shows two more pattern features.

The first arm has a *guard*: `if pages >= 100` after the pattern. The arm
runs only if the pattern matches and the guard is true. If the guard is
false, matching moves on to the next arm, which is why the 40-page command
falls through to the plain `Command.Read` arm. A guard can be any `bool`
expression, and it can use the names the pattern bound.

The last arm joins two patterns with `|`, so it matches either a `List` or a
`Quit`. Each alternative in an or-pattern has to bind the same names, which
here is none.

Guards don't count towards exhaustiveness, because the compiler can't know
in general whether a condition will be true. If we deleted the unguarded
`Command.Read` arm, the compiler would reject the `match`: a `Read` with
fewer than 100 pages would have nowhere to go.

## Matching literal values

A pattern can also be a literal: an integer, a `bool`, a string, or a float.
That makes `match` a natural way to dispatch on words typed by a user:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
def parse_command(line: str) -> str:
    return match line:
        case "list": "List"
        case "quit" | "exit": "Quit"
        case other: f"unknown: {other}"

def main():
    print(parse_command("list"))
    print(parse_command("exit"))
    print(parse_command("dance"))
```

<span class="caption">Listing 6-7: Matching string literals, with a catch-all binding</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
List
Quit
unknown: dance
```

The last arm's pattern is a plain lowercase name, `other`. A name pattern
matches anything and binds the whole scrutinee, so it works like `_` except
that the arm can use the value. Like `_`, it has to be the last arm.

There are infinitely many strings and integers, so a literal `match` can
never list them all. The compiler insists on a catch-all arm, and names the
exact fix:

```aura check-fail:AU2999
def describe(count: int64) -> str:
    match count:
        case 0:
            return "none"
        case 1:
            return "one"
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2999]: `match` over `int64` with literal patterns requires a final `case _:` arm
 --> src/main.au:2:5
  |
2 |     match count:
  |     ^
```

A `bool` is the exception: `case true:` and `case false:` together cover
every value, so no catch-all is needed.

## Matching and ownership

A `match` reads its scrutinee the same way a function with a bare parameter
does: with shared access. The payload bindings are borrowed from the value
being matched, so you can read them but not take them. Let's see what
happens when an arm tries to keep a title:

```aura check-fail:AU3002
enum Command:
    Read(title: str, pages: int64)
    Finish(str)
    List
    Quit

def finished_title(command: Command, done: mut list[str]):
    match command:
        case Command.Finish(title):
            done.append(title)
        case _:
            pass

def main():
    mut done = list[str]()
    finished_title(Command.Finish("Beloved"), done)
    print(done)
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU3002]: cannot move `title` out of a shared match on `command`
 --> src/main.au:10:25
   |
10 |             done.append(title)
   |                         ^
  = related src/main.au:9:29: value is borrowed here
  = help: write `match own command` to consume the scrutinee, or call `.clone()` to consume an independent copy
  = fix: replace src/main.au:10:30-10:30 with `.clone()`
```

`append` takes ownership of what it stores. The `title` binding only borrows
the string inside `command`, which still belongs to whoever owns `command`.
This is the same rule as moving a field out of a borrowed class in
[Chapter 4](/book/ch04-02-shared-and-mutable-access), and the help line gives
the same two fixes. Cloning keeps the command intact. Writing `match own`
consumes the command and hands each arm owned payloads, which needs the
function to own `command` in the first place:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
enum Command:
    Read(title: str, pages: int64)
    Finish(str)
    List
    Quit

def record_finish(command: own Command, done: mut list[str]):
    match own command:
        case Command.Finish(title):
            done.append(title)
        case _:
            pass

def main():
    mut done = list[str]()
    record_finish(Command.Finish("Beloved"), done)
    record_finish(Command.List, done)
    print(done)
```

<span class="caption">Listing 6-8: `match own` gives the arm ownership of the payload</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
[Beloved]
```

`match own` uses up the command, and the string moves from the command into
the list without being copied. There is also `match mut`, which lends the
arms mutable access to the payloads so they can change them in place. The
pattern is the one you've seen for parameters and loops: bare for reading,
`mut` for changing, `own` for taking. Copy payloads, like the `pages` count,
are copied into their bindings in every form, so they never cause these
errors.

## A recursive match

Now we can evaluate the `Expr` tree from the previous section. Each variant
gets an arm, and the arms for `Add` and `Multiply` call the function again on
their sub-expressions:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
enum Expr:
    Number(int64)
    Add(Expr, Expr)
    Multiply(Expr, Expr)

def evaluate(expr: Expr) -> int64:
    return match expr:
        case Expr.Number(value): value
        case Expr.Add(left, right): evaluate(left) + evaluate(right)
        case Expr.Multiply(left, right): evaluate(left) * evaluate(right)

def main():
    expr = Expr.Add(Expr.Number(2), Expr.Multiply(Expr.Number(3), Expr.Number(4)))
    print(evaluate(expr))
    print(expr)
```

<span class="caption">Listing 6-9: Evaluating an expression tree with a recursive `match`</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
14
Expr.Add(Expr.Number(2), Expr.Multiply(Expr.Number(3), Expr.Number(4)))
```

The structure of `evaluate` follows the structure of `Expr` exactly: one arm
per variant, and a recursive call wherever the variant contains another
`Expr`. Because `evaluate` takes shared access and `match` borrows, `left`
and `right` are borrowed sub-trees, and nothing is copied or consumed as the
function walks down. `main` can still print `expr` afterwards. If someone adds
a `Subtract` variant to `Expr`, `evaluate` stops compiling until it learns
what to do with one.

Patterns can nest, too: `case Expr.Add(Expr.Number(0), right):` would match
only additions whose left operand is the number zero. Aura also has patterns
for tuples, lists, and class fields. The
[Manual](/manual/enums-and-match) describes them all, along with the precise
coverage rules.
