We have one more kind of "one of several things" to look at, and it's the
most common of all: a value that might not be there.

## Source: docs/book/ch06-03-optional-values.md

# `T | None` and concise matching

Some functions don't always have an answer. Searching a shelf for a title
might find it or might not. Stripping a prefix from a string only works if
the prefix is there. In Python, such a function returns `None` when it has
nothing to give, and the caller is supposed to check. When the caller
forgets, the program carries on with a `None` until something tries to use
it, and then fails with a `TypeError` or `AttributeError` somewhere else.
Tony Hoare, who introduced null references in 1965, later called them his
"billion-dollar mistake", and this is the reason.

Aura keeps `None`, but it puts the possibility in the type. A function that
might not return a title has the return type `str | None`, read "a `str` or
`None`". The `|` makes a *union* type, and a union with `None` is how Aura
spells an optional value. You can't use a `str | None` as a `str` until you've
checked which one it is, and the compiler makes sure you do.

## A function that might find nothing

Here is a search over a list of titles that returns the position of a match,
or `None` if there isn't one:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
def find(titles: list[str], wanted: str) -> int64 | None:
    mut index: int64 = 0
    for title in titles:
        if title == wanted:
            return index
        index += 1
    return None

def main():
    titles = ["Dune", "Emma", "Beloved"]
    print(find(titles, "Emma"))
    print(find(titles, "Ulysses"))
```

<span class="caption">Listing 6-10: A search that returns `int64 | None`</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
1
None
```

Both `return index` and `return None` are allowed, because each one is a
member of the declared return type. You don't wrap the integer in anything:
an `int64` is already an `int64 | None`.

If you know Python's type hints, this is the same idea as
`Optional[int]`, which Python also lets you write as `int | None`. The
difference is that Python's hints are advice for tools like mypy, and the
interpreter ignores them. In Aura the type is checked every time you build.

## Using an optional value

Let's try to use the result as if it were a number:

```aura check-fail:AU2003
def find(titles: list[str], wanted: str) -> int64 | None:
    mut index: int64 = 0
    for title in titles:
        if title == wanted:
            return index
        index += 1
    return None

def main():
    titles = ["Dune", "Emma", "Beloved"]
    position = find(titles, "Emma")
    print(position + 1)
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2003]: operator `+` is not supported for union `int64 | None`: unions have no ordering or arithmetic
 --> src/main.au:12:11
   |
12 |     print(position + 1)
   |           ^
  = help: select one member with a type pattern before comparing or computing
```

`position` has the type `int64 | None`, and there is no sensible meaning for
`None + 1`. So the compiler refuses to add anything to the union as a whole.
The same thing happens when you pass an optional value to a function that
wants the plain type. `strip_prefix` on a string returns `str | None`, since
the prefix may not be there:

```aura check-fail:AU2002
def shout(text: str) -> str:
    return text.to_upper()

def main():
    rest = "finish Dune".strip_prefix("finish ")
    print(shout(rest))
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2002]: argument type mismatch for function `shout`: expected `str`, found `str | None`
 --> src/main.au:6:17
  |
6 |     print(shout(rest))
  |                 ^
```

We know the prefix is there in this case, but the compiler checks types, not
the contents of string literals. In real code the string would come from a
user, and the check would be the only thing standing between a typo and a
crash.

The help line in the first error says to "select one member". There are two
ways to do that.

## Checking with `is None`

The most direct is an `if` that tests for `None`. Inside each branch, the
compiler knows which member it has:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
def find(titles: list[str], wanted: str) -> int64 | None:
    mut index: int64 = 0
    for title in titles:
        if title == wanted:
            return index
        index += 1
    return None

def report(titles: list[str], wanted: str):
    position = find(titles, wanted)
    if position is None:
        print(f"{wanted} is not on the shelf")
        return
    print(f"{wanted} is book number {position + 1}")

def main():
    titles = ["Dune", "Emma", "Beloved"]
    report(titles, "Emma")
    report(titles, "Ulysses")
    match find(titles, "Beloved"):
        case int64 as index:
            print(f"found at index {index}")
        case None:
            print("missing")
```

<span class="caption">Listing 6-11: Narrowing with `is None`, and matching on a union member</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
Emma is book number 2
Ulysses is not on the shelf
found at index 2
```

After `if position is None: ... return`, the rest of `report` can only run
when `position` holds an integer, and the compiler knows it. From that line
on, `position` has the type `int64`, so `position + 1` is fine. This is
called *narrowing*. It works with `is None` and `is not None`, inside the
`if` and `else` branches, after an early `return` (or `continue` or `break`
in a loop), and through `and`, `or`, and `not`.

Narrowing applies to a binding you can name: a local, a parameter, or a field
of one of those. A function call like `find(titles, wanted)` gives a new
value every time it runs, so to narrow its result, bind it to a name first,
as `report` does.

Narrowing lasts only as long as the compiler can be sure of it. Assign a new
value to the binding and the fact goes away, even inside the branch that
tested it:

```aura check-fail:AU2003
def main():
    mut position: int64 | None = 3
    if position is not None:
        position = None
        print(position + 1)
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2003]: operator `+` is not supported for union `int64 | None`: unions have no ordering or arithmetic
 --> src/main.au:5:15
  |
5 |         print(position + 1)
  |               ^
  = help: select one member with a type pattern before comparing or computing
```

Only `is None` and `is not None` narrow. `position == None` is an ordinary
comparison that returns a `bool` and tells the compiler nothing.

## Matching on a union member

The `match` at the end of Listing 6-11 is the other way. A union is matched
by the type of its members: `case int64 as index:` matches when the value is
an integer and binds it as `index`, and `case None:` matches the absence. As
with enums, the arms must cover every member, so a `match` over
`int64 | None` without a `None` arm doesn't compile.

Which should you use? `is None` with an early return reads best when the
missing case is a short detour, like printing a message and stopping, and the
rest of the function works on the value. `match` reads best when both cases
do real work, or when the union has more than two members, as in
`int64 | str | None`.

## No `Option`, no `T?`

If you've used Rust, Swift, or Kotlin, you might reach for `Option[str]` or
`str?`. Neither exists in Aura:

```aura check-fail:AU2001
def main():
    nickname: Option[str] = None
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2001]: unknown type `Option`
 --> src/main.au:2:15
  |
2 |     nickname: Option[str] = None
  |               ^
```

```aura check-fail:AU1101
def main():
    nickname: str? = None
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU1101]: expected Newline
 --> src/main.au:2:13
  |
2 |     nickname: str? = None
  |             ^
```

Aura uses the union because it says exactly what the value can be, in the
words a Python programmer already uses, and because it needs no wrapping: a
`str` is a valid `str | None` as it stands, with no `Some(...)` around it.

There is one place where Aura does use an enum for "maybe missing". Looking
up a position in a list with `titles.get(5)` returns `Lookup[str]`, with the
variants `Lookup.Found(value)` and `Lookup.Missing`. That keeps "there is no
entry" separate from "the entry is `None`" in a collection that stores
optional values. We'll meet `Lookup` properly in
[Chapter 8](/book/ch08-00-collections).

## Putting it together

Let's finish the chapter by parsing commands for the reading tracker. The
parser takes a line of text and returns a `Command`, or `None` if it can't
make sense of the line. The main loop then uses everything from this
chapter: narrowing to skip lines that didn't parse, a `match` over the
command's variants, and a `match` over the result of `find`:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
enum Command:
    Finish(str)
    List
    Quit

def find(titles: list[str], wanted: str) -> int64 | None:
    mut index: int64 = 0
    for title in titles:
        if title == wanted:
            return index
        index += 1
    return None

def parse_command(line: str) -> Command | None:
    words = line.trim()
    match words:
        case "list":
            return Command.List
        case "quit":
            return Command.Quit
        case _:
            pass
    title = words.strip_prefix("finish ")
    if title is not None:
        return Command.Finish(title)
    return None

def main():
    titles = ["Dune", "Emma", "Beloved"]
    for line in ["list", "finish Emma", "finish Ulysses", "dance", " quit "]:
        command = parse_command(line)
        if command is None:
            print(f"I don't understand '{line}'")
            continue
        match command:
            case Command.Finish(title):
                match find(titles, title):
                    case int64 as index:
                        print(f"finished book {index + 1}: {title}")
                    case None:
                        print(f"{title} is not on the shelf")
            case Command.List:
                print(titles)
            case Command.Quit:
                print("bye")
```

<span class="caption">Listing 6-12: Parsing and running tracker commands</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
[Dune, Emma, Beloved]
finished book 2: Emma
Ulysses is not on the shelf
I don't understand 'dance'
bye
```

`parse_command` handles the one-word commands with a literal `match`, and
the `case _: pass` arm lets every other line fall through to the code after
it. `strip_prefix("finish ")` returns the rest of the line when it starts
with `finish `, and `None` otherwise. Inside the `if title is not None`
branch, `title` is a `str`, and because it is an owned local, it can move
into `Command.Finish`.

In `main`, `if command is None: ... continue` narrows `command` to a plain
`Command` for the rest of the loop body, so the `match` that follows only
needs arms for the three variants. Each place where a value might be
missing is visible in a type, and each one is handled before the value is
used. The [Manual](/manual/enums-and-match) has the full narrowing and union
matching rules.

## Summary

Enums let you say that a value is exactly one of several shapes, each with
its own data, so that combinations that make no sense can't be built. `match`
takes them apart: it binds payloads to names, tests literals, refines arms
with guards, and combines patterns with `|`, and the compiler checks that
every variant is handled. Like function parameters, a `match` borrows by
default, with `match own` and `match mut` when an arm needs to take or change
the payload. For values that might be missing, `T | None` puts the
possibility in the type, and `is None` or a type pattern selects the member
before you can use it.

Our programs are getting long enough to want more than one file. In the next
chapter we'll split code into modules, decide what each module exposes, and
organize a growing program into a package.

## Source: docs/book/ch07-00-modules-and-packages.md

# Managing growing programs with modules and packages

Every program we have written so far fits in one file. That works for a
while, and then it doesn't. The file gets long enough that you scroll past
the class definitions to find `main`. Two unrelated helpers both want to be
called `format`. A function you wrote for one program would be handy in the
next one, and the only way to share it is to copy and paste. Python solves
these problems with modules, packages, and `pip`, and Aura solves them with
the same three ideas, held to stricter rules.

In Aura a *module* is one `.au` file. A file decides which of its names other
files may use by marking them `public`; everything else stays private, and
the compiler enforces that. A *package* is a directory with an `Aura.toml`
manifest and a `src/` folder of modules. Packages can depend on other
packages, from a path on your disk or from a git repository, and a
*workspace* lets several packages live side by side in one repository with a
single lockfile.

We'll learn all of this on one small program. It starts as a single file that
tracks a reading list, and over the next three sections we split it into
modules, decide which parts of it other code is allowed to touch, and finally
pull a reusable piece out into its own package that the reading list depends
on. By the end of the chapter you'll be able to lay out a multi-file Aura
project, read the compiler's import and visibility errors, and manage
dependencies with `Aura.toml` and `Aura.lock`.

## Source: docs/book/ch07-01-modules-and-imports.md

# Modules and imports

Our program for this chapter keeps track of a reading list: which books are
on it, how many pages each has, and how far through the list we are. Let's
start a fresh package for it:

```console
$ aura new shelf
created `shelf`
```

`aura new` gives us the layout you saw in
[Chapter 1](/book/ch01-00-getting-started):

```text
shelf
├── .gitignore
├── Aura.toml
├── src
│   └── main.au
└── tests
    └── smoke.au
```

We'll come back to `Aura.toml` in the [last section of this
chapter](/book/ch07-03-packages-and-workspaces). For now, the only thing that
matters is that `src/` is where our modules live. Replace the contents of
`src/main.au` with Listing 7-1.

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
class Book:
    title: str
    author: str
    pages: int64
    read: bool

def pages_left(books: list[Book]) -> int64:
    mut total: int64 = 0
    for book in books:
        if not book.read:
            total += book.pages
    return total

def main() -> int32:
    books = [
        Book(title="Dune", author="Frank Herbert", pages=412, read=true),
        Book(title="Kindred", author="Octavia Butler", pages=264, read=false),
        Book(title="Piranesi", author="Susanna Clarke", pages=272, read=false),
    ]
    print(f"{books.len()} books, {pages_left(books)} pages to go")
    return 0
```

<span class="caption">Listing 7-1: The whole reading list in one file</span>

```console
$ cd shelf
$ aura run src/main.au
3 books, 536 pages to go
```

Nothing here is new. A `Book` class, a function that adds up the pages we
haven't read yet, and a `main` that builds a list and prints a line. But you
can already see where this is heading. The class and its helpers are the part
of the program that knows what a book *is*, and `main` is the part that
decides what to *do* with books today. As the program grows, those two parts
will grow at different speeds, and we'd like them in different files.

## Moving code into a module

Let's move `Book` and `pages_left` into a new file, `src/books.au`, exactly as
they are:

*Filename: src/books.au*

```aura
class Book:
    title: str
    author: str
    pages: int64
    read: bool

def pages_left(books: list[Book]) -> int64:
    mut total: int64 = 0
    for book in books:
        if not book.read:
            total += book.pages
    return total
```

<span class="caption">Listing 7-2: `Book` and `pages_left` in their own file</span>

That file is now a module named `books`. Aura doesn't need any declaration to
make it one: one `.au` file is one module, and its name comes from its path
under `src/`, without the `.au`. So `src/books.au` is the module `books`, and
`src/main.au` is the module `main`.

Code in `main` can't see what's in `books` until it asks for it. We ask with
an `import` statement at the top of the file, and then reach the module's
contents through the module's name, the way you would in Python:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura fragment
import books

def main() -> int32:
    books = [
        books.Book(title="Dune", author="Frank Herbert", pages=412, read=true),
        books.Book(title="Kindred", author="Octavia Butler", pages=264, read=false),
        books.Book(title="Piranesi", author="Susanna Clarke", pages=272, read=false),
    ]
    print(f"{books.len()} books, {books.pages_left(books)} pages to go")
    return 0
```

<span class="caption">Listing 7-3: Importing the `books` module (this won't compile yet)</span>

The caption gives it away. Let's see what the compiler thinks:

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU2001]: module `books` has no callable member `Book`
 --> src/main.au:5:15
  |
5 |         books.Book(title="Dune", author="Frank Herbert", pages=412, read=true),
  |               ^
```

The import itself worked: the compiler found `src/books.au` and knows there is
a module called `books`. What it can't find is anything called `Book` that
`main` is allowed to call, even though the class is right there in the
file.

The reason is that in Aura, everything at the top of a module is private
unless you say otherwise. A private name can be used anywhere inside the file that declares
it, and nowhere else. From `main`'s point of view, a private `Book` and a
`Book` that doesn't exist look the same, which is why the message reads the
way it does. To let other modules use a name, put `public` in front of it.
Let's do that for the class and the function:

*Filename: src/books.au*

```aura fragment
public class Book:
    title: str
    ...

public def pages_left(books: list[Book]) -> int64:
    ...
```

and run again:

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU2999]: field `title` is private on `Book`
 --> src/main.au:5:20
  |
5 |         books.Book(title="Dune", author="Frank Herbert", pages=412, read=true),
  |                    ^
```

Progress. `main` can see the class now, but not its fields. Visibility in
Aura is decided name by name, and a class's fields and methods each have
their own. Marking a class `public` lets other modules name the type; it
doesn't hand them its insides. Because `main` builds books with keyword
arguments, it needs to set every field, so every field has to be public. We'll
question that choice in the [next section](/book/ch07-02-visibility). For now,
mark them all:

*Filename: src/books.au*

```aura
public class Book:
    public title: str
    public author: str
    public pages: int64
    public read: bool

public def pages_left(books: list[Book]) -> int64:
    mut total: int64 = 0
    for book in books:
        if not book.read:
            total += book.pages
    return total
```

<span class="caption">Listing 7-4: Making the class, its fields, and the function public</span>

One more try:

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU3003]: cannot assign to immutable binding `books`; declare it with `mut` to rebind it
 --> src/main.au:4:5
  |
4 |     books = [
  |     ^
```

This one is a surprise if you're coming from Python, so let's slow down. Look
at what the error points to: line 4, `books = [`. That line was fine in
Listing 7-1. What changed is the `import books` at the top of the file. An
import puts a name into the module's namespace, the same namespace that holds
its functions and classes. Inside `main`, the name `books` already exists, so
`books = [...]` isn't creating a new local binding at all. It's an attempt to
assign to the existing name, and that name is an imported module, which can't
be reassigned. The `mut` hint is the compiler's standard advice for assigning
to an existing binding; it doesn't help here.

Python would let the local list hide the module for the rest of the function,
and the next line, `books.pages_left(books)`, would then fail at run time
because a list has no `pages_left`. Aura won't let one spelling mean two
different things inside a function, so it stops us at the assignment. The fix
is a better name for the list:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura fragment
import books

def main() -> int32:
    reading_list = [
        books.Book(title="Dune", author="Frank Herbert", pages=412, read=true),
        books.Book(title="Kindred", author="Octavia Butler", pages=264, read=false),
        books.Book(title="Piranesi", author="Susanna Clarke", pages=272, read=false),
    ]
    left = books.pages_left(reading_list)
    print(f"{reading_list.len()} books, {left} pages to go")
    return 0
```

<span class="caption">Listing 7-5: `main` using the `books` module</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
3 books, 536 pages to go
```

The same output as before, from two files. Notice that we still pass only
`src/main.au` to `aura run`. The compiler starts from the file you name, finds
the `Aura.toml` above it, treats the `src/` directory beside that manifest as
the *source root*, and loads whatever the imports ask for. You never list the
other files anywhere.

## How paths map to modules

Let's add a second module, one that draws a text progress bar. We'll put it
one level down, in a `report` directory, because we expect more reporting
code to join it later:

*Filename: src/report/progress.au*

```aura
public def progress_bar(done: int64, total: int64) -> str:
    width: int64 = 20
    filled = done * width // total
    return "[" + "#".repeat(filled) + "-".repeat(width - filled) + "]"
```

<span class="caption">Listing 7-6: A progress bar module in a subdirectory</span>

We'll also add a `total_pages` function to `src/books.au`, so `main` can work
out how much we've read:

*Filename: src/books.au*

```aura fragment
public def total_pages(books: list[Book]) -> int64:
    mut total: int64 = 0
    for book in books:
        total += book.pages
    return total
```

The project now looks like this:

```text
shelf
├── Aura.lock
├── Aura.toml
├── src
│   ├── books.au
│   ├── main.au
│   └── report
│       └── progress.au
└── tests
    └── smoke.au
```

(The `Aura.lock` file appeared the first time we ran the program. It records
how the compiler resolved our package, and we'll read it in [section
7.3](/book/ch07-03-packages-and-workspaces).)

The module name for `src/report/progress.au` is its path under `src/` with
dots in place of slashes: `report.progress`. You might try importing the
directory, the way a Python package with an `__init__.py` lets you:

```aura fragment
import books
import report
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU2999]: cannot resolve module `report` at `src/report.au`
 --> src/main.au:2:1
  |
2 | import report
  | ^
```

The message tells us exactly where the compiler looked: for `import report`
it wanted a file called `src/report.au`. A directory on its own is not a
module in Aura, and there is no `__init__` file. Every import names a file:

```aura fragment
import books
import report.progress

def main() -> int32:
    reading_list = [
        books.Book(title="Dune", author="Frank Herbert", pages=412, read=true),
        books.Book(title="Kindred", author="Octavia Butler", pages=264, read=false),
        books.Book(title="Piranesi", author="Susanna Clarke", pages=272, read=false),
    ]
    total = books.total_pages(reading_list)
    done = total - books.pages_left(reading_list)
    print(report.progress.progress_bar(done, total))
    return 0
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
[########------------]
```

That works, but `report.progress.progress_bar(done, total)` is a mouthful.
An import of a dotted path binds its *first* component, `report`, and you
spell out the rest every time you use something from it. That's useful when
the full path helps the reader, and tedious when it doesn't.

## Importing names directly

When one or two names from a module carry most of the weight in a file,
import them directly with `from ... import ...`:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura fragment
import books
from report.progress import progress_bar

def main() -> int32:
    reading_list = [
        books.Book(title="Dune", author="Frank Herbert", pages=412, read=true),
        books.Book(title="Kindred", author="Octavia Butler", pages=264, read=false),
        books.Book(title="Piranesi", author="Susanna Clarke", pages=272, read=false),
    ]
    total = books.total_pages(reading_list)
    done = total - books.pages_left(reading_list)
    print(f"{progress_bar(done, total)} {done}/{total} pages")
    return 0
```

<span class="caption">Listing 7-7: Mixing a module import and a direct import</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
[########------------] 412/948 pages
```

A from-import binds only the names you list. After this line `progress_bar`
is a name in `main`, but `report` is not, so `report.progress.progress_bar`
would no longer resolve. You can import any public function, class, enum,
trait, or module constant this way.

Listing 7-7 uses both styles on purpose. `books.Book`
and `books.total_pages` read well with their prefix: it tells the reader
which part of the program a name belongs to, and keeps `Book` from looking
like something `main` defined. `progress_bar` is a single, distinctive name
that `main` uses once, and the prefix would add nothing. A good default is to
keep the module prefix when you use several things from a module and to
import directly when one name is the point.

Each entry of a from-import can take its own spelling with `as`, and a long
list can go in parentheses across several lines, with a trailing comma:

```aura fragment
from books import (
    Book,
    pages_left,
    total_pages as count_pages,
)
```

`as` works on a whole module too. This is handy for long paths:

```aura fragment
import books
import report.progress as progress

def main() -> int32:
    reading_list = [
        books.Book(title="Dune", author="Frank Herbert", pages=412, read=true),
        books.Book(title="Kindred", author="Octavia Butler", pages=264, read=false),
    ]
    total = books.total_pages(reading_list)
    print(progress.progress_bar(412, total))
    print(report.progress.progress_bar(412, total))
    return 0
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU2001]: unknown name `report`
 --> src/main.au:11:11
   |
11 |     print(report.progress.progress_bar(412, total))
   |           ^
```

An aliased module import binds only the alias. `progress.progress_bar` works,
and `report` is unknown, because nothing put it in scope. An alias changes
only how *this* file spells the name. The function is still
`report.progress.progress_bar` everywhere else, with the same type, the same
visibility, and the same documentation.

## One name, one meaning

Imports share a namespace with everything else at the top of a module. That
rule caught us with the `books` list earlier, and it applies to declarations
too. Suppose `main` imports `progress_bar` and then defines its own:

```aura fragment
from report.progress import progress_bar

def progress_bar(done: int64, total: int64) -> str:
    return f"{done} of {total}"
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU2999]: duplicate item `progress_bar` (previously declared as function at 1:8)
 --> src/main.au:3:1
  |
3 | def progress_bar(done: int64, total: int64) -> str:
  | ^
```

The "1:8" in the message is the position of the original declaration inside
`src/report/progress.au`, line 1, column 8, right after `public`; the message
doesn't name that file, so it's worth knowing where to look. Python would
let the second definition replace the imported one without a word. Aura
treats it as a mistake, because a reader who sees `progress_bar` in this file
should be able to tell which function it is. If you really want both, give
one of them another name with `as`.

## An import is not a copy

It's tempting to think of `import` as pasting another file's text into this
one. It isn't, and the difference shows up as soon as two modules define
things with the same name. Let's try defining a second `Book` class in `main`
and handing a list of them to `books.pages_left`:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura fragment
import books

class Book:
    title: str
    author: str
    pages: int64
    read: bool

def main() -> int32:
    mine = [Book(title="Dune", author="Frank Herbert", pages=412, read=false)]
    print(books.pages_left(mine))
    return 0
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU2002]: argument type mismatch for function `pages_left`: expected `books.Book`, found `Book`
 --> src/main.au:11:28
   |
11 |     print(books.pages_left(mine))
   |                            ^
```

The two classes have the same name and the same fields, but they are
different types. Every declaration keeps the identity of the module that
defines it, so the class in `books` is `books.Book` wherever you use it, and
the compiler says so in the message. This is what makes private names
possible at all: the compiler always knows which module a declaration belongs
to, and so it can tell whether the code reaching for it is inside that module
or outside.

## What happens when a module is imported

In Python, importing a module runs it. Every top-level statement executes the
first time something imports the file, which is how modules set up global
state, and also how an innocent `import` can open a network connection or
print to the terminal. Aura doesn't do that. Let's add a stray `print` to the
bottom of `src/report/progress.au`:

*Filename: src/report/progress.au*

```aura
public def progress_bar(done: int64, total: int64) -> str:
    width: int64 = 20
    filled = done * width // total
    return "[" + "#".repeat(filled) + "-".repeat(width - filled) + "]"

print("loading report.progress")
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
[########------------] 412/948 pages
$ aura run src/report/progress.au
loading report.progress
```

Importing the module gave `main` its declarations and nothing else. The
`print` only runs when `progress.au` is itself the program we asked to run.
So you can read an Aura file's import list and know that none of those
imports will do anything at run time. The one thing that does happen before
`main` starts is that module *constants* get their values, which we'll meet
in the next section.

Aura also needs the imports between modules to form a tree with no loops,
so every module can be checked after the modules it depends on. If `books.au` imports
`report.progress` and `report/progress.au` imports `books`, the compiler
refuses the whole program:

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU2999]: cyclic import involving `src/books.au`
 --> src/main.au
```

When you hit this, the usual fix is to move whatever both modules need into
a third module that both of them import.

We now have three modules that can see each other's public names. So far we
made things public whenever the compiler asked, which got the program
running but gave `main` the run of `Book`'s insides. In the next section
we'll go back and decide what each module should really expose.

## Source: docs/book/ch07-02-visibility.md

# Visibility and private names

At the end of the last section, every field of `Book` was public because the
compiler asked us to make it so. That got the program running, but it also
means any module that imports `books` can build a `Book` with any values it
likes and change those values whenever it wants. For a class with four plain
fields that might seem harmless. Let's give `Book` a field where it isn't.

So far a book is either read or not. A reading tracker ought to know how far
into a book we are, so let's replace `read: bool` with a bookmark: the number
of pages we've read. A bookmark only makes sense between zero and the book's
page count. If a module can write `bookmark=9000` into a 412-page book, then
`pages_left` will happily return a negative number, and the bug will show up
far away from the line that caused it. We want `books` to be the only module
that can move a bookmark, so it can keep that promise.

In Python, you'd signal this by naming the field `_bookmark` and hoping
everyone respects the underscore. Aura makes it a rule the compiler checks.

## Private fields

A field without `public` is private. Let's write the new `Book` that way, and
give it a method that moves the bookmark safely:

*Filename: src/books.au*

```aura
public class Book:
    public title: str
    public author: str
    public pages: int64
    bookmark: int64

    public def read_to(mut self, page: int64):
        self.bookmark = max(0, min(page, self.pages))

    public def is_finished(self) -> bool:
        return self.bookmark == self.pages

public def pages_left(books: list[Book]) -> int64:
    mut total: int64 = 0
    for book in books:
        total += book.pages - book.bookmark
    return total

public def total_pages(books: list[Book]) -> int64:
    mut total: int64 = 0
    for book in books:
        total += book.pages
    return total
```

<span class="caption">Listing 7-8: `Book` with a private bookmark (this won't work from `main` yet)</span>

`read_to` clamps whatever page it's given into the range `0` to `pages`, using
the two-argument forms of `min` and `max`. `pages_left` reads
`book.bookmark` directly, and that's fine: it lives in the same module as the
class, and inside its own module a private name is as usable as a public one.
Visibility is about module boundaries, not about classes. There's no
equivalent of a "private to this class" field that a free function in the
same file can't touch.

Now `main` stops passing `read=...` and records progress with `read_to`:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura fragment
import books
from report.progress import progress_bar

def main() -> int32:
    mut reading_list = [
        books.Book(title="Dune", author="Frank Herbert", pages=412),
        books.Book(title="Kindred", author="Octavia Butler", pages=264),
        books.Book(title="Piranesi", author="Susanna Clarke", pages=272),
    ]
    reading_list[0].read_to(412)
    reading_list[1].read_to(100)
    total = books.total_pages(reading_list)
    done = total - books.pages_left(reading_list)
    print(f"{progress_bar(done, total)} {done}/{total} pages")
    return 0
```

<span class="caption">Listing 7-9: `main` moving bookmarks through a method</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU2999]: class constructor `Book` cannot initialize private field `bookmark` from another module
 --> src/main.au:6:15
  |
6 |         books.Book(title="Dune", author="Frank Herbert", pages=412),
  |               ^
```

This is the other side of making a field private. `main` isn't allowed to set
`bookmark`, but the constructor has to give it *some* value, and `main` is the
one calling the constructor. With no default and no permission, there's no
way for this call to produce a complete `Book`.

There are two ways out. One is a public method on `Book` that builds the
object from inside the module, where private fields are reachable; you'll see
that pattern in many libraries. The other, which fits here, is a default
value. A new book starts with the bookmark at page zero, so let's say so:

```aura fragment
    bookmark: int64 = 0
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
[##########----------] 512/948 pages
```

We've read all 412 pages of *Dune* and 100 of *Kindred*, which is 512 of 948.
Let's check that the compiler really keeps `main` away from the bookmark.
First, passing it to the constructor:

```aura fragment
        books.Book(title="Dune", author="Frank Herbert", pages=412, bookmark=412),
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU2999]: field `bookmark` is private on `Book`
 --> src/main.au:6:69
  |
6 |         books.Book(title="Dune", author="Frank Herbert", pages=412, bookmark=412),
  |                                                                     ^
```

and then assigning it directly:

```aura fragment
    reading_list[1].bookmark = 100
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU2999]: field `bookmark` is private on `Book`
 --> src/main.au:11:5
   |
11 |     reading_list[1].bookmark = 100
   |     ^
```

Both are refused with the same message, which names the field and the class.
The only way for `main` to move a bookmark now is `read_to`, so we can try the
case that worried us:

```aura fragment
    reading_list[1].read_to(9000)
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
[##############------] 676/948 pages
```

*Kindred* counts as finished at 264 pages, not 9000, and `pages_left` can't
go negative. The promise "a bookmark stays inside its book" is now kept by
the code in `books.au`, and no amount of code elsewhere can break it.
If we later decide to store the bookmark differently, say as a percentage,
we can change `books.au` alone, because nothing outside it ever saw the field.

Keep in mind that a `public` field is public for writing as well as reading.
`main` could still write `reading_list[1].pages = 50` and shrink a book. If
that ever matters, the same treatment applies: make the field private and
expose a method that reads it.

## Private methods and functions

Methods follow the same rule. Suppose `read_to` grows complicated enough that
we pull the clamping out into its own method:

```aura fragment
    public def read_to(mut self, page: int64):
        self.bookmark = self.clamp(page)

    def clamp(self, page: int64) -> int64:
        return max(0, min(page, self.pages))
```

`clamp` has no `public`, so it's a detail of the `books` module. If `main`
tries to call it, say with `print(reading_list[1].clamp(9000))`, the compiler
refuses:

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU2999]: method `clamp` is private on `Book`
 --> src/main.au:11:27
   |
11 |     print(reading_list[1].clamp(9000))
   |                           ^
```

Top-level functions work the same way. Here is `report.progress` with a
private helper:

*Filename: src/report/progress.au*

```aura
public def progress_bar(done: int64, total: int64) -> str:
    width: int64 = 20
    filled = done * width // total
    return "[" + segment("#", filled) + segment("-", width - filled) + "]"

def segment(mark: str, count: int64) -> str:
    return mark.repeat(count)
```

<span class="caption">Listing 7-10: A private helper beside a public function</span>

If `main` tries to import the helper by name, the compiler tells us exactly
what's wrong:

```aura fragment
from report.progress import progress_bar, segment
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU2999]: item `segment` is private in module `report.progress`
 --> src/main.au:2:43
  |
2 | from report.progress import progress_bar, segment
  |                                           ^
```

Reaching for a private item through the module prefix, as in
`report.progress.segment(...)`, gives the "has no callable member" message we
met in the last section. Both mean the same thing: the name exists, but not
for you.

An alias doesn't get around any of this. `from report.progress import segment
as seg` fails the same way, because an alias renames a name you're already
allowed to use; it doesn't change who is allowed.

## Module constants

The progress bar's width is buried inside the function. Let's give it, and
the heading we print above the bar, a home of their own. A binding at the top
level of a module is a *module constant*:

*Filename: src/settings.au*

```aura
public shelf_name = "Reading list"
public bar_width: int64 = 20
```

<span class="caption">Listing 7-11: Constants in their own module</span>

Constants follow the same visibility rule as everything else, so we mark both
`public`. `report.progress` can now use the shared width:

*Filename: src/report/progress.au*

```aura fragment
import settings

public def progress_bar(done: int64, total: int64) -> str:
    filled = done * settings.bar_width // total
    empty = settings.bar_width - filled
    return "[" + segment("#", filled) + segment("-", empty) + "]"

def segment(mark: str, count: int64) -> str:
    return mark.repeat(count)
```

and `main` imports `settings` too, to print the heading:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura fragment
import books
import settings
from report.progress import progress_bar

def main() -> int32:
    mut reading_list = [
        books.Book(title="Dune", author="Frank Herbert", pages=412),
        books.Book(title="Kindred", author="Octavia Butler", pages=264),
        books.Book(title="Piranesi", author="Susanna Clarke", pages=272),
    ]
    reading_list[0].read_to(412)
    reading_list[1].read_to(100)
    total = books.total_pages(reading_list)
    done = total - books.pages_left(reading_list)
    print(settings.shelf_name)
    print(f"{progress_bar(done, total)} {done}/{total} pages")
    return 0
```

<span class="caption">Listing 7-12: Two modules sharing the `settings` constants</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
Reading list
[##########----------] 512/948 pages
```

Two modules import `settings`, and that's fine. Each module is loaded and
initialized once, however many files import it. The compiler gives every
reachable module's constants their values before `main` starts, dependencies
first, so by the time `progress_bar` runs, `settings.bar_width` is already 20.
Within one module, constants are set in the order they're written, and one
constant can use an earlier one but not a later one:

```aura fragment
public shelf_name = "Reading list"
public bar_width: int64 = full_width - 4
full_width: int64 = 24
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU2001]: module constant `full_width` is used before initialization
 --> src/settings.au:2:27
  |
2 | public bar_width: int64 = full_width - 4
  |                           ^
  = related src/settings.au:3:1: `full_width` is declared here
```

Swap the two lines and it compiles, with `full_width` usable inside
`settings.au` but invisible outside it.

### Constants really are constant

A module constant can't change. That's true from inside its module and from
outside it. Here's `main` trying to widen the bar at run time:

```aura fragment
    settings.bar_width = 30
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU3003]: cannot assign through immutable place `settings.bar_width`
 --> src/main.au:15:5
   |
15 |     settings.bar_width = 30
   |     ^
```

and a module can't declare a mutable top-level binding in the first place:

```aura check-fail:AU3003
mut pages_read: int64 = 0

def main():
    print(pages_read)
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU3003]: module bindings are immutable; `mut` module state is not supported
 --> src/main.au:1:5
  |
1 | mut pages_read: int64 = 0
  |     ^
  = help: put mutable state in a local value owned by `main` or another explicit owner
```

The help line is the whole design in one sentence. Python modules are a
common place to keep global state: a cache, a counter, a configuration
object that gets patched in tests. Every function that touches that state is
quietly coupled to every other one, and once tasks run in parallel (Chapter
15), shared mutable globals become data races. Aura removes the option.
Mutable state lives in a value with an owner, usually created in `main`, and
it's passed to the functions that need it, where their signatures say whether
they read it or change it.

One more consequence follows from constants belonging to their module. A
constant like `shelf_name` is an owned `str` stored in `settings`, and other
modules get shared access to it, never ownership:

```aura fragment
    title = settings.shelf_name
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU3001]: cannot move `settings.shelf_name` out of immutable module storage
 --> src/main.au:15:22
   |
15 |     title = settings.shelf_name
   |                      ^
  = help: keep shared access or construct an independent owned value
```

`title = ...` would make `main` the new owner of the string, which would leave
`settings` without its constant. You can use the constant directly, as
`print(settings.shelf_name)` does, or ask for your own copy with
`settings.shelf_name.clone()`. Copy values such as `bar_width` have no such
issue; reading one gives you a copy.

## Documenting the public surface

Once a module has a deliberate public surface, it's worth saying what that
surface is for. A docstring at the top of the file describes the module, and
one as the first line of each public declaration describes that declaration:

*Filename: src/books.au*

```aura
"""Books on the reading list, and the page counts we track for them."""

public class Book:
    """One book, and how far into it we are."""

    public title: str
    public author: str
    public pages: int64
    bookmark: int64 = 0

    public def read_to(mut self, page: int64):
        """Move the bookmark to `page`, keeping it inside the book."""
        self.bookmark = max(0, min(page, self.pages))

    public def is_finished(self) -> bool:
        """Report whether the bookmark has reached the last page."""
        return self.bookmark == self.pages

public def pages_left(books: list[Book]) -> int64:
    """Count the pages we have not read yet, across every book."""
    mut total: int64 = 0
    for book in books:
        total += book.pages - book.bookmark
    return total

public def total_pages(books: list[Book]) -> int64:
    """Count every page on the list."""
    mut total: int64 = 0
    for book in books:
        total += book.pages
    return total
```

<span class="caption">Listing 7-13: The `books` module with docstrings</span>

Your editor shows these when you hover over `books.Book` in `main`, and
`aura doc` turns them into a reference page:

```console
$ aura doc src/books.au --out api
wrote api/books.md
```

The page lists `Book` with its `title`, `author`, and `pages` fields, its two
public methods, and the two public functions. `bookmark` isn't there. The
documentation shows exactly what other modules can use, which is also exactly
what you're promising to keep working when you change the module.

That last point is the best guide to choosing what to make public. Every
public name is something other code may come to depend on, and changing it
means changing them. A private name can be renamed, rewritten, or deleted
with only one file to check. So start private, and make a name public when
another module has a real reason to use it. For classes, that usually means
public methods that describe behavior, like `read_to` and `is_finished`, and
private fields that hold the representation.

Our modules now have clean boundaries, but they all live inside one package.
The progress bar has nothing to do with books, and it would be useful in
other programs. In the next section we'll move it into a package of its own
and make `shelf` depend on it.

## Source: docs/book/ch07-03-packages-and-workspaces.md

# Packages, dependencies, and workspaces

Modules organize the code inside one program. Packages are how programs
share code with each other. Our `report.progress` module draws a text
progress bar, and nothing about it is specific to books: a download tool, a
test runner, or a backup script could all use it. Copying the file into each
of those projects would work until the day we fix a bug in one copy and
forget the others. A package lets us write it once and depend on it from
anywhere.

We've been inside a package all along. `aura new` made one for us, and the
compiler has been reading its manifest every time we ran the program. Let's
look at that manifest properly before we make a second package.

## The manifest

*Filename: Aura.toml*

```toml
[package]
name = "shelf"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2026"
```

All three fields are required. The `edition` names the version of the
language the package is written against, and today `"2026"` is the only
edition there is; anything else is refused:

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU2999]: manifest `Aura.toml` uses unsupported package edition `2024`; the current Aura compiler supports edition `2026`
 --> src/main.au
```

The `version` is the package's own version number, which must start with a
digit. The `name` is the one with real consequences, because it's more than
a label. When another package depends on this one, the name becomes the first
part of every import path, as in `import shelf.books`. That's why a package
name has to be a valid Aura identifier: letters, digits, and underscores, not
starting with a digit. A hyphenated name, common in other languages, is
refused:

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU2999]: manifest `Aura.toml` has an invalid package name `my-shelf`; package names must match `[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*`
 --> src/main.au
```

If it were allowed, `import my-shelf.books` would parse as `my` minus
`shelf.books`. `aura new` knows this rule and fixes the name for you: `aura new
my-shelf` creates a directory called `my-shelf` whose manifest says `name =
"my_shelf"`.

Two more rules come with every package. The source root is always `src/`,
and the file you hand to `aura run`, `aura check`, or `aura build` has to live
under it (test files under `tests/` are the exception, as you'll see in
[Chapter 11](/book/ch11-00-testing)). There's no setting to move it, which
means every Aura package you open is laid out the same way.

## The lockfile

You've probably noticed `Aura.lock` sitting next to the manifest. Here is
what it says for `shelf` today:

*Filename: Aura.lock*

```toml
version = 1

[[package]]
name = "shelf"
version = "0.1.0"
source = "path"
path = "."
```

The lockfile records how the compiler resolved every package in the program:
which packages there are, and exactly where each one came from. Right now
that's one package, found at `.`. It will become more interesting in a
moment. The compiler writes this file itself when `check`, `run`, or `build`
succeeds, so you never edit it by hand. Commit it to version control along
with the manifest, so that everyone who builds the project resolves the same
code.

## Making a library package

Let's make the progress bar into a package called `gauge`. It goes next to
`shelf`, not inside it, so first we step up a directory. We don't need the
`main.au` that `aura new` creates, because `gauge` is a library: other
programs will import it, and it has no program of its own to run.

```console
$ cd ..
$ aura new gauge
created `gauge`
$ rm gauge/src/main.au
```

Now we move the bar into `gauge/src/bar.au`. In `shelf` it read its width
from `settings`, but a library can't import its users' modules, so the width
becomes a parameter:

*Filename: gauge/src/bar.au*

```aura
"""Text progress bars."""

public def progress_bar(done: int64, total: int64, width: int64) -> str:
    """Draw `done` out of `total` as a bar `width` characters wide."""
    filled = done * width // total
    return "[" + segment("#", filled) + segment("-", width - filled) + "]"

def segment(mark: str, count: int64) -> str:
    return mark.repeat(count)
```

<span class="caption">Listing 7-14: The progress bar as a library module</span>

Back in `shelf`, we delete `src/report/progress.au` and import the bar from
its new home. Imports from another package start with that package's name, so
the path is `gauge.bar`:

*Filename: shelf/src/main.au*

```aura fragment
import books
import settings
from gauge.bar import progress_bar

def main() -> int32:
    mut reading_list = [
        books.Book(title="Dune", author="Frank Herbert", pages=412),
        books.Book(title="Kindred", author="Octavia Butler", pages=264),
        books.Book(title="Piranesi", author="Susanna Clarke", pages=272),
    ]
    reading_list[0].read_to(412)
    reading_list[1].read_to(100)
    total = books.total_pages(reading_list)
    done = total - books.pages_left(reading_list)
    bar = progress_bar(done, total, settings.bar_width)
    print(settings.shelf_name)
    print(f"{bar} {done}/{total} pages")
    return 0
```

<span class="caption">Listing 7-15: `shelf` importing from the `gauge` package</span>

```console
$ cd shelf
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU2999]: cannot resolve module `gauge.bar` at `src/gauge/bar.au`
 --> src/main.au:3:1
  |
3 | from gauge.bar import progress_bar
  | ^
```

The compiler doesn't know `gauge` is a package, so it reads `gauge.bar` as a
local module and looks for `src/gauge/bar.au` inside `shelf`. Aura never goes
looking for packages on its own: not in the parent directory, not in a global
install location, not on the network. A package uses another package only if
its manifest says so. Let's say so:

*Filename: shelf/Aura.toml*

```toml
[package]
name = "shelf"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2026"

[dependencies]
gauge = { path = "../gauge" }
```

<span class="caption">Listing 7-16: Declaring a path dependency</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
Reading list
[##########----------] 512/948 pages
```

A *path dependency* points at another package's directory, relative to the
manifest that declares it. It's the natural choice for packages that live in
the same repository, or for trying out a change to a library before you
publish it. The two packages now look like this:

```text
projects
├── gauge
│   ├── Aura.toml
│   ├── src
│   │   └── bar.au
│   └── tests
│       └── smoke.au
└── shelf
    ├── Aura.lock
    ├── Aura.toml
    ├── src
    │   ├── books.au
    │   ├── main.au
    │   └── settings.au
    └── tests
        └── smoke.au
```

and the lockfile has grown an entry for the dependency:

*Filename: shelf/Aura.lock*

```toml
version = 1

[[package]]
name = "gauge"
version = "0.1.0"
source = "path"
path = "../gauge"

[[package]]
name = "shelf"
version = "0.1.0"
source = "path"
path = "."
```

Inside `gauge`, imports are still relative to `gauge`'s own `src/`. If
`gauge` later splits `bar.au` into several modules, `bar.au` would import
them as, say, `import blocks`, without a `gauge.` prefix, exactly the way
`shelf/src/main.au` imports `books`. Only code *outside* a package uses its
name as a prefix.

Package boundaries add no new visibility rules, because the module rules
already cover them. `segment` is private to `gauge.bar`, and that doesn't
change because `shelf` has declared a dependency:

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU2999]: item `segment` is private in module `gauge.bar`
 --> src/main.au:3:37
  |
3 | from gauge.bar import progress_bar, segment
  |                                     ^
```

### The dependency's name is not a nickname

In the `[dependencies]` table, the key on the left of `=` must be the
dependency's real package name. You might want to call `gauge` something else
in `shelf`:

```toml
[dependencies]
meter = { path = "../gauge" }
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU2999]: dependency name `meter` does not match package name `gauge` at `/home/you/projects/gauge`
 --> src/main.au
```

The compiler opened `../gauge/Aura.toml`, found `name = "gauge"`, and refused
the mismatch. (It prints the full path of the package it found; we've written ours as
`/home/you/projects`.) This rule means that the name you read in an import, the
name in your manifest, and the name in the dependency's own manifest are
always the same word, so you can find the code behind any import without
guessing. If you want a shorter spelling in one file, that's what `import
gauge.bar as bars` is for.

## Git dependencies

Path dependencies are perfect for packages that sit next to each other on
your disk. For a package someone else maintains, you point at a git
repository instead:

```toml
[dependencies]
gauge = { git = "https://github.com/example/gauge.git", tag = "v0.1.0" }
```

You import a git dependency exactly as you'd import a path dependency, by its
package name. What changes is how the compiler finds the code. It fetches the
repository into a cache under your home directory, checks out the version you
asked for, and records the exact commit in `Aura.lock`. A git dependency can
say which version it wants in one of three ways. `rev = "..."` names one
commit by its hash, and never moves. `tag = "v0.1.0"` names a tag, and
`branch = "release"` names a branch; with none of the three, the dependency
follows the `main` branch. You may pick at most one:

```toml
[dependencies]
gauge = { git = "https://github.com/example/gauge.git", tag = "v0.1.0", branch = "main" }
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU2999]: dependency `gauge` must choose at most one git selector: `rev`, `tag`, or `branch`
 --> src/main.au
```

A branch is a moving target: tomorrow `main` may point at a different commit
than it does today. If the compiler followed it on every build, the same
source could compile one day and fail the next, with no change on your side.
So it doesn't. The first time it resolves a branch or tag, it writes the
commit it found into `Aura.lock`, and every later build uses that commit. For
a branch dependency the lock entry looks something like this:

```toml
[[package]]
name = "gauge"
version = "0.1.0"
source = "git"
git = "https://github.com/example/gauge.git"
rev = "0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567"
branch = "main"
```

When you *want* the newer code, ask for it by running `aura deps update`
from inside the package. That re-resolves every branch and tag dependency in
the package and rewrites the lockfile. `aura deps update gauge` refreshes one dependency by name. A
`rev` dependency is already pinned to one commit, so there's nothing to
update, and naming a path dependency is an error:

```console
$ aura deps update gauge
error[AU2999]: package `gauge` is not a git dependency in the current package graph
 --> /home/you/projects/shelf
```

That's the whole story for where packages come from today: a path or a git
repository. Aura has no package registry yet, so there's no `pip install`
equivalent and no version solving. If you write a dependency the way you
would in many other languages, with only a version number, the compiler tells
you what to do instead:

```toml
[dependencies]
gauge = "0.1.0"
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU2999]: version-only dependencies are not supported yet for `gauge` (requested `0.1.0`); use `gauge = { path = "..." }` or `gauge = { git = "..." }` instead
 --> src/main.au
```

One thing to keep in mind about git dependencies: Aura is careful about how
it fetches and caches them, but it can't tell you whether the code inside is
trustworthy. Pin a `rev` or a `tag` for anything you run in production, and
read what you depend on. The [Manual](/manual/packages) has the details of
the cache and the checks it performs.

## Workspaces

`shelf` and `gauge` are separate packages, and right now each would keep its
own lockfile. That's awkward for two packages that we develop together in one
repository: the two lockfiles could disagree, and every command has to be run
from inside one package or the other. A *workspace* ties them together. It's
a manifest in the parent directory that lists the member packages and has no
`[package]` table of its own:

*Filename: projects/Aura.toml*

```toml
[workspace]
members = ["shelf", "gauge"]
```

<span class="caption">Listing 7-17: A workspace manifest</span>

Each member is still an ordinary package with its own `Aura.toml`, its own
`src/`, and its own dependencies. What changes is where the lockfile lives.
Let's delete `shelf/Aura.lock` and run the program from the workspace root:

```console
$ cd ..
$ rm shelf/Aura.lock
$ aura run shelf/src/main.au
Reading list
[##########----------] 512/948 pages
```

The compiler found `shelf/Aura.toml`, noticed that the manifest one level up
lists `shelf` as a member, and wrote one lockfile for the whole workspace, at
the root:

*Filename: projects/Aura.lock*

```toml
version = 1

[[package]]
name = "gauge"
version = "0.1.0"
source = "path"
path = "gauge"

[[package]]
name = "shelf"
version = "0.1.0"
source = "path"
path = "shelf"
```

Paths in the lockfile are now relative to the workspace root. Here is the
final layout:

```text
projects
├── Aura.lock
├── Aura.toml
├── gauge
│   ├── Aura.toml
│   ├── src
│   │   └── bar.au
│   └── tests
│       └── smoke.au
└── shelf
    ├── Aura.toml
    ├── src
    │   ├── books.au
    │   ├── main.au
    │   └── settings.au
    └── tests
        └── smoke.au
```

`aura deps update` run from the root works on every member at once, and
`aura test` can run the tests of both packages in one go:

```console
$ aura deps update
Aura.lock is already up to date
$ aura test shelf/tests gauge/tests
ok gauge/tests/smoke.au
ok shelf/tests/smoke.au
2 passed; 0 failed
```

Being in the same workspace doesn't make packages depend on each other. If we
took the `[dependencies]` table out of `shelf/Aura.toml`, the workspace would
not fill the gap:

```console
$ aura run shelf/src/main.au
error[AU2999]: cannot resolve module `gauge.bar` at `shelf/src/gauge/bar.au`
 --> shelf/src/main.au:3:1
  |
3 | from gauge.bar import progress_bar
  | ^
```

This is deliberate. A workspace is about building packages together, and a
dependency is about one package using another. Keeping them separate means
you can read any one package's manifest and see everything it uses, and that
`gauge` stays usable on its own when someone outside the workspace adds it as
a git dependency. Membership is also listed by exact path; there are no glob
patterns such as `"libs/*"`, so every member is named in the root manifest.

## Summary

You can now grow an Aura program past one file. A module is one file, named
by its path under `src/`, and other files reach it with `import` or `from
... import ...`. Everything in a module is private unless it's marked
`public`, which lets you keep a class's fields private and offer methods that
protect its invariants, as `Book.read_to` does for the bookmark. Imports bring
in declarations only, module constants are set once before `main` runs and
never change, and mutable state belongs to a value with an owner.

Packages carry those ideas across projects. A package is a directory with an
`Aura.toml` and a `src/`, and its name is the root of every import other
packages write. Dependencies come from a path or a git repository, the
lockfile pins exactly what was resolved, and a workspace lets several packages
share one lockfile without letting them use each other by accident. The
[Manual](/manual/packages) has the complete rules for manifests, lockfiles,
and dependency resolution, and the [Names and scopes](/manual/names-and-scopes)
page covers imports and visibility in full.

The reading list stores its books in a `list`, and the `gauge` package builds
strings by repeating characters. In the [next
chapter](/book/ch08-00-collections) we'll look closely at those two types and
at their relatives, dictionaries and sets, which are the containers most
Aura programs are built from.

## Source: docs/book/ch08-00-collections.md

# Common collections

Most of the data a program handles comes in groups: the lines of a file, the
scores of a class, the words in a document and how often each one appears.
Aura gives you a small set of collection types for holding those groups, and
if you've written Python they will look familiar. A `list[T]` keeps values in
order. A `dict[K, V]` maps keys to values. A `set[T]` holds each value once.
`str`, which you've been using since the first chapter, is a sequence of
text with its own rules, and `Array[T]` is a block of numbers for arithmetic
on a whole table at a time.

The familiar shapes come with two differences that run through the whole
chapter. First, every collection holds exactly one type of element, written
in its type: a `list[int64]` can't hold a string, and the compiler checks
that when it reads the literal. Second, collections own what they hold. When
you put a string into a list, the list becomes its owner, and when you take
something out, ownership moves to you. The ownership rules from
[Chapter 4](/book/ch04-00-understanding-ownership) explain almost every error
you'll meet in this chapter, and we'll point back to them as they come up.

We'll work through these types with a gradebook: a few students, a few
assignments, and the questions a teacher asks of them: who passed, what the
class average is, and who needs help. By the end of the chapter you'll be
able to pick the right collection for a job, read and change it without
fighting the ownership checker, and use comprehensions and
builtins such as `sum`, `sorted`, and `max` to answer questions in a line or
two.

## Source: docs/book/ch08-01-lists.md

# Lists

A `list[T]` holds values of one type `T`, in order, and grows as you add to
it. It's the collection you'll reach for most, so it's where we'll start our
gradebook: one student's scores on a run of assignments.

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
def main():
    mut scores = [72, 95, 88]
    scores.append(64)
    print(scores)
    print(f"{scores.len()} scores, first {scores[0]}, last {scores[-1]}")
```

<span class="caption">Listing 8-1: Building a list, adding to it, and reading from both ends</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
[72, 95, 88, 64]
4 scores, first 72, last 64
```

So far this is Python with a `mut` in front. The square-bracket literal makes
a list, `append` adds to the end, `len()` counts the elements (the builtin
`len(scores)` does the same thing), and indexing starts at zero. A negative
index counts back from the end, so `scores[-1]` is the last element.

The `mut` matters. `append` changes the list, and Aura only lets you change a
value through a mutable binding. Leave it off and the compiler points at the
call:

```aura check-fail:AU3003
def main():
    scores = [72, 95, 88]
    scores.append(64)
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU3003]: method `append` requires a mutable receiver
 --> src/main.au:3:12
  |
3 |     scores.append(64)
  |            ^
  = help: declare the receiver place with `mut` before calling a mutating method
```

## One element type

What type is `scores`? We didn't write one, so the compiler worked it out from
the literal: the elements are integer literals, so the list is a
`list[int64]`. Every element has to agree with that. A gradebook might be
tempted to record a missing assignment as a word:

```aura check-fail:AU2002
def main():
    scores = [72, "absent", 88]
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2002]: list literal elements must all have type `int64`, found `str`
 --> src/main.au:2:19
  |
2 |     scores = [72, "absent", 88]
  |                   ^
```

Python would accept this list, and then some later line that adds up the
scores would fail when it reached the string. Because an Aura list has one
element type, any code that reads an element knows exactly what it will get,
and the compiler can check every use. When you really do have a value that may
be missing, say so in the type: a `list[int64 | None]` holds numbers or
`None`, and code reading it has to handle both, as you saw in
[Chapter 6](/book/ch06-00-enums-and-match).

The other side of inference is that an empty list gives the compiler nothing
to infer from:

```aura check-fail:AU2002
def main():
    scores = []
    print(scores)
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2002]: empty list literals require an expected `list[T]` type annotation in the bootstrap compiler
 --> src/main.au:2:14
  |
2 |     scores = []
  |              ^
```

Give the binding a type, or call the list type as a constructor. Both of these
make an empty `list[int64]`:

```aura
def main():
    mut first: list[int64] = []
    mut second = list[int64]()
    first.append(1)
    second.append(2)
```

When you know roughly how many elements a list will end up with,
`list[int64].with_capacity(1_000)` makes an empty list with room for that
many, so it doesn't have to grow in steps as you append. The contents are the
same either way; only the amount of copying behind the scenes changes.

## Reading elements

Indexing is checked at run time. An index past the end doesn't wrap around or
return a placeholder; it stops the task:

```aura
def main():
    scores = [72, 95, 88]
    print(scores[3])
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU4003]: list index `3` is out of bounds for length `3`
 --> src/main.au:3:18
  |
3 |     print(scores[3])
  |                  ^
  = note: Aura call chain (innermost first): main at 1:1
```

This is a *trap*, a runtime failure that ends the task, and the program
exits with an error. Notice that `aura check` accepted the code: the compiler
doesn't try to prove indexes are in range, so the check happens when the line
runs. A trap is the right outcome when a bad index means the program has a
bug. [Chapter 9](/book/ch09-00-error-handling) talks about when to let a
program stop and when to recover.

When a missing element is an ordinary situation, not a bug, use `get`
instead. It returns a `Lookup[T]`, an enum with two variants, and `match`
makes you handle both:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
def main():
    scores = [72, 95, 88]
    match scores.get(5):
        case Lookup.Found(score):
            print(f"sixth score: {score}")
        case Lookup.Missing:
            print("there is no sixth score")
```

<span class="caption">Listing 8-2: Reading an element that might not be there</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
there is no sixth score
```

Aura uses a separate `Lookup` type here, not `int64 | None`, because a list
can hold `None` itself. In a `list[int64 | None]`, a `get` that returned
`None` couldn't tell you whether the element was missing or present and equal
to `None`. `Lookup.Missing` can only mean one thing.

Indexes are `int64`. A narrower integer, such as an `int32` position, widens
automatically when you use it as an index, because no `int32` value can be
out of the `int64` range. An unsigned `uint64` can, so it's refused with
`AU2002`, and you'd convert it with `as` first.

### Elements that aren't copy values

Our scores are copy values, so `scores[0]` hands you a copy of the number and
the list keeps its own. A list of strings behaves differently: `first =
names[0]` is an error, because it would create a second owner for a string
the list already owns. [Chapter 4](/book/ch04-00-understanding-ownership)
walked through that error and its three fixes: view the element in place with
`view first = names[0]`, make your own copy with `names[0].clone()`, or take
it out of the list with `pop`. Passing an element straight to a function, as
in `print(names[0])`, lends it for the call and needs none of them.

## Changing a list

Lists have the methods you'd expect, with names borrowed from Python. Let's
use most of them on our scores at once:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
def main():
    mut scores = [72, 95, 88]
    scores.insert(0, 50)
    scores.extend([64, 91])
    print(scores)

    dropped = scores.pop(0)
    last = scores.pop()
    print(f"dropped {dropped} and {last}: {scores}")

    old = scores.set(1, 96)
    print(f"replaced {old}: {scores}")

    scores.remove(88)
    print(scores)
    print(f"64 is at {scores.index(64)}, and appears {scores.count(64)} time")
```

<span class="caption">Listing 8-3: Inserting, removing, and replacing elements</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
[50, 72, 95, 88, 64, 91]
dropped 50 and 91: [72, 95, 88, 64]
replaced 95: [72, 96, 88, 64]
[72, 96, 64]
64 is at 2, and appears 1 time
```

`insert(position, value)` puts a value before `position`; like Python, it
clamps positions that are out of range, so `insert(100, x)` appends.
`extend` moves every element of another list onto the end. `pop()` removes
and returns the last element, and `pop(0)` the first. `set` is the one you may
not have met: it replaces an element and *returns the old one*. Assigning with
`scores[1] = 96` works too, but `set` hands the previous value back to you,
which matters when the elements are owned values you don't want to lose.
`remove(value)` deletes the first element equal to `value`, `index(value)`
finds its position, and `count(value)` counts how many there are.

`remove` and `index` have a sharp edge. If the value isn't there, they trap:

```aura
def main():
    mut scores = [72, 95, 88]
    scores.remove(50)
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU4008]: collection value was not found
 --> src/main.au
  = note: Aura call chain (innermost first): main at 1:1
  = help: check `value in values` before removing when absence is expected
```

The help line says what to do: when the value may legitimately be missing,
test first with `if 50 in scores:`. The `in` operator works on every
collection in this chapter. `pop` and `set` trap the same way when the
position is out of range, and `pop()` traps on an empty list.

Other changes you can make in place are `clear()`, which empties the list,
`reverse()`, and `swap(i, j)`. Sorting gets its own section below.

## Looping over a list

A `for` loop visits the elements in order. How it visits them depends on
what you ask for, and the three choices are the three access modes from
[Chapter 4](/book/ch04-00-understanding-ownership):

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
def main():
    mut scores = [72, 95, 64, 88]

    mut total: int64 = 0
    for score in scores:
        total += score
    print(f"total before curve: {total}")

    for score in mut scores:
        score += 3
    print(f"after curve: {scores}")

    for position, score in enumerate(scores):
        print(f"assignment {position + 1}: {score}")
```

<span class="caption">Listing 8-4: Reading, changing, and numbering elements in loops</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
total before curve: 319
after curve: [75, 98, 67, 91]
assignment 1: 75
assignment 2: 98
assignment 3: 67
assignment 4: 91
```

A bare `for score in scores` gives the loop shared access: it reads each
element and leaves the list as it was. `for score in mut scores` gives it
mutable access, so `score += 3` changes the element inside the list, which is
how the curve takes effect. In Python, assigning to the loop variable would
change nothing but the variable. A third form, `for name in own names`, moves
each element out of the list and into the loop, consuming the list; after
that loop the list is gone, and using it is the familiar `AU3001`.

`enumerate(scores)` gives each element with its position, as a `(int64, T)`
pair, and `zip(first, second)` walks two lists side by side and stops at the
shorter one. Both are only valid as the thing a `for` loop iterates over.

While a bare loop is reading a list, the list is frozen. Here's an attempt to
add a make-up score for every failing grade while we're still looking at the
grades:

```aura check-fail:AU3002
def main():
    mut scores = [72, 95, 64, 88]
    for score in scores:
        if score < 70:
            scores.append(70)
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU3002]: cannot mutate `scores` while `scores` is borrowed for iteration
 --> src/main.au:5:20
  |
5 |             scores.append(70)
  |                    ^
  = related src/main.au:3:18: `scores` is borrowed for this loop here
  = help: perform owner mutation after the loop; use `for item in mut scores:` when mutating elements through the loop binding
```

In Python, appending to a list you're iterating over is a classic bug: the
loop may run forever or skip elements, depending on what you add and where.
Aura rules it out before the program runs. The two `related` and `help` lines
give the options: collect the changes and apply them after the loop, or use
`for score in mut scores` if what you want is to change each element in
place.

## Sorting

`sort()` puts a list in order, in place:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
def last_name(name: str) -> str:
    parts = name.split(" ")
    return parts[-1].clone()

def main():
    mut names = ["Grace Hopper", "Ada Lovelace", "Alan Turing", "Katherine Johnson"]
    names.sort()
    print(names)
    names.sort(key=last_name)
    print(names)
    names.sort(key=lambda name: name.len(), reverse=true)
    print(names)
```

<span class="caption">Listing 8-5: Sorting naturally, by a key function, and in reverse</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
[Ada Lovelace, Alan Turing, Grace Hopper, Katherine Johnson]
[Grace Hopper, Katherine Johnson, Ada Lovelace, Alan Turing]
[Katherine Johnson, Grace Hopper, Ada Lovelace, Alan Turing]
```

With no arguments, `sort` uses the natural order of the element type:
numbers by value, strings by their UTF-8 bytes. (That second rule means
uppercase letters sort before lowercase ones, so `"Zebra"` comes before
`"apple"`.) `key=` takes a function that computes a sort key for each
element, here a named function and then a lambda; the key is computed once
per element, before anything moves. `reverse=true` flips the order.

Look closely at the last line of output. Grace Hopper and Ada Lovelace have
names of the same length, and they stay in the order they had before the
sort, even with `reverse=true`. Aura's sort is *stable*: elements with equal
keys keep their relative order, in both directions. That lets you sort by
one thing and then another and keep the first order as a tiebreaker.

Natural sorting needs a type that has an order. A class of your own doesn't
have one until you give it one:

```aura check-fail:AU2002
class Student:
    name: str
    scores: list[int64]

def main():
    mut roster = [
        Student(name="Ada", scores=[72, 95]),
        Student(name="Grace", scores=[88]),
    ]
    roster.sort()
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2002]: `list.sort` cannot order list element type `Student`
 --> src/main.au:10:12
   |
10 |     roster.sort()
   |            ^
  = help: use an existing naturally ordered type, or implement `Ord[T].lt` returning `bool`
```

Implementing the `Ord` trait is a topic for [Chapter
10](/book/ch10-00-generics-traits-conversions). The quick fix is a key:
`roster.sort(key=lambda student: student.name.clone())` sorts by name.

## Lists of richer values

Real gradebooks hold more than numbers. Let's give each student a name and a
list of scores, and see how a list of class values behaves:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
class Student:
    name: str
    scores: list[int64]

def main():
    mut roster = [
        Student(name="Ada", scores=[72, 95]),
        Student(name="Grace", scores=[88]),
    ]
    roster[1].scores.append(91)
    match mut roster.lookup(0):
        case Lookup.Found(student):
            student.scores.append(64)
        case Lookup.Missing:
            print("no first student")
    for student in roster:
        print(f"{student.name}: {student.scores}")
    roster.sort(key=lambda student: student.scores.len())
    print(roster[0].name)
```

<span class="caption">Listing 8-6: Changing elements of a list of classes in place</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
Ada: [72, 95, 64]
Grace: [88, 91]
Grace
```

`roster[1].scores.append(91)` reaches through the index to the student's
field and changes it where it lies, without copying the student out. That
works because `roster` is mutable and we're not trying to make a new owner,
only to change one that already exists.

The `match mut roster.lookup(0)` is the in-place cousin of `get`. `get` hands
you a *clone* of the element, which is fine for a number and wasteful for a
student with a long list of scores, and impossible for elements that can't be
cloned. `lookup` doesn't produce a value at all. It exists only as the subject
of a `match`: if the position is valid, the `Found` arm runs with `student`
naming the element inside the list, and with `match mut` the arm can change
it. While that arm runs, the list can't grow or shrink, so the view can't be
left pointing at nothing.

## Matching on a list's shape

`match` can look at a list's length and pull out its elements at the same
time. Here's a function that describes a student's progress in words:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
def describe(scores: list[int64]) -> str:
```
