```aura
    return match scores:
        case []: "no scores yet"
        case [only]: f"one score: {only}"
        case [first, second]: f"two scores: {first} and {second}"
        case [first, *rest]: f"{first}, then {len(rest)} more"

def main():
    print(describe([]))
    print(describe([88]))
    print(describe([88, 91]))
    print(describe([75, 98, 67, 91]))
```

<span class="caption">Listing 8-7: Sequence patterns</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
no scores yet
one score: 88
two scores: 88 and 91
75, then 3 more
```

Each pattern matches lists of one exact length, except the last, where
`*rest` collects whatever the other positions leave into a new list. The arms
are tried in order, so the specific lengths go first. The
[Manual](/manual/enums-and-match) has the full rules for sequence patterns.

## Making new lists from old ones

Two list methods build a fresh list and leave the original alone. `filter`
keeps the elements a function accepts, and `map` transforms every element:

```aura
def passed(score: int64) -> bool:
    return score >= 70

def main():
    scores = [75, 98, 67, 91]
    print(scores.filter(passed))
    print(scores.map(lambda score: score * 10 // 9))
    print(scores)
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
[75, 98, 91]
[83, 108, 74, 101]
[75, 98, 67, 91]
```

Both run immediately and give you a complete list, not a lazy iterator. A
slice such as `scores[1:3]` also makes a new list, copying the elements it
selects; [Chapter 4](/book/ch04-00-understanding-ownership) covered how
slices work and what they cost. If you need to work on part of a list
*without* copying it, Aura has views of a range, called spans, which the
[Manual](/manual/collections) describes.

`map` and `filter` are fine, but for anything longer than one function call,
most Aura code uses comprehensions instead, along with builtins such as
`sorted` and `sum`. We'll get to those in [section
8.4](/book/ch08-04-comprehensions-and-builtins). First, though, our students
have names, and names are strings, which have more going on than they first
appear to.

## Source: docs/book/ch08-02-strings.md

# Strings

Our gradebook's data will arrive as text, one student per line:

```text
Ada Lovelace: 72, 95, 88
```

Turning a line like that into a name and a list of numbers means trimming,
splitting, and parsing, and printing a report afterwards means padding and
joining. All of that happens on `str`, Aura's string type. You've used `str`
since the first chapter, and most of its methods will be familiar from
Python. The parts that differ are the ones that come from two decisions: a
`str` is UTF-8 text, and a `str` is an owned value that never changes.

## What a `str` is

A `str` holds a sequence of Unicode characters, stored as UTF-8 bytes. The
string owns those bytes, the way a list owns its elements, and nothing can
change them after the string is made. Every method that seems to modify a
string, such as `replace`, `to_upper`, or `trim`, returns a new string and
leaves the original as it was.

Because a `str` is an owned value, not a copy value, assignment moves it:

```aura check-fail:AU3001
def main():
    s = "abc"
    t = s
    print(s)
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU3001]: use of moved value `s`
 --> src/main.au:4:11
  |
4 |     print(s)
  |           ^
  = related src/main.au:3:9: value moved here
  = help: pass shared access when ownership is not needed, or call `.clone()` at the move site when an independent value is required
  = fix: replace src/main.au:3:10-3:10 with `.clone()`
```

That's the same rule you met in [Chapter 4](/book/ch04-00-understanding-ownership),
and the fix the compiler offers is the same: `t = s.clone()` makes an
independent copy. Note the spelling. Strings copy with `.clone()`, while
lists, dictionaries, and sets copy with `.copy()`. A function that only reads
a string should take it as a plain `str` parameter, which lends it for the
call and doesn't move anything.

## Length, and what counts as a character

Let's look at a name with an accent in it:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
def main():
    name = "Zoë"
    print(name.len())
    print(name.byte_len())
    print(name[2:])
    print(name[:-1])
    print(name[::-1])
    cheer = "A🎉"
    print(f"{cheer.len()} scalars, {cheer.byte_len()} bytes")
```

<span class="caption">Listing 8-8: Counting and slicing Unicode text</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
3
4
ë
Zo
ëoZ
2 scalars, 5 bytes
```

`len()` counts *Unicode scalar values*, which for most text means the
characters you see: `Zoë` has three. `byte_len()` counts the UTF-8 bytes
behind them, and `ë` takes two bytes, so there are four. The emoji takes four
bytes on its own. The two numbers have different costs as well as different
meanings: `byte_len()` is stored with the string and is instant, while
`len()` has to walk the bytes to count scalars, so it takes time proportional
to the length of the string. In a loop over a long string, that difference is
worth remembering.

Slices count scalar values too, so `name[2:]` is the `ë` and never half of
it. Every slice of a `str` is a new, valid string: you can't cut a character
in two. Slices follow the same rules as list slices: the end is exclusive,
negative positions count from the end, and a step of `-1` walks backwards,
which reverses the string.

One caution about "characters". A scalar value is not always what a reader
would call one character. Some accented letters can also be written as a
plain letter followed by a combining accent, and some emoji are built from
several scalars joined together. Aura counts scalars, not those visual
clusters, which is also what Python's `len` does.

A string slice that goes past the end doesn't quietly stop at the end the way
Python's does. Like a list slice, it traps:

```aura
def main():
    word = "café"
    print(word[1:9])
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU4003]: slice end `9` is outside `0..=4`
 --> src/main.au:3:17
  |
3 |     print(word[1:9])
  |                 ^
  = note: Aura call chain (innermost first): main at 1:1
```

The message tells you the valid range. Aura chooses a trap over clamping
because a slice that asks for nine characters of a four-character word
usually means the program's idea of the text is wrong, and silently
returning less hides that.

## No indexing by position

If you try to take one character with an index, as you might in Python, the
compiler stops you:

```aura check-fail:AU2999
def main():
    word = "café"
    print(word[0])
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2999]: cannot index non-Array, list, or dict value `str`
 --> src/main.au:3:11
  |
3 |     print(word[0])
  |           ^
```

and a `for` loop over a string isn't available either:

```aura check-fail:AU2999
def main():
    word = "café"
    for ch in word:
        print(ch)
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2999]: `for` currently requires a `Range`, `Queue[T]`, `list[T]`, or `set[T]` iterable, found `str`
 --> src/main.au:3:5
  |
3 |     for ch in word:
  |     ^
```

This is a real gap if you're used to Python, so let's be clear about why it
exists and what to do instead. Aura has no character type: a single letter is
a `str` of length one. Finding the scalar at position `n` in UTF-8 means
walking from the start, so `word[n]` inside a loop would quietly turn a
linear algorithm into a quadratic one. Aura would rather not offer an
operation that looks cheap and isn't. `chars()`, `ord()`, and `chr()` aren't
available yet.

In practice, most text processing doesn't need single characters. You want
words, fields, lines, and prefixes, and the methods in the rest of this
section work on those directly. When you do need one character, a slice such
as `word[0:1]` gives it to you as a one-character `str`.

## Searching

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
def main():
    comment = "Great work on the essay; revise the essay intro."
    print(comment.contains("essay"))
    print(comment.starts_with("Great"))
    print(comment.count("essay"))
    print(comment.find("revise"))
    print(comment.find("excellent"))
    match comment.find(";"):
        case int64 as at:
            print(comment[:at])
        case None:
            print(comment)
    print(comment.replace("essay", "report"))
    print(comment.to_upper())
```

<span class="caption">Listing 8-9: Searching and transforming a string</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
true
true
2
25
None
Great work on the essay
Great work on the report; revise the report intro.
GREAT WORK ON THE ESSAY; REVISE THE ESSAY INTRO.
```

`contains`, `starts_with`, and `ends_with` answer yes-or-no questions.
`count` counts non-overlapping matches. `find` returns the position of the
first match, counted in scalars like `len()` and slices, so you can feed it
straight into a slice. When there's no match it returns `None`, not Python's
`-1`, so its type is `int64 | None` and you have to deal with both cases before
you can use the number. The `match` with a type pattern does that, as you saw
in [Chapter 6](/book/ch06-00-enums-and-match). A `-1` that slips through
unchecked would slice from the end of the string, which is exactly the kind
of bug the type rules out.

`strip_prefix` and `strip_suffix` follow the same pattern. They return the
rest of the string if the prefix or suffix was there, and `None` if it
wasn't:

```aura
def main():
    file_name = "term1-grades.csv"
    match file_name.strip_suffix(".csv"):
        case str as stem:
            print(stem)
        case None:
            print("not a CSV file")
```

## Splitting and parsing

Now we have what we need to read a gradebook line. Let's write a function
that turns the text after the colon into a list of scores, and use it from
`main`:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
def parse_scores(text: str) -> list[int64]:
    mut scores: list[int64] = []
    for part in text.split(","):
        match parse_int64(part.trim()):
            case Result.Ok(score):
                scores.append(score)
            case Result.Err(message):
                print(f"skipping {part.trim()}: {message}")
    return scores

def main():
    line = "  Ada Lovelace: 72, 95, x, 88  "
    trimmed = line.trim()
    pair = trimmed.split_once(":")
    if pair is not None:
        name, rest = pair
        scores = parse_scores(rest)
        print(f"{name} has {scores.len()} scores: {scores}")
    else:
        print(f"no colon in {trimmed}")
```

<span class="caption">Listing 8-10: Parsing a line of text into a name and scores</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
skipping x: invalid digit found in string
Ada Lovelace has 3 scores: [72, 95, 88]
```

Let's take it from the top of `main`. `trim()` returns a copy of the line
without the whitespace at either end; `trim_start()` and `trim_end()` trim one
side. `split_once(":")` splits at the first colon and returns both halves as
a `(str, str)` tuple, or `None` if there's no colon, so its type is
`(str, str) | None`. The `if pair is not None:` test narrows it to the tuple,
and `name, rest = pair` unpacks it. (`rsplit_once` splits at the last
occurrence instead.)

In `parse_scores`, `split(",")` breaks the rest of the line into a
`list[str]` at every comma. The pieces still have their spaces, so each one
gets trimmed before `parse_int64` tries to read it as a number.
`parse_int64` returns a `Result`, because text from outside the program might
not be a number at all, and the `x` in our line shows the `Err` case. Here we
print a note and keep going; [Chapter 9](/book/ch09-00-error-handling) shows
how to pass the error up to the caller instead. `parse_int32` and
`parse_float64` work the same way.

For whole blocks of text, two more splitting methods help. `lines()` breaks
text at newlines, and handles Windows-style line endings as well.
`split_whitespace()` splits on any run of spaces, tabs, or newlines, and drops
the empty pieces that `split(" ")` would leave between two spaces:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
def main():
    report = """Ada Lovelace: 72, 95, 88
Grace Hopper: 88, 91
Alan Turing: 64, 70, 91
"""
    for line in report.lines():
        print(line.split_whitespace())
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
[Ada, Lovelace:, 72,, 95,, 88]
[Grace, Hopper:, 88,, 91]
[Alan, Turing:, 64,, 70,, 91]
```

The triple-quoted string keeps its text exactly as written, newlines
included, and the final newline doesn't produce an empty last line. Notice,
too, that a printed list of strings shows them without quotation marks.

While we're on literals: the usual escapes `\n`, `\t`, `\\`, `\"`, and `\'`
work in ordinary strings, along with `\0`, `\xHH`, and `\u{...}`. A Python
habit that doesn't carry over is `\r`, which isn't a supported escape; the
compiler reports `AU1001` for it, and you can write `\x0d` if you need a
carriage return. A string with an `r` prefix, such as `r"C:\grades"`, treats
backslashes as ordinary characters.

## Building strings

There are three common ways to put a string together. The first is `+`,
which joins two strings. *Two strings*, that is:

```aura check-fail:AU2999
def main():
    total = 255
    print("total: " + total)
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2999]: binary operator operands must match, found `str` and `int64`
 --> src/main.au:3:11
  |
3 |     print("total: " + total)
  |           ^
```

Aura doesn't convert numbers to text behind your back, any more than it
converts an `int32` to an `int64`. Write the conversion: `total.to_string()`
or `str(total)` both give `"255"`.

The second way, and usually the best one, is an f-string. You've been using
them all along, and they also take a format specification after a colon that
controls width, alignment, and precision. The third is `join`, which glues a
list of strings together with the receiver as the separator. Here's a small
report that uses all of them:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
def score_line(name: str, scores: list[int64]) -> str:
    mut parts: list[str] = []
    for score in scores:
        parts.append(f"{score:>3}")
    return f"{name:<14}|" + " ".join(parts)

def main():
    rule = "-".repeat(26)
    print(f"{'Student':<14}| Scores")
    print(rule)
    print(score_line("Ada Lovelace", [72, 95, 88]))
    print(score_line("Grace Hopper", [88, 91]))
    print(rule)
    average = 84.6
    print(f"class average: {average:.1f} ({average / 100.0:.0%})")
```

<span class="caption">Listing 8-11: Formatting a report with f-strings, `join`, and `repeat`</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
Student       | Scores
--------------------------
Ada Lovelace  | 72  95  88
Grace Hopper  | 88  91
--------------------------
class average: 84.6 (85%)
```

`{score:>3}` right-aligns a number in three columns, `{name:<14}`
left-aligns a name in fourteen, `.1f` shows one decimal place, and `.0%`
multiplies by a hundred and adds a percent sign. The compiler checks each
specification against the type of the value before the program runs, so a
`.1f` on a string is a compile-time error rather than a surprise in the
output. `"-".repeat(26)` makes a string of 26 dashes; it's the same method the
progress bar used in [Chapter 7](/book/ch07-00-modules-and-packages).

The pattern in `score_line`, collecting pieces in a `list[str]` and joining
them once at the end, is the clearest way to build a string out of many
parts. For a few pieces in a loop, `+=` on a mutable string works too:

```aura
def main():
    mut summary = "scores:"
    for score in [72, 95, 88]:
        summary += f" {score}"
    print(summary)
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
scores: 72 95 88
```

Strings compare with `==` and `!=`, and order with `<` and friends by their
UTF-8 bytes, which is the same order `sort` uses. The full list of string
methods is in the Manual's [API index](/manual/api-index), and
[Types](/manual/types) covers `to_bytes` and `str.from_bytes` for converting
to and from raw bytes.

We can now read a student's name and scores out of a line of text. A
gradebook has many such lines, and the natural way to hold them is to look up
scores by name. That's what dictionaries are for.

## Source: docs/book/ch08-03-dicts-and-sets.md

# Dictionaries and sets

A list answers "what's at position 3?". Most questions a gradebook asks are
different: "what are Grace's scores?", "has Alan handed anything in?". For
questions by name, you want a `dict[K, V]`, which maps keys of type `K` to
values of type `V`. For questions of membership alone, you want a `set[T]`.
Both work much as they do in Python, and both follow the ownership rules of
the last section, with one twist for keys that's worth slowing down for.

## Creating and reading a dictionary

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
def main():
    mut grades = {"ada": 72, "grace": 95}
    grades["alan"] = 64
    grades["ada"] = 78
    print(grades)
    print(grades["grace"])
    print(f"{grades.len()} students")
    print("kathy" in grades)
    match grades.get("kathy"):
        case Lookup.Found(grade):
            print(f"kathy: {grade}")
        case Lookup.Missing:
            print("no grade for kathy")
    match grades.remove("alan"):
        case Lookup.Found(grade):
            print(f"removed alan, who had {grade}")
        case Lookup.Missing:
            print("alan was not there")
    print(grades)
```

<span class="caption">Listing 8-12: Adding, updating, reading, and removing entries</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
{ada: 78, grace: 95, alan: 64}
95
3 students
false
no grade for kathy
removed alan, who had 64
{ada: 78, grace: 95}
```

The literal `{"ada": 72, "grace": 95}` makes a `dict[str, int64]`, inferred
from the keys and values the same way a list's element type is. Every key has
to have the key type and every value the value type; mixing them is an
`AU2002`, as it is for lists. An empty dictionary needs its type written
down, either as `grades: dict[str, int64] = {}` or as `dict[str, int64]()`.

Assigning to `grades["alan"]` adds a new entry, and assigning to an existing
key, as with `"ada"`, replaces its value. A dictionary keeps its keys in the
order they were first inserted, and updating a value doesn't move its key,
which is why `ada` is still first after the update. Printing, `keys()`,
`values()`, and `items()` all follow that order.

Reading a missing key with brackets is a trap, as an out-of-range list index
is:

```aura
def main():
    grades = {"ada": 72, "grace": 95}
    print(grades["kathy"])
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU4003]: dict key `kathy` was not present
 --> src/main.au:3:18
  |
3 |     print(grades["kathy"])
  |                  ^
  = note: Aura call chain (innermost first): main at 1:1
```

So the rule is the one from lists. Use `grades[key]` when the key must be
there and its absence would be a bug. Use `key in grades` to test first, or
`get(key)` when absence is ordinary. `get` returns the same `Lookup` enum that
list `get` does, with `Lookup.Found(value)` holding a copy of the value, and
for the same reason: a dictionary's value could itself be `None`, and
`Lookup.Missing` can't be confused with it. Unlike Python's `dict.get`, it
takes no default argument; the `Missing` arm is where the default goes.

`remove(key)` takes the entry out and gives you its value, moved out of the
dictionary, inside a `Lookup.Found`. If the key wasn't there you get
`Lookup.Missing`, not a trap.

Dictionary keys can be any type that supports equality: numbers, strings,
tuples such as `("ada", 3)` for a student and an assignment number, and your
own classes. Lookups, insertions, and `in` take constant time on average,
however big the dictionary grows.

## Looping over a dictionary

You can't loop over a dictionary directly:

```aura check-fail:AU2999
def main():
    grades = {"ada": 72, "grace": 95}
    for name in grades:
        print(name)
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2999]: `for` currently requires a `Range`, `Queue[T]`, `list[T]`, or `set[T]` iterable, found `dict[str, int64]`
 --> src/main.au:3:5
  |
3 |     for name in grades:
  |     ^
```

In Python, `for name in grades` loops over the keys, and it's a common
surprise for newcomers that it doesn't give the values. Aura asks you to say
which you want, using one of three methods that each return a list:

```aura
def main():
    grades = {"ada": 72, "grace": 95}
    for name, grade in grades.items():
        print(f"{name}: {grade}")
    for name in grades.keys():
        print(name)
    print(grades.values())
    print(sorted(grades.keys()))
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
ada: 72
grace: 95
ada
grace
[72, 95]
[ada, grace]
```

`items()` gives a list of `(key, value)` tuples, which a `for` loop can
unpack. These lists are *snapshots*: new lists holding copies of the keys and
values, taken when you call the method. Changing the dictionary afterwards
doesn't change a snapshot, and changing the snapshot doesn't touch the
dictionary. That makes them safe to loop over even while you update the
dictionary, which Python forbids with a runtime error. The price is the copy,
so for a dictionary of large values, prefer reading entries by key. The last
line uses `sorted`, which we'll meet properly in the [next
section](/book/ch08-04-comprehensions-and-builtins), to print the names in
alphabetical order instead of insertion order.

## Grouping scores by student

Now let's do something real. Our gradebook arrives as lines with a student
and one score each, in no particular order, and we want each student's
scores together, plus each student's best score. A `dict[str, list[int64]]`
holds the first, and a `dict[str, int64]` the second:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura check-fail:AU3001
def main():
    lines = ["ada 72", "grace 95", "ada 88", "alan 64", "grace 91"]
    mut scores: dict[str, list[int64]] = {}
    mut best: dict[str, int64] = {}
    for line in lines:
        pair = line.split_once(" ")
        if pair is not None:
            name, text = pair
            match parse_int64(text):
                case Result.Ok(score):
                    match best.get(name):
                        case Lookup.Found(current):
                            if score > current:
                                best[name] = score
                        case Lookup.Missing:
                            best[name] = score
                    if name in scores:
                        scores[name].append(score)
                    else:
                        scores[name] = [score]
                case Result.Err(message):
                    print(f"bad score for {name}: {message}")
    print(scores)
    print(best)
```

<span class="caption">Listing 8-13: Grouping scores by name (this won't compile yet)</span>

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU3001]: use of moved value `name`
 --> src/main.au:17:24
   |
17 |                     if name in scores:
   |                        ^
  = related src/main.au:14:38: value moved here
  = help: pass shared access when ownership is not needed, or call `.clone()` at the move site when an independent value is required
  = fix: replace src/main.au:14:42-14:42 with `.clone()`
```

The compiler says `name` was moved on line 14, by `best[name] = score`. It
looks odd that *storing a score* would move the name.

Think about what the dictionary needs. When `name` isn't already a key,
`best[name] = score` adds a new entry, and the dictionary has to own that
entry's key from now on, for as long as the entry exists. It can't borrow
the key from our loop, because `name` is gone by the next iteration. So
assigning through an index *moves the key in*, along with the value. The
compiler applies that rule to every indexed assignment on a dictionary, even
when the key happens to be present already, so `best[name] += 1` would move
`name` too. The same goes for line 16, the `Missing` arm: on either path,
`name` has been handed to `best` by the time we reach line 17.

Lookups are different. `best.get(name)`, `name in scores`, and `scores[name]`
on the right-hand side only need to compare `name` with the keys, so they
borrow it and give it back. That's why line 11 was fine.

There are two fixes. One is to put the moves last, so nothing needs `name`
afterwards. The other, which keeps our code in the order we'd describe it, is
to give `best` its own copy of the name, with `.clone()`, as the `fix` line
suggests. The `fix` only points at line 14, the first move the compiler
found, but both arms of the inner `match` store the name, so both need it:

```aura fragment
                    match best.get(name):
                        case Lookup.Found(current):
                            if score > current:
                                best[name.clone()] = score
                        case Lookup.Missing:
                            best[name.clone()] = score
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
{ada: [72, 88], grace: [95, 91], alan: [64]}
{ada: 88, grace: 95, alan: 64}
```

Now look at the second half of the loop, which never caused trouble:

```aura fragment
                    if name in scores:
                        scores[name].append(score)
                    else:
                        scores[name] = [score]
```

`scores[name].append(score)` changes the list stored under `name` in place,
without moving `name` and without copying the list out. The `else` arm moves
`name` into the dictionary as a new key, and since nothing uses `name` after
it, that's fine.

### Looking up and changing in one step

The `if name in scores` version looks the key up twice: once for `in` and
again for the index. For a value you want to change, the `lookup` method from
lists does it in one step, and works the same way on dictionaries:

```aura
def record(scores: mut dict[str, list[int64]], name: own str, score: int64):
    match mut scores.lookup(name):
        case Lookup.Found(existing):
            existing.append(score)
        case Lookup.Missing:
            scores[name] = [score]

def main():
    mut scores: dict[str, list[int64]] = {}
    record(scores, "ada", 72)
    record(scores, "ada", 88)
    record(scores, "grace", 95)
    print(scores)
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
{ada: [72, 88], grace: [95]}
```

`lookup` is only allowed as the subject of a `match`. When the key is
present, the `Found` arm runs with `existing` naming the list inside the
dictionary, and `match mut` lets the arm change it. When the key is missing,
the `Missing` arm runs and is free to insert. The parameter types tell the
same story as the loop did: `scores` is `mut` because `record` changes it, and
`name` is `own` because `record` may store it as a new key.

Two more methods round out dictionaries. `update(other)` moves every entry of
another dictionary into this one, replacing values for keys that already
exist, and `copy()` makes an independent copy of the whole dictionary. Note
that `update` consumes `other`: after `grades.update(more)`, `more` has been
moved. Two dictionaries are equal with `==` when they hold the same keys with
equal values, whatever order they were inserted in.

## Sets

A `set[T]` holds values with no duplicates, and its main job is answering
"is this in here?" quickly. Let's find the students who scored below 70 on
anything:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
def main():
    scores = {"ada": [72, 88], "grace": [95, 91], "alan": [64, 58]}
    mut struggling = set[str]()
    for name, list_of_scores in scores.items():
        for score in list_of_scores:
            if score < 70:
                struggling.add(name.clone())
    print(struggling)
    print(struggling.len())
    print("alan" in struggling)
    print("ada" not in struggling)
    struggling.discard("ada")
    struggling.remove("alan")
    print(struggling)
```

<span class="caption">Listing 8-14: Collecting names in a set</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
{alan}
1
true
true
set()
```

Alan has two low scores, so `add` is called for him twice, and the set still
holds him once. That's the whole point of a set: you can add freely without
first checking for a duplicate. We call `name.clone()` because the set needs
to own each name it holds, and `name` belongs to the snapshot list that
`items()` returned.

`in` and `not in` test membership, in constant time on average, which is the
reason to choose a set over a list when membership is the question. To take
a value out, use `remove`, which traps with `AU4008` if the value isn't there,
or `discard`, which does nothing in that case. An empty set prints as
`set()`, because `{}` would read as an empty dictionary.

That last point applies to literals too. A brace literal with colons is a
dictionary and one without is a set, so `{1, 2, 3}` is a `set[int64]`. An
empty `{}` is a dictionary, unless the binding's type says `set[...]`:

```aura
def main():
    sections = {1, 2, 2, 3}
    mut empty: set[str] = {}
    empty.add("math")
    print(sections)
    print(empty)
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
{1, 2, 3}
{math}
```

A set has no positions, so it has no indexing and no `get`. You can loop over
one with a bare `for` or consume it with `for value in own`, but not with
`for value in mut`. Changing a value in place could make it equal to another
value already in the set, and the set would no longer hold each value once.
Sets currently iterate in the order values were added, but that order isn't
part of the contract, so if you need a particular order, sort:
`sorted(struggling)` gives you a sorted list.

You may be used to Python's set operators, `a | b` for union and `a & b` for
intersection. Aura doesn't have them yet; `|` on two sets is an `AU2003`
error, because the compiler only knows `|` as a bitwise operator on integers.
For now, a comprehension or a short loop does the job, and comprehensions are
where we're going next.

## Choosing a collection

With three collection types, the choice usually comes down to the question
you'll ask most. If order matters, or duplicates do, use a list. If you look
things up by a key, use a dictionary. If you only need to know whether
something is present, use a set. When a program needs more than one view of
the same data, as our gradebook does with `scores` and `best`, it's normal to
keep more than one collection, each owning its own copy of the keys.

In the next section we'll stop writing so many loops. Comprehensions build a
list, a set, or a dictionary from another collection in one expression, and a
handful of builtins compute sums, minimums, and sorted copies without a loop
at all.

## Source: docs/book/ch08-04-comprehensions-and-builtins.md

# Comprehensions and builtins

By now our gradebook code has a lot of loops that look the same: make an
empty collection, walk another one, maybe test something, append. Python
programmers write most of those as comprehensions, and Aura has the same
syntax for lists, sets, and dictionaries. It also has the builtins you'd
reach for next, such as `sum`, `max`, and `sorted`, so that a question like
"what's the best score in the class?" takes one line instead of five.

## List, set, and dictionary comprehensions

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
def main():
    scores = [72, 95, 64, 88, 91]
    curved = [score + 5 for score in scores]
    passing = [score for score in scores if score >= 70]
    bands: set[int64] = {score // 10 * 10 for score in scores}
    print(curved)
    print(passing)
    print(bands)
```

<span class="caption">Listing 8-15: A list comprehension, a filtered one, and a set comprehension</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
[77, 100, 69, 93, 96]
[72, 95, 88, 91]
{70, 90, 60, 80}
```

A comprehension reads the way it does in Python. The expression at the front
is what goes into the new collection, the `for` clause says where the values
come from, and an optional `if` keeps only some of them. Square brackets make
a list and braces make a set, which here collapses the five scores into the
four distinct grade bands they fall into.

Each comprehension runs as soon as it's evaluated and produces a complete,
owned collection. There's nothing lazy about it. The source is read with
shared access, as in a bare `for` loop, so `scores` is unchanged afterwards
and can't be changed while the comprehension is running.

The loop name, `score` here, belongs to the comprehension alone. It doesn't
exist after the closing bracket, and it can't reuse a name that's already in
use around it:

```aura check-fail:AU2999
def main():
    score = 100
    scores = [72, 95]
    curved = [score + 5 for score in scores]
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2999]: comprehension binding `score` would shadow an existing name
 --> src/main.au:4:29
  |
4 |     curved = [score + 5 for score in scores]
  |                             ^
```

In Python 3 the comprehension's `score` would quietly hide the outer one
inside the brackets, and `score + 5` would mean the loop value. That's
probably what you meant, but a reader has to know the scoping rule to be
sure. Aura applies the same no-shadowing rule it uses for `for` loops, so one
spelling means one thing throughout a function.

You can have more than one `for` clause, and the clauses nest the same way
written-out loops would, with the first clause outermost:

```aura
def main():
    names = ["ada", "grace", "alan"]
    assignments = [1, 2]
    slots = [f"{name}-{number}" for name in names for number in assignments if name != "alan"]
    print(slots)
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
[ada-1, ada-2, grace-1, grace-2]
```

A dictionary comprehension uses braces with a `key: value` pair at the
front. Let's map each name to its length:

```aura check-fail:AU3002
def main():
    names = ["ada", "grace", "alan"]
    lengths = {name: name.len() for name in names}
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU3002]: cannot move borrowed value `name`
 --> src/main.au:3:16
  |
3 |     lengths = {name: name.len() for name in names}
  |                ^
  = related src/main.au:3:37: value is borrowed here
  = help: comprehensions store owned values; call `.clone()` on this shared value, or use an explicit consuming loop when the source should be transferred
  = fix: replace src/main.au:3:20-3:20 with `.clone()`
```

This is the same situation as the dictionary keys in the last section, seen
from another angle. The comprehension walks `names` with shared access, so
each `name` is borrowed from the list. The new dictionary has to own its keys,
and it can't own a string that the list still owns. The numbers in the first
listing didn't have this problem because they're copy values. The help line
gives both ways out: clone each name, or, if you're done with `names`, write
a `for name in own names` loop that moves each string into the dictionary
without copying.

```aura
def main():
    names = ["ada", "grace", "alan"]
    lengths = {name.clone(): name.len() for name in names}
    print(lengths)
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
{ada: 3, grace: 5, alan: 4}
```

`name.len()` needed no clone, because it produces a new number rather than
storing the name. The rule to remember is that whatever ends up *in* the new
collection must be owned by it: copy values copy, freshly computed values
such as `name.len()` or `name.to_upper()` are already owned, and owned values
borrowed from the source need `.clone()`.

Comprehensions only take the bare form of `for`. Writing `for name in mut
names` or `for name in own names` inside the brackets is a syntax error
(`AU1101`), and the message tells you to use a statement loop for those.

### Two things comprehensions don't do

Python lets you drop the brackets inside a function call, as in `sum(score *
2 for score in scores)`, to make a *generator expression* that produces
values one at a time. Aura has no generators:

```aura check-fail:AU2005
def main():
    scores = [72, 95]
    print(sum(s * 2 for s in scores))
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2005]: generator expressions are unavailable; use an eager owned list comprehension or an explicit loop
 --> src/main.au:3:21
  |
3 |     print(sum(s * 2 for s in scores))
  |                     ^
```

Add the brackets, `sum([s * 2 for s in scores])`, and you get a list
comprehension, which builds the whole list first. For the collection sizes in
most programs that's fine.

The second limitation is a bug in the current compiler rather than a design
choice, and it's easy to trip over. A comprehension whose output calls a
method on the loop name, written directly as an argument to a function, isn't
resolved properly:

```aura check-fail:AU2001
def main():
    names = ["ada", "grace"]
    print([name.len() for name in names])
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2001]: unknown name `name`
 --> src/main.au:3:12
  |
3 |     print([name.len() for name in names])
  |            ^
```

The same comprehension works when you bind it to a name first, as in
`lengths = [name.len() for name in names]` followed by `print(lengths)`, and
that's the style this book uses.

## Reducing a collection to one value

Five builtins take a collection and boil it down to a single answer:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
def main():
    scores = [72, 95, 64, 88, 91]
    print(sum(scores))
    print(min(scores))
    print(max(scores))
    print(any([score < 65 for score in scores]))
    print(all([score >= 60 for score in scores]))
    print(sum(range(1, 11)))
    print(max(72, 95, 64))
    average = sum(scores).to_float() / len(scores).to_float()
    print(f"average {average:.1f}")
```

<span class="caption">Listing 8-16: `sum`, `min`, `max`, `any`, and `all`</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
410
64
95
true
true
55
95
average 82.0
```

`sum`, `min`, and `max` work on a list, a set, or a range of numbers, and
return the element type: these scores are `int64`, so the sum is an `int64`.
`any` and `all` take a collection of `bool`s, which a comprehension is good
at producing; `any` stops at the first `true` and `all` at the first `false`.
`min` and `max` also accept two or more separate numbers of the same type, as
in `max(72, 95, 64)`. All of them read the collection with shared access and
leave it as it was.

The average shows a step you'll write often. `sum(scores)` and `len(scores)`
are both integers, and Aura doesn't do integer `/`, so we convert each to a
`float64` with `.to_float()` before dividing. Python's `/` silently turns two
integers into a float; Aura makes you say so, for the reasons we saw in
[Chapter 3](/book/ch03-00-common-concepts).

Each builtin has a defined answer for an empty collection where one makes
sense. `sum` of nothing is zero, `any` of nothing is `false`, and `all` of
nothing is `true`. There's no sensible minimum or maximum of nothing, so
`min` and `max` trap:

```aura
def main():
    empty: list[int64] = []
    print(max(empty))
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU4001]: `max(...)` of an empty collection
 --> src/main.au:3:11
  |
3 |     print(max(empty))
  |           ^
  = note: Aura call chain (innermost first): main at 1:1
```

Python raises a `ValueError` here. When a list may be empty, check
`values.is_empty()` before asking for its maximum.

One more note on `sum`: it uses the same checked `+` as the rest of the
language, so adding up `int64` values that overflow stops with `AU4002`
instead of wrapping around to a negative number.

## Building new lists

Another group of builtins and operators make a new list from existing ones:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
def main():
    scores = [72, 95, 64, 88, 91]
    print(sorted(scores))
    print(sorted(scores, reverse=true))
    print(reversed(scores))
    print(scores[::-1])
    print(scores[::2])
    print(scores + [100, 59])
    print([0] * 3)
    print(list(range(1, 6)))
    print(scores)
```

<span class="caption">Listing 8-17: Making sorted, reversed, joined, and repeated lists</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
[64, 72, 88, 91, 95]
[95, 91, 88, 72, 64]
[91, 88, 64, 95, 72]
[91, 88, 64, 95, 72]
[72, 64, 91]
[72, 95, 64, 88, 91, 100, 59]
[0, 0, 0]
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
[72, 95, 64, 88, 91]
```

The last line is the important one: none of these touched `scores`. Each
one copies elements into a fresh list. That's the difference between
`sorted(scores)` and `scores.sort()`, and between `reversed(scores)` and
`scores.reverse()`: the builtin gives you a new list and works on a value you
only have shared access to, while the method rearranges a list you can
change. `sorted` takes the same keyword arguments as `sort`, `key=` and
`reverse=`, and is stable in the same way. Unlike Python's `reversed`, which
returns a lazy iterator, Aura's returns a list.

A slice with a third number takes a step: `scores[::2]` keeps every second
element, and `scores[::-1]` walks backwards from the end, which reverses the
list. Steps work on lists and on strings. A step of zero traps, and so does
a negative step whose start and end don't make sense going backwards. Aura
never clamps a slice to fit, for steps or otherwise.

`+` joins two lists of the same element type into a new list, and `*`
repeats one. `list(range(1, 6))` turns a range into a real list, and
`list(some_set)` turns a set into one. When you want to *grow* a list rather
than build a new one, `scores += [100, 59]` on a mutable list adds the
elements in place, without copying the existing ones. That makes `+=` the
right choice inside a loop, where `scores = scores + more` would copy the
whole list on every step.

There are a few limits to know about. `sorted`, `reversed`, and `list` don't
take a `str` or a dictionary; to sort a dictionary's keys, write
`sorted(table.keys())`, as we did in the last section. And because each of
these copies elements, the element type has to be one that can be copied:
copy values, strings, lists, and classes made of those are all fine.

The names `sum`, `min`, `max`, `any`, `all`, `sorted`, `reversed`, and
`list` belong to the builtins, so a top-level function can't use them:
`def sum(...)` is rejected with `AU2007`. A local binding can still have one
of those names, although giving a binding the same name as a builtin is
rarely a kindness to the reader.

## Putting it together

Let's put this section to work on the whole gradebook: rank the students by
average, find who needs help, and report the best single score.

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
def average(values: list[int64]) -> float64:
    return sum(values).to_float() / len(values).to_float()

def main():
    scores = {
        "ada": [72, 88, 95],
        "grace": [95, 91, 84],
        "alan": [64, 58, 77],
        "kathy": [81, 79, 90],
    }
    averages = [(name.clone(), average(marks)) for name, marks in scores.items()]
    ranking = sorted(averages, key=lambda entry: entry[1], reverse=true)
    for name, mean in ranking:
        print(f"{name:<6} {mean:.1f}")

    struggling = {name.clone() for name, marks in scores.items() if min(marks) < 70}
    print(f"needs help: {', '.join(sorted(struggling))}")

    best_marks = [max(marks) for marks in scores.values()]
    print(f"best single score: {max(best_marks)}")
    print(f"everyone has a pass: {all([mark >= 70 for mark in best_marks])}")
```

<span class="caption">Listing 8-18: Ranking, filtering, and summarizing the gradebook</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
grace  90.0
ada    85.0
kathy  83.3
alan   66.3
needs help: alan
best single score: 95
everyone has a pass: true
```

The first comprehension builds a list of `(name, average)` tuples, one per
student, cloning each name because the new list has to own it. `sorted` then
orders those tuples by their second element, highest first, and the `for`
loop unpacks each tuple back into a name and an average.

You might have expected a dictionary from name to average here. It would be
natural, and `sorted(scores.keys(), key=lambda name: averages[name])` is what
you'd write in Python. In Aura that lambda would *take ownership* of
`averages`, because a lambda that uses a local value captures it by moving it
in, and then the `print` loop couldn't read `averages` any more. The compiler
says exactly that ("value moved into closure here") if you try.
[Chapter 13](/book/ch13-00-closures-and-decorators) explains closures and
captures properly. Sorting a list of tuples sidesteps the question, because
the lambda only uses its own parameter.

The rest is the builtins at work: a set comprehension with a filter for the
students who scored below 70 at least once, `sorted` to print them in a
predictable order, and `max` used twice, once inside a comprehension for each
student's best and once over those bests.

Everything in this section has worked on general-purpose collections, where
each element can be any type. For tables of numbers there's one more type,
which trades that flexibility for speed and arithmetic on a whole table at
once.

## Source: docs/book/ch08-05-numeric-arrays.md

# Numeric arrays

Our gradebook is really a table: one row per student, one column per
assignment, a number in every cell. We've been storing it as a dictionary of
lists, which is flexible, and that flexibility costs something. Each list is
its own allocation, each row can have a different length, and every
calculation is a loop we write by hand. When the data is a rectangular table
of numbers and the work is arithmetic, Aura has a type built for it:
`Array[T]`.

If you've used NumPy, `Array` will feel like a small, strict version of it.
It holds numbers of one type in a single contiguous block of memory, laid out
row by row, with a *shape* that says how many rows and columns (or more
dimensions) there are. You can add two arrays, multiply one by a number, or
take the mean of all of them without writing a loop, and those operations run
as tight loops over the block.

## Making an array

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
def main():
    scores = Array[float64].from_list(
        [72.0, 88.0, 95.0,
         95.0, 91.0, 84.0,
         64.0, 58.0, 77.0],
        [3, 3],
    )
    print(scores)
    print(scores.shape())
    print(scores.len())
    print(scores[1, 2])
    print(scores[-1, 0])
    print(scores.get([0, 1]))
    print(scores.get([5, 1]))
```

<span class="caption">Listing 8-19: Building a 3-by-3 array and reading from it</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
Array[float64](shape=[3, 3], values=[72.0, 88.0, 95.0, 95.0, 91.0, 84.0, 64.0, 58.0, 77.0])
[3, 3]
9
84.0
64.0
88.0
None
```

`Array[float64].from_list(values, shape)` copies the numbers from a list and
arranges them into the shape you give, filling the first row, then the
second, and so on. The line breaks in the list are only for us; to Aura it's
nine numbers. `shape()` gives the shape back as a `list[int64]`, and `len()`
is the total number of elements, here 3 times 3.

The type in brackets is the array's *dtype*, its element type, and there are
exactly four choices: `int32`, `int64`, `float32`, and `float64`. Anything
else is refused:

```aura check-fail:AU2002
def main():
    a = Array[str].zeros([2])
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2002]: Array dtype must be one of `int32`, `int64`, `float32`, or `float64`, found `str`
 --> src/main.au:2:9
  |
2 |     a = Array[str].zeros([2])
  |         ^
```

Two other constructors make arrays without a list:
`Array[int64].zeros([2, 3])` fills a shape with zeros, and
`Array[float64].full([2, 2], 0.5)` fills it with a value you choose.

The shape is a runtime value, not part of the type. A 3-by-3 array and a
1-by-100 array are both `Array[float64]`, so the compiler can't check that a
shape matches its data. That check happens when the array is built:

```aura
def main():
    a = Array[float64].from_list([1.0, 2.0, 3.0], [2, 2])
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU4007]: array shape [2, 2] requires 4 values, but storage contains 3
 --> src/main.au
  = note: Aura call chain (innermost first): main at 1:1
```

`AU4007` is the trap code for array shape problems, and you'll see it again.

### Reading one element

An array index has one coordinate per dimension, separated by commas:
`scores[1, 2]` is row 1, column 2, counting from zero. Negative coordinates
count from the end of their own axis, as with lists. The number of
coordinates has to match the number of dimensions, and since the shape is
only known at run time, so is this check:

```aura
def main():
    a = Array[float64].zeros([2, 2])
    print(a[1])
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU4007]: array rank 2 requires 2 coordinates, found 1
 --> src/main.au:3:13
  |
3 |     print(a[1])
  |             ^
  = note: Aura call chain (innermost first): main at 1:1
```

A coordinate that's out of range traps with `AU4003`. For coordinates that
might be bad, `get` takes them as a list and returns `T | None`, so
`scores.get([5, 1])` is `None` instead of a trap. An array element is always
a number, never `None`, so a plain optional is enough here; there's no need
for the `Lookup` type that lists and dictionaries use.

## Changing an array

Changing an array follows the same rule as changing anything else: you need a
mutable binding.

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
def main():
    mut grid = Array[int64].zeros([2, 3])
    grid[0, 1] = 7
    old = grid.set([1, 2], 3)
    print(grid)
    print(old)
    mut bonus = Array[float64].full([2, 2], 0.5)
    bonus.fill(1.5)
    print(bonus)
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
Array[int64](shape=[2, 3], values=[0, 7, 0, 0, 0, 3])
0
Array[float64](shape=[2, 2], values=[1.5, 1.5, 1.5, 1.5])
```

Indexed assignment writes one element. `set` does the same and hands back
the value it replaced, and `fill` overwrites every element. Without `mut`,
the compiler stops at the first write:

```aura check-fail:AU3003
def main():
    a = Array[float64].zeros([2, 2])
    a[0, 0] = 1.0
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU3003]: cannot assign through immutable place `a[..]`
 --> src/main.au:3:5
  |
3 |     a[0, 0] = 1.0
  |     ^
```

An array can't grow or shrink. Its shape is fixed when it's made, and there's
no `append`, `reshape`, or `transpose`. To get a different shape, build a new
array.

## Arithmetic on whole arrays

Here's where arrays earn their place:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
def to_percent(score: float64) -> float64:
    return score / 100.0

def main():
    scores = Array[float64].from_list([72.0, 88.0, 95.0, 64.0], [2, 2])
    weights = Array[float64].from_list([0.5, 0.5, 0.25, 0.75], [2, 2])
    print(scores + 5.0)
    print(scores * weights)
    print(scores.map(to_percent))
    print(scores.sum())
    print(scores.min())
    print(scores.max())
    print(scores.mean())
    print(sum(scores))
```

<span class="caption">Listing 8-20: Elementwise arithmetic, `map`, and reductions</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
Array[float64](shape=[2, 2], values=[77.0, 93.0, 100.0, 69.0])
Array[float64](shape=[2, 2], values=[36.0, 44.0, 23.75, 48.0])
Array[float64](shape=[2, 2], values=[0.72, 0.88, 0.95, 0.64])
319.0
64.0
95.0
79.75
319.0
```

`scores + 5.0` adds five to every element and returns a new array.
`scores * weights` multiplies the two arrays element by element, which is
*not* matrix multiplication; Aura arrays don't have that. `+`, `-`, `*`, and,
for floating-point arrays, `/` all work this way, with either two arrays or
an array and a single number. `map` applies a function to every element and
returns a new array of the results. `sum`, `min`, and `max` reduce the whole
array to one number of its dtype, and the builtin `sum(scores)` does the same
as `scores.sum()`. `mean` always returns a `float64`, even for an integer
array, so you never lose the fraction.

Every one of these produces a new array and leaves `scores` alone. Arrays are
owned values, so assigning one to another name moves it, and `.clone()` makes
an independent copy when you need two.

### The rules are strict on purpose

NumPy will happily combine arrays of different shapes by *broadcasting*, and
arrays of different types by promoting one of them. Those rules are
convenient and also a common source of results that are subtly wrong: a
column added to a row silently becomes a table. Aura has neither. Two arrays
in one operation must have exactly the same shape:

```aura
def main():
    a = Array[float64].zeros([2, 2])
    b = Array[float64].zeros([2, 3])
    print(a + b)
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU4007]: array operands require the same shape and dtype, found [2, 2] float64 and [2, 3] float64
 --> src/main.au:4:11
  |
4 |     print(a + b)
  |           ^
  = note: Aura call chain (innermost first): main at 1:1
```

and the same dtype, which the compiler can check before the program runs,
because the dtype is part of the type:

```aura check-fail:AU2002
def main():
    a = Array[float64].zeros([2, 2])
    b = Array[float32].zeros([2, 2])
    print(a + b)
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2002]: Array arithmetic requires matching dtypes, found `Array[float64]` and `Array[float32]`
 --> src/main.au:4:11
  |
4 |     print(a + b)
  |           ^
```

A single number has to have exactly the array's dtype, too. An `int64`
binding doesn't become a `float64` because it's next to a float array:

```aura check-fail:AU2002
def main():
    a = Array[float64].zeros([2, 2])
    bonus: int64 = 5
    print(a + bonus)
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2002]: Array arithmetic requires scalar dtype `float64`, found `int64`
 --> src/main.au:4:11
  |
4 |     print(a + bonus)
  |           ^
```

Write the number as a float literal, `5.0`, or convert the binding with
`bonus.to_float()`. Be careful with integer literals in particular. At the
time of writing, `a + 5` on a `float64` array gets past `aura check` and
then traps when it runs:

```aura
def main():
    a = Array[float64].zeros([2, 2])
    print(a + 5)
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU4007]: array float64 storage requires float64 scalar at flat index 0, found 5
 --> src/main.au:3:11
  |
3 |     print(a + 5)
  |           ^
  = note: Aura call chain (innermost first): main at 1:1
```

That's a compiler bug, not a rule; the checker ought to reject it with
`AU2002`, as it does for the `int64` binding. Until it's fixed, write
`5.0`.

Integer arrays don't support `/` at all, for the same reason integers don't:
it's unclear whether you want floor division or a fraction.

```aura check-fail:AU2003
def main():
    a = Array[int64].zeros([2, 2])
    print(a / 2)
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2003]: integer Array `/` is not supported
 --> src/main.au:3:11
  |
3 |     print(a / 2)
  |           ^
  = help: map the values to `float32` or `float64` before using true division
```

Integer arrays keep Aura's checked arithmetic: an `int64` array sum that
overflows traps rather than wrapping. If you want wrapping or saturating
arithmetic, integer arrays have the same `wrapping_add`, `saturating_mul`,
and related methods as integer scalars.

Last, a reduction needs something to reduce. `sum` of an empty array is
zero, but there's no mean of nothing:

```aura
def main():
    a = Array[float64].zeros([2, 0])
    print(a.len())
    print(a.sum())
    print(a.mean())
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
0
0.0
error[AU4007]: cannot compute array mean over an empty array
 --> src/main.au
  = note: Aura call chain (innermost first): main at 1:1
```

`min` and `max` behave the same way. A dimension of zero is allowed, so a
2-by-0 array exists; it has no elements.

## Slicing rows

A slice of an array selects whole rows: `scores[1:3]` is a new array with
rows 1 and 2 and every column. It works only on the first axis, and it's a
copy, not a view, so changing the slice doesn't change the original. There's
no step, either; `a[::2]` is refused with `AU2003` and a suggestion to
convert to a list first. That's enough for our gradebook, which needs one
student's row at a time:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
def column_mean(table: Array[float64], column: int64) -> float64:
    rows = table.shape()[0]
    mut total = 0.0
    for row in range(rows):
        total += table[row, column]
    return total / rows.to_float()

def main():
    names = ["ada", "grace", "alan", "kathy"]
    scores = Array[float64].from_list(
        [72.0, 88.0, 95.0,
         95.0, 91.0, 84.0,
         64.0, 58.0, 77.0,
         81.0, 79.0, 90.0],
        [4, 3],
    )
    for i, name in enumerate(names):
        row = scores[i:i + 1]
        print(f"{name:<6} mean {row.mean():.1f}, best {row.max():.0f}")

    assignments = scores.shape()[1]
    for column in range(assignments):
        print(f"assignment {column + 1}: {column_mean(scores, column):.1f}")

    overall = scores.mean()
    spread = scores - overall
    print(f"class mean {overall:.2f}, from {spread.min():.2f} to {spread.max():+.2f}")
```

<span class="caption">Listing 8-21: The gradebook as an array</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
ada    mean 85.0, best 95
grace  mean 90.0, best 95
alan   mean 66.3, best 77
kathy  mean 83.3, best 90
assignment 1: 78.0
assignment 2: 79.0
assignment 3: 86.5
class mean 81.17, from -23.17 to +13.83
```

The per-student numbers come from row slices, so they need no loop of our
own. The per-assignment averages are columns, and since slices only cut
rows, `column_mean` walks down a column with a loop. That's the honest cost
of a deliberately small array type: you get exact, predictable arithmetic,
and for column operations you sometimes write the loop. The last two lines
subtract the class mean from every score in one step and report how far the
lowest and highest scores sit from it.

Arrays have a few more limits worth knowing before you plan a program around
them. They live in ordinary memory on the CPU. They have no equality, so `a
== b` is an `AU2003` error, no views, and no reshaping. The
[Manual](/manual/numeric-arrays) lists exactly what's there, along with
measured performance against NumPy and Rust.

## Summary

You now know the collections that most Aura programs are built from. Lists
keep values in order and give you indexing, slicing, sorting, and in-place
changes through `mut`. Strings are owned UTF-8 text that counts characters as
Unicode scalars, slices without ever splitting one, and offers methods for
the splitting, searching, and formatting that text processing needs.
Dictionaries map keys to values in insertion order, sets answer membership
questions, and both make you be explicit about absence with `Lookup` or
`in`. Comprehensions and builtins such as `sum`, `max`, and `sorted` turn
most of the loops you'd write over these into one expression, and `Array[T]`
handles rectangular tables of numbers with whole-array arithmetic.

Running through all of it is ownership. A collection owns its elements, so
storing a value moves it in, reading one gives you shared access or a copy,
and the compiler tells you when a string or a list would end up with two
owners. You've also met a lot of traps along the way: indexes past the end,
missing keys, `remove` of a value that isn't there, the `max` of an empty
list. In the [next chapter](/book/ch09-00-error-handling) we'll look at
errors properly: when a trap is the right response, and how to use `Result`
to report a problem to the caller and let it decide what to do.

## Source: docs/book/ch09-00-error-handling.md

# Error handling

Programs fail. A file is missing, a user types `80a` where a port number should
be, a loop reads one element past the end of a list. Python treats all of these
the same way: something raises an exception, the exception travels up the call
stack until a `try` block catches it, and if nothing catches it the program
prints a traceback and exits. That model is convenient to write, but a reader
looking at a function call cannot tell whether it might raise, or what it might
raise, without reading every function it calls.

Aura splits failures into two kinds and gives each its own mechanism. A failure
that means the program itself is wrong, such as an index out of range or a
broken invariant, is a *trap*: the current task stops at once, cleanup runs,
and the diagnostic points at the line that failed. A failure that a working
program should expect, such as bad input or a missing file, is a value. The
function returns a `Result`, its signature says so, and the compiler makes the
caller decide what to do with it. There is no third route. Aura has no
exceptions, no `raise`, and no way to catch a trap.

In this chapter we'll write a small loader for a settings file made of `key =
value` lines. The first version trusts its input and traps when the input is
wrong. We'll read those traps together, then rebuild the loader around
`Result`, the `try` operator, and an error enum of our own, so every way the
input can be wrong becomes something the caller can report. We finish with the
question you'll face in every program you write: for this particular failure,
should the program trap, or should it return an error?

By the end you will be able to read a trap diagnostic and its call chain, use
`assert` to state what must be true, design an error type for a small module,
propagate errors with `try` without losing information, and choose between the
two mechanisms with reasons you can explain to a reviewer.

## Source: docs/book/ch09-01-traps.md

# Traps: failures that stop a task

Our settings loader starts out with a hopeful view of its input. Every line of
a settings file should look like `port = 9000`: a key, an equals sign, a value.
So the first version splits each line on `=` and takes the two halves. Create a
file called `src/main.au` (in a new package from `aura new settings`, or
anywhere you like) and type this in:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
def parse_line(line: str) -> (str, str):
    parts = line.split("=")
    return (parts[0].trim(), parts[1].trim())

def main():
    lines = ["port = 9000", "workers = 4", "verbose"]
    for line in lines:
        (key, value) = parse_line(line)
        print(f"{key} -> {value}")
    print("loaded")
```

<span class="caption">Listing 9-1: A settings parser that assumes every line contains `=`</span>

The third line, `verbose`, is the kind of thing people write in settings files
all the time: a flag with no value. The program compiles, because nothing about
it is wrong as far as types and ownership go. Let's run it:

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
port -> 9000
workers -> 4
error[AU4003]: list index `1` is out of bounds for length `1`
 --> src/main.au:3:36
  |
3 |     return (parts[0].trim(), parts[1].trim())
  |                                    ^
  = note: Aura call chain (innermost first): parse_line at 1:1 -> main at 5:1
```

The first two lines worked. On the third, `"verbose".split("=")` produced a
list with one element, and `parts[1]` asked for a second one. Aura stopped the
program right there. This is a *trap*: a runtime failure that ends the current
task immediately. `loaded` never printed.

## Reading a trap

The diagnostic has the same shape as the compiler errors you've already met,
and it's worth reading line by line.

The header, `error[AU4003]: list index `1` is out of bounds for length `1``,
gives the code and a sentence with the actual values involved. Every runtime
diagnostic has a code in the `AU4xxx` range. `AU4003` is the code for bounds
and lookup failures; the [Manual](/manual/diagnostics) lists every code.
Because the message includes both the index and the length, you often know what
went wrong before you look at the source.

The `-->` line and the snippet under it point at the exact spot: line 3, column
36, the `1` inside `parts[1]`. The caret marks the operation that failed, not
the start of the statement.

The last line is the call chain. It reads innermost first: the trap happened in
`parse_line`, which is defined at line 1, and `parse_line` was called from
`main`, defined at line 5. In a small program that's obvious. In a program with
forty functions, the call chain is how you find the route the bad value took.
These are Aura frames only. You won't see interpreter internals or generated
code in them, and a native binary built with `aura build` reports the same
frames as `aura run`.

Notice also what happened to the output. The two lines printed before the trap
are still there. Aura writes program output to standard output and the
diagnostic to standard error, and it doesn't throw away output that was already
produced. If we hide standard error, we can see the exit status the shell gets:

```console
$ aura run src/main.au 2>/dev/null; echo $?
port -> 9000
workers -> 4
1
```

The final `1` comes from `echo $?`. A trapped program always exits with status
1, so a shell script or a CI job knows that something went wrong.

## What traps

Index errors aren't the only failures that trap. Every one of the following
stops the task with a diagnostic, and none of them can be ignored by accident.

Integer arithmetic is checked. If a result doesn't fit its type, Aura traps
with `AU4002` instead of wrapping around:

```aura
def main():
    mut retries: int8 = 125
    for attempt in range(5):
        retries += 1
    print(retries)
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU4002]: integer value `128` does not fit in `int8`
 --> src/main.au:4:9
  |
4 |         retries += 1
  |         ^
  = note: Aura call chain (innermost first): main at 1:1
```

C would quietly turn `128` into `-128` here, and Python would quietly grow the
integer. Aura does neither, because a counter that silently changes sign is a
bug that surfaces far from where it happened.

Dividing by zero traps with `AU4004`:

```aura
def share(budget: int64, workers: int64) -> int64:
    return budget // workers

def main():
    print(share(1000, 4))
    print(share(1000, 0))
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
250
error[AU4004]: division by zero
 --> src/main.au:2:12
  |
2 |     return budget // workers
  |            ^
  = note: Aura call chain (innermost first): share at 1:1 -> main at 4:1
```

A few other operations trap for the same reason: they were asked to do
something impossible with the values they were given. Reading a dictionary key
that isn't there with `settings["timeout"]` traps with `AU4003`. A numeric
conversion with `as` that doesn't fit, such as `5000000000 as int32`, traps
with `AU4002` (we'll look at conversions closely in [Chapter
10](/book/ch10-00-generics-traits-conversions)). And an assertion that turns
out to be false traps with `AU4001`, which brings us to the one trap you write
on purpose.

## Assertions

An `assert` statement states something that must be true for the program to
continue. If the condition is `false`, the task traps at the `assert`. Let's
say `share` should never be called with zero workers, and we want the program
to say so clearly rather than failing inside the division:

```aura
def share(budget: int64, workers: int64) -> int64:
    assert workers > 0, f"share() needs at least one worker, got {workers}"
    return budget // workers

def main():
    print(share(1000, 0))
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU4001]: share() needs at least one worker, got 0
 --> src/main.au:2:5
  |
2 |     assert workers > 0, f"share() needs at least one worker, got {workers}"
  |     ^
  = note: left = 0
  = note: right = 0
  = note: Aura call chain (innermost first): share at 1:1 -> main at 5:1
```

The message after the comma became the diagnostic's message. Without one, the
message is `assertion failed`. The two `note` lines are something the compiler
added for us: when the condition is a single comparison such as `workers > 0`,
a failed assertion reports the value on each side. Here `left` is `workers` and
`right` is the literal `0`. You'll come to rely on this in tests, where seeing
the actual value saves you from adding a `print` and running again. [Chapter
11](/book/ch11-00-testing) has more on how those values are reported.

The message is evaluated only when the assertion fails. So you can build an
expensive message, or call a function to describe the state, and pay for it
only on the failure path:

```aura
def explain(workers: int64) -> str:
    print("building the message")
    return f"bad worker count {workers}"

def main():
    workers = 4
    assert workers > 0, explain(workers)
    print("ok")
```

This prints only `ok`. The condition was true, so `explain` never ran.

The condition has to be a `bool`. If you're coming from Python you might write
`assert workers` to mean "workers is not zero", and Aura won't accept it:

```aura check-fail:AU2002
def share(budget: int64, workers: int64) -> int64:
    assert workers, "share() needs at least one worker"
    return budget // workers
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2002]: `assert` condition must have type `bool`, found `int64`
 --> src/main.au:2:5
  |
2 |     assert workers, "share() needs at least one worker"
  |     ^
  = help: Aura has no implicit truthiness; compare the value explicitly, for example `value != 0`
```

Aura has no truthiness anywhere in the language, so `assert` is no exception.
Write the comparison you mean.

One more property of assertions matters a great deal: Aura never removes them.
There's no release mode, optimization flag, or environment variable that strips
assertions out, the way `python -O` does. An `assert` you write runs in every
build. That makes assertions trustworthy for checking your own program's logic,
and it also means they are the wrong tool for checking input from the outside
world, as we'll see in [To trap or not to trap](/book/ch09-03-to-trap-or-not).

## What happens when a task traps

A trap stops the task it happens in. It doesn't stop instantly, though: before
the task ends, Aura runs any cleanup that the task had registered with `with`.
Here's a lock file that has to be removed however the block ends:

```aura
class Lockfile:
    path: str

    def __exit__(mut self) -> None:
        print(f"removing {self.path}")

def main():
    lines = ["port = 9000", "verbose"]
    with lock = Lockfile(path="settings.lock"):
        print(f"holding {lock.path}")
        parts = lines[1].split("=")
        print(parts[1])
    print("finished")
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
holding settings.lock
removing settings.lock
error[AU4003]: list index `1` is out of bounds for length `1`
 --> src/main.au:12:21
   |
12 |         print(parts[1])
   |                     ^
  = note: Aura call chain (innermost first): main at 7:1
```

`removing settings.lock` printed before the diagnostic, and `finished` never
printed. The `with` block's cleanup ran on the way out, and then the trap ended
`main`. If a cleanup step itself fails during a trap, the original trap stays
the one you see, because that's the failure you need to fix. [Chapter
14](/book/ch14-00-resources-and-cleanup) covers `with` and cleanup order in
full.

When `main` is the task that traps, the whole program ends. A task started
inside a task group is different. A trap ends that task only, and the task that
started it finds out by looking at the result:

```aura
def value_of(line: str) -> str:
    parts = line.split("=")
    return parts[1].trim()

def main():
    with group = TaskGroup():
        good = group.start(value_of, "port = 9000")
        bad = group.start(value_of, "verbose")
        match good.result():
            case TaskResult.Ready(value):
                print(f"good task: {value}")
            case TaskResult.Error(message):
                print(f"good task trapped: {message}")
            case TaskResult.Cancelled:
                print("good task was cancelled")
            case TaskResult.TimedOut:
                print("good task timed out")
        match bad.result():
            case TaskResult.Ready(value):
                print(f"bad task: {value}")
            case TaskResult.Error(message):
                print(f"bad task trapped: {message}")
            case TaskResult.Cancelled:
                print("bad task was cancelled")
            case TaskResult.TimedOut:
                print("bad task timed out")
    print("main is still running")
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
good task: 9000
bad task trapped: list index `1` is out of bounds for length `1`
main is still running
```

The second task trapped on the same `parts[1]` as before. Its trap became a
`TaskResult.Error` value in `main`, and `main` carried on. This is how a server
keeps running when one request handler hits a bug: the handler's task is the
unit that fails. Don't worry about the task group syntax yet; [Chapter
15](/book/ch15-00-concurrency) builds it up properly. The point here is the
boundary. A trap always ends a whole task, and the only place you can observe
it is from outside that task.

## No catching

If you've written Python, you may be reaching for `try` and `except` to wrap
`parse_line` and recover from the bad line. Aura doesn't have them, and the
compiler tells you so:

```aura check-fail:AU2005
def parse_port(text: str) -> int64:
    try:
        return int(text)
    except ValueError:
        return 8080
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2005]: `try`/`except` is not supported; use `Result` with `match` today
 --> src/main.au:2:5
  |
2 |     try:
  |     ^
```

There is no way, inside a task, to catch a trap and continue. Aura does this
deliberately. A trap means the program reached a state its author didn't plan
for. Code that catches every failure and carries on tends to carry on with
half-updated data, and the real bug shows up later somewhere unrelated. By
making traps uncatchable, Aura guarantees that when one happens you see it, at
the line where it happened, with the values that caused it.

That leaves our settings loader in an awkward spot. A line without `=` isn't a
bug in our program. It's a mistake in a file that some person wrote, and a good
loader should report it politely and keep its own state intact. For failures
like that, Aura has a second mechanism, and it's the subject of the next
section.

## Source: docs/book/ch09-02-recoverable-errors.md

# Recoverable errors with `Result`

When `parse_line` meets a line without `=`, the right response depends on who
is asking. A command-line tool should print a helpful message and exit with a
non-zero status. An editor plugin should underline the line. A server reloading
its configuration should keep the old settings and log a warning. `parse_line`
can't know which of these it's part of, so it shouldn't decide. Its job is to
say what went wrong and hand that answer back.

In Aura that answer is a value of type `Result[T, E]`. A `Result` is a generic
enum with two variants: `Result.Ok(value)` holds a successful value of type
`T`, and `Result.Err(error)` holds an error of type `E`. Because it's an
ordinary enum, everything you learned about enums and `match` in [Chapter
6](/book/ch06-00-enums-and-match) applies to it.

## Returning a `Result`

Let's change `parse_line` so a malformed line is an error the caller receives, instead of a trap:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
def parse_line(line: str) -> Result[(str, str), str]:
    parts = line.split("=")
    if parts.len() != 2:
        return Result.Err(f"expected `key = value`, found `{line}`")
    return Result.Ok((parts[0].trim(), parts[1].trim()))

def main():
    lines = ["port = 9000", "workers = 4", "verbose"]
    for line in lines:
        match parse_line(line):
            case Result.Ok((key, value)):
                print(f"{key} -> {value}")
            case Result.Err(message):
                print(f"skipping line: {message}")
    print("loaded")
```

<span class="caption">Listing 9-2: `parse_line` returns a `Result` and `main` decides what to do with each outcome</span>

The return type now reads as a sentence: on success, a pair of strings; on
failure, a `str` explaining why. Before indexing, the function checks the one
thing that made Listing 9-1 trap, and returns `Result.Err` with a message if
the line doesn't split into exactly two parts. The success path wraps the pair
in `Result.Ok`.

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
port -> 9000
workers -> 4
skipping line: expected `key = value`, found `verbose`
loaded
```

This time the program reached the end. `main` chose to skip the bad line and
say so, which is a policy, and the policy lives in `main` where it belongs.

### The compiler keeps you honest

A `Result[(str, str), str]` is not a pair of strings, and Aura won't let you
pretend it is. If we keep the old line from Listing 9-1 that destructured the
result directly, the checker stops us:

```aura check-fail:AU2999
def parse_line(line: str) -> Result[(str, str), str]:
    parts = line.split("=")
    if parts.len() != 2:
        return Result.Err(f"expected `key = value`, found `{line}`")
    return Result.Ok((parts[0].trim(), parts[1].trim()))

def main():
    lines = ["port = 9000", "workers = 4", "verbose"]
    for line in lines:
        (key, value) = parse_line(line)
        print(f"{key} -> {value}")
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2999]: tuple binding requires a tuple value, found `Result[(str, str), str]`
 --> src/main.au:10:10
   |
10 |         (key, value) = parse_line(line)
   |          ^
```

You have to look inside the `Result` before you can use the pair. And when you
do look with `match`, you have to handle both variants. Here's what happens if
we only write the case we're hoping for:

```aura check-fail:AU2999
def parse_line(line: str) -> Result[(str, str), str]:
    parts = line.split("=")
    if parts.len() != 2:
        return Result.Err(f"expected `key = value`, found `{line}`")
    return Result.Ok((parts[0].trim(), parts[1].trim()))

def main():
    match parse_line("verbose"):
        case Result.Ok((key, value)):
            print(f"{key} -> {value}")
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2999]: non-exhaustive match over `Result`: missing `Err(_)`
 --> src/main.au:8:5
  |
8 |     match parse_line("verbose"):
  |     ^
```

This is the core difference from exceptions. In Python, the fact that
`int(text)` can raise `ValueError` lives in the documentation, and forgetting
about it costs nothing until the day it happens. In Aura, the possibility of
failure is part of the return type, so you can't reach the value without
passing the place where the error would be.

## Parsing returns a `Result` too

Our values are numbers, so the next step is turning `"9000"` into an `int64`.
The builtin parsers `parse_int32`, `parse_int64`, and `parse_float64` all
return a `Result` whose error is a `str`:

```aura
def main():
    print(parse_int64("9000"))
    print(parse_int64("90o0"))
    print(parse_int64(""))
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
Result.Ok(9000)
Result.Err(invalid digit found in string)
Result.Err(cannot parse integer from empty string)
```

Printing a `Result` shows its variant and payload, which is handy while you're
exploring. Let's combine the two steps into a function that turns a line into a
key and a number:

```aura
def parse_line(line: str) -> Result[(str, str), str]:
    parts = line.split("=")
    if parts.len() != 2:
        return Result.Err(f"expected `key = value`, found `{line}`")
    return Result.Ok((parts[0].trim(), parts[1].trim()))

def parse_setting(line: str) -> Result[(str, int64), str]:
    match own parse_line(line):
        case Result.Ok((key, text)):
            match own parse_int64(text):
                case Result.Ok(number):
                    return Result.Ok((key, number))
                case Result.Err(message):
                    return Result.Err(message)
        case Result.Err(message):
            return Result.Err(message)

def main():
    print(parse_setting("port = 9000"))
    print(parse_setting("port = nine"))
    print(parse_setting("verbose"))
```

<span class="caption">Listing 9-3: Passing errors up by hand with nested `match`</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
Result.Ok((port, 9000))
Result.Err(invalid digit found in string)
Result.Err(expected `key = value`, found `verbose`)
```
