Two details are new here. The first is `match own`. A plain `match` on a value
looks at it through shared access, which is fine when you only read the
payload, as `main` did in Listing 9-2 when it printed `message`. Here we want
to move `key` into a new `Result.Ok` and move `message` into a new
`Result.Err`, and you can only move something out of a value you own. `match
own` consumes the scrutinee, so its payloads become owned bindings we're free
to hand on. If you leave `own` off, the compiler names the problem and suggests
both fixes: `match own`, or `.clone()` to move a copy instead. We'll see that
diagnostic in full a little later.

The second detail is the shape. Most of Listing 9-3 is plumbing: unwrap the
success, or return the error unchanged. The two lines that do the actual work
are buried in it. That pattern is so common that Aura has an operator for it.

## Propagating errors with `try`

`try expr` evaluates `expr`, which must produce a `Result`. If it's
`Result.Ok(value)`, the `try` expression produces `value` and execution
continues. If it's `Result.Err(error)`, the current function returns
`Result.Err(error)` immediately. Here's Listing 9-3 again with `try`:

```aura
def parse_line(line: str) -> Result[(str, str), str]:
    parts = line.split("=")
    if parts.len() != 2:
        return Result.Err(f"expected `key = value`, found `{line}`")
    return Result.Ok((parts[0].trim(), parts[1].trim()))

def parse_setting(line: str) -> Result[(str, int64), str]:
    (key, text) = try parse_line(line)
    number = try parse_int64(text)
    return Result.Ok((key, number))

def main():
    print(parse_setting("port = 9000"))
    print(parse_setting("port = nine"))
    print(parse_setting("verbose"))
```

<span class="caption">Listing 9-4: The same function with `try`</span>

The output is identical. `parse_setting` now reads top to bottom as the steps
it performs, and each `try` marks a place where it might return early. That
last part matters. A Python function can stop at any call that raises, and
nothing at the call site tells you. In Aura every early exit is either a
`return` or a `try`, so you can find all of them by reading the function.

`try` can't make a function fallible behind its caller's back. It only works
inside a function whose return type is a `Result`:

```aura check-fail:AU2999
def main():
    number = try parse_int64("9000")
    print(number)
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2999]: `try` requires the enclosing function to return `Result`, found `None`
 --> src/main.au:2:14
  |
2 |     number = try parse_int64("9000")
  |              ^
```

This `main` returns nothing, so a failed parse would have nowhere to go. At the
top of the program there's no caller left to pass the error to, which is why
`main` uses `match` and decides for itself.

## An error type of our own

So far every error has been a `str`. Strings are fine for a quick program, but
they have a cost: the only thing a caller can do with a string is show it to
someone. A caller that wants to treat a missing setting differently from a typo
has to search the message text, and the message text isn't a contract.

The better tool is an enum that lists the ways our loader can fail. Let's also
record line numbers, because "line 2: expected `key = value`" is far more
useful to whoever edits the file:

```aura
enum ConfigError:
    MissingEquals(int64)
    BadNumber(int64, str)
    MissingKey(str)
```

`MissingEquals` carries the line number. `BadNumber` carries the line number
and the parser's message. `MissingKey` names a required setting that never
appeared. Each variant holds exactly the data needed to describe that failure,
and nothing more.

Now `parse_line` returns `Result[(str, str), ConfigError]`. When we try to use
`try` on `parse_int64` in a function that returns that type, the compiler
objects:

```aura check-fail:AU2002
enum ConfigError:
    MissingEquals(int64)
    BadNumber(int64, str)

def parse_line(number: int64, line: str) -> Result[(str, str), ConfigError]:
    parts = line.split("=")
    if parts.len() != 2:
        return Result.Err(ConfigError.MissingEquals(number))
    return Result.Ok((parts[0].trim(), parts[1].trim()))

def parse_setting(number: int64, line: str) -> Result[(str, int64), ConfigError]:
    (key, text) = try parse_line(number, line)
    value = try parse_int64(text)
    return Result.Ok((key, value))
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2002]: `try` error type `str` does not match enclosing `Result` error type `ConfigError`
 --> src/main.au:13:13
   |
13 |     value = try parse_int64(text)
   |             ^
```

The first `try` is fine, because `parse_line` already returns a `ConfigError`.
The second would return a `str` from a function that promised a `ConfigError`.
`try` never changes an error's type silently, so we have two ways forward.

The first is to convert the error ourselves, at the point where we know the
line number. A small helper does it:

```aura check-fail:AU3002
enum ConfigError:
    MissingEquals(int64)
    BadNumber(int64, str)

def parse_value(number: int64, text: str) -> Result[int64, ConfigError]:
    match parse_int64(text):
        case Result.Ok(value):
            return Result.Ok(value)
        case Result.Err(message):
            return Result.Err(ConfigError.BadNumber(number, message))
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU3002]: cannot move `message` out of a shared match on `parse_int64(...)`
 --> src/main.au:10:61
   |
10 |             return Result.Err(ConfigError.BadNumber(number, message))
   |                                                             ^
  = related src/main.au:9:25: value is borrowed here
  = help: write `match own parse_int64(...)` to consume the scrutinee, or call `.clone()` to consume an independent copy
  = fix: replace src/main.au:10:68-10:68 with `.clone()`
```

This is the diagnostic promised earlier. We forgot `own`, so `message` is only
borrowed from the `Result`, and we're trying to move it into a new enum value.
The `related` line points at the binding, and the help line offers `match own`
or a clone. The parser's `Result` is a temporary we never use again, so
consuming it is the right fix: write `match own parse_int64(text):` and the
helper compiles.

The second way is to teach Aura how to turn a `str` into a `ConfigError`, so
`try` can do the conversion for us. When the error types differ, `try` looks
for an implementation of a trait named `From` whose source is the inner error
type. Aura doesn't predeclare `From`, so a module that wants this conversion
declares the trait itself and then implements it:

```aura
trait From[Source]:
    def from(value: own Source) -> Self

enum ConfigError:
    MissingEquals(int64)
    BadNumber(int64, str)
    Invalid(str)

impl From[str] for ConfigError:
    def from(value: own str) -> ConfigError:
        return ConfigError.Invalid(value)

def parse_line(number: int64, line: str) -> Result[(str, str), ConfigError]:
    parts = line.split("=")
    if parts.len() != 2:
        return Result.Err(ConfigError.MissingEquals(number))
    return Result.Ok((parts[0].trim(), parts[1].trim()))

def parse_setting(number: int64, line: str) -> Result[(str, int64), ConfigError]:
    (key, text) = try parse_line(number, line)
    value = try parse_int64(text)
    return Result.Ok((key, value))

def main():
    print(parse_setting(1, "port = 9000"))
    print(parse_setting(1, "port = nine"))
    print(parse_setting(2, "verbose"))
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
Result.Ok((port, 9000))
Result.Err(ConfigError.Invalid(invalid digit found in string))
Result.Err(ConfigError.MissingEquals(2))
```

Now `try parse_int64(text)` compiles. On failure, Aura calls `ConfigError.from`
with the `str` error and returns the converted value. Look at what we lost,
though. `from` receives only the string, so the `Invalid` variant has no line
number. `From` is the right tool when one error type maps naturally onto
another, such as a module's own I/O error wrapped into an application error.
When the conversion needs context that only the caller has, a helper like
`parse_value` keeps that context. We'll use the helper. Traits, including how
`From` fits into conversions generally, are the subject of [Chapter
10](/book/ch10-00-generics-traits-conversions).

## Looking up a required key

Once each line is parsed, we need to check that the required settings were
present. We'll collect the values in a `dict[str, int64]` and look up each
required key.

You already know from [Chapter 8](/book/ch08-03-dicts-and-sets) that
`values["port"]` traps when the key is missing, and that `get` returns a
`Lookup[T]` instead: `Lookup.Found(value)` or `Lookup.Missing`. `Lookup` isn't
a `Result`, because a missing key isn't an error in itself. It's a fact about
the dictionary, and the caller decides whether it's a problem:

```aura fragment
def require(values: dict[str, int64], key: own str) -> Result[int64, ConfigError]:
    match values.get(key):
        case Lookup.Found(value):
            return Result.Ok(value)
        case Lookup.Missing:
            return Result.Err(ConfigError.MissingKey(key))
```

For our loader a missing `port` is an error, so `require` turns
`Lookup.Missing` into `ConfigError.MissingKey`. The parameter is `own str`
because the error keeps the key; when we call `require(values, "port")`, the
string literal moves in.

This is also why `get` doesn't return `int64 | None`, even though the optional
values from Chapter 6 are the right type for "maybe there's a value" in your
own code. A dictionary can store optional values too. If a `dict[str, int64 |
None]` holds `None` for some key, `get` must be able to tell you "the key is
present and its value is `None`", which is `Lookup.Found(None)`, apart from
"the key isn't there", which is `Lookup.Missing`. A plain `T | None` would
collapse those two answers into one.

## The finished loader

Here is the whole program, with the error enum, both helpers, and a `main` that
runs four sample files:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
enum ConfigError:
    MissingEquals(int64)
    BadNumber(int64, str)
    MissingKey(str)

class Settings:
    port: int64
    workers: int64

def parse_line(number: int64, line: str) -> Result[(str, str), ConfigError]:
    parts = line.split("=")
    if parts.len() != 2:
        return Result.Err(ConfigError.MissingEquals(number))
    return Result.Ok((parts[0].trim(), parts[1].trim()))

def parse_value(number: int64, text: str) -> Result[int64, ConfigError]:
    match own parse_int64(text):
        case Result.Ok(value):
            return Result.Ok(value)
        case Result.Err(message):
            return Result.Err(ConfigError.BadNumber(number, message))

def require(values: dict[str, int64], key: own str) -> Result[int64, ConfigError]:
    match values.get(key):
        case Lookup.Found(value):
            return Result.Ok(value)
        case Lookup.Missing:
            return Result.Err(ConfigError.MissingKey(key))

def parse_settings(lines: list[str]) -> Result[Settings, ConfigError]:
    mut values: dict[str, int64] = {}
    for (index, line) in enumerate(lines):
        number = index + 1
        (key, text) = try parse_line(number, line)
        values[key] = try parse_value(number, text)
    port = try require(values, "port")
    workers = try require(values, "workers")
    return Result.Ok(Settings(port=port, workers=workers))

def describe(error: ConfigError) -> str:
    match error:
        case ConfigError.MissingEquals(number):
            return f"line {number}: expected `key = value`"
        case ConfigError.BadNumber(number, message):
            return f"line {number}: value is not a number ({message})"
        case ConfigError.MissingKey(key):
            return f"missing required setting `{key}`"

def load(lines: list[str]) -> int32:
    match parse_settings(lines):
        case Result.Ok(settings):
            print(f"listening on {settings.port} with {settings.workers} workers")
            return 0
        case Result.Err(error):
            print(f"config error: {describe(error)}")
            return 2

def main() -> int32:
    samples = [
        ["port = 9000", "workers = 4"],
        ["port = 9000", "verbose"],
        ["port = 90o0", "workers = 4"],
        ["port = 9000"],
    ]
    mut status: int32 = 0
    for sample in samples:
        if load(sample) != 0:
            status = 2
    return status
```

<span class="caption">Listing 9-5: A settings loader where every input mistake is a `ConfigError`</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au; echo $?
listening on 9000 with 4 workers
config error: line 2: expected `key = value`
config error: line 1: value is not a number (invalid digit found in string)
config error: missing required setting `workers`
2
```

Read `parse_settings` again and notice how little error handling it seems to
contain. Four `try` expressions mark the four places it can stop early, and
every one of them returns a `ConfigError` the caller can inspect. `describe`
turns each variant into a message, and because it's a `match` over the enum,
adding a fifth variant later will make the compiler point at `describe` until
we handle it.

`load` is where the policy lives. It prints the error and returns `2`, and
`main` passes a non-zero status back to the shell when any sample failed. A
`main` declared `-> int32` sets the process exit status to the value it
returns, which lets a script tell "the settings file was wrong" (status 2, from
our code) apart from "the program hit a bug" (status 1, from a trap).

The loader no longer traps on anything a user could type into a settings file.
It still contains code that could trap, though: `parts[0]` in `parse_line`
would trap on an empty list, and `index + 1` would trap on overflow. Those
aren't input problems. `split` always returns at least one part, and no list is
long enough for its index to overflow. Deciding which failures belong in a
`ConfigError` and which can safely stay traps is the question of the next
section.

## Source: docs/book/ch09-03-to-trap-or-not.md

# To trap or not to trap

You now have two ways for a function to fail. It can trap, which ends the task
with a diagnostic, or it can return `Result.Err`, which hands the problem to
its caller. Neither is better in general. Each one makes a different promise,
and choosing well is mostly a matter of asking one question about the failure:
whose mistake is it?

If the failure means the program itself is wrong, it should trap. If the
failure comes from the world the program lives in, such as a person, a file,
the network, or another service, it should be a `Result`. The rest of this
section works through that rule with the settings loader and shows where the
edges are.

## Mistakes in the world are values

Everything a user can put in a settings file is something our loader has to
expect. A missing `=`, a misspelled number, a forgotten key: none of these mean
our code is wrong, and all of them will happen. That's why Listing 9-5 turns
each one into a `ConfigError`. The caller can print it, log it, or fall back to
defaults, and the program keeps whatever state it had.

The same goes for anything that crosses the program's edge. Aura's own
libraries follow this rule. Reading a file returns `Result[str, io.Error]`,
because files go missing on working systems. Spawning a process, opening a
socket, and parsing JSON all return typed results. Even timeouts and
cancellations in the concurrency APIs come back as values you match on, not as
traps. If the standard library had to guess what your program wanted when a
file was missing, it would guess wrong for half its callers, so it doesn't
guess.

There's a second reason to keep input checks out of assertions. Aura never
strips `assert`, so an assertion would technically catch bad input in every
build. But a trap is a bad way to tell a user they made a typo. It prints a
diagnostic aimed at a programmer, names a line of *our* source, and exits with
status 1 as though the program crashed. A `ConfigError` lets us say "line 2:
expected `key = value`" and exit with a status we chose.

## Mistakes in the program are traps

Now consider the other side. Suppose the loader also checks that `workers` is
between 1 and 64, and reports `ConfigError.OutOfRange` otherwise. Once the
loader has done that, a `Settings` value with zero workers can only exist if
some code built one without going through the loader. That's a bug, and a bug
is exactly what a trap is for:

```aura
enum ConfigError:
    OutOfRange(str, int64)

class Settings:
    port: int64
    workers: int64

def checked_workers(workers: int64) -> Result[int64, ConfigError]:
    if workers < 1 or workers > 64:
        return Result.Err(ConfigError.OutOfRange("workers", workers))
    return Result.Ok(workers)

def share(budget: int64, settings: Settings) -> int64:
    assert settings.workers >= 1, "Settings.workers is checked when settings are loaded"
    return budget // settings.workers

def main():
    print(checked_workers(0))
    match checked_workers(4):
        case Result.Ok(workers):
            settings = Settings(port=9000, workers=workers)
            print(share(1000, settings))
        case Result.Err(error):
            print(error)
```

<span class="caption">Listing 9-6: Validate at the edge with `Result`, then state the invariant with `assert`</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
Result.Err(ConfigError.OutOfRange(workers, 0))
250
```

`checked_workers` is the edge, so it returns a `Result`. `share` sits inside
the program, where the check has already happened, so it asserts. Giving
`share` a `Result[int64, ConfigError]` return type would be a mistake: every
caller would have to handle an error that can't happen, and sooner or later
someone would handle it with a `match` arm that does nothing. The assertion
says something truer. It tells the reader what `share` relies on, and if a
later change breaks that, the trap will name `share` and the message will say
where the guarantee was supposed to come from.

The same reasoning applies to the operations that trap on their own. An index
out of range, a division by zero, an integer overflow: when these happen, the
code made an assumption that wasn't true. Aura traps on them because returning
a `Result` from every `+` and every `[i]` would bury real errors under
impossible ones.

## When you know more than the compiler

Sometimes the types say a call can fail and you know it can't. `parse_int64`
returns a `Result` whatever you pass it, even a constant you wrote yourself.
Aura has no `unwrap` method to say "I'm sure, trap if I'm wrong", so you write
that intent out with a `match` and an assertion in the branch that shouldn't
happen. Our first try is missing something:

```aura check-fail:AU1101
DEFAULT_PORT = "9000"

def parse_constant(text: str) -> int64:
    match parse_int64(text):
        case Result.Ok(value):
            return value
        case Result.Err(message):
            assert false, f"built-in constant `{text}` is not a number: {message}"

def main():
    print(parse_constant(DEFAULT_PORT))
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU1101]: function `parse_constant` is missing a return
 --> src/main.au:3:1
  |
3 | def parse_constant(text: str) -> int64:
  | ^
```

The checker treats `assert` as a statement that can fall through, even when its
condition is the literal `false`, so it sees a path through the `Err` branch
that never returns an `int64`. Adding `return 0` after the assertion satisfies
it. That line never runs, but writing it keeps the rule simple: only `return`
ends a function. With the return in place, changing the constant to `"9OOO"`
shows what the trap looks like:

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU4001]: built-in constant `9OOO` is not a number: invalid digit found in string
 --> src/main.au:8:13
  |
8 |             assert false, f"built-in constant `{text}` is not a number: {message}"
  |             ^
  = note: Aura call chain (innermost first): parse_constant at 3:1 -> main at 11:1
```

Use this sparingly, and only when the input really is under your control. If
the text could ever come from a file or a user, it belongs in a `Result`.

## Examples, prototypes, and tests

There are three places where trapping freely is fine. In a short example,
careful error handling can hide the idea being shown, so the example might
index a list without checking it. In a prototype, you often don't know yet how
a failure should be handled, and a trap marks the spot clearly. When you come
back to make the program solid, searching for `assert` and for direct indexing
gives you the list of places to decide.

Tests are the third place, and there trapping is the whole mechanism. A failed
`assert` in a test is how the test reports failure, as [Chapter
11](/book/ch11-00-testing) shows. Tests also push in the other direction,
though. Aura's test runner has no way to say "this case should trap", because
nothing in Aura can catch a trap. A function that returns `Result.Err` for bad
input can be tested directly: call it and match on the error. That makes
`Result` the easier design to test, which is one more reason to use it at your
program's edges.

## A few rules of thumb

When you're unsure, these questions usually settle it:

1. Could this failure happen while the program is working correctly, because of
   something outside it? Return a `Result`.
2. Would a caller ever want to react differently to different failures? Give
   the error an enum type, not a `str`.
3. Can the failure happen only if some code in this program is wrong? Trap, and
   use an `assert` with a message that explains the broken assumption.
4. Is a missing value normal and not an error at all? Return `T | None`, or, for collection lookups, use the `Lookup` that `get` gives you.

One honest warning before we move on. Aura makes you handle a `Result` before
you can use the value inside it, but it doesn't currently stop you from calling
a function that returns `Result[None, str]` and ignoring the result entirely:

```aura
def save(path: str) -> Result[None, str]:
    return Result.Err(f"disk full while writing {path}")

def main():
    save("settings.conf")
    print("saved")
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
saved
```

The error was dropped without a word. When a function returns a `Result` only
to report failure, make sure every call site matches on it or passes it on with
`try`.

## Summary

Aura gives failures two shapes. A trap stops the current task at the line that
failed, runs cleanup, and reports a diagnostic with a code, the values
involved, and the call chain. Traps can't be caught, which keeps bugs from
hiding. A `Result[T, E]` is an ordinary value that carries either a success or
an error. The compiler makes you look inside it before using the success,
`match` makes you handle both cases, and `try` passes an error up to the
caller, changing its type only through a `From` conversion you wrote. A small
enum like `ConfigError` lets callers act on errors without parsing messages,
and `Lookup` separates "not there" from "there, but `None`".

You've seen generic types several times now without our stopping to explain
them: `Result[T, E]` works for any `T` and `E`, `Lookup[T]` for any `T`, and
the `From` conversion was a trait we declared ourselves. [Chapter
10](/book/ch10-00-generics-traits-conversions) explains how to write generic
code of your own, how traits describe what a type can do, and how Aura converts
between types without ever doing it behind your back.

## Source: docs/book/ch10-00-generics-traits-conversions.md

# Generics, traits, and conversions

Every program eventually grows two functions that are the same except for a
type. One finds the largest `int64` in a list, the other the largest `str`. One
stack holds undo actions, another holds numbers. Copying the code works for a
while, and then a bug gets fixed in one copy and not the other. Python avoids
the problem by not checking types until the program runs, so one function can
accept anything and fail later if the thing doesn't support what the function
does with it. Aura checks types before the program runs, so it needs a way to
write code once and still say exactly what that code requires.

That way has two parts. *Generics* let a function, class, or enum take type
parameters, so `Stack[T]` works for any `T`. *Traits* describe behavior that a
type can promise, such as "has a price" or "can be compared with `<`", and let
generic code ask for exactly the behavior it uses. You've already been using
both without seeing their definitions: `Result[T, E]`, `Lookup[T]`, and
`list[T]` are generic types, and the `From` trait in the previous chapter told
`try` how to convert one error into another.

The third part of this chapter is conversions. Aura never converts a value from
one type to another unless you write the conversion, not even an `int32` to an
`int64`. We'll look at why, at the three ways to convert numbers and text, and
at how traits let your own types join in.

We'll build a generic stack and a `largest` function that first refuses to
compile, then use traits to describe priced items in a small shop and fix
`largest` along the way. By the end you'll be able to write generic code,
define and implement traits, give your own types operators and custom printing,
and convert between types deliberately.

## Source: docs/book/ch10-01-generics.md

# Generic functions and classes

Let's start with the duplication problem in its plainest form. Here are two
functions that find the largest value in a list, one for integers and one for
strings:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
def largest_int(values: own list[int64]) -> int64:
    mut rest = values
    mut best = rest.pop()
    while rest.len() > 0:
        candidate = rest.pop()
        if candidate > best:
            best = candidate
    return best

def largest_str(values: own list[str]) -> str:
    mut rest = values
    mut best = rest.pop()
    while rest.len() > 0:
        candidate = rest.pop()
        if candidate > best:
            best = candidate
    return best

def main():
    print(largest_int([3, 9, 4]))
    print(largest_str(["pear", "fig", "plum"]))
```

<span class="caption">Listing 10-1: Two functions that differ only in their types</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
9
plum
```

The functions take the list with `own` because they pull values out of it with
`pop`, and the result has to be an owned value we can return. An `own`
parameter can't be mutated in place, so the first line moves it into a `mut`
binding called `rest`. Apart from the types in the signatures, the two bodies
are character for character the same. We'd like to write the body once. We'll
come back to `largest` at the end of this section, because making it generic
turns out to need one more idea. First let's look at a case that works straight
away.

## A generic class

An editor keeps an undo history: a stack of actions, newest on top. A tool that
walks a directory tree keeps a stack of depths. Both are stacks, and the code
that pushes and pops doesn't care what's on the stack. Here is one `Stack`
class for both:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
class Stack[T]:
    items: list[T]

    def push(mut self, item: own T):
        self.items.append(item)

    def pop(mut self) -> T | None:
        if self.items.len() == 0:
            return None
        return self.items.pop()

    def size(self) -> int64:
        return self.items.len()

def main():
    mut undo: Stack[str] = Stack(items=[])
    undo.push("type hello")
    undo.push("delete word")
    print(undo.size())
    print(undo.pop())
    print(undo.pop())
    print(undo.pop())

    mut depths = Stack[int64](items=[])
    depths.push(3)
    print(depths.size())
    print(depths)
```

<span class="caption">Listing 10-2: A `Stack` class with a type parameter `T`</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
2
delete word
type hello
None
1
Stack(items=[3])
```

The `[T]` after the class name declares a *type parameter*. Inside the class,
`T` stands for whatever type a particular stack holds. The field `items` is a
`list[T]`, `push` takes a `T`, and `pop` returns `T | None` so that popping an
empty stack is an ordinary outcome instead of a trap. You could name the
parameter anything, but a single capital letter is the convention, and `T` is
the usual first choice.

`main` creates two stacks in the two ways Aura offers. The first annotates the
binding as `Stack[str]`, and the constructor call takes its type from that
annotation. The second writes the type argument on the constructor itself,
`Stack[int64](items=[])`. Both mean the same thing. What you can't do is leave
the type out entirely when nothing determines it: `Stack(items=[])` with no
annotation gives the compiler an empty list and no way to know what `T` is.
When the fields do determine it, as in `Stack(items=["a", "b"])`, you can leave
the type out and Aura will infer `Stack[str]`.

Once a stack has a type, it holds only that type. If we annotate a
`Stack[int64]` and give it strings, the checker catches the mismatch:

```aura check-fail:AU2002
class Stack[T]:
    items: list[T]

def main():
    s: Stack[int64] = Stack(items=["a"])
    print(s)
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2002]: list literal elements must all have type `int64`, found `str`
 --> src/main.au:5:36
  |
5 |     s: Stack[int64] = Stack(items=["a"])
  |                                    ^
```

A `Stack[int64]` and a `Stack[str]` are different types, and there's no general
"stack of anything" type that both fit into. Aura's generic arguments are
invariant: a `Stack[int32]` isn't a `Stack[int64]` either, even though every
`int32` value fits in an `int64`.

### Ownership in a generic signature

Look again at `push(mut self, item: own T)`. The `own` is there for a reason,
and the quickest way to see it is to take it away:

```aura check-fail:AU3002
class Stack[T]:
    items: list[T]

    def push(mut self, item: T):
        self.items.append(item)
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU3002]: parameter `item` is borrowed; declare it as `own T` to take ownership
 --> src/main.au:5:27
  |
5 |         self.items.append(item)
  |                           ^
  = related src/main.au:4:24: parameter `item` is borrowed here
  = help: declare the parameter as `own T` when the function should consume this non-cloneable value
```

A bare parameter gives the function shared access, as you learned in [Chapter
4](/book/ch04-00-understanding-ownership). Shared access lets `push` look at
`item` but not keep it, and storing it in the list is keeping it. For a
concrete type like `int64` that wouldn't matter, because integers are copy
values. But Aura checks a generic body once, for every possible `T`, before any
particular `T` is chosen. Some `T`s will be owned values like `str` or a list,
so the body has to be correct for them. The ownership mode you write in a
generic signature is fixed when the function is declared, and it stays the same
for every type the function is used with.

That gives you a simple rule. If a generic function stores, returns, or
otherwise consumes a `T` it receives, the parameter needs `own T`.

## Generic functions

Functions take type parameters the same way, in brackets after the name. Here
are two helpers that work on any stack:

```aura
class Stack[T]:
    items: list[T]

    def push(mut self, item: own T):
        self.items.append(item)

    def pop(mut self) -> T | None:
        if self.items.len() == 0:
            return None
        return self.items.pop()

    def size(self) -> int64:
        return self.items.len()

def pop_or[T](stack: mut Stack[T], fallback: own T) -> T:
    item = stack.pop()
    if item is None:
        return fallback
    return item

def drain[T](stack: mut Stack[T]) -> list[T]:
    mut out: list[T] = []
    while stack.size() > 0:
        item = stack.pop()
        if item is not None:
            out.append(item)
    return out

def main():
    mut undo: Stack[str] = Stack(items=[])
    undo.push("type hello")
    print(pop_or(undo, "nothing to undo"))
    print(pop_or(undo, "nothing to undo"))
    mut depths: Stack[int64] = Stack(items=[])
    depths.push(1)
    depths.push(2)
    print(drain(depths))
    print(depths.size())
```

<span class="caption">Listing 10-3: Generic functions that work on any `Stack[T]`</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
type hello
nothing to undo
[2, 1]
0
```

When we call `pop_or(undo, "nothing to undo")`, the compiler works out `T` from
the arguments: `undo` is a `Stack[str]`, so `T` is `str`, and the fallback must
be a `str` too. We never write `pop_or[str](...)`, although we could.

Inside `pop_or`, the test `item is None` narrows `item`. After the `if`
returns, the compiler knows `item` is a `T` and not `None`, so `return item`
matches the declared return type. `drain` uses the opposite test, `is not
None`, to append only real items. This is the same narrowing you saw for
optional values in [Chapter 6](/book/ch06-00-enums-and-match), and it works on
a type parameter as well as on a concrete type.

Sometimes there's nothing to infer from. Here's a small function that picks a value or a fallback:

```aura
def unwrap_or[T](value: own T | None, fallback: own T) -> T:
    if value is None:
        return fallback
    return value

def main():
    missing: int64 | None = None
    print(unwrap_or(missing, 5))
    print(unwrap_or("x".strip_prefix("y"), "default"))
    print(unwrap_or[str](None, "z"))
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
5
default
z
```

The first two calls give the compiler a typed first argument. In the third, a
bare `None` says nothing about `T`, so we write the type argument explicitly
with `unwrap_or[str]`. That bracket syntax is called explicit specialization,
and it works on constructors (`Stack[int64](...)`) and on enum variants
(`Result[int64, str].Ok(7)`) too.

## Generic enums

You've been using generic enums for a while, and Chapter 9 leaned on them
heavily. `Result[T, E]` is an enum with two type parameters, and `Lookup[T]`
has one. Your own enums can take parameters the same way:

```aura
enum Reply[T]:
    Value(T)
    Pending
    Failed(str)

def main():
    first: Reply[int64] = Reply.Value(42)
    second: Reply[int64] = Reply.Failed("timed out")
    for reply in [first, second]:
        match reply:
            case Reply.Value(number):
                print(number + 1)
            case Reply.Pending:
                print("pending")
            case Reply.Failed(reason):
                print(reason)
```

In the `Reply.Value(number)` arm, `number` has type `int64`, because the match
is over a `Reply[int64]`. The compiler substitutes the type argument into each
variant's payload.

## What generic code costs

When you build a native binary, Aura compiles a generic function separately for
each set of type arguments the program uses. `pop_or` called with a
`Stack[str]` and with a `Stack[int64]` becomes two pieces of machine code, each
working directly on its own type. You don't pay at run time for having written
the function once. The cost is in compile time and binary size, which grow a
little with every distinct instantiation. A diagnostic always names the
function as you wrote it, `pop_or`, never a generated copy.

Generic code is also checked against everything it does. If a generic body
copies a value of type `T`, the compiler remembers that `T` must be safe to
copy and checks it at every call site. Most types are, but a random-number
generator isn't, because duplicating it would make two generators produce the
same "random" sequence:

```aura check-fail:AU3007
import random

def snapshot[T](values: list[T]) -> list[T]:
    return values.copy()

def main():
    scores = [3, 9, 4]
    print(snapshot(scores))
    generators = [random.Rng(seed=1)]
    print(snapshot(generators).len())
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU3007]: cannot use function `snapshot` because `random.Rng` contains non-cloneable `random.Rng` state
 --> src/main.au:10:11
   |
10 |     print(snapshot(generators).len())
   |           ^
  = help: move or remove the value so it has one owner, or construct an independent generator with an explicit seed
```

The call with `scores` is fine. The call with a list of generators is rejected
at the call, with a message that says why. You didn't have to write the
requirement down; the compiler inferred it from the `.copy()` in the body. The
[Manual](/manual/generics-and-traits) has the full rules for these inferred
requirements.

## Back to `largest`

Now let's try to merge the two functions from Listing 10-1 into one:

```aura check-fail:AU2999
def largest[T](values: own list[T]) -> T:
    mut rest = values
    mut best = rest.pop()
    while rest.len() > 0:
        candidate = rest.pop()
        if candidate > best:
            best = candidate
    return best

def main():
    print(largest([3, 9, 4]))
```

<span class="caption">Listing 10-4: A generic `largest` that doesn't compile yet</span>

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2999]: unsupported operands for binary expression: `T`
 --> src/main.au:6:12
  |
6 |         if candidate > best:
  |            ^
```

The compiler points at the `>`. Everything else in the body works for any `T`:
popping, comparing lengths, assigning. But `>` isn't defined for every type:
there's no obvious meaning for comparing two stacks, or two settings files.
Because the body is checked once for all possible `T`s, and some `T`s have no
`>`, the body is rejected, even though our one call uses integers.

Python would run this and fail at run time on the first type without `>`. Aura
wants the requirement in the signature, so that a caller can see from the
declaration alone what `largest` needs from `T`, and so that the error lands at
the call that passes an unsuitable type instead of deep inside the function.
The way to state "T must support `>`" is a trait bound, and traits are the
subject of the next section.

## Source: docs/book/ch10-02-traits.md

# Traits

A trait names a set of methods that a type can promise to provide. Code that
works with "any type that has these methods" asks for the trait, and the
compiler checks the promise on both sides: that each type claiming the trait
really has the methods, and that generic code only calls methods the trait
provides. If you've used Python's abstract base classes, Go's interfaces, or
Rust's traits, the idea will be familiar. The Aura version is closest to
Rust's.

We'll leave `largest` broken for a moment and build up traits with a different
example: a small shop that sells books and coffee. Different items are priced
in different ways, but the till only needs to know a name and a price.

## Declaring and implementing a trait

Here's a trait for things with a price, and two classes that implement it:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
trait Priced:
    def name(self) -> str
    def price_cents(self) -> int64

    def label(self) -> str:
        return f"{self.name()}: {self.price_cents()} cents"

class Book:
    title: str
    pages: int64

class Coffee:
    size: str
    shots: int64

impl Priced for Book:
    def name(self) -> str:
        return self.title.clone()

    def price_cents(self) -> int64:
        return 500 + self.pages * 2

impl Priced for Coffee:
    def name(self) -> str:
        return f"{self.size} coffee"

    def price_cents(self) -> int64:
        return 300 + self.shots * 75

    def label(self) -> str:
        return f"{self.name()} ({self.shots} shots): {self.price_cents()} cents"

def main():
    novel = Book(title="Emma", pages=400)
    latte = Coffee(size="large", shots=2)
    print(novel.price_cents())
    print(novel.label())
    print(latte.label())
```

<span class="caption">Listing 10-5: A `Priced` trait with two required methods and one default method</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
1300
Emma: 1300 cents
large coffee (2 shots): 450 cents
```

The `trait` block lists method signatures. `name` and `price_cents` end at the
signature, with no body: they're *required*, and every implementation must
supply them. `label` has a body, which makes it a *default* method. An
implementation gets it for free and may replace it. A default method can call
the trait's other methods, as `label` does, because every type that implements
`Priced` is guaranteed to have them.

An `impl Priced for Book:` block is where `Book` keeps its promise. `Book` uses
the default `label`. `Coffee` overrides it to show the number of shots. Once
the implementation exists, the trait's methods are called like any other
method: `novel.label()`.

`Book.name` returns `self.title.clone()`. The method has shared access to
`self`, so it can't hand out the title it doesn't own; `clone` makes an
independent owned `str` to return.

The compiler holds implementations to the trait's contract. Leave out a
required method and the `impl` block is rejected where it starts:

```aura check-fail:AU2999
trait Priced:
    def price_cents(self) -> int64
    def name(self) -> str

class Sticker:
    design: str

impl Priced for Sticker:
    def price_cents(self) -> int64:
        return 99
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2999]: impl of `Priced` for `Sticker` is missing method `name`
 --> src/main.au:8:1
  |
8 | impl Priced for Sticker:
  | ^
```

Changing a signature is rejected too, even a change that looks harmless, like
returning `int32` where the trait says `int64`:

```aura check-fail:AU2999
trait Priced:
    def price_cents(self) -> int64

class Sticker:
    design: str

impl Priced for Sticker:
    def price_cents(self) -> int32:
        return 99
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2999]: method `price_cents` in impl of `Priced` does not match the trait signature
 --> src/main.au:8:5
  |
8 |     def price_cents(self) -> int32:
  |     ^
```

The receiver, the parameter types and their ownership modes, and the return
type all have to match. That strictness is what lets generic code rely on a
trait without seeing the implementations.

## Trait bounds

Now for the payoff. A generic function can require that its type parameter
implements a trait by writing a *bound* after the parameter: `T: Priced`.
Inside the function, any method of `Priced` can be called on a `T`:

```aura
trait Priced:
    def name(self) -> str
    def price_cents(self) -> int64

    def label(self) -> str:
        return f"{self.name()}: {self.price_cents()} cents"

class Book:
    title: str
    pages: int64

class Coffee:
    size: str
    shots: int64

impl Priced for Book:
    def name(self) -> str:
        return self.title.clone()

    def price_cents(self) -> int64:
        return 500 + self.pages * 2

impl Priced for Coffee:
    def name(self) -> str:
        return f"{self.size} coffee"

    def price_cents(self) -> int64:
        return 300 + self.shots * 75

    def label(self) -> str:
        return f"{self.name()} ({self.shots} shots): {self.price_cents()} cents"

def total_cents[T: Priced](items: list[T]) -> int64:
    mut total = 0
    for item in items:
        total += item.price_cents()
    return total

def print_receipt[T: Priced](items: list[T]):
    for item in items:
        print(item.label())
    print(f"total: {total_cents(items)} cents")

def main():
    books = [Book(title="Dune", pages=600), Book(title="Emma", pages=400)]
    print_receipt(books)
    order: list[Book | Coffee] = [Book(title="Dune", pages=600), Coffee(size="large", shots=2)]
    print_receipt(order)
```

<span class="caption">Listing 10-6: Generic functions bounded by `Priced`</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
Dune: 1700 cents
Emma: 1300 cents
total: 3000 cents
Dune: 1700 cents
large coffee (2 shots): 450 cents
total: 2150 cents
```

The bound works in both directions. Inside `total_cents`, it's what allows
`item.price_cents()`. Without it, the compiler has no reason to think a `T` has
that method:

```aura check-fail:AU2999
def total_cents[T](items: list[T]) -> int64:
    mut total = 0
    for item in items:
        total += item.price_cents()
    return total
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2999]: unsupported method call `price_cents` on `T`
 --> src/main.au:4:23
  |
4 |         total += item.price_cents()
  |                       ^
```

At the call site, the bound is a requirement the argument must meet.
`print_receipt(books)` is fine because `Book` implements `Priced`.

The second call is more interesting. `order` is a list of `Book | Coffee`, a
union of two types. A union satisfies a bound when every member implements the
trait with the same method signatures, so `print_receipt` accepts it, and each
`item.label()` call runs the implementation for whichever type that element
actually is. That's how you put different kinds of items in one list. Aura has
no "trait object" type that means "any `Priced` thing"; the union names the
exact set of types, and the compiler checks every one of them.

### Traits are nominal

Here's a mistake that comes naturally to a Python programmer. A `Sticker` class
has a `price_cents` method with exactly the right signature, but nobody wrote
`impl Priced for Sticker`:

```aura check-fail:AU2002
trait Priced:
    def price_cents(self) -> int64

class Sticker:
    design: str

    def price_cents(self) -> int64:
        return 99

def total_cents[T: Priced](items: list[T]) -> int64:
    mut total = 0
    for item in items:
        total += item.price_cents()
    return total

def main():
    print(total_cents([Sticker(design="cat")]))
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2002]: type `Sticker` does not implement trait `Priced`
 --> src/main.au:17:11
   |
17 |     print(total_cents([Sticker(design="cat")]))
   |           ^
```

In Python's duck typing, having the method would be enough. In Aura a type
implements a trait only through an `impl` block, never because its method names
happen to line up. A method called `price_cents` on a sticker might mean
something unrelated to the till's idea of a price, and `impl Priced for
Sticker` is where someone states that it means the same thing. It's one line of
ceremony in exchange for never being surprised by an accidental match.

### Several bounds, and traits that build on traits

A type parameter can have more than one bound, joined with `+`, as in `T:
Priced + Display`. The function can then call the methods of every trait in the
list, and the argument must implement all of them. We'll use that form shortly.

A trait can also require another trait. If every priced thing needs a name, we
can split `name` into its own trait and make `Priced` depend on it:

```aura
trait Named:
    def name(self) -> str

trait Priced: Named:
    def price_cents(self) -> int64

    def label(self) -> str:
        return f"{self.name()}: {self.price_cents()} cents"

class Book:
    title: str
    pages: int64

impl Priced for Book:
    def price_cents(self) -> int64:
        return 500 + self.pages * 2

impl Named for Book:
    def name(self) -> str:
        return self.title.clone()

def show[T: Priced](item: T):
    print(item.name())
    print(item.label())

def main():
    show(Book(title="Emma", pages=400))
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
Emma
Emma: 1300 cents
```

`trait Priced: Named:` reads "`Priced` requires `Named`". The second colon ends
the header. `Named` is a *supertrait* of `Priced`, so the default `label` can
call `self.name()`, and a bound of `T: Priced` gives `show` access to `name` as
well. Implementing `Priced` doesn't implement `Named` for you, though. If we
delete the `impl Named for Book` block, the compiler reports `impl of `Priced`
for `Book` requires supertrait `Named``.

## Traits the language knows about

A few traits have names the compiler recognizes, and implementing them changes
how your type behaves with the language's own syntax.

### `Display`: how a value prints

Prices in cents are awkward to read. Let's give them a type of their own:

```aura
copy class Money:
    cents: int64

impl Display for Money:
    def display(self) -> str:
        return f"${self.cents // 100}.{self.cents % 100:02}"

def main():
    price = Money(cents=1250)
    print(price)
    print(f"due today: {price}")
    print([price, Money(cents=5)])
    print(str(price).len())
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
$12.50
due today: $12.50
[$12.50, $0.05]
6
```

`Display` is part of every module's prelude, so we can implement it without
declaring it. Its one method, `display`, returns the text for the value.
`print`, `str()`, and f-strings all use it, and so does printing a `Money`
inside a list, which is why the third line shows `$12.50` instead of
`Money(cents=1250)`. A type without a `Display` implementation keeps the
structural rendering you've seen all along.

`Money` is a `copy class`, which makes its values copy values like integers. It
holds a single integer, so copying it is as cheap as copying the integer, and
we're about to pass prices around freely.

You can implement `Display` only for a class or enum declared in the same
module, and only once per type. One type gets one rendering, decided by the
module that owns it.

### Operators

Adding two `Money` values seems natural, but the compiler doesn't know what `+` means for them:

```aura check-fail:AU2999
copy class Money:
    cents: int64

def main():
    print(Money(cents=1300) + Money(cents=450))
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2999]: unsupported operands for binary expression: `Money`
 --> src/main.au:5:11
  |
5 |     print(Money(cents=1300) + Money(cents=450))
  |           ^
```

When no builtin rule applies, Aura turns `a + b` into a call to the `add`
method of a trait named `Add`. Unlike `Display`, the operator traits aren't
predeclared, so a module that wants one declares it with the shape the compiler
expects:

```aura
trait Add[Rhs, Out]:
    def add(self, rhs: Rhs) -> Out

copy class Money:
    cents: int64

impl Display for Money:
    def display(self) -> str:
        return f"${self.cents // 100}.{self.cents % 100:02}"

impl Add[Money, Money] for Money:
    def add(self, rhs: Money) -> Money:
        return Money(cents=self.cents + rhs.cents)

def main():
    book = Money(cents=1300)
    coffee = Money(cents=450)
    print(book + coffee)
    mut total = Money(cents=0)
    for price in [book, coffee, coffee]:
        total += price
    print(total)
```

<span class="caption">Listing 10-7: Implementing `Add` gives `Money` a `+` operator</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
$17.50
$22.00
```

`Add` is a generic trait with two parameters: the type on the right of the `+`
and the type of the result. `impl Add[Money, Money] for Money` says "a `Money`
plus a `Money` is a `Money`". Once that exists, `book + coffee` calls our
`add`, and `total += price` works too.

The other operators follow the same pattern: `Sub`, `Mul`, `Div`, `FloorDiv`,
and `Mod` for `-`, `*`, `/`, `//`, and `%`, `Neg` and `Not` for unary `-` and
`not`, and `Ord` for the comparisons `<`, `<=`, `>`, and `>=`. The
[Manual](/manual/generics-and-traits) lists each trait's exact shape. Two
things stay fixed: `==` and `!=` always use Aura's builtin structural equality,
and `and` and `or` can't be overloaded.

## Fixing `largest`

We now have everything `largest` needs. Its body uses `>`, and `>` on a type
parameter is a call to `Ord.gt`. So the bound we want is `T: Ord[T]`: "a `T`
can be compared with another `T`". Let's write it, and call it with integers
first:

```aura check-fail:AU2002
trait Ord[Rhs]:
    def lt(self, rhs: Rhs) -> bool
    def le(self, rhs: Rhs) -> bool
    def gt(self, rhs: Rhs) -> bool
    def ge(self, rhs: Rhs) -> bool

def largest[T: Ord[T]](values: own list[T]) -> T | None:
    mut rest = values
    if rest.len() == 0:
        return None
    mut best = rest.pop()
    while rest.len() > 0:
        candidate = rest.pop()
        if candidate > best:
            best = candidate
    return best

def main():
    print(largest([3, 9, 4]))
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2002]: type `int64` does not implement trait `Ord[int64]`
 --> src/main.au:19:11
   |
19 |     print(largest([3, 9, 4]))
   |           ^
```

The body compiles now. The error moved to the call, which is where the bound
puts it. The message may surprise you, because `3 < 9` obviously works. But
integer comparison is a builtin rule, not an implementation of our `Ord` trait,
and the bound asks for the trait. Traits can be implemented for builtin types
as well as your own, so we can supply one. While we're at it, we'll give
`largest` an empty-list answer of `None` instead of trapping on `pop`, and
implement `Ord` for `Money`:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
trait Ord[Rhs]:
    def lt(self, rhs: Rhs) -> bool
    def le(self, rhs: Rhs) -> bool
    def gt(self, rhs: Rhs) -> bool
    def ge(self, rhs: Rhs) -> bool

copy class Money:
    cents: int64

impl Display for Money:
    def display(self) -> str:
        return f"${self.cents // 100}.{self.cents % 100:02}"

impl Ord[Money] for Money:
    def lt(self, rhs: Money) -> bool:
        return self.cents < rhs.cents

    def le(self, rhs: Money) -> bool:
        return self.cents <= rhs.cents

    def gt(self, rhs: Money) -> bool:
        return self.cents > rhs.cents

    def ge(self, rhs: Money) -> bool:
        return self.cents >= rhs.cents

impl Ord[int64] for int64:
    def lt(self, rhs: int64) -> bool:
        return self < rhs

    def le(self, rhs: int64) -> bool:
        return self <= rhs

    def gt(self, rhs: int64) -> bool:
        return self > rhs

    def ge(self, rhs: int64) -> bool:
        return self >= rhs

def largest[T: Ord[T]](values: own list[T]) -> T | None:
    mut rest = values
    if rest.len() == 0:
        return None
    mut best = rest.pop()
    while rest.len() > 0:
        candidate = rest.pop()
        if candidate > best:
            best = candidate
    return best

def announce[T: Ord[T] + Display](values: own list[T]):
    winner = largest(values)
    if winner is None:
        print("nothing to compare")
    else:
        print(f"largest: {winner}")

def main():
    print(largest([3, 9, 4]))
    announce([Money(cents=1300), Money(cents=450), Money(cents=1700)])
    empty: list[Money] = []
    announce(empty)
```

<span class="caption">Listing 10-8: A generic `largest` bounded by `Ord`, used with integers and with `Money`</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
9
largest: $17.00
nothing to compare
```

One function now serves both types, and the signature says exactly what it
needs. Inside `impl Ord[int64] for int64`, `self < rhs` uses the builtin
integer comparison, so there's no recursion. Builtin rules always take
precedence over trait dispatch.

`announce` shows the `+` form of bounds: it calls `largest`, which needs
`Ord[T]`, and prints the winner, which needs `Display`. Its bound states both.
The `Display` bound is a real requirement, not a formality. `announce([3, 9,
4])` is rejected with `type `int64` does not implement trait `Display``,
because integers print through a builtin rule rather than through a `Display`
implementation.

That's a fair amount of code to make integers comparable, and it's an honest
cost of Aura 0.11: the operator traits are a protocol the compiler recognizes,
not a library of ready-made implementations for the builtin types. In practice
you'll mostly write bounds like `Ord[T]` for your own domain types, where you
have to say what "larger" means anyway.

## Limits worth knowing

Traits on builtin types come with one rule. A trait method can't have the same
name as a builtin method of the type it's implemented for, because the builtin
would always win and your method would never run. The compiler rejects the
collision up front:

```aura check-fail:AU2006
trait Sized:
    def len(self) -> int64

impl Sized for str:
    def len(self) -> int64:
        return 0
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2006]: trait method `len` collides with builtin method `str.len`
 --> src/main.au:5:5
  |
5 |     def len(self) -> int64:
  |     ^
  = help: rename the trait method; builtin methods cannot be shadowed by trait implementations
```

A few features you may know from other languages don't exist in Aura today:
trait objects and dynamic dispatch, associated types and constants, and `where`
clauses. Every trait call is resolved at compile time to one implementation.
When you need a list of mixed types, use a union, as Listing 10-6 did. The
[Manual](/manual/generics-and-traits) has the complete rules for
implementations, overlap, and dispatch.

There's one more kind of trait method we haven't used: a method with no `self`,
called on the type instead of on a value. It's how you write "make a `Money`
from this text", which brings us to converting between types.

## Source: docs/book/ch10-03-conversions.md

# Converting between types

In Python, `2 + 0.5` is `2.5`, `len(items) / 2` is a float, and an integer
quietly grows as large as it needs to be. Aura does none of these things. A
value keeps its type until you write a conversion, and every conversion you
write either produces an exact result, traps, or returns a `Result`. This
section shows the three tools for numbers and text, explains why Aura is this
strict, and ends with conversions between your own types.

## No implicit conversions

The error that surprises most newcomers is a good place to begin. A sensor
gives us an `int32`, and a helper takes an `int64`:

```aura check-fail:AU2002
def scale(value: int64) -> int64:
    return value * 2

def main():
    reading: int32 = 21
    print(scale(reading))
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2002]: argument type mismatch for function `scale`: expected `int64`, found `int32`
 --> src/main.au:6:17
  |
6 |     print(scale(reading))
  |                 ^
```

Every `int32` fits in an `int64`, so this looks like a conversion the compiler
could do for us. Aura won't, and the reason is that silent widening never comes
alone. A language that widens `int32` to `int64` on the way into a function
soon needs rules for which way to convert when an `int32` meets a `uint32`, or
an `int64` meets a `float64`, and somewhere in those rules a value gets
narrowed or rounded without anyone writing it. Overflow and precision bugs live
in exactly those places. Aura's answer is that the code shows every conversion,
so you can find them.

The same rule applies to operators. Both sides of `+` must have the same type:

```aura check-fail:AU2999
def main():
    a: int32 = 2
    b: int64 = 3
    print(a + b)
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2999]: binary operator operands must match, found `int32` and `int64`
 --> src/main.au:4:11
  |
4 |     print(a + b)
  |           ^
```

In practice this comes up less often than you might fear. An integer literal
with no other type information is an `int64`, a float literal is a `float64`,
and lengths and indices are `int64`, so most code uses one integer type and one
float type throughout. Mixed widths appear at the edges: a file format with
32-bit fields, a C library, a protocol. There is one deliberate exception. An
index position, such as `names[i]`, accepts smaller integer types like `int32`
and widens them, because widening an index can't lose information and indexing
with a narrow counter is common.

## `as` for numbers

To convert between numeric types, write `value as Type`:

```aura
def scale(value: int64) -> int64:
    return value * 2

def main():
    reading: int32 = 21
    print(scale(reading as int64))
```

`as` works between any two numeric types, and it follows one rule: the result
is exact, or the program traps. Widening is always exact. Narrowing is exact
when the value fits, and traps when it doesn't:

```aura
def main():
    small: int32 = 7
    print(small as int64)
    big: int64 = 300
    print(big as int16)
    print(3 as float64)
    print(3.9 as int64)
    print(-3.9 as int64)
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
7
300
3.0
3
-3
```

Converting a float to an integer truncates toward zero, so `3.9` becomes `3`
and `-3.9` becomes `-3`. That's the only kind of loss `as` allows, and it's the
one you'd expect from the operation's name. Now let's narrow a value that
doesn't fit:

```aura
def main():
    count: int64 = 300
    as_byte = count as uint8
    print(as_byte)
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU4002]: integer value `300` does not fit in `uint8`
 --> src/main.au:3:15
  |
3 |     as_byte = count as uint8
  |               ^
  = note: Aura call chain (innermost first): main at 1:1
```

In C, `(uint8_t)300` is `44`, and the program carries on with a number nobody
asked for. Aura traps with the same `AU4002` you saw for arithmetic overflow in
[Chapter 9](/book/ch09-01-traps). When the value is a literal, the compiler
doesn't wait for run time: `300 as uint8` is rejected by `aura check` with
`integer literal `300` does not fit in `uint8``.

Integer to float conversion follows the same rule, which is less obvious. A
`float64` has 53 bits of precision, so not every `int64` has an exact
`float64`:

```aura
def main():
    n: int64 = 9007199254740993
    f = n as float64
    print(f)
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU4002]: integer value `9007199254740993` cannot be represented exactly as `float64`
 --> src/main.au:3:9
  |
3 |     f = n as float64
  |         ^
  = note: Aura call chain (innermost first): main at 1:1
```

The nearest `float64` is `9007199254740992`, one less. `as` won't give you that
silently. A float that isn't a number at all can't become an integer either:
casting infinity to `int64` traps with `cannot cast non-finite float to
`int64``.

Read `as` as a claim you're making: "this value fits the target type". If the
claim is false, you find out at the line that made it.

## `.to_float()` when rounding is the point

Sometimes you want the nearest float and don't care about the last bit.
Computing an average is the usual case. Every integer type has a `.to_float()`
method that returns a `float64`, rounding to the nearest representable value
instead of trapping:

```aura
def average(prices: list[int64]) -> float64:
    mut total = 0
    for price in prices:
        total += price
    return total.to_float() / prices.len().to_float()

def main():
    print(average([1300, 450, 1700]))
    n: int64 = 9007199254740993
    print(n.to_float())
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
1150.0
9007199254740992.0
```

`average` shows the other reason you'll meet `.to_float()` often. Aura doesn't
define `/` on two integers:

```aura check-fail:AU2003
def average(total: int64, count: int64) -> float64:
    return total / count
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2003]: integer `/` is not supported; use `//` for floor division, or call `.to_float()` on both operands for true division
 --> src/main.au:2:12
  |
2 |     return total / count
  |            ^
```

Python 2 had `7 / 2 == 3`, Python 3 changed it to `3.5`, and code broke in both
directions. Aura makes you say which one you mean. `//` is floor division and
stays an integer; `.to_float()` on both sides gives true division. The help
line in the diagnostic says exactly that.

Choose between `as float64` and `.to_float()` by intent. `as float64` says the
value must be exact. `.to_float()` says rounding is acceptable.

## Text and numbers

`as` refuses anything that isn't numeric:

```aura check-fail:AU2002
def main():
    text = "12"
    n = text as int64
```

```console
$ aura check src/main.au
error[AU2002]: casts are only supported between numeric types, found `str` and `int64`
 --> src/main.au:3:9
  |
3 |     n = text as int64
  |         ^
```

Converting text to a number can fail for reasons that have nothing to do with
bugs, so it isn't a cast: it's parsing, and parsing returns a `Result`. You
used `parse_int64` throughout Chapter 9; `parse_int32` and `parse_float64` work
the same way.

Going the other direction always succeeds, so it returns a plain `str`. Use
`str(value)`, or put the value in an f-string, which also lets you format it:

```aura
def main():
    count: int64 = 42
    print(str(count) + " items")
    ratio = 1300.to_float() / 3.to_float()
    print(f"{ratio:.2f}")
```

For your own types, `str()` and f-strings use `Display`, which you implemented
for `Money` in the previous section.

## Converting your own types

There's no `as` for classes. To turn one of your types into another, or a
builtin value into one of yours, you write a function or a method, and two
traits give that code a conventional shape.

The first is `From`, which you met in [Chapter
9](/book/ch09-02-recoverable-errors) as the way `try` converts one error type
into another. Nothing about it is specific to errors. `From[Source]` has a
single method, `from`, with no `self`: it takes a `Source` and returns a value
of the implementing type. A method with no `self` is called an *associated
method*, and you call it on the type, as in `Money.from(12)`.

The second is a trait we'll define ourselves for parsing text into a value. Its
method also has no `self`, and returns `Result[Self, str]`, where `Self` means
"the type implementing this trait". Here are both, implemented for `Money`:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
trait From[Source]:
    def from(value: own Source) -> Self

trait Parse:
    def parse(text: str) -> Result[Self, str]

copy class Money:
    cents: int64

impl Display for Money:
    def display(self) -> str:
        return f"${self.cents // 100}.{self.cents % 100:02}"

impl From[int64] for Money:
    def from(value: own int64) -> Money:
        return Money(cents=value * 100)

impl Parse for Money:
    def parse(text: str) -> Result[Money, str]:
        if text.starts_with("-"):
            return Result.Err(f"`{text}`: a price cannot be negative")
        parts = text.split(".")
        if parts.len() == 1:
            dollars = try parse_int64(parts[0])
            return Result.Ok(Money.from(dollars))
        if parts.len() != 2 or parts[1].len() != 2:
            return Result.Err(f"`{text}` is not a price like 12.50")
        dollars = try parse_int64(parts[0])
        cents = try parse_int64(parts[1])
        return Result.Ok(Money(cents=dollars * 100 + cents))

def parse_all[T: Parse](texts: list[str]) -> Result[list[T], str]:
    mut values: list[T] = []
    for text in texts:
        values.append(try T.parse(text))
    return Result.Ok(values)

def average_dollars(prices: list[Money]) -> float64:
    mut total = 0
    for price in prices:
        total += price.cents
    return total.to_float() / prices.len().to_float() / 100.0

def main():
    print(Money.from(12))
    print(Money.parse("4.05"))
    print(Money.parse("4.5"))
    print(Money.parse("-3"))
    match parse_all[Money](["12.50", "3", "0.99"]):
        case Result.Ok(prices):
            print(prices)
            print(f"average: {average_dollars(prices):.2f}")
        case Result.Err(message):
            print(message)
```

<span class="caption">Listing 10-9: Converting integers and text into `Money` with `From` and a `Parse` trait</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
$12.00
Result.Ok($4.05)
Result.Err(`4.5` is not a price like 12.50)
Result.Err(`-3`: a price cannot be negative)
[$12.50, $3.00, $0.99]
average: 5.50
```

`Money.from(12)` reads as what it does: make a `Money` from the integer `12`,
meaning twelve dollars. Because `From` is a trait, the conversion has a
predictable name that every reader of the code will recognize, and it's the
same name `try` looks for when it has to convert an error.

`Money.parse` shows how conversions and errors fit together. Every way the text
can be wrong becomes a `Result.Err`, and the two `try parse_int64(...)` calls
pass the parser's own message up unchanged, because `parse` returns the same
`str` error type.

The most interesting line is in `parse_all`: `try T.parse(text)`. `T` is a type
parameter, and `T: Parse` promises it has an associated `parse` method, so the
generic function can call it through the type. `parse_all[Money]` uses
`Money.parse`; a `Port` or `Mode` type with its own `impl Parse` would get its
own. We have to specialize the call explicitly, as in `parse_all[Money](...)`,
because a list of strings says nothing about which type to parse into. As with
`Ord` in the previous section, builtin types don't come with our trait:
`parse_all[int64]` is rejected until someone writes `impl Parse for int64`.

Calling an associated method through a type parameter has a few restrictions in
Aura 0.11. The call has to be in a module-level function, not in a method, and
a function that makes it can't be started directly as a task. The
[Manual](/manual/generics-and-traits) lists them.

## Summary

Generics let you write a function, class, or enum once and use it with many
types. Type parameters are checked once, for every possible type, so the
ownership modes and operations in a generic body have to make sense for all of
them: `own T` for values the body keeps, and a trait bound for any method or
operator it calls. Traits name behavior, implementations promise it explicitly,
and bounds put the requirement in the signature where callers can read it. A
few traits connect to the language itself: `Display` controls printing, `Add`,
`Ord`, and friends give your types operators, and `From` lets `try` convert
errors.

Conversions follow the same philosophy of saying what you mean. `as` converts
numbers exactly or traps, `.to_float()` rounds on purpose, parsing text returns
a `Result`, and `str()` and f-strings render anything. Nothing converts behind
your back.

With error handling and generics in hand, you're ready to make sure your code
does what you think it does. [Chapter 11](/book/ch11-00-testing) introduces
`aura test`, and we'll use it to find a real bug in some code that looks
correct.

## Source: docs/book/ch11-00-testing.md

# Writing automated tests

By now the compiler checks a great deal for you. It knows every value's type,
it knows who owns what, and it won't let you reach the inside of a `Result`
without handling the error. What it can't know is what you meant. If a function
is supposed to apply a 10% discount and it applies 1%, the types are perfect
and the program is wrong. Tests are how you write down what you meant, so a
machine can check it every time the code changes.

Aura ships its own test runner as part of the `aura` command, so there's no
framework to choose and nothing to install. A test is an ordinary function
whose name starts with `test_`, it uses the `assert` statement you met in
[Chapter 9](/book/ch09-01-traps), and `aura test` finds it, runs it, and
reports the result.

In this chapter we'll create a small package called `checkout` that totals a
shopping cart, applies discounts, and formats prices. We'll write tests for it,
watch one of them catch a real bug in code that looks correct, learn to read
failure output and select which tests run, and then organize a growing test
suite with shared fixtures, parameterized cases, and machine-readable output
for CI.

## Source: docs/book/ch11-01-writing-tests.md

# How to write tests

Tests live in a package, so we begin with an empty one. `aura new` creates it,
and as you saw in [Chapter 1](/book/ch01-03-hello-packages), it already
includes a place for tests:

```console
$ aura new checkout
created `checkout`
$ cd checkout
$ find . -type f | sort
./.gitignore
./Aura.toml
./src/main.au
./tests/smoke.au
```

Open `tests/smoke.au`:

*Filename: tests/smoke.au*

```aura
def main() -> int32:
    return 0
```

It's the smallest test there is: a program that exits with status 0. Run the package's tests:

```console
$ aura test
ok tests/smoke.au
1 passed; 0 failed
```

With no arguments, `aura test` looks through the `tests/` directory for `.au`
files and runs each one. `smoke.au` has no test functions in it, so the runner
treats the whole file as one test case and runs its `main`. It passes if `main`
returns 0 and fails if `main` returns anything else or traps. That makes the
file a smoke test, a quick check that the package builds and starts. You'll
also notice a new `Aura.lock` file next to `Aura.toml`; package commands such
as `aura run` and `aura test` write it to record the package's resolved
dependencies.

File-level cases are useful for end-to-end scripts, but most tests are smaller
than a whole program. For those, Aura has test functions.

## The code we'll test

Our package will total a shopping cart. Prices are in cents, as an `int64`,
because floating-point money accumulates rounding errors. Create `src/cart.au`
with one function:

*Filename: src/cart.au*

```aura
public def subtotal(prices: list[int64]) -> int64:
    mut total = 0
    for price in prices:
        total += price
    return total
```

<span class="caption">Listing 11-1: The first function of the `cart` module</span>

The function is `public` because the tests live in a different module and can
only import public names, as [Chapter 7](/book/ch07-00-modules-and-packages)
explained.

## Your first test function

Now create `tests/cart_test.au`:

*Filename: tests/cart_test.au*

```aura fragment
from cart import subtotal

def test_adds_prices():
    assert subtotal([250, 125]) == 375

def test_empty_cart_is_zero():
    assert subtotal([]) == 0
```

<span class="caption">Listing 11-2: Two test functions for `subtotal`</span>

The file imports `subtotal` from the `cart` module, the same way any other
module in the package would. Test files under `tests/` are part of the package,
so `import` and `from ... import` resolve against `src/` exactly as they do for
`src/main.au`.

Each test is a function that follows three rules. Its name starts with `test_`.
It takes no parameters. It returns `None`, which is what a function with no
`->` annotation returns. Inside, it calls the code under test and asserts what
should be true about the result. If every assertion holds, the function returns
normally and the test passes. If any assertion fails, the test traps, and a
trapped test is a failed test.

```console
$ aura test
ok tests/cart_test.au::test_adds_prices
ok tests/cart_test.au::test_empty_cart_is_zero
ok tests/smoke.au
3 passed; 0 failed
```

Each test function is reported as its own case, named by its file and its
function joined with `::`. Files run in path order, and the functions in a file
run in the order they're written.

## Making sure a test can fail

A test that has never failed hasn't proved much. It might not be testing what
you think, or it might not be running at all. So before trusting
`test_adds_prices`, let's break `subtotal` on purpose and watch the test catch
it. Change `+=` to `=` in the loop:

*Filename: src/cart.au*

```aura
public def subtotal(prices: list[int64]) -> int64:
    mut total = 0
    for price in prices:
        total = price
    return total
```

The function now returns the last price instead of the sum. Run the tests again:

```console
$ aura test
FAILED tests/cart_test.au::test_adds_prices
error[AU4001]: assertion failed
 --> tests/cart_test.au:4:5
  |
4 |     assert subtotal([250, 125]) == 375
  |     ^
  = note: left = 125
  = note: right = 375
  = note: Aura call chain (innermost first): test_adds_prices at 3:1
ok tests/cart_test.au::test_empty_cart_is_zero
ok tests/smoke.au
2 passed; 1 failed
```

The failing case is marked `FAILED` and followed by the assertion's diagnostic.
Two lines in it do most of the work: `left = 125` is what `subtotal` returned,
and `right = 375` is what we expected. Because the assertion's condition is a
single `==` comparison, Aura captured both operands when the comparison failed
and printed them. You don't need to add a `print` and run again to find out
what the function actually returned.

Notice too that `test_empty_cart_is_zero` still passed. The broken function
returns 0 for an empty list, the same as the correct one. That's a useful
reminder that each test checks one specific behavior, and a suite needs enough
cases to pin the function down. Change `=` back to `+=` before moving on.

## Testing a `Result`

Let's give the cart two more abilities. A discount takes a percentage off the
total, and a percentage outside 0 to 100 is a mistake by whoever configured the
discount, so it's a `Result`, following the reasoning in [Chapter
9](/book/ch09-03-to-trap-or-not). And prices need to be shown as dollars and
cents.

*Filename: src/cart.au*

```aura
public def subtotal(prices: list[int64]) -> int64:
    mut total = 0
    for price in prices:
        total += price
    return total

public def apply_discount(total: int64, percent: int64) -> Result[int64, str]:
    if percent < 0 or percent > 100:
        return Result.Err(f"discount must be between 0 and 100, got {percent}")
    return Result.Ok(total - total * percent // 100)

public def format_cents(cents: int64) -> str:
    return f"${cents // 100}.{cents % 100:02}"
```

<span class="caption">Listing 11-3: Adding `apply_discount` and `format_cents`</span>

There are two ways to test a function that returns a `Result`. When you know
exactly which value to expect, compare the whole `Result` with `==`, since
`Result` values compare structurally. When you only care about part of the
outcome, `match` on it and assert inside the arm. Here are tests that use both,
plus two for `format_cents`:

*Filename: tests/cart_test.au*

```aura fragment
from cart import subtotal, apply_discount, format_cents

def test_adds_prices():
    assert subtotal([250, 125]) == 375

def test_empty_cart_is_zero():
    assert subtotal([]) == 0

def test_ten_percent_off():
    assert apply_discount(2000, 10) == Result.Ok(1800)

def test_rejects_discount_over_100():
    match apply_discount(2000, 150):
        case Result.Ok(total):
            assert false, f"expected an error, got {total}"
        case Result.Err(message):
            assert message.contains("between 0 and 100")

def test_formats_cents():
    assert format_cents(1805) == "$18.05"

def test_formats_refunds():
    assert format_cents(-250) == "-$2.50"
```

<span class="caption">Listing 11-4: Tests for discounts and formatting</span>

`test_rejects_discount_over_100` uses `assert false` with a message for the
branch that shouldn't happen. An assertion message is evaluated only when the
assertion fails, so the f-string costs nothing on the passing path, and if the
branch is ever reached the message says what came back instead. In the `Err`
arm we check that the message mentions the valid range. We don't compare the
whole string, because the exact wording of an error message is the kind of
detail that changes without the behavior changing.

The last test is about refunds. A refund of $2.50 is stored as `-250` cents,
and it should print as `-$2.50`. Let's run everything:

```console
$ aura test
ok tests/cart_test.au::test_adds_prices
ok tests/cart_test.au::test_empty_cart_is_zero
ok tests/cart_test.au::test_ten_percent_off
ok tests/cart_test.au::test_rejects_discount_over_100
ok tests/cart_test.au::test_formats_cents
FAILED tests/cart_test.au::test_formats_refunds
error[AU4001]: assertion failed
 --> tests/cart_test.au:23:5
   |
23 |     assert format_cents(-250) == "-$2.50"
   |     ^
  = note: left = $-3.50
  = note: right = -$2.50
  = note: Aura call chain (innermost first): test_formats_refunds at 22:1
ok tests/smoke.au
6 passed; 1 failed
```

This time we didn't break anything on purpose. `format_cents` looked right, and
it is right for every positive amount, but `left = $-3.50` says a $2.50 refund
prints as minus three dollars fifty. The reason is in how Aura's `//` and `%`
treat negative numbers. `//` is floor division, so it rounds toward negative
infinity: `-250 // 100` is `-3`, not `-2`. And `%` takes the sign of the
divisor, so `-250 % 100` is `50`. Put together, they give `$-3.50`. Python
