``unknown type `stats.Record` `` at an unrelated line. Naming the type through
its module, as `records.Record`, avoids it. Plain functions and fields are not
affected.

## The report module

In the single-file version, `print_report` printed as it went. That is fine
for a program and awkward for a test, because a test has no easy way to look
at what was printed. So `report.render` builds the lines in a list and returns them
joined into one string, and `main` does the printing. The report now also
lists each skipped line with its reason, and leaves out the errors block when
there were no errors.

*Filename: src/report.au*

```aura fragment
from records import Level, level_name
from stats import Summary

public def render(path: str, summary: Summary) -> str:
    mut out: list[str] = []
    out.append(f"{path}: {summary.total} records, {summary.skipped.len()} skipped")
    out.append("")
    out.append("by level")
    for level in [Level.Debug, Level.Info, Level.Warn, Level.Error]:
        match summary.by_level.get(level):
            case Lookup.Found(count):
                out.append(row(level_name(level), count))
            case Lookup.Missing:
                pass
    out.append("")
    out.append("by service")
    for service in sorted(summary.by_service.keys()):
        out.append(row(service, summary.by_service[service]))
    if summary.errors_by_service.len() > 0:
        out.append("")
        out.append("errors by service")
        for service in sorted(summary.errors_by_service.keys()):
            out.append(row(service, summary.errors_by_service[service]))
    if summary.skipped.len() > 0:
        out.append("")
    for skipped in summary.skipped:
        out.append(f"skipped line {skipped.line}: {skipped.reason}")
    return "\n".join(out)

def row(name: str, count: int64) -> str:
    return f"  {name:<8s}{count:>5d}"
```

<span class="caption">Listing 12-16: The report as a function from a summary to text</span>

The repeated format string became the private helper `row`, so the column
widths are written once. Separating "compute the text" from "write the text"
is worth doing in almost any program that produces output. It is what lets the
test at the end of this section check the report without capturing standard
output.

## Arguments as a Config

So far `main` has looked at `args[0]` directly. With an option to support, the
argument handling grows enough to deserve its own module and its own error
type. The goal is that every mistake a user can make on the command line turns
into a specific message, and none of them turns into a trap.

*Filename: src/config.au*

```aura fragment
from records import Level, parse_level

public class Config:
    public path: str
    public min_level: Level

public enum ConfigError:
    MissingPath
    MissingValue(flag: str)
    UnknownFlag(flag: str)
    BadLevel(text: str)
    ExtraArgument(text: str)

public def parse_args(args: list[str]) -> Result[Config, ConfigError]:
    mut path: str | None = None
    mut min_level = Level.Debug
    mut index = 0
    while index < args.len():
        arg = args[index].clone()
        if arg == "--min-level":
            if index + 1 >= args.len():
                return Err(ConfigError.MissingValue(flag=arg))
            text = args[index + 1].clone()
            match parse_level(text):
                case Level as level:
                    min_level = level
                case None:
                    return Err(ConfigError.BadLevel(text=text))
            index += 2
        elif arg.starts_with("-"):
            return Err(ConfigError.UnknownFlag(flag=arg))
        elif path is not None:
            return Err(ConfigError.ExtraArgument(text=arg))
        else:
            path = arg
            index += 1
    match own path:
        case str as found:
            return Ok(Config(path=found, min_level=min_level))
        case None:
            return Err(ConfigError.MissingPath)

public def describe(error: ConfigError) -> str:
    match error:
        case ConfigError.MissingPath:
            return "missing the log file to read"
        case ConfigError.MissingValue(flag):
            return f"`{flag}` needs a value"
        case ConfigError.UnknownFlag(flag):
            return f"unknown option `{flag}`"
        case ConfigError.BadLevel(text):
            return f"`{text}` is not a level; use debug, info, warn, or error"
        case ConfigError.ExtraArgument(text):
            return f"unexpected argument `{text}`; logscan reads one file"
```

<span class="caption">Listing 12-17: Parsing the command line into a `Config`, or a specific error</span>

`parse_args` takes the argument list as a parameter instead of calling
`sys.args()` itself. That one decision is what makes it testable: a test can
pass `["app.log", "--min-level", "warn"]` without starting a process.

The loop walks the arguments with an explicit index, because `--min-level`
consumes two of them. Each argument is cloned into an owned `arg`, since most
paths through the loop store it somewhere: in `path`, or in an error variant
that outlives the list. Every check that could go wrong returns a
`ConfigError` naming the exact argument at fault. A path is `str | None` until
we find one, and the final `match own` turns it into a `Config` or a
`MissingPath` error. `own` moves the string out of `path` into `found`, so the
`Config` takes it over without a copy.

The flag names a minimum level, and it reuses `parse_level` from the records
module. That reuse is a small win of the module split: the set of valid levels
is defined in one place, and the log parser and the command line can't drift
apart.

## A thin main

What's left for `main.au` is the glue: parse the arguments, run, and turn
each failure into a message and an exit status.

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura fragment
import config
import fs
import io
import report
import stats
import sys

def run(settings: config.Config) -> Result[None, io.Error]:
    text = try fs.read_to_string(settings.path)
    summary = stats.summarize(text, settings.min_level)
    print(report.render(settings.path, summary))
    return Ok(None)

def explain(error: io.Error) -> str:
    match error:
        case io.Error.NotFound:
            return "no such file"
        case io.Error.PermissionDenied:
            return "permission denied"
        case io.Error.IsDirectory:
            return "it is a directory, not a file"
        case io.Error.InvalidData:
            return "the file is not valid UTF-8 text"
        case _:
            return f"{error}"

def main() -> int32:
    match config.parse_args(sys.args()):
        case Ok(settings):
            match run(settings):
                case Ok(_):
                    return 0
                case Err(error):
                    print(f"logscan: cannot read {settings.path}: {explain(error)}")
                    return 1
        case Err(error):
            print(f"logscan: {config.describe(error)}")
            print("usage: logscan <path> [--min-level LEVEL]")
            return 2
```

<span class="caption">Listing 12-18: `main.au` reduced to wiring and error messages</span>

`explain` translates the `io.Error` variants a user is likely to cause into
plain words, and falls back to the variant's own rendering for the rest.
`InvalidData` is what `fs.read_to_string` reports when a file isn't valid
UTF-8, which is worth a clear message, since pointing a text tool at a binary
file by mistake is common. We kept the `io.Error` value all the way up to this
function instead of turning it into a string inside `run`. That way the
decision about wording is made once, at the top, where we know who is reading.

Usage errors exit with 2 and print the usage line. A file that can't be read
exits with 1 and doesn't, because the usage was fine. Here is every failure we
know how to cause:

```console
$ aura run src/main.au --
logscan: missing the log file to read
usage: logscan <path> [--min-level LEVEL]
$ aura run src/main.au -- --verbose app.log
logscan: unknown option `--verbose`
usage: logscan <path> [--min-level LEVEL]
$ aura run src/main.au -- app.log --min-level
logscan: `--min-level` needs a value
usage: logscan <path> [--min-level LEVEL]
$ aura run src/main.au -- app.log --min-level loud
logscan: `loud` is not a level; use debug, info, warn, or error
usage: logscan <path> [--min-level LEVEL]
$ aura run src/main.au -- app.log other.log
logscan: unexpected argument `other.log`; logscan reads one file
usage: logscan <path> [--min-level LEVEL]
$ aura run src/main.au -- nope.log
logscan: cannot read nope.log: no such file
$ aura run src/main.au -- src
logscan: cannot read src: it is a directory, not a file
```

Compare these with the first section's `io.Error.NotFound`. Each message now
names the thing that was wrong and, where it helps, what would be right.

## Testing each module

`aura new` created a `tests/` directory with a placeholder in it. Delete
`tests/smoke.au`; we'll replace it with one test file per module. As
[Chapter 11](/book/ch11-00-testing) explained, `aura test` runs every
parameterless function whose name starts with `test_` in the files under
`tests/`, and a test fails when it traps, for example on a failed `assert`.
Test files import the package's modules the same way `main.au` does.

Start with the parser. A test for a good line checks the fields, and a test
for a bad line checks which `ParseError` came back:

*Filename: tests/test_records.au*

```aura fragment
from records import Level, ParseError, parse_line

def test_parses_a_well_formed_line():
    match parse_line("2026-10-31T09:14:09 ERROR db connection reset by peer"):
        case Ok(record):
            assert record.level == Level.Error
            assert record.service == "db"
            assert record.message == "connection reset by peer"
        case Err(error):
            assert false, f"unexpected error {error}"

def test_short_line_reports_field_count():
    match parse_line("connection pool exhausted"):
        case Ok(_):
            assert false, "a three-field line should not parse"
        case Err(error):
            assert error == ParseError.TooFewFields(found=3)
```

<span class="caption">Listing 12-19: Tests for `parse_line`</span>

Because `ParseError` is an enum with data, the second test compares the whole
value, `TooFewFields(found=3)`, which checks both the kind of failure and the
count it carries.

For `stats`, a small log written inline as a string is enough. It has a good
`INFO` line, a blank line, a good `ERROR` line, and a bad one:

*Filename: tests/test_stats.au*

```aura fragment
from records import Level
from stats import summarize

LOG = "2026-10-31T09:00:00 INFO api up\n\n2026-10-31T09:00:01 ERROR api down\ngarbage\n"

def test_counts_records_and_skips_bad_lines():
    summary = summarize(LOG, Level.Debug)
    assert summary.total == 2
    assert summary.skipped.len() == 1
    assert summary.skipped[0].line == 4
    assert summary.by_service["api"] == 2
    assert summary.errors_by_service["api"] == 1

def test_min_level_filters_records():
    summary = summarize(LOG, Level.Error)
    assert summary.total == 1
    assert summary.by_level.len() == 1
```

<span class="caption">Listing 12-20: Tests for `summarize`</span>

The first test pins down two decisions we made on purpose: the blank line is
not counted as skipped, and the skipped line is reported as line 4, counting
from 1. Those are exactly the details a later edit could break without anyone
noticing, so they are the details worth testing.

It's good practice to see a test fail once, to know that it can. Change
`summary.total == 2` to `== 3` and run only this file:

```console
$ aura test tests/test_stats.au
FAILED tests/test_stats.au::test_counts_records_and_skips_bad_lines
error[AU4001]: assertion failed
 --> tests/test_stats.au:8:5
  |
8 |     assert summary.total == 3
  |     ^
  = note: left = 2
  = note: right = 3
  = note: Aura call chain (innermost first): test_counts_records_and_skips_bad_lines at 6:1
ok tests/test_stats.au::test_min_level_filters_records
1 passed; 1 failed
```

For a comparison, the failure shows both operands, so you can see what the
code produced without adding a `print`. Put the 2 back.

The report test uses `summarize` to build its input and checks two lines of
the output:

*Filename: tests/test_report.au*

```aura fragment
from records import Level
from report import render
from stats import summarize

def test_report_lists_skipped_lines_with_reasons():
    summary = summarize("2026-10-31T09:00:00 INFO api up\nshort line\n", Level.Debug)
    text = render("test.log", summary)
    assert text.starts_with("test.log: 1 records, 1 skipped")
    assert text.contains("skipped line 2: expected at least 4 fields, found 2")
```

And the configuration tests try a good command line, the default, and two
mistakes:

*Filename: tests/test_config.au*

```aura fragment
from config import ConfigError, parse_args
from records import Level

def test_path_and_level():
    match parse_args(["app.log", "--min-level", "warn"]):
        case Ok(settings):
            assert settings.path == "app.log"
            assert settings.min_level == Level.Warn
        case Err(error):
            assert false, f"unexpected error {error}"

def test_level_defaults_to_debug():
    match parse_args(["app.log"]):
        case Ok(settings):
            assert settings.min_level == Level.Debug
        case Err(error):
            assert false, f"unexpected error {error}"

def test_rejects_unknown_flag():
    match parse_args(["--verbose", "app.log"]):
        case Ok(_):
            assert false, "--verbose should be rejected"
        case Err(error):
            assert error == ConfigError.UnknownFlag(flag="--verbose")

def test_missing_path():
    match parse_args([]):
        case Ok(_):
            assert false, "no arguments should be rejected"
        case Err(error):
            assert error == ConfigError.MissingPath
```

<span class="caption">Listing 12-21: Tests for `parse_args`</span>

## Letting a test find a bug

We wrote `test_path_and_level` the way a user would type the command, with a
lowercase `warn`, and that is a problem: `parse_level` only knows the
upper-case spellings. Logs from some other services spell levels in lower case
too, so let's state that requirement as a test in `tests/test_records.au`
before we fix anything:

```aura fragment
def test_level_is_case_insensitive():
    match parse_line("2026-10-31T09:20:00 warn api retrying upstream"):
        case Ok(record):
            assert record.level == Level.Warn
        case Err(error):
            assert false, f"unexpected error {error}"
```

Now run the whole suite:

```console
$ aura test
FAILED tests/test_config.au::test_path_and_level
error[AU4001]: unexpected error config.ConfigError.BadLevel(warn)
 --> tests/test_config.au:10:13
   |
10 |             assert false, f"unexpected error {error}"
   |             ^
  = note: Aura call chain (innermost first): test_path_and_level at 4:1
ok tests/test_config.au::test_level_defaults_to_debug
ok tests/test_config.au::test_rejects_unknown_flag
ok tests/test_config.au::test_missing_path
ok tests/test_records.au::test_parses_a_well_formed_line
ok tests/test_records.au::test_short_line_reports_field_count
FAILED tests/test_records.au::test_level_is_case_insensitive
error[AU4001]: unexpected error records.ParseError.UnknownLevel(warn)
 --> tests/test_records.au:24:13
   |
24 |             assert false, f"unexpected error {error}"
   |             ^
  = note: Aura call chain (innermost first): test_level_is_case_insensitive at 19:1
ok tests/test_report.au::test_report_lists_skipped_lines_with_reasons
ok tests/test_stats.au::test_counts_records_and_skips_bad_lines
ok tests/test_stats.au::test_min_level_filters_records
8 passed; 2 failed
```

Two failures with one cause, and the messages from our `assert false, ...`
lines say what the cause is: `warn` was rejected as a level, once on the
command line and once in a log line. This is where the `ParseError` and
`ConfigError` enums earn their keep in tests, too. The failure shows the exact
variant and its payload, not a bare "parse failed".

The fix belongs in one place, `parse_level`, and it is one word. Match on the
upper-cased text:

```aura fragment
public def parse_level(text: str) -> Level | None:
    match text.to_upper():
        case "DEBUG":
            return Level.Debug
```

`to_upper()` returns a new string, and the `match` compares that against the
literal cases. Run the tests again:

```console
$ aura test
ok tests/test_config.au::test_path_and_level
ok tests/test_config.au::test_level_defaults_to_debug
ok tests/test_config.au::test_rejects_unknown_flag
ok tests/test_config.au::test_missing_path
ok tests/test_records.au::test_parses_a_well_formed_line
ok tests/test_records.au::test_short_line_reports_field_count
ok tests/test_records.au::test_level_is_case_insensitive
ok tests/test_report.au::test_report_lists_skipped_lines_with_reasons
ok tests/test_stats.au::test_counts_records_and_skips_bad_lines
ok tests/test_stats.au::test_min_level_filters_records
10 passed; 0 failed
```

Both tests pass, because the command line and the parser share
`parse_level`. When you are working on one module, `-k` narrows the run to
test names containing a substring. Use the file name, since a word like
`records` also appears in some test names in `test_stats.au`:

```console
$ aura test -k test_records.au
ok tests/test_records.au::test_parses_a_well_formed_line
ok tests/test_records.au::test_short_line_reports_field_count
ok tests/test_records.au::test_level_is_case_insensitive
3 passed; 0 failed
```

Run the refactored program against the sample log. The counts are the same as
before the split, and the skipped lines now explain themselves:

```console
$ aura run src/main.au -- app.log

by level
  DEBUG       1
  INFO        4
  WARN        1
  ERROR       3

by service
  api         4
  db          2
  worker      3

errors by service
  api         1
  db          1
  worker      1

skipped line 7: expected at least 4 fields, found 3
skipped line 11: unknown level `NOTICE`
```

And as a native binary, which behaves the same and reads its arguments from
the real command line:

```console
$ aura build -o target/logscan src/main.au

$ ./target/logscan app.log --min-level ERROR
app.log: 3 records, 2 skipped

by level
  ERROR       3

by service
  api         1
  db          1
  worker      1

errors by service
  api         1
  db          1
  worker      1

skipped line 7: expected at least 4 fields, found 3
skipped line 11: unknown level `NOTICE`
```

There is plenty left you could add. A `--service` option would be a few lines
in `config` and one more check in `summarize`. Reading from standard input
when no path is given would use `io.read_line()` in a loop, and only `main`
would need to change. Parsing timestamps would let the report show a time
range. The structure we have now means each of these touches one or two
modules and comes with a place to put its tests.

## Summary

You've built a complete command-line tool in Aura. It reads its arguments with
`sys.args()` and a file with `fs.read_to_string`, keeps the `Result`-returning
work in `run` and leaves exit statuses to `main`, and parses untrusted text
into typed `Record` values at the boundary. Along the way you met ownership in
everyday code: views and `.clone()` for strings in a list, `own` keys for a
dictionary, and `mut self` for a method that updates counts. You saw the
choice between `T | None` for an absence with nothing to say and
`Result[T, E]` with an error enum when the caller needs a reason, and you
split the program into modules with deliberate `public` boundaries and a test
file for each.

Several helpers in this chapter took a value and did one fixed thing with it.
The next chapter is about values that *are* behavior: closures that capture
their surroundings, such as a filter that remembers the minimum level it was
built with, and decorators that wrap a function once so every call goes
through the same code.

## Source: docs/book/ch13-00-closures-and-decorators.md

# Closures and decorators

So far, the functions in this book have been things we call. In this chapter
they become things we pass around. A sort that should order requests by
duration needs to be told how to get the duration out of a request. A filter
that keeps "requests slower than the limit the user typed" needs to carry that
limit with it. A tool runner that should log every call needs a way to put the
same logging around many different functions without editing each one.

Aura's answer to the first two is the *closure*, written with `lambda`: a small
function value that can capture bindings from the place where it was created.
If you know Python's lambdas, the syntax will look familiar. What is new is
that every capture has an owner. A closure either copies a value, takes it
over, or borrows it for a limited time, and the compiler checks which one you
meant, as it does for any other binding. That is what lets Aura run
closures without a garbage collector, and it is why some closures can be
called many times while others can be called only once.

The answer to the third is the *decorator*. A line such as `@traced("count")`
above a function replaces that function, once, when the module starts, with a
wrapped version built from a closure. We'll use decorators together with
derived JSON codecs to build the core of a typed tool runner: a program that
receives a tool call as JSON text, decodes its arguments into a class, calls a
decorated function, and sends back JSON, with every malformed call turned into
a precise error message.

By the end of the chapter you'll be able to read and write function types such
as `def(ms: int64) -> bool`, choose between capturing by copy, by move, and by
loan, store closures in `Callable[...]` values that can be returned and kept,
and write decorators, including generic ones that adapt to each function they
wrap.

## Source: docs/book/ch13-01-closures.md

# Closures

Let's start from a question we could ask of the log in the last chapter: which
requests were slow? Suppose we already have the durations, in milliseconds, in
a list. Finding the slow ones is a filter, and a list's `filter` method takes a
function that says yes or no for each element.

## Functions are values

We can hand `filter` an ordinary named function:

*Filename: slow.au*

```aura
def is_slow(ms: int64) -> bool:
    return ms > 100

def is_tiny(ms: int64) -> bool:
    return ms < 10

def main():
    durations = [12, 1840, 35, 410, 7]
    print(durations.filter(is_slow))
    check: def(ms: int64) -> bool = is_slow
    print(check(250))
    checks: list[def(ms: int64) -> bool] = [is_slow, is_tiny]
    for keep in checks:
        print(durations.filter(keep))
```

<span class="caption">Listing 13-1: Passing, storing, and calling named functions as values</span>

```console
$ aura run slow.au
[1840, 410]
true
[1840, 410]
[7]
```

Writing `is_slow` without parentheses doesn't call it. It names the function as
a value, which we can pass to `filter`, store in a binding, or put in a list.
The type of that value is written the way the function was declared, with the
body and the name left out: `def(ms: int64) -> bool`. You can use a function
type anywhere a type is allowed, including a parameter, a class field, or a
list's element type as in `checks`.

The parameter name is part of the type. That may be surprising if you come
from languages where only the parameter types matter, so let's see what
happens if we leave it out:

```aura check-fail:AU2015
def is_slow(ms: int64) -> bool:
    return ms > 100

def main():
    check: def(int64) -> bool = is_slow
    print(check(250))
```

```console
$ aura run slow.au
error[AU2015]: callable contract mismatch: positional parameter 1 differs from parameter `ms` in its name; declare `type Adapter = def(int64) -> bool` and use `Adapter(is_slow)`
 --> slow.au:5:33
  |
5 |     check: def(int64) -> bool = is_slow
  |                                 ^
  = help: preserve identical complete contracts at bare destinations; apply safe restrictions through an explicit thin alias or owned callable constructor such as `Alias(function)`
```

Aura calls the full description of how a function may be called its
*contract*: the parameter names, their modes and types, any defaults, and the
result. `is_slow` can be called as `is_slow(ms=250)`, but a `def(int64) -> bool`
could only be called positionally, so storing one as the other would quietly
throw away part of the contract. The compiler won't do that implicitly. If you
want a value without the name, the message tells you how to ask for it: define
`type Adapter = def(int64) -> bool` and write `Adapter(is_slow)`. In practice
you usually don't need to write the type at all. `check = is_slow` infers the
complete contract, names and all.

Named functions like these are *thin* function values: a pointer to code, with
nothing else attached. They are copy values, so passing one around never moves
anything, and they can go anywhere a value can go, including across tasks.

## Capturing the limit

`is_slow` has its limit, 100, written into its body. In a real tool the limit
comes from the user. A named function at module level can't see the local
bindings of `main`, so it has no way to read a `limit` chosen at run time.
This is the job of a closure:

*Filename: slow.au*

```aura
def main():
    durations = [12, 1840, 35, 410, 7]
    limit = 30
    print(durations.filter(lambda ms: ms > limit))
    print(durations.map(lambda ms: f"{ms}ms"))
    print(sorted(durations, key=lambda ms: -ms))
```

<span class="caption">Listing 13-2: Lambdas as callbacks, one of them capturing `limit`</span>

```console
$ aura run slow.au
[1840, 35, 410]
[12ms, 1840ms, 35ms, 410ms, 7ms]
[1840, 410, 35, 12, 7]
```

`lambda ms: ms > limit` is a function value with one parameter, `ms`, and a body
of one expression. The body mentions `limit`, which is not a parameter, so the
lambda *captures* it from the surrounding scope. `map` builds a new list from
each element's result, and `sorted` uses the lambda as a key, here sorting by
the negated duration to get the slowest first.

An Aura lambda's body is always exactly one expression. There are no statement
bodies and no `return`. When a callback needs more than one step, write a named
function, and pass the closure's captured values to it as arguments; we'll do
that with decorators in the next section.

## Where a lambda's types come from

The lambdas above never say that `ms` is an `int64`. They don't have to,
because each one is passed straight to a method that knows what it will pass
in. Take the lambda out of the call and give it a name, and that context is
gone:

```aura check-fail:AU2002
def main():
    limit = 30
    is_slow = lambda ms: ms > limit
    print(is_slow(150))
```

```console
$ aura check slow.au
error[AU2002]: lambda parameter types require an expected `def(...) -> ...` context
 --> slow.au:3:15
  |
3 |     is_slow = lambda ms: ms > limit
  |               ^
  = help: add a `def(...) -> ...` annotation to the immutable local, or pass the lambda directly to a callback parameter
```

Aura doesn't guess a parameter's type from how the body uses it. `ms > limit`
would work for several numeric types, and a guess that is right today can
become wrong when someone edits the body. So a lambda with parameters needs an
expected function type, either from the callback it is passed to or from an
annotation. Lambda parameters themselves can't carry type annotations; the type
always comes from outside. (A lambda with no parameters, such as
`lambda: limit * 2`, can infer its result from the body, because there is
nothing to guess about its inputs.)

Add the annotation the help line suggests:

```aura
def main():
    limit = 30
    is_slow: def(int64) -> bool = lambda ms: ms > limit
    print(is_slow(150))
    print(is_slow(20))
    print(limit)
```

```console
$ aura run slow.au
true
false
30
```

## What a capture does with its value

Notice the last line of that output. `limit` is still usable after the
closure captured it. That's because `limit` is an `int64`, a copy value, and a
lambda without a capture list copies each copy value it uses at the moment the
lambda is created. The closure holds its own 30, independent of the binding
outside.

An owned value can't be copied implicitly, so a lambda captures it by moving it
in. Here is a filter that keeps lines from one service:

```aura check-fail:AU3001
def main():
    service = "db"
    from_service: def(str) -> bool = lambda name: name == service
    print(from_service("db"))
    print(service)
```

```console
$ aura check slow.au
error[AU3001]: use of moved value `service`
 --> slow.au:5:11
  |
5 |     print(service)
  |           ^
  = related slow.au:3:59: value moved into closure here
  = help: pass shared access when ownership is not needed, or call `.clone()` at the move site when an independent value is required
  = fix: replace slow.au:3:66-3:66 with `.clone()`
```

This is the same move error as passing `service` to an `own` parameter, and the
`related` line points at the place inside the lambda where the move happened.
The closure now owns the string, so `main` can't print it.

Aura moves by default, rather than borrowing, because a closure is a value,
and values travel. A closure that borrowed `service` would be tied to the scope
where `service` lives, and it would become invalid the moment that scope ended
if it had been returned or stored somewhere. A closure that owns its captures
can go anywhere. Python makes the other choice, capturing a reference to the
variable, which is why a Python lambda created in a loop famously sees the
loop variable's *last* value. In Aura a capture is taken when the lambda is
created, so that surprise can't happen.

There are two ways to keep `service` usable. The help line offers one: clone
the string, so the closure gets its own copy. The other is to say explicitly
that the closure should borrow, with a *capture list* in square brackets after
`lambda`:

```aura
def main():
    service = "db"
    from_service: def(str) -> bool = lambda [service] name: name == service
    print(from_service("db"))
    print(from_service("api"))
    print(service)
```

<span class="caption">Listing 13-3: Borrowing a capture with an explicit capture list</span>

```console
$ aura run slow.au
true
false
db
```

A capture list names every outer binding the body uses, and the form of each
entry sets how it is captured:

- `name` borrows the binding with shared access, for as long as the closure is
  in use.
- `mut name` borrows it with mutable access, so the closure can change it.
- `own name` copies a copy value or moves an owned one, which is what a lambda
  without a list does.

Once you write a list, it must be complete. A name the body uses but the list
leaves out is an error, and so is a listed name the body never uses. That
keeps the list honest as a description of what the closure touches. A
borrowing closure is tied to the scope of what it borrows, so it can't be
stored in a long-lived place or returned; we'll see the owned alternative for
that shortly.

## Call once, call many, or call and change

What a closure does with its captures when it runs decides how often it can be
called. Aura sorts every closure into one of three *call kinds*.

A closure whose body only reads its captures is *shared*: it can be called any
number of times, through any binding. Every closure we've written so far is
shared.

A closure whose body gives an owned capture away can run only once, because
after the first call it no longer has the value. This one returns its captured
string:

```aura check-fail:AU3001
def main():
    banner = "slow requests"
    take_banner = lambda: banner
    print(take_banner())
    print(take_banner())
```

```console
$ aura check slow.au
error[AU3001]: use of moved value `take_banner`
 --> slow.au:5:11
  |
5 |     print(take_banner())
  |           ^
  = related slow.au:4:11: value moved here
  = help: pass shared access when ownership is not needed, or transfer this non-cloneable value only once
```

The first call moved the string out of the closure and handed it to `print`,
so calling the closure consumed the closure itself, and the second call is a
use after a move. This is a *consuming* closure. It is useful for work that
should happen exactly once, such as handing a finished result to its new
owner, and the compiler guarantees it does happen at most once.

The third kind changes its captures. Here a closure owns a counter and bumps
it on each call:

```aura check-fail:AU3003
class Counter:
    total: int64

    def bump(mut self) -> int64:
        self.total += 1
        return self.total

def main():
    counter = Counter(total=0)
    next_id = lambda [own counter]: counter.bump()
    print(next_id())
```

```console
$ aura check slow.au
error[AU3003]: a mutable-repeatable closure must be called through a mutable closure place
 --> slow.au:11:11
   |
11 |     print(next_id())
   |           ^
  = help: store the closure in a `mut` local before calling it
```

Calling `next_id` changes the counter it owns, so calling it changes
`next_id`. The rule for that is the one we know from methods: changing a value
requires a `mut` binding. Write `mut next_id = ...` and the closure keeps its
counter between calls:

```aura
class Counter:
    total: int64

    def bump(mut self) -> int64:
        self.total += 1
        return self.total

def main():
    counter = Counter(total=0)
    mut next_id = lambda [own counter]: counter.bump()
    print(next_id())
    print(next_id())
    print(next_id())
```

<span class="caption">Listing 13-4: A mutable closure that owns its state</span>

```console
$ aura run slow.au
1
2
3
```

The counter moved into the closure when we wrote `[own counter]`, and from then
on it lives in the closure's environment. A Python programmer would build this
with a class or with `nonlocal`; here it is one line, and the `mut` on the
binding tells the reader that calls have an effect.

A closure can also change a binding outside itself, through a `mut` entry in
the capture list. That is a mutable loan, and it follows the same rule as any
mutable loan: while it is live, nothing else may touch the borrowed value.

```aura check-fail:AU3002
def main():
    durations = [12, 1840, 35, 410, 7]
    mut slow: list[int64] = []
    mut keep: def(int64) -> None = lambda [mut slow] ms: slow.append(ms)
    keep(1840)
    print(slow)
    keep(410)
```

```console
$ aura check slow.au
error[AU3002]: cannot read `slow` while mutable view `keep` remains live; use the view instead
 --> slow.au:6:11
  |
6 |     print(slow)
  |           ^
  = related slow.au:4:48: mutable view `keep` starts here
  = related slow.au:7:5: last use of view `keep` keeps this loan live
```

The two `related` lines mark the span of the loan: it starts where the closure
is created and lasts until its last call on line 7. Reading `slow` in the
middle of that span would mean reading a list while something else holds the
right to change it. Finish using the closure first, and the loan ends in time:

```aura
def main():
    durations = [12, 1840, 35, 410, 7]
    mut slow: list[int64] = []
    mut keep: def(int64) -> None = lambda [mut slow] ms: slow.append(ms)
    for ms in durations:
        if ms > 100:
            keep(ms)
    print(slow)
```

```console
$ aura run slow.au
[1840, 410]
```

## Passing closures to your own functions

Built-in callback sites such as `filter`, `map`, and `sorted` accept capturing
closures directly. Your own functions are a different matter. Let's write a
`count_where` that takes a predicate:

```aura check-fail:AU2002
def count_where(values: list[int64], keep: def(int64) -> bool) -> int64:
    mut total = 0
    for value in values:
        if keep(value):
            total += 1
    return total

def main():
    durations = [12, 1840, 35, 410, 7]
    print(count_where(durations, lambda ms: ms > 100))
    limit = 30
    print(count_where(durations, lambda ms: ms > limit))
```

```console
$ aura check slow.au
error[AU2002]: argument type mismatch for function `count_where`: expected `def(int64) -> bool`, found `closure def(int64) -> bool`
 --> slow.au:12:34
   |
12 |     print(count_where(durations, lambda ms: ms > limit))
   |                                  ^
```

The first call is accepted and the second is not. The difference is the
capture. `lambda ms: ms > 100` captures nothing, so it is a thin function
value like `is_slow`. `lambda ms: ms > limit` carries an environment holding
its copy of `limit`, and a `def(...)` parameter has room for a code pointer
only. The message spells the difference as `def(int64) -> bool` versus
`closure def(int64) -> bool`.

To accept closures with captures, a function says so with an owned callable
type, `Callable[def(...) -> R]`. It is usually given a short name with `type`:

*Filename: slow.au*

```aura
type Check = Callable[def(int64) -> bool]

def count_where(values: list[int64], keep: Check) -> int64:
    mut total = 0
    for value in values:
        if keep(value):
            total += 1
    return total

def slower_than(limit: own int64) -> Check:
    return Check(lambda ms: ms > limit)

def main():
    durations = [12, 1840, 35, 410, 7]
    over_a_second = slower_than(1000)
    print(count_where(durations, over_a_second))
    print(count_where(durations, slower_than(30)))
    print(durations.filter(over_a_second))
```

<span class="caption">Listing 13-5: Returning and passing closures as `Callable` values</span>

```console
$ aura run slow.au
1
3
[1840]
```

A `Check` holds a closure together with its environment. You make one by
calling the type with a lambda, `Check(lambda ms: ...)`, which is called
*packing*. Packing is always written out. Assigning a bare lambda to a `Check`
binding is rejected with `AU2015` and a message saying that a lambda becomes a
`Callable` only through the constructor. The reason is that a packed closure
is a different kind of value from a thin one: it owns an environment, it is
not a copy value, and it can't be cloned. Aura wants that change visible where
it happens.

Once packed, the closure can go where thin function values go: into
parameters like `keep`, out of functions like `slower_than`, into fields and
lists. `slower_than` is a function that builds functions, and each one it
returns remembers its own limit. `count_where` borrows `over_a_second` with a
shared parameter, so we can use it again afterward, and `filter` accepts it
too.

`slower_than` takes its parameter as `own int64`. Try it with a bare `limit:
int64` and the compiler explains why:

```aura check-fail:AU3002
type Check = Callable[def(int64) -> bool]

def slower_than(limit: int64) -> Check:
    return Check(lambda ms: ms > limit)

def main():
    over_a_second = slower_than(1000)
    print(over_a_second(1840))
```

```console
$ aura check slow.au
error[AU3002]: lambda cannot capture shared parameter `limit` by value
 --> slow.au:4:34
  |
4 |     return Check(lambda ms: ms > limit)
  |                                  ^
  = related slow.au:3:17: shared parameter `limit` is declared here
  = help: clone `limit` into an owned local before creating the lambda, or declare the enclosing parameter as `own int64`
```

A bare parameter is shared access to a value the caller still owns, even when
the type is a copy value. A lambda without a capture list takes its captures
by value, and Aura doesn't let it turn a borrowed parameter into a value of its
own without saying so. Taking the parameter as `own` makes `slower_than` the
owner of its argument, and then the lambda is free to keep it.

## Closures over records

Closures are at their most useful with collections of class values. Here is a
list of requests, queried three ways:

*Filename: slow.au*

```aura check-fail:AU3002
class Request:
    service: str
    ms: int64

def main():
    requests = [
        Request(service="api", ms=12),
        Request(service="db", ms=1840),
        Request(service="api", ms=410),
    ]
    slowest = sorted(requests, key=lambda request: request.ms, reverse=true)
    print(slowest.map(lambda request: request.service))
```

```console
$ aura check slow.au
error[AU3002]: cannot move non-copy field `service` out of borrowed value `request`
 --> slow.au:12:47
   |
12 |     print(slowest.map(lambda request: request.service))
   |                                               ^
  = related slow.au:12:30: `request` is borrowed here
  = help: take `request` as `own Request` when the field should be moved, or call `.clone()` on the field to return an independent value
  = fix: replace slow.au:12:54-12:54 with `.clone()`
```

`map` passes each element to the callback with shared access, because the list
still owns its elements after `map` is done. Returning `request.service` would
move the string out of an element the list still owns. The key lambda,
`request.ms`, is fine, since an `int64` copies. This is the same rule we met
with `Summary.add` in the last chapter, and the same fix applies:

```aura
class Request:
    service: str
    ms: int64

def main():
    requests = [
        Request(service="api", ms=12),
        Request(service="db", ms=1840),
        Request(service="api", ms=410),
    ]
    wanted = "api"
    from_api = requests.filter(lambda request: request.service == wanted)
    print(from_api.len())
    slowest = sorted(requests, key=lambda request: request.ms, reverse=true)
    print(slowest.map(lambda request: request.service.clone()))
    print(sum(requests.map(lambda request: request.ms)))
```

<span class="caption">Listing 13-6: Filtering, sorting, and mapping a list of class values</span>

```console
$ aura run slow.au
2
[db, api, api]
2262
```

`filter` and `map` are eager: each returns a new list right away and leaves
the original in place. `filter` gives back copies of the elements it keeps, so
the list `requests` is still whole for the `sorted` and `sum` that follow.

## Choosing between a lambda and a named function

A lambda earns its place when the behavior is short and only makes sense next
to the call that uses it, as a sort key or a filter condition usually does.
When the logic needs a statement, a name, or a test of its own, a named
function is clearer, and you can still give it captured values by passing them
as arguments from a small lambda. The [Manual](/manual/closures) has the full
rules, including how closures cross into tasks, which [Chapter 15](/book/ch15-00-concurrency)
takes up.

The pattern from Listing 13-5, a function that takes some configuration and
returns a closure built from it, is more general than it looks. If the
configuration is itself a function, the result is a wrapped version of that
function. That is a decorator, and it is where we go next.

## Source: docs/book/ch13-02-decorators.md

# Decorators

The last section ended with `slower_than`, a function that took a
limit and returned a closure built around it. Now suppose the thing we hand in
is not a number but another function, and what we get back is a new function
that does a little extra work around each call to the old one: print a trace
line, count the calls, retry on failure. Writing that by hand at every place we
define a function would be tedious and easy to forget. A *decorator* does it
once, at the definition.

We'll build up to a small typed tool runner, the core of a program that an
AI agent or a script talks to. It receives a tool call as JSON text, such as
`{"tool": "count", "args": {"level": "Error"}}`, decodes the arguments into a
class, runs the matching tool, and replies with JSON. The decorator puts the
same tracing around every tool, and derived JSON codecs do the decoding and
encoding, including precise errors for calls that don't match.

## A first decorator

Here is a decorator that traces each call of a function that takes a line of
text and returns a number:

*Filename: tools.au*

```aura
type Handler = Callable[def(line: str) -> int64]

def traced(f: own Handler) -> Handler:
    print("wrapping a handler")
    return Handler(lambda [own f] line: report(f, line))

def report(f: Handler, line: str) -> int64:
    print(f"-> {line}")
    result = f(line)
    print(f"<- {result}")
    return result

@traced
def field_count(line: str) -> int64:
    return line.split_whitespace().len()

def main():
    print("main starts")
    field_count("2026-10-31T09:14:09 ERROR db connection reset")
    field_count("connection pool exhausted")
```

<span class="caption">Listing 13-7: A decorator that wraps a function with trace output</span>

```console
$ aura run tools.au
wrapping a handler
main starts
-> 2026-10-31T09:14:09 ERROR db connection reset
<- 5
-> connection pool exhausted
<- 3
```

The line `@traced` above `def field_count` means: define `field_count` as
written, then call `traced` with it, and let the name `field_count` refer to
whatever `traced` returns. Every later call of `field_count`, including from
other modules, goes through the wrapper.

Read the output from the top. `wrapping a handler` appears once, *before*
`main starts`. Decorators run when the module initializes, in the order the
decorated functions are declared, not on each call. Each call then goes
through the closure that `traced` returned, which is why every call prints its
`->` and `<-` lines.

Everything inside `traced` is something we met in the last section.
`Handler` is an owned callable type, `Callable[def(line: str) -> int64]`, and
the decorated name `field_count` has exactly this type, because Aura builds it
from the function's parameter names, modes, and result. `traced` takes `f`
with `own` because the closure it returns has to keep `f`, and the capture
list `[own f]` moves the original function into that closure. Since a
lambda's body is one expression, the real work happens in `report`, a named
function that receives the captured `f` and the call's argument. This split
between a one-line lambda and a helper is the usual shape of an Aura
decorator.

That `own` is required, and if you forget it the compiler says what to write:

```aura check-fail:AU3002
type Handler = Callable[def(line: str) -> int64]

def traced(f: Handler) -> Handler:
    print("wrapping a handler")
    return Handler(lambda [own f] line: report(f, line))

def report(f: Handler, line: str) -> int64:
    print(f"-> {line}")
    result = f(line)
    print(f"<- {result}")
    return result

@traced
def field_count(line: str) -> int64:
    return line.split_whitespace().len()

def main():
    print("main starts")
    field_count("2026-10-31T09:14:09 ERROR db connection reset")
    field_count("connection pool exhausted")
```

```console
$ aura check tools.au
error[AU3002]: parameter `f` is borrowed; declare it as `own Callable[def(line: str) -> int64]` to take ownership
 --> tools.au:5:32
  |
5 |     return Handler(lambda [own f] line: report(f, line))
  |                                ^
  = related tools.au:3:12: parameter `f` is borrowed here
  = help: declare the parameter as `own Callable[def(line: str) -> int64]` when the function should consume this non-cloneable value
```

A bare parameter only borrows `f` for the duration of the call to `traced`, but
the closure we return outlives that call. A packed callable can't be cloned
either, so the only way for the wrapper to have `f` later is to own it.

## What a decorator can wrap

Because the decorator's type names the parameter, the decorated function must
use the same name. Rename `line` to `text` in `field_count` and the decorator
no longer fits:

```aura check-fail:AU2015
type Handler = Callable[def(line: str) -> int64]

def traced(f: own Handler) -> Handler:
    print("wrapping a handler")
    return Handler(lambda [own f] line: report(f, line))

def report(f: Handler, line: str) -> int64:
    print(f"-> {line}")
    result = f(line)
    print(f"<- {result}")
    return result

@traced
def field_count(text: str) -> int64:
    return text.split_whitespace().len()

def main():
    print("main starts")
    field_count("2026-10-31T09:14:09 ERROR db connection reset")
    field_count("connection pool exhausted")
```

```console
$ aura check tools.au
error[AU2015]: decorator on `field_count` must take and return `Callable[def(text: str) -> int64]`: callable contract mismatch: parameter `text` would be renamed to `line`; renaming requires an explicit wrapper
 --> tools.au:13:1
   |
13 | @traced
   | ^
  = help: a decorator's callable type names each parameter, so the decorated function must use the same names
```

The message states the rule in its first clause: a decorator on `field_count`
must take and return a callable with `field_count`'s exact contract. Here the
contract has a parameter named `text`, and `Handler` has one named `line`.
This is the same contract rule as in the last section. A caller could write
`field_count(text="...")`, and a wrapper that only answers to `line` would
break that call, so the compiler insists the two agree.

Some functions can't be decorated at all. A parameter with a default is one:

```aura check-fail:AU2047
type Handler = Callable[def(line: str) -> int64]

def traced(f: own Handler) -> Handler:
    print("wrapping a handler")
    return Handler(lambda [own f] line: report(f, line))

def report(f: Handler, line: str) -> int64:
    print(f"-> {line}")
    result = f(line)
    print(f"<- {result}")
    return result

@traced
def field_count(line: str, sep: str = " ") -> int64:
    return line.split_whitespace().len()

def main():
    print("main starts")
    field_count("2026-10-31T09:14:09 ERROR db connection reset")
    field_count("connection pool exhausted")
```

```console
$ aura check tools.au
error[AU2047]: decorated function `field_count` cannot give parameter `sep` a default
 --> tools.au:14:28
   |
14 | def field_count(line: str, sep: str = " ") -> int64:
   |                            ^
  = help: a decorator returns a closure, and a closure has no parameter defaults
```

The help line gives the reason. What replaces a decorated function is a
closure, and closures have no default values for their parameters, so a
caller who left out `sep` would have nothing to fall back on. The same check,
`AU2047`, rejects decorating `main`, a generic function, or a function that
returns a view. Decorators also apply only to module-level functions, not to
methods, classes, or functions inside other functions.

Python programmers sometimes use a decorator to register a function in a
global table as a side effect. That doesn't carry over, because Aura modules
have no mutable state:

```aura check-fail:AU3003
mut calls = 0

def main():
    calls += 1
```

```console
$ aura check tools.au
error[AU3003]: module bindings are immutable; `mut` module state is not supported
 --> tools.au:1:5
  |
1 | mut calls = 0
  |     ^
  = help: put mutable state in a local value owned by `main` or another explicit owner
```

A decorator in Aura transforms one function and nothing else. When we need a
table of tools later, we'll write it out explicitly.

## Stacking decorators

More than one decorator can sit above a function. The decorator expressions
are evaluated top to bottom, and the results are applied bottom to top, so the
one nearest `def` wraps the function first. A decorator can also be a call,
such as `@tag("outer")`, that returns the real decorator. This program shows
both orders at once:

*Filename: tools.au*

```aura
type Step = Callable[def(n: int64) -> int64]
type Wrapper = Callable[def(f: own Step) -> Step]

def tag(label: own str) -> Wrapper:
    print(f"evaluate {label}")
    return Wrapper(lambda [own label] own f: wrap(label.clone(), f))

def wrap(label: own str, f: own Step) -> Step:
    print(f"apply {label}")
    return Step(lambda [own label, own f] n: show(label, f, n))

def show(label: str, f: Step, n: int64) -> int64:
    print(f"call {label}")
    return f(n)

@tag("outer")
@tag("inner")
def double(n: int64) -> int64:
    return n * 2

def main():
    print(double(21))
```

<span class="caption">Listing 13-8: A decorator factory, stacked twice</span>

```console
$ aura run tools.au
evaluate outer
evaluate inner
apply inner
apply outer
call outer
call inner
42
```

`tag` is a *decorator factory*: it takes a label and returns a `Wrapper`, a
callable that takes a `Step` and returns a `Step`. Both `tag` calls run first,
in source order. Then the inner wrapper is applied to `double` and the outer
wrapper to that result. At call time, the outermost wrapper runs first, so the
trace reads `call outer`, then `call inner`, then the real `double`.

The lambda inside `tag` is worth reading slowly:
`lambda [own label] own f: wrap(label.clone(), f)`. It captures `label`, and it
takes its own parameter `f` with `own`, matching `Wrapper`'s `own Step`. Its
body clones `label` before passing it on. That clone matters: if the lambda
moved `label` out, it would become a consuming closure, callable once, and
`Wrapper` describes a callable that can be called any number of times.

## One decorator for every tool

`traced` and `tag` work only for one exact signature. A tool runner has many
tools with different argument and result types, and we don't want a separate
tracing decorator for each. A generic decorator solves this. Its type
parameters are inferred from each function it decorates:

*Filename: tools.au*

```aura
type Tool[A, R] = Callable[def(args: A) -> R]
type Decorator[A, R] = Callable[def(f: own Tool[A, R]) -> Tool[A, R]]

def traced[A, R](name: own str) -> Decorator[A, R]:
    return Decorator[A, R](lambda [own name] own f: wrap(name.clone(), f))

def wrap[A, R](name: own str, f: own Tool[A, R]) -> Tool[A, R]:
    return Tool[A, R](lambda [own name, own f] args: call_traced(name, f, args))

def call_traced[A, R](name: str, f: Tool[A, R], args: A) -> R:
    print(f"call {name}")
    return f(args)

@traced("fields")
def field_count(args: str) -> int64:
    return args.split_whitespace().len()

@traced("double")
def double(args: int64) -> int64:
    return args * 2

def main():
    print(field_count("connection pool exhausted"))
    print(double(21))
```

<span class="caption">Listing 13-9: A generic decorator factory that fits any one-argument tool</span>

```console
$ aura run tools.au
call fields
3
call double
42
```

`traced("fields")` can't work out `A` and `R` from its own argument, a string.
The function under it supplies them: for `field_count`, `A` is `str` and `R` is
`int64`; for `double`, both are `int64`. Each use is inferred on its own.

A type parameter stands for a type, never for a whole parameter list, so
`Tool[A, R]` still fixes the shape of the function: exactly one parameter,
named `args`. That is why both tools call their parameter `args`. A tool that
names it anything else gets the same `AU2015` we saw earlier:

```console
$ aura check tools.au
error[AU2015]: decorator on `double` must take and return `Callable[def(n: int64) -> int64]`: callable contract mismatch: parameter `n` would be renamed to `args`; renaming requires an explicit wrapper
 --> tools.au:18:1
   |
18 | @traced("double")
   | ^
  = help: a decorator's callable type names each parameter, so the decorated function must use the same names
```

One parameter called `args` sounds limiting until you make `A` a class. A tool
that needs a level and an optional service takes one argument of a class with
those two fields. And a class is something the compiler can teach to read and
write JSON.

## Deriving a JSON codec

The `json` module's `json.Codec` trait describes a type that converts to and
from `json.Value`, the module's tree of JSON data. We'll use only a few of the
module's functions here; [Chapter 16](/book/ch16-04-json) covers it in full. You can implement it by
hand, but for an ordinary class or enum you write the `impl` line with no body
and the compiler writes the implementation:

*Filename: tools.au*

```aura
import json

class CountArgs:
    """Counts log records at one level, optionally for one service."""

    level: str
    service: str | None = None

impl json.Codec for CountArgs

def main():
    inputs = [
        '{"level": "ERROR", "service": "db"}',
        '{"level": "ERROR"}',
        '{"level": 3}',
        '{"service": "db"}',
        '{"level": "ERROR", "limit": 5}',
        '{"level": ',
    ]
    for text in inputs:
        match own json.decode_text[CountArgs](text):
            case Ok(args):
                print(f"ok level={args.level} service={args.service}")
            case Err(error):
                print(f"error {error}")
    print(json.dumps(json.encode(CountArgs(level="WARN", service=None))))
```

<span class="caption">Listing 13-10: Decoding and encoding a class through a derived codec</span>

```console
$ aura run tools.au
ok level=ERROR service=db
ok level=ERROR service=None
error $.level: expected string, found integer
error $: missing field `level`
error $: unknown field `limit`
error $: invalid JSON at line 1, column 11: EOF while parsing a value
{"level":"WARN","service":null}
```

One empty `impl` gave `CountArgs` three things: `encode`, which turns a value
into a JSON tree; `decode`, which goes the other way; and `schema`, which we'll
come to shortly. `json.decode_text[CountArgs](text)` parses the text and
decodes it in one step, returning `Result[CountArgs, json.DecodeError]`.

The decoder is strict, and each error names the place in the document it was
reading, as a path from the root `$`:

- `{"level": 3}` has the right key with the wrong kind of value, so the error
  is at `$.level`.
- `{"service": "db"}` leaves out `level`, which has no default, so it is a
  missing field.
- `{"level": "ERROR", "limit": 5}` has a key `CountArgs` doesn't declare.
  Rather than ignore it, the decoder rejects it as an unknown field. That
  catches a misspelled key, which would otherwise be silently dropped and
  replaced with a default.
- `{"level": ` isn't JSON at all, so the error is a parse error at the root,
  with a line and column.

`service` is declared `str | None = None`. The `= None` default is what makes
it optional in the input; a `T | None` field without a default must still be
present, even if its value is `null`. On the way out, `encode` writes every
field, so `None` comes out as `null`.

Decoding stops at the first error. The result is either a complete, valid
`CountArgs` or an error, never a half-filled value, which is the property we
want at a boundary where text from outside enters the program.

The field types themselves need a JSON form. Strings, numbers, booleans,
lists, `dict[str, T]`, optionals, and other classes and enums with a codec all
have one. A field of a class without a codec stops the derivation:

```aura check-fail:AU2002
import json

class Window:
    start: str
    end: str

class CountArgs:
    level: str
    window: Window

impl json.Codec for CountArgs
```

```console
$ aura check tools.au
error[AU2002]: derived `json.Codec` for `CountArgs`: type `Window` does not implement trait `json.Codec`
 --> tools.au:11:1
   |
11 | impl json.Codec for CountArgs
   | ^
```

Adding `impl json.Codec for Window` fixes it. The [Manual](/manual/json#derived-codecs)
lists every field type and its JSON form.

## Telling a caller what a tool accepts

The third derived method is `schema`. It returns a JSON Schema document that
describes exactly what `decode` accepts:

```aura
import json

class CountArgs:
    """Counts log records at one level, optionally for one service."""

    level: str
    service: str | None = None

impl json.Codec for CountArgs

def main():
    print(json.dumps(json.schema[CountArgs](), indent=2))
```

```console
$ aura run tools.au
{
  "additionalProperties": false,
  "description": "Counts log records at one level, optionally for one service.",
  "properties": {
    "level": {
      "type": "string"
    },
    "service": {
      "anyOf": [
        {
          "type": "string"
        },
        {
          "type": "null"
        }
      ]
    }
  },
  "required": [
    "level"
  ],
  "type": "object"
}
```

The class docstring became the schema's `description`. Only `level` is
`required`, because `service` has a default, and `additionalProperties` is
`false`, matching the decoder's refusal of unknown keys. This is the document
you would hand to a language model or another program that wants to call the
tool: because it is derived from the same class as the decoder, the two can't
disagree about what a valid call looks like.

An enum without payloads encodes as its variant name. That lets us use our
`Level` enum from Chapter 12 directly as a field type instead of a string, and
the schema then lists the allowed names, `"Debug"`, `"Info"`, `"Warn"`, and
`"Error"`. A caller that sends `"ERROR"` gets an error rather than a level we
didn't define.

## The tool runner

Now we can put the pieces together. Each tool is a decorated function that
takes one argument class and returns one result class, both with derived
codecs. A `ToolCall` class decodes the outer envelope. Its `args` field has
the type `json.Value`, which passes whatever JSON it finds through unchanged,
so the envelope can be decoded before we know which tool's argument class to
use.

*Filename: tools.au*

```aura
import json

enum Level:
    Debug
    Info
    Warn
    Error

impl json.Codec for Level

class Record:
    level: Level
    service: str

class CountArgs:
    """Counts log records at one level, optionally for one service."""

    level: Level
    service: str | None = None

impl json.Codec for CountArgs

class Count:
    matched: int64

impl json.Codec for Count

class ServicesArgs:
    """Lists the services that logged at one level."""

    level: Level

impl json.Codec for ServicesArgs

class Services:
    names: list[str]

impl json.Codec for Services

class ToolCall:
    tool: str
    args: json.Value

impl json.Codec for ToolCall

type Tool[A, R] = Callable[def(args: A) -> R]
type Decorator[A, R] = Callable[def(f: own Tool[A, R]) -> Tool[A, R]]

def traced[A, R](name: own str) -> Decorator[A, R]:
    return Decorator[A, R](lambda [own name] own f: wrap(name.clone(), f))

def wrap[A, R](name: own str, f: own Tool[A, R]) -> Tool[A, R]:
    return Tool[A, R](lambda [own name, own f] args: call_traced(name, f, args))

def call_traced[A, R](name: str, f: Tool[A, R], args: A) -> R:
    print(f"call {name}")
    return f(args)

def sample() -> list[Record]:
    return [
        Record(level=Level.Info, service="api"),
        Record(level=Level.Error, service="api"),
        Record(level=Level.Error, service="db"),
        Record(level=Level.Warn, service="db"),
        Record(level=Level.Error, service="worker"),
    ]

@traced("count")
def count(args: CountArgs) -> Count:
    mut matched = 0
    for record in sample():
        if record.level != args.level:
            continue
        match args.service:
            case str as wanted:
                if record.service == wanted:
                    matched += 1
            case None:
                matched += 1
    return Count(matched=matched)

@traced("services")
def services(args: ServicesArgs) -> Services:
    mut names: list[str] = []
    for record in sample():
        if record.level == args.level and record.service not in names:
            names.append(record.service.clone())
    return Services(names=names)

def run[A: json.Codec, R: json.Codec](f: Tool[A, R], args: own json.Value) -> Result[json.Value, str]:
    match own json.decode[A](args):
        case Ok(decoded):
            result = f(decoded)
            return Ok(json.encode(result))
        case Err(error):
            return Err(f"bad arguments: {error}")

def dispatch(text: str) -> Result[json.Value, str]:
    match own json.decode_text[ToolCall](text):
        case Ok(call):
            if call.tool == "count":
                return run(count, call.args)
            if call.tool == "services":
                return run(services, call.args)
            return Err(f"unknown tool `{call.tool}`")
        case Err(error):
            return Err(f"bad call: {error}")

def main():
    calls = [
        '{"tool": "count", "args": {"level": "Error"}}',
        '{"tool": "count", "args": {"level": "Error", "service": "db"}}',
        '{"tool": "services", "args": {"level": "Error"}}',
        '{"tool": "count", "args": {"level": "ERROR"}}',
        '{"tool": "count", "args": {"level": "Error", "limit": 5}}',
        '{"tool": "grep", "args": {}}',
        '{"args": {}}',
    ]
    for text in calls:
        match dispatch(text):
            case Ok(value):
                print(f"result {json.dumps(value)}")
            case Err(message):
                print(f"error {message}")
```

<span class="caption">Listing 13-11: A typed tool runner with decorated tools and derived codecs</span>

```console
$ aura run tools.au
call count
result {"matched":3}
call count
result {"matched":1}
call services
result {"names":["api","db","worker"]}
error bad arguments: $.level: unknown variant `ERROR`
error bad arguments: $: unknown field `limit`
error unknown tool `grep`
error bad call: $: missing field `tool`
```

Let's trace one call through the program. `dispatch` decodes the text as a
`ToolCall`. If the envelope is malformed, as in the last call that has no
`tool` key, it stops there with the decoder's message. Otherwise it picks the
tool by name and hands it, with the still-undecoded `args`, to `run`.

`run` is generic over the argument type `A` and the result type `R`, and its
bounds `A: json.Codec` and `R: json.Codec` say that both must have codecs. The
type arguments are inferred from the tool we pass: `run(count, call.args)`
fixes `A = CountArgs` and `R = Count`. So `json.decode[A](args)` decodes the
arguments as exactly the class `count` expects, and `json.encode(result)`
encodes whatever it returned. `f` is a bare parameter, so `run` borrows the
decorated binding for the call and leaves it in place for the next one.
(Writing `json.encode(f(decoded))` on one line fails to infer `encode`'s type
parameter in Aura 0.11, with `AU2002`; binding the result to `result` first,
as the listing does, gives the compiler the type it needs.)

Each successful call prints `call count` or `call services` before its result.
Those lines come from `traced`, and neither tool contains any tracing code. The
two bad-argument calls never reach a tool at all, and never print a `call`
line, because the decoder rejects them first. A tool body can rely on its
argument being a valid `CountArgs`: `args.level` is a real `Level`, and an
unknown key in the JSON can't have slipped through as a silent default.

`dispatch` lists the tools with plain `if` tests. As we saw, a decorator can't
add a function to a module-level registry, so the list of tools lives in one
function where you can read it. Adding a tool means writing the decorated
function, its two classes, and one more `if`. The reference agent in the
repository, under `examples/agents/tool_runner`, grows this same design into a
package with a separate tool layer and more tools.

## Summary

Functions in Aura are values with a full contract: parameter names, modes,
types, and result. Named functions and capture-free lambdas are thin values
you can store and pass anywhere. A lambda that captures becomes a closure,
and you choose how each capture is held: copied or moved in by default,
borrowed with `[name]` or `[mut name]`, or taken with `[own name]`. What the
body does with its captures makes it callable any number of times, once, or
only through a `mut` binding. To return or store a capturing closure, you pack
it into a `Callable[...]` type, explicitly.

Decorators are built from those pieces. A decorator is a function from a
`Callable` to a `Callable` of the same contract, applied once when the module
starts, and a generic decorator factory such as `traced[A, R](name)` serves
every function with one parameter named `args`. Paired with derived
`json.Codec` implementations, that gives a typed boundary for JSON: input is
decoded strictly into classes, with path-precise errors and a schema that
describes it, before any of your code runs. The [Manual](/manual/functions#decorators)
has the full decorator rules.

Several of the values in this chapter owned something that needed to be given
back at the end, a borrowed list or a captured counter. The next chapter looks
at resources that need cleanup at a known moment, such as files and network
connections, and at how `with` makes that moment explicit.

## Source: docs/book/ch14-00-resources-and-cleanup.md

# Resources and cleanup

Programs hold on to things that belong to the outside world. An open file is a
slot in the operating system's file table. A socket is a connection that the
machine on the other end is keeping alive for us. A temporary file sits on disk
until somebody deletes it. Each of these has to be given back, and the hard part
is not remembering to give it back on the happy path. The hard part is giving it
back when the function returns early, when an error propagates out through
`try`, or when a trap stops the task halfway through.

Python answers this with the `with` statement and context managers, and if you
have written `with open(path) as f:` you already know the shape. Aura keeps that
shape and tightens the contract. A `with` block in Aura runs its cleanup exactly
once on every way out of the block, including traps, in an order you can predict
from the source. Because Aura has no garbage collector, there is no "eventually"
in that sentence: cleanup happens at the line where the block ends.

In this chapter we'll first use `with` on files the standard library gives us,
and look closely at when and in what order cleanup runs. Then we'll write our
own resource manager, a scratch file that deletes itself, and push it through
every failure we can think of: an error from `try`, a cleanup that fails, a trap
in the middle of the body, and a trap inside the cleanup itself. By the end you
will be able to read any `with` block and say exactly what runs when it ends,
and why.

The last piece of the chapter points forward. A `TaskGroup`, which we use for
concurrency in [Chapter 15](/book/ch15-00-concurrency), is also a resource
managed by `with`. The rules you learn here are the reason a group of tasks can
promise that none of them outlives the block that started it.

## Source: docs/book/ch14-01-with-and-cleanup.md

# `with` and deterministic cleanup

Let's start with a small, ordinary job: count the lines in a text file. Make a
new package with `aura new line_count`, put a `notes.txt` with three lines next
to `Aura.toml`, and replace `src/main.au` with this:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
import fs
import io

def line_count(path: str) -> Result[int64, io.Error]:
    with file = try fs.open(path):
        text = try file.read_all()
        return Result.Ok(len(text.split("\n")) - 1)

def report(path: str):
    match line_count(path):
        case Result.Ok(count):
            print(f"{path}: {count} lines")
        case Result.Err(error):
            print(f"{path}: {error}")

def main():
    report("notes.txt")
    report("missing.txt")
```

<span class="caption">Listing 14-1: Reading a file inside a `with` block</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
notes.txt: 3 lines
missing.txt: io.Error.NotFound
```

If you have written Python, the `with` line reads the way you expect. `fs.open`
opens the file, the block uses it, and when the block ends the file is closed.
There are two small differences in spelling. Aura writes the binding first,
`with file = ...`, although `with ... as file` also works and means the same
thing. And `fs.open` returns a `Result`, because opening a file can fail, so we
put `try` in front of it. When the file is missing, `try` returns the error from
`line_count` before the block is ever entered, which is the second line of
output.

The interesting part is the line that is not there. Nowhere do we call
`file.close()`. The `return` on the last line of the block leaves `line_count`
while the file is open, and Aura closes it on the way out. The same happens if
`file.read_all()` fails and `try` propagates the error: the file is closed
before the error reaches `report`.

## Forgetting `try`

It is easy to forget that `fs.open` gives back a `Result` and not a file. Let's
see what happens if we leave out the `try`:

```aura check-fail:AU2017
import fs
import io

def line_count(path: str) -> Result[int64, io.Error]:
    with file = fs.open(path):
        text = try file.read_all()
        return Result.Ok(len(text.split("\n")) - 1)

def main():
    print(line_count("notes.txt"))
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU2017]: `with` requires a context manager, found `Result[fs.File, io.Error]`
 --> src/main.au:5:5
  |
5 |     with file = fs.open(path):
  |     ^
```

The compiler points at the `with` and tells us what it found:
`Result[fs.File, io.Error]`. A `Result` has no cleanup of its own, so it can't
manage a scope. `AU2017` is the code Aura uses for everything that goes wrong
with the context manager protocol, and we'll meet it again in the next section
when we write our own managers. The fix is the one the type suggests: unwrap the
`Result` with `try` (or `match` on it) so that the `with` gets the `fs.File`
inside.

## Every way out runs the exit

Files don't print anything when they close, so to watch cleanup happen we need a
resource that talks. Here is a tiny class, `Section`, that prints a line when a
block starts and another when it ends. We'll look at how `__enter__` and
`__exit__` work in detail in the next section. For now, read them as "run this
at the start" and "run this at the end".

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
class Section:
    name: str

    def __enter__(mut self) -> None:
        print("  enter " + self.name)

    def __exit__(mut self) -> None:
        print("  exit " + self.name)

def main():
    for n in range(4):
        with section = Section(name=f"round {n}"):
            if n == 1:
                print("  skipping")
                continue
            if n == 3:
                print("  stopping")
                break
            print("  working")
    print("done")
```

<span class="caption">Listing 14-2: Leaving a `with` block by falling through, `continue`, and `break`</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
  enter round 0
  working
  exit round 0
  enter round 1
  skipping
  exit round 1
  enter round 2
  working
  exit round 2
  enter round 3
  stopping
  exit round 3
done
```

Each round leaves the block in a different way. Rounds 0 and 2 fall off the end.
Round 1 leaves with `continue`, which jumps to the next iteration of the loop
around the block. Round 3 leaves with `break`, which jumps out of the loop
entirely. Every round prints its `exit` line before control goes anywhere else.

That is the core promise of `with`. Once the block has been entered, its exit
runs exactly once, whichever way control leaves the block:

- falling through the end of the block
- `return`
- `break` or `continue` that leaves the block
- `try` propagating an error
- a trap, such as a failed assertion or an index out of range
- cancellation of the task the block is running in

We've seen the first four. The next section covers traps in detail, and
[Chapter 15](/book/ch15-00-concurrency) covers cancellation. They follow the
same rule.

"Exactly once" matters as much as "always". An exit can't run twice because two
paths both tried to clean up, and it can't be skipped because one path forgot.
The compiler plans the cleanup for every exit edge of the block when it compiles
the function, so it is not something you can get wrong by adding a new `return`
later.

## Bindings in the body stay in the body

Python programmers sometimes rely on a detail of Python's `with`: names bound
inside the block are still visible after it. That isn't true in Aura. A `with`
body is a block like the body of an `if` or a `for`, and bindings made inside it
end with it. Suppose we try to move the `return` out of the block in Listing
14-1:

```aura check-fail:AU2001
import fs
import io

def line_count(path: str) -> Result[int64, io.Error]:
    with file = try fs.open(path):
        text = try file.read_all()
    return Result.Ok(len(text.split("\n")) - 1)

def main():
    print(line_count("notes.txt"))
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU2001]: unknown name `text`
 --> src/main.au:7:26
  |
7 |     return Result.Ok(len(text.split("\n")) - 1)
  |                          ^
```

As far as the compiler is concerned, there is no `text` on line 7. It is the same scoping
rule we met in [Chapter 3](/book/ch03-00-common-concepts), and it has a pleasant
consequence here: nothing that was computed while the file was open can be
mistaken for the file itself after it closes. If you need a value after the
block, declare it before the block with `mut` and assign it inside, or return
from inside the block as Listing 14-1 does.

## Several resources in one header

Copying a file needs two open files at once: one to read and one to write. A
`with` header can list several items separated by commas:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
import fs
import io

def copy_file(source: str, target: str) -> Result[None, io.Error]:
    with input = try fs.open(source), output = try fs.create(target):
        text = try input.read_all()
        try output.write_all(text)
    return Result.Ok(None)

def report(source: str, target: str):
    match copy_file(source, target):
        case Result.Ok(_):
            print(f"copied {source} to {target}")
        case Result.Err(error):
            print(f"could not copy {source}: {error}")

def main():
    report("notes.txt", "notes.bak")
    report("missing.txt", "missing.bak")
```

<span class="caption">Listing 14-3: Two resources in one `with` header</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
copied notes.txt to notes.bak
could not copy missing.txt: io.Error.NotFound
$ ls
Aura.lock
Aura.toml
notes.bak
notes.txt
src
tests
```

Items are set up from left to right, and each one is fully entered before the
next is evaluated. That means a later item may use an earlier one's binding,
which is handy when the second resource is derived from the first. It also
explains what `ls` shows: there is no `missing.bak`. When `fs.open("missing.txt")`
failed, `try` left the function before `fs.create` was ever evaluated, so no
empty target file was created.

When the block ends, the items are cleaned up in the opposite order: `output`
first, then `input`. We can see the order with two `Section`s:

```aura
class Section:
    name: str

    def __enter__(mut self) -> None:
        print("enter " + self.name)

    def __exit__(mut self) -> None:
        print("exit " + self.name)

def main():
    with Section(name="outer") as outer, inner = Section(name="inner"):
        print("body")
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
enter outer
enter inner
body
exit inner
exit outer
```

This also shows the two spellings side by side: `Section(name="outer") as outer`
and `inner = Section(name="inner")` mean the same thing, and you can mix them in
one header.

Reverse order is the only order that is safe in general. A resource entered
later may depend on one entered earlier: a buffered writer wrapping a file, a
transaction on a connection, a lock that protects a data structure. If the
earlier one were torn down first, the later one's cleanup would run against
something already gone. Closing in reverse means each cleanup runs while
everything it might need is still alive. Writing one header with two items is
the same as nesting one `with` inside another, and nested blocks naturally unwind
from the inside out.

## What Aura closes for you without `with`
