You might wonder what happens if we open a file without `with` at all. Aura
doesn't leak it. An `fs.File` is an owned value, and like every owned value
(see [Chapter 4](/book/ch04-00-understanding-ownership)) it is released when its
owner goes out of scope. A file bound with `mut file = try fs.create(path)` in a
function is flushed and closed when that function returns.

So why use `with`? There are three reasons, and the third is the important one.

The first is that `with` puts the end of the resource's life on the page. The
indented block is the region where the file is open, and anyone reading the code
can see it without tracing ownership.

The second is that it keeps the resource from going anywhere else. The `with`
binding is managed by the block, and the compiler won't let you move it out:
writing `return Result.Ok(file)` inside the block of Listing 14-1 is rejected
with ``cannot move managed `with` resource `file` ``. We'll come back to that
error in [Chapter 15](/book/ch15-00-concurrency), where it is the rule that keeps
tasks from outliving their group.

The third is that `with` is how your own code gets to run at cleanup. Aura
classes have no destructor. A class can define `__exit__`, but only a `with`
block calls it. Watch what happens to the same `Section` with and without
`with`:

```aura
class Section:
    name: str

    def __enter__(mut self) -> None:
        print("enter " + self.name)

    def __exit__(mut self) -> None:
        print("exit " + self.name)

def loose():
    section = Section(name="loose")
    print("using " + section.name)

def main():
    loose()
    with section = Section(name="scoped"):
        print("using " + section.name)
    print("done")
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
using loose
enter scoped
using scoped
exit scoped
done
```

The loose `Section` is dropped at the end of `loose`: its memory is freed and
its `name` string with it. But no `enter` or `exit` line appears for it, because
dropping a value only releases what it owns. It doesn't run arbitrary code.
The `with` version runs both.

This is a deliberate choice, and Python is a useful contrast. Python has
`__del__`, which runs when an object is collected, but *when* that is depends on
the implementation: right away in CPython when the last reference goes, at some
later collection in PyPy, possibly never for an object caught in a reference
cycle at shutdown. That is why Python style says to use `with` for files even
though CPython would usually close them anyway. Aura removes the ambiguity from
the other side. Memory and the standard library's handles are released when
their owner's scope ends, which is always a known point. Code you write runs at
cleanup only through `with`, which is always visible in the source.

## Resources the standard library gives you

You can use these standard library types in a `with` header, and each knows how
to clean itself up:

- `fs.File`, from `fs.open`, `fs.create`, and `fs.append`
- the `net` socket, listener, and HTTP types
- `process.Child`, `process.Pipe`, and `process.Supervisor`
- `TaskGroup`

For files, sockets, and pipes the cleanup is a close. For a `TaskGroup` it is
something richer: waiting for every task the group started. That is the subject
of [Chapter 15](/book/ch15-00-concurrency). The details for each resource are in
its Manual page, and the full contract of the statement is in the Manual's
[Statements](/manual/statements) chapter.

So far every exit we have watched has succeeded. Real cleanup can fail: deleting
a file that someone else already deleted, flushing to a disk that is full. And
real bodies can trap. In the next section we'll build a resource of our own and
find out exactly what Aura does in each of those cases.

## Source: docs/book/ch14-02-resource-managers.md

# Writing your own resource manager

The standard library's resources close themselves, but plenty of cleanup is
specific to your program. A test fixture deletes the directory it set up. A
progress bar erases itself when the work is done. A transaction rolls back if it
was never committed. In Aura, any class can take part in `with` by following a
small protocol, and once it does, it gets the same guarantees as `fs.File`.

We'll build one example through the whole section: a scratch file that a
function writes intermediate results into and that is deleted when the function
is done with it, however it finishes.

## The protocol

A class becomes a context manager by defining one or two methods:

- `__exit__(mut self)`, which runs once when control leaves the block. Instead
  of `__exit__`, a class may define `close(mut self) -> None`, and Aura uses
  that as the exit.
- `__enter__(mut self)`, which is optional and runs after the item expression
  has produced the value and before the body starts.

Both methods take `mut self` and nothing else. Here is the scratch file:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
import fs
import io

class Scratch:
    path: str

    def create(path: own str) -> Result[Scratch, io.Error]:
        try fs.write_string(path, "")
        print("created " + path)
        return Result.Ok(Scratch(path=path))

    def append(self, line: str) -> Result[None, io.Error]:
        return fs.append_string(self.path, line + "\n")

    def read(self) -> Result[str, io.Error]:
        return fs.read_to_string(self.path)

    def __exit__(mut self) -> Result[None, io.Error]:
        try fs.remove_file(self.path)
        print("removed " + self.path)
        return Result.Ok(None)

def summarize(values: list[int64]) -> Result[int64, io.Error]:
    with scratch = try Scratch.create("work.tmp"):
        for value in values:
            try scratch.append(str(value))
        text = try scratch.read()
        print(text)
    return Result.Ok(len(values))

def main():
    match summarize([3, 1, 4]):
        case Result.Ok(count):
            print(f"summarized {count} values")
        case Result.Err(error):
            print(f"error: {error}")
```

<span class="caption">Listing 14-4: A scratch file that deletes itself</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
created work.tmp
3
1
4

removed work.tmp
summarized 3 values
$ ls
Aura.lock
Aura.toml
src
tests
```

The output reads in the order the program runs: the file is created, filled,
read back, and removed before `summarize` returns. Afterwards `ls` shows no
`work.tmp`.

There are a few design choices in `Scratch` worth looking at, because each one
comes from a rule of the protocol.

Creating the file happens in `Scratch.create`, an associated function that
returns `Result[Scratch, io.Error]`, and not in `__enter__`. That is because
`__enter__` can't fail in a recoverable way. It must return `None` (or a view,
which we'll get to at the end of this section), so it has no way to hand an
`io.Error` back to the caller. The pattern that works is to put the fallible
setup in the item expression and use `try` there, exactly as we did with
`try fs.open(path)`. If `create` fails, the `with` never registers an exit,
because there is nothing yet to clean up.

The exit, on the other hand, is allowed to fail, and ours can: `fs.remove_file`
returns a `Result`. So `__exit__` is declared to return `Result[None, io.Error]`
and uses `try` like any other function. We'll see what Aura does with that error
shortly.

`create` takes `path` as `own str`. The new `Scratch` stores the string in its
field, so it has to own it. If you write `path: str`, the compiler stops you at
`Scratch(path=path)` with an `AU3002` and suggests either `own str` or
`.clone()`. Taking ownership is the better fit: the caller passes a literal, and
nobody else needs the string afterwards.

If the methods have the wrong shape, the class isn't a context manager at all.
Here `__exit__` forgot the `mut` on `self`:

```aura check-fail:AU2017
class Scratch:
    path: str

    def __exit__(self) -> None:
        print("removing " + self.path)

def main():
    with scratch = Scratch(path="work.tmp"):
        print("working")
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU2017]: class `Scratch` is not a context manager: `__exit__(mut self)` is missing or has the wrong shape
 --> src/main.au:8:5
  |
8 |     with scratch = Scratch(path="work.tmp"):
  |     ^
```

The error lands on the `with`, not on the method, because the method is
perfectly fine as an ordinary method. It only becomes a problem when we ask the
class to manage a scope. The reason for `mut self` is that cleanup almost always
changes the resource: it closes a handle, marks a transaction finished, empties a
buffer. Requiring `mut` means the exit has the access it needs, and it tells
readers that calling it changes the object.

## When cleanup itself fails

What should happen if the scratch file is already gone when the block ends?
Let's make that happen on purpose, by deleting the file in the body:

```aura
import fs
import io

class Scratch:
    path: str

    def create(path: own str) -> Result[Scratch, io.Error]:
        try fs.write_string(path, "")
        print("created " + path)
        return Result.Ok(Scratch(path=path))

    def __exit__(mut self) -> Result[None, io.Error]:
        try fs.remove_file(self.path)
        print("removed " + self.path)
        return Result.Ok(None)

def tidy() -> Result[None, io.Error]:
    with scratch = try Scratch.create("work.tmp"):
        try fs.remove_file("work.tmp")
        print("someone removed work.tmp early")
    print("after the block")
    return Result.Ok(None)

def main():
    match tidy():
        case Result.Ok(_):
            print("tidy finished")
        case Result.Err(error):
            print(f"tidy failed: {error}")
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
created work.tmp
someone removed work.tmp early
tidy failed: io.Error.NotFound
```

The body finished normally, then the exit ran and its `fs.remove_file` failed
with `NotFound`. Aura treated that `Err` the way `try` treats one: it returned
from `tidy` with the error, so `after the block` never printed. An exit that
returns `Result` behaves as if there were an invisible `try` at the end of the
block.

That has a consequence for every function that uses such a manager. The
enclosing function must be able to return the error. If we use `Scratch` in a
`main` that returns nothing, the compiler tells us so:

```aura check-fail:AU2017
import fs
import io

class Scratch:
    path: str

    def __exit__(mut self) -> Result[None, io.Error]:
        try fs.remove_file(self.path)
        return Result.Ok(None)

def main():
    with scratch = Scratch(path="work.tmp"):
        print("working")
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU2017]: exit of `Scratch` may fail with `io.Error`; the enclosing function must return `Result[_, io.Error]`
 --> src/main.au:12:5
   |
12 |     with scratch = Scratch(path="work.tmp"):
   |     ^
```

This is the same reasoning Aura applies to `try` everywhere: an error has to go
somewhere you can see in the signature. Python's `__exit__` can raise, and the
exception then flies out of the `with` statement with nothing in the function's
signature to warn the caller. In Aura, a fallible cleanup shows up as a
`Result` return type on every function that uses it. The error type can also be
one that has a `From` conversion from the exit's error, as described in
[Chapter 9](/book/ch09-00-error-handling).

If you don't want callers to deal with cleanup errors, decide inside the exit:
log the problem and return `None` from a `__exit__(mut self) -> None`. That is a
legitimate choice for best-effort cleanup like deleting a temporary file. The
point is that the choice is written down in one place.

### When the body is already failing

What if the body fails and then the cleanup fails too? Only one error can come
out of the block, and Aura picks the body's. Here both fail:

```aura
class Flush:
    name: str

    def __exit__(mut self) -> Result[None, str]:
        print("exit " + self.name)
        return Result.Err("exit of " + self.name + " failed")

def step() -> Result[int64, str]:
    return Result.Err("body failed")

def run() -> Result[int64, str]:
    with flush = Flush(name="flush"):
        value = try step()
        print(value)
    return Result.Ok(0)

def main():
    print(run())
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
exit flush
Result.Err(body failed)
```

The exit still ran (it printed `exit flush`), but its error was dropped and
`body failed` came out. That is the right priority. The body's error describes
what actually went wrong. The cleanup failure is often a consequence of it, a
half-written file that couldn't be flushed because the write that filled it
failed. Reporting the cleanup error instead would send you looking in the wrong
place.

## Traps unwind through every `with`

A `Result` is an error the program expects and handles. A trap is different: an
index out of range, a failed assertion, an overflow. As
[Chapter 9](/book/ch09-00-error-handling) explains, a trap stops the task. But
"stops" does not mean "abandons its resources". Let's add a line to
`summarize` that traps when the list is empty, and call it with an empty list:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
import fs
import io

class Scratch:
    path: str

    def create(path: own str) -> Result[Scratch, io.Error]:
        try fs.write_string(path, "")
        print("created " + path)
        return Result.Ok(Scratch(path=path))

    def append(self, line: str) -> Result[None, io.Error]:
        return fs.append_string(self.path, line + "\n")

    def read(self) -> Result[str, io.Error]:
        return fs.read_to_string(self.path)

    def __exit__(mut self) -> Result[None, io.Error]:
        try fs.remove_file(self.path)
        print("removed " + self.path)
        return Result.Ok(None)

def summarize(values: list[int64]) -> Result[int64, io.Error]:
    with scratch = try Scratch.create("work.tmp"):
        print(f"first value: {values[0]}")
        for value in values:
            try scratch.append(str(value))
        text = try scratch.read()
        print(text)
    return Result.Ok(len(values))

def main():
    match summarize([3, 1, 4]):
        case Result.Ok(count):
            print(f"summarized {count} values")
        case Result.Err(error):
            print(f"error: {error}")
    match summarize([]):
        case Result.Ok(count):
            print(f"summarized {count} values")
        case Result.Err(error):
            print(f"error: {error}")
```

<span class="caption">Listing 14-5: A trap inside the body of a `with`</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
created work.tmp
first value: 3
3
1
4

removed work.tmp
summarized 3 values
created work.tmp
removed work.tmp
error[AU4003]: list index `0` is out of bounds for length `0`
 --> src/main.au:25:38
   |
25 |         print(f"first value: {values[0]}")
   |                                      ^
  = note: Aura call chain (innermost first): summarize at 23:1 -> main at 32:1
$ ls
Aura.lock
Aura.toml
src
tests
```

The first call behaves as before. The second creates the scratch file and then
traps on `values[0]`. Look at the order of the last lines: `removed work.tmp`
comes *before* the diagnostic. When the trap happened, Aura did not stop on the
spot. It walked back out of the block, ran the scratch file's exit, and only
then reported the trap and ended the program with a failure status. The `ls`
confirms that no `work.tmp` was left behind.

The diagnostic itself is the ordinary trap report. `AU4003` is the
out-of-bounds code, the arrow points at the `0` in `values[0]`, and the note
lists the call chain from the innermost frame outwards.

### Cleanup order during a trap

A trap doesn't only unwind the block it happens in. It unwinds every block that
is active, in this function and in all the functions that called it, innermost
first. Here is a program with `with` blocks at two levels, and a manager whose
exit fails:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
class Section:
    name: str

    def __enter__(mut self) -> None:
        print("enter " + self.name)

    def __exit__(mut self) -> None:
        print("exit " + self.name)

class Journal:
    entries: list[str]

    def __exit__(mut self) -> Result[None, str]:
        if len(self.entries) == 0:
            return Result.Err("journal is empty")
        print(f"flushed {len(self.entries)} entries")
        return Result.Ok(None)

def lookup(values: list[int64], index: int64) -> Result[int64, str]:
    with journal = Journal(entries=[]), section = Section(name="lookup"):
        return Result.Ok(values[index])

def main():
    with section = Section(name="main"):
        print(lookup([1, 2, 3], 1))
        print(lookup([1, 2, 3], 9))
```

<span class="caption">Listing 14-6: A trap unwinding through two functions</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
enter main
enter lookup
exit lookup
Result.Err(journal is empty)
enter lookup
exit lookup
exit main
error[AU4003]: list index `9` is out of bounds for length `3`
 --> src/main.au:21:33
   |
21 |         return Result.Ok(values[index])
   |                                 ^
  = note: `Journal.__exit__` also failed during cleanup: journal is empty
  = note: Aura call chain (innermost first): lookup at 19:1 -> main at 23:1
```

Let's read this from the top. The first call to `lookup` succeeds in its body,
but the `Journal` is empty, so its exit returns an `Err`. The `Section` exit runs
first (it was entered second), and then the journal's `Err` replaces the
function's result, which is why `main` prints `Result.Err(journal is empty)`
instead of `Result.Ok(2)`. That's the rule from the previous part: on a normal
exit, an exit's error is returned like `try`.

The second call traps on `values[9]`. Now three exits are active: the
`Section` and the `Journal` in `lookup`, and the `Section` in `main`. All three
run, in reverse order of entry: `exit lookup`, then the journal's exit (which
prints nothing because it fails), then `exit main`. Only after the last one does
the diagnostic appear.

Look at the first note. The journal's exit failed during the unwind, but its
error didn't replace the trap, and it wasn't thrown away silently either. Aura
attached it to the trap report as a note. The trap stays the primary
diagnostic because it is the reason the program stopped. The cleanup failure is
extra information you may need while debugging it.

### An exit that traps doesn't stop the others

An exit is ordinary code, so it can trap too. What happens to the exits that
haven't run yet? Here three managers are entered and the middle one's exit
fails an assertion:

```aura
class Step:
    name: str
    fail: bool

    def __enter__(mut self) -> None:
        print("enter " + self.name)

    def __exit__(mut self) -> None:
        print("exit " + self.name)
        assert not self.fail, "cleanup of " + self.name + " failed"

def main():
    with a = Step(name="a", fail=false), b = Step(name="b", fail=true), c = Step(name="c", fail=false):
        print("body")
```

<span class="caption">Listing 14-7: A trap inside an exit</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
enter a
enter b
enter c
body
exit c
exit b
exit a
error[AU4001]: cleanup of b failed
 --> src/main.au:10:9
   |
10 |         assert not self.fail, "cleanup of " + self.name + " failed"
   |         ^
  = note: Aura call chain (innermost first): Step.__exit__ at 8:5 -> main at 12:1
```

`exit b` traps, and `exit a` still runs afterwards. This is the rule that makes
the whole system dependable: *every remaining `with` exit runs after one traps.*
Each exit that was registered before the failing one still runs, in this frame
and in the callers' frames. If a failing cleanup could cancel the cleanups after
it, one buggy manager deep in a library could leave your files open and your
temporary directories on disk. Aura isolates each exit from the others.

When more than one thing traps, Aura has to choose which diagnostic to report.
If the body was already failing, the body's diagnostic stays primary, as in
Listing 14-5. If the body finished cleanly, as here, the first exit to trap is
the one reported. You can see that in the call chain: the innermost frame is
`Step.__exit__`.

### Failing while entering

There is one more place a failure can happen: partway through a header with
several items. Suppose the second item's `__enter__` traps:

```aura
class Step:
    name: str
    fail: bool

    def __enter__(mut self) -> None:
        assert not self.fail, "could not start " + self.name
        print("enter " + self.name)

    def __exit__(mut self) -> None:
        print("exit " + self.name)

def main():
    with a = Step(name="a", fail=false), b = Step(name="b", fail=true), c = Step(name="c", fail=false):
        print("body")
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
enter a
exit a
error[AU4001]: could not start b
 --> src/main.au:6:9
  |
6 |         assert not self.fail, "could not start " + self.name
  |         ^
  = note: Aura call chain (innermost first): Step.__enter__ at 5:5 -> main at 12:1
```

`a` was fully entered, so its exit runs. `b` failed while entering, so its exit
does *not* run, and `c` was never constructed at all. An exit is registered only
after the item's expression and its `__enter__` have both succeeded. That's
the right line to draw: cleanup code is allowed to assume that setup finished.
If `b`'s exit ran after a failed enter, it would have to defend against a
half-initialized object, which is exactly the kind of code that has bugs.

## Things `__exit__` can't do

If you're coming from Python, you'll notice that Aura's `__exit__` takes no
arguments besides `self`. Python passes `exc_type`, `exc_value`, and
`traceback`, and an `__exit__` that returns `True` swallows the exception. In
Aura, the exit can't see why the block ended and can't stop a failure from
continuing.

That's a real limitation. You can't write a manager that rolls back on failure
and commits on success purely by looking at how the block ended. The usual
workaround is to make the success explicit: give the manager a `commit(mut
self)` method that the body calls as its last step, and have `__exit__` roll
back if `commit` was never called. That's arguably clearer anyway, because the
commit point is visible in the body.

The other half of the limitation is deliberate. Because no exit can suppress a
trap, a trap always reaches the top of the task. A library's context manager
can't hide your bug from you, and reading a `with` block never requires you to
check whether the manager might silently swallow failures.

## Entering with a view

So far the `with` name has bound the manager itself. A manager can instead hand
the body a view into part of itself, by returning `view` or `view mut` from
`__enter__`. This is how you write a guard: the body gets access to the
protected data, and the manager stays out of reach until the exit.

```aura
class Lock:
    name: str
    values: list[int64]

    def __enter__(mut self) -> view mut list[int64] from self:
        print("lock " + self.name)
        return view mut self.values

    def __exit__(mut self) -> None:
        print(f"unlock {self.name} with {len(self.values)} values")

def main():
    with Lock(name="counter", values=[]) as values:
        values.append(1)
        values.append(2)
        print(f"inside: {len(values)}")
```

<span class="caption">Listing 14-8: An entry view</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
lock counter
inside: 2
unlock counter with 2 values
```

Inside the block, `values` is a mutable view of the lock's list. The `Lock`
itself is held in a hidden binding that the body can't name, so the body can't
call methods on it or move it while the view is live. The view ends before the
exit runs, which is why `__exit__` can read `self.values` freely.

Two rules keep this sound, and you'll run into both. The first is that a `with`
item consumes its expression. If we bind the lock first and then manage it,
the lock is gone afterwards:

```aura check-fail:AU3001
class Lock:
    name: str
    values: list[int64]

    def __enter__(mut self) -> view mut list[int64] from self:
        print("lock " + self.name)
        return view mut self.values

    def __exit__(mut self) -> None:
        print(f"unlock {self.name} with {len(self.values)} values")

def main():
    lock = Lock(name="counter", values=[])
    with lock as values:
        values.append(1)
    print(len(lock.values))
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU3001]: use of moved value `lock`
 --> src/main.au:16:15
   |
16 |     print(len(lock.values))
   |               ^
  = related src/main.au:14:10: value moved here
  = help: pass shared access when ownership is not needed, or transfer this non-cloneable value only once
```

This is the ordinary moved-value error from
[Chapter 4](/book/ch04-00-understanding-ownership). The `with` took ownership
of `lock` on line 14, ran its exit at the end of the block, and dropped it. A
managed resource belongs to its block; that is how the block can promise to
clean it up.

The second rule is that the view can't escape the block. Storing it somewhere
that outlives the block is rejected:

```aura check-fail:AU3010
class Lock:
    name: str
    values: list[int64]

    def __enter__(mut self) -> view mut list[int64] from self:
        print("lock " + self.name)
        return view mut self.values

    def __exit__(mut self) -> None:
        print(f"unlock {self.name} with {len(self.values)} values")

class Cache:
    items: list[int64]

def main():
    mut cache = Cache(items=[])
    with Lock(name="counter", values=[]) as values:
        values.append(1)
        cache.items = values
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU3010]: a view cannot be stored as a class field
 --> src/main.au:19:23
   |
19 |         cache.items = values
   |                       ^
  = help: keep it in a matching `view` binding, or produce an explicit owned value
```

If this were allowed, `cache.items` would point into the lock's list after the
lock had been unlocked and dropped. `AU3010` is the code for a view that would
outlive what it borrows from. If you need the data afterwards, make an owned
copy inside the block with `values.copy()`.

## The one case where exits don't run

Everything in this section is about Aura control flow leaving a block: a
return, a `try`, a trap, or a cancellation. There is one situation outside
that, and you should know about it before the next chapter. If the program's
`main` finishes while some task is still suspended in the middle of its work,
the runtime abandons that task. An abandoned task's `with` exits do not run.

That sounds alarming, but it can only happen to a task that escaped structured
concurrency, and the next chapter shows how `TaskGroup` keeps every task inside
a `with` block that waits for it. Treat abandonment as a last-resort cleanup of
the runtime's own state, never as a way your cleanup code gets called. The
Manual's [Execution Model](/manual/execution-model) has the precise rules.

## Summary

A `with` block ties a resource to a region of code. Items enter left to right,
exits run right to left, and each registered exit runs exactly once on every way
out: falling through, `return`, `break` and `continue`, `try`, traps, and
cancellation. An exit that returns `Result` acts like a `try` at the end of the
block on normal paths. When the body is already failing, the body's error or
trap stays primary, and a cleanup error becomes a note on the trap rather than
replacing it. A trap inside one exit doesn't stop the exits registered before
it, so one bad cleanup can't leak every other resource.

You can now write your own managers with `__enter__` and `__exit__` (or
`close`), keep fallible setup in the item expression where `try` can reach it,
and hand the body a view when the manager should guard its data. You also know
the edges of the design: an exit can't inspect or suppress a failure, and a
managed value belongs to its block.

The next chapter puts all of this to work. A `TaskGroup` is a resource whose
exit waits for every task it started, and the cleanup rules from this chapter
are what let Aura promise that no task outlives the block that created it.

## Source: docs/book/ch15-00-concurrency.md

# Structured concurrency

Sooner or later a program needs to do more than one thing at a time. A server
handles many connections. A build tool compiles several files at once. A
crawler waits on dozens of slow network requests and would like to do something
useful while it waits. Concurrency is how a program overlaps that work, and it
has a reputation for producing the worst bugs in software: work that keeps
running after everyone has forgotten it, failures that vanish because nobody
was listening, two pieces of code changing the same data at the same moment.

Aura's concurrency is built to rule out the first two by structure and the
third by the type system. Every task starts inside a `TaskGroup`, and a task
group is a resource managed by `with`, exactly like the files and scratch
managers of [Chapter 14](/book/ch14-00-resources-and-cleanup). When the block
ends, the group waits for its tasks. So a task can't outlive the block that
started it, and a failure in a task always has somewhere to go. Tasks don't
share mutable data at all: they exchange owned values through typed queues, and
the compiler checks that everything crossing from one task to another is safe to
move.

If you've used Python, you have probably met two older models. Threads from the
`threading` module can be started anywhere and run until they finish, and the
code that started them can return long before. `asyncio.create_task` has the
same shape for coroutines. Python 3.11 added `asyncio.TaskGroup`, which works
much like Aura's groups, and we'll compare the two along the way. The
difference is that in Aura the structured form is the only form there is.

Through the chapter we'll grow one program, a word counter that splits its
input between tasks, from a single background task up to a worker pool with a
producer, several workers, a results queue, and a deadline that cancels
everything if the pool gets stuck. By the end you'll be able to read any Aura
concurrent program and answer two questions about every task in it: which block
started it, and which block waits for it.

## Source: docs/book/ch15-01-tasks-and-task-groups.md

# Tasks and task groups

A *task* is a function call that runs concurrently with the code that started
it. Tasks are lightweight: each has its own small stack, and the Aura runtime
schedules thousands of them over a handful of operating system threads. You
never create a task on its own. You ask a `TaskGroup` to start one, and the
group is responsible for it from then on.

Let's count the words in a sentence on a separate task:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
def count_words(text: str) -> int64:
    return len(text.split(" "))

def main():
    with group = TaskGroup():
        task = group.start(count_words, "the quick brown fox")
        match task.result(timeout=1s):
            case TaskResult.Ready(count):
                print(f"words: {count}")
            case TaskResult.Error(message):
                print("failed: " + message)
            case TaskResult.TimedOut:
                print("timed out")
            case TaskResult.Cancelled:
                print("cancelled")
    print("group closed")
```

<span class="caption">Listing 15-1: Starting one task and waiting for its result</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
words: 4
group closed
```

There are three pieces here. `TaskGroup()` creates the group, and `with` makes
the group's lifetime the indented block. `group.start(count_words, "the quick
brown fox")` starts a task that will call `count_words` with that argument. Notice
that we pass the function and its arguments separately, rather than calling
`count_words(...)` ourselves. Calling it would run it here and now, on the
current task. Passing it lets the group run it somewhere else.

`start` returns a `Task[int64]`, a handle to the result that will exist once the
task finishes. `task.result(timeout=1s)` waits for that result, for at most one
second. The wait can end in four ways, and `TaskResult[T]` has a case for each:
the task returned a value, the task trapped, our wait ran out of time, or our
wait was cancelled. Aura makes us handle all four because each is a real
possibility in concurrent code, and each usually needs different handling. A
timeout, in particular, says nothing about the task itself; it only means *we*
stopped waiting. We'll come back to timeouts in
[Section 15.3](/book/ch15-03-cancellation-and-shutdown).

The timeout is a `Duration`. Literals like `1s`, `100ms`, and `2m` cover the
common cases, and you'll see how to compute durations at runtime later in the
chapter.

## Why the group is a `with` block

The line that matters most in Listing 15-1 is the one with no code on it: the
end of the `with` block. Leaving the block runs the group's exit, and a task
group's exit *waits for every task the group started*. So by the time `group
closed` prints, `count_words` has finished, whatever happened to it. No task
started inside the block is still running after it.

That is what *structured concurrency* means. A task's lifetime is nested inside
a block of code, the same way a binding's lifetime is nested inside its scope.
You can read the structure of the concurrent program off the indentation.

To see why that's worth a rule, think about the alternative. In Python, this is
legal and common:

```python
import threading

def save_report(): ...

def handle_request():
    threading.Thread(target=save_report).start()
    return "ok"
```

`handle_request` returns while `save_report` is still running. Nothing in the
code says who is waiting for it, so if it fails, the exception is printed to
standard error by the thread machinery and the caller never hears about it. If
the program exits while it runs, a daemon thread is killed mid-write, and a
non-daemon thread holds the exit up until it finishes. `asyncio.create_task`
has the same shape, plus a twist: the event loop holds only a weak reference to
the task, so a task nobody keeps a reference to can be garbage collected before
it finishes. Every one of these is a bug that comes from a task outliving the
code that started it.

Python's answer, since version 3.11, is `asyncio.TaskGroup`, which follows the
"nurseries" of the Trio library. Inside `async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:`,
tasks started with `tg.create_task` are awaited when the block ends. Aura's
`TaskGroup` is the same idea. The difference is that Python still has
`create_task` and threads alongside it, so structure is a convention you have to
keep. Aura has no way to start a detached task.

### The group can't leave its block

What stops us from smuggling the group out of its block, so that its tasks keep
running after the function returns? Let's try:

```aura check-fail:AU2999
def count_words(text: str) -> int64:
    return len(text.split(" "))

def launch() -> TaskGroup:
    with group = TaskGroup():
        group.start_soon(count_words, "the quick brown fox")
        return group

def main():
    group = launch()
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU2999]: cannot move managed `with` resource `group`
 --> src/main.au:7:16
  |
7 |         return group
  |                ^
```

This is the rule from [Chapter 14](/book/ch14-01-with-and-cleanup): a value
managed by `with` belongs to its block, and the compiler won't let it move out.
For a file, that guarantees the file is closed where the block ends. For a task
group, it guarantees the tasks are finished where the block ends.

You can still pass the group to a helper function, as long as the helper only
borrows it. The helper starts tasks that belong to the caller's group, and the
caller's block waits for them:

```aura
def report(name: str, text: str):
    print(f"{name}: {len(text.split(" "))} words")

def start_reports(group: TaskGroup, documents: own list[str]):
    mut n = 0
    for text in own documents:
        group.start_soon(report, f"doc {n}", text)
        n += 1

def main():
    with group = TaskGroup():
        start_reports(group, ["the quick brown fox", "jumps over"])
    print("all reports done")
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
doc 0: 4 words
doc 1: 2 words
all reports done
```

### Always open a group with `with`

The current compiler accepts a `TaskGroup()` that isn't bound with `with`, and
that is a hole you should know about. Such a group has no block, so nothing
waits for its tasks:

```aura
def work():
    sleep(100ms)
    print("child finished")

def launch():
    group = TaskGroup()
    group.start_soon(work)
    print("launch returning")

def main():
    launch()
    print("back in main")
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
launch returning
back in main
```

`launch` returned with its task still running, and when `main` finished, the
runtime abandoned the task before it could print. As we saw at the end of
[Chapter 14](/book/ch14-02-resource-managers), an abandoned task's `with` exits
don't run either. Every guarantee in this chapter assumes the group is opened
with `with`, so always write it that way.

## Starting several tasks

One task isn't much use. Let's count three documents at once, keep the handles
in a list, and wait for all of them. Here's the obvious first attempt:

```aura check-fail:AU3002
def count_words(text: str) -> int64:
    return len(text.split(" "))

def main():
    documents = ["the quick brown fox", "jumps over", "the lazy dog again"]
    mut tasks: list[Task[int64]] = []
    with group = TaskGroup():
        for doc in documents:
            tasks.append(group.start(count_words, doc))
        match wait_all(tasks, timeout=1s):
            case WaitAll.Ready(counts):
                print(counts)
            case WaitAll.Error(index, message):
                print(f"document {index} failed: {message}")
            case WaitAll.TimedOut:
                print("timed out")
            case WaitAll.Cancelled:
                print("cancelled")
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU3002]: cannot move borrowed value `doc`
 --> src/main.au:9:51
  |
9 |             tasks.append(group.start(count_words, doc))
  |                                                   ^
  = related src/main.au:8:13: value is borrowed here
  = help: take `doc` as `own str` when ownership is required, or call `.clone()` to consume an independent copy
  = fix: replace src/main.au:9:54-9:54 with `.clone()`
```

The error points at `doc` in the call to `start`, and the related line tells us
that `doc` is borrowed from the loop on line 8. A plain `for doc in documents`
gives the body shared access to each element (that's
[Chapter 4](/book/ch04-00-understanding-ownership)), and `start` wants to
*move* its arguments.

That's the key ownership rule for tasks: starting a task moves (or copies) each
argument into storage that belongs to the task. The child never borrows from the
parent's stack. It has to be this way, because the child runs concurrently with
the parent. If the child borrowed `doc`, the parent could change or drop the
list while the child was still reading from it, and there would be no point at
which the compiler could check that the borrow had ended. Moving the argument
makes the child the only owner of its input.

The help line offers two fixes. We could `.clone()` each string, which leaves
`documents` intact. Here we don't need `documents` afterwards, so the cheaper
fix is to hand each string over with `for doc in own documents`:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
def count_words(text: str) -> int64:
    return len(text.split(" "))

def main():
    documents = ["the quick brown fox", "jumps over", "the lazy dog again"]
    mut tasks: list[Task[int64]] = []
    with group = TaskGroup():
        for doc in own documents:
            tasks.append(group.start(count_words, doc))
        match wait_all(tasks, timeout=1s):
            case WaitAll.Ready(counts):
                print(counts)
            case WaitAll.Error(index, message):
                print(f"document {index} failed: {message}")
            case WaitAll.TimedOut:
                print("timed out")
            case WaitAll.Cancelled:
                print("cancelled")
```

<span class="caption">Listing 15-2: Starting a task per document and waiting for all of them</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
[4, 2, 4]
```

`wait_all` takes the list of handles and waits until every task has produced a
value, or one has failed, or the timeout passes. On success, `WaitAll.Ready`
carries the results in the same order as the handles, not the order in which
the tasks finished. There's a matching `wait_any` that returns as soon as the
first task finishes, with the index of the one that won.

Notice that the parameter of `count_words` is a plain `text: str`. The
function borrows its argument as usual; what it borrows from is the task's own
copy. The same holds for `own` parameters, which consume the task's copy. The one
kind of parameter a task target can't have is `mut`, because there's nobody to
write the change back to:

```aura check-fail:AU3002
def add_one(counts: mut list[int64]):
    counts.append(1)

def main():
    mut counts: list[int64] = []
    with group = TaskGroup():
        group.start_soon(add_one, counts)
    print(counts)
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU3002]: task starting does not support mutable parameter `counts` on function `add_one`; child tasks cannot write back through the starting call frame
 --> src/main.au:7:26
  |
7 |         group.start_soon(add_one, counts)
  |                          ^
```

If a task needs to produce something, it returns it, or sends it through a
queue, which is the subject of the next section.

## Fire and forget, inside a scope

When we don't need a task's result, `start_soon` starts it without returning a
handle:

```aura
def report(name: str, text: str):
    print(f"{name}: {len(text.split(" "))} words")

def main():
    with group = TaskGroup():
        group.start_soon(report, "a", "the quick brown fox")
        group.start_soon(report, "b", "jumps over")
        group.start_soon(report, "c", "the lazy dog again")
    print("all reports done")
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
a: 4 words
c: 4 words
b: 2 words
all reports done
```

Run this a few times and the first three lines may come out in different
orders. The order in which independent tasks run, and so the order of their
output, is deliberately unspecified. The last line, though, is always last,
because the group's exit waits for all three. "Fire and forget" in Aura means
you forget the handle, not the task: the group still owns it.

## When a task fails

A task can trap, like any code. What happens next depends on whether anybody is
looking at its result. Let's put an assertion in `count_words` and give it an
empty document:

```aura
def count_words(text: str) -> int64:
    assert len(text) > 0, "empty document"
    return len(text.split(" "))

def main():
    documents = ["the quick brown fox", "", "the lazy dog again"]
    mut tasks: list[Task[int64]] = []
    with group = TaskGroup():
        for doc in own documents:
            tasks.append(group.start(count_words, doc))
        match wait_all(tasks, timeout=1s):
            case WaitAll.Ready(counts):
                print(counts)
            case WaitAll.Error(index, message):
                print(f"document {index} failed: {message}")
            case WaitAll.TimedOut:
                print("timed out")
            case WaitAll.Cancelled:
                print("cancelled")
    print("after the group")
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
document 1 failed: empty document
after the group
```

The trap stopped the task, not the program. `wait_all` reported it as
`WaitAll.Error` with the index of the failing task and the assertion's message,
and because we observed the failure, it's handled: the group closes normally.

Now the same failure with `start_soon`, where there is no handle to observe it
through:

```aura
def report(text: str):
    assert len(text) > 0, "empty document"
    print(f"{len(text.split(" "))} words")

def main():
    with group = TaskGroup():
        group.start_soon(report, "the quick brown fox")
        group.start_soon(report, "")
        group.start_soon(report, "jumps over")
    print("after the group")
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
4 words
2 words
error[AU4001]: empty document
 --> src/main.au:2:5
  |
2 |     assert len(text) > 0, "empty document"
  |     ^
  = note: left = 0
  = note: right = 0
  = note: Aura call chain (innermost first): report at 1:1
  = note: Aura task entry: report at 1:1
  = note: Aura task ancestry (youngest first): report spawned from main at 8:15
```

This time `after the group` never prints. An unread failure doesn't disappear:
when the group closes, it raises the child's trap in the parent. The two notes
at the bottom are specific to tasks. `Aura task entry` names the function the
task was started with, and `Aura task ancestry` says which code started it: line
8 of `main`, the second `start_soon`. In a program with many tasks, that's
how you find which one went wrong.

Compare this with the Python thread from earlier, whose exception would be
printed and then forgotten. In Aura, a failure always reaches some code that can
see it: the code reading the result, or failing that, the block that owns the
task.

### A failure doesn't cancel the siblings

There's one more detail worth testing, because it differs from Python's
`asyncio.TaskGroup`. When one child fails and nobody reads its result, what
happens to its siblings?

```aura
def slow():
    sleep(2s)
    print("slow child finished")

def bad():
    assert false, "bad child"

def main():
    with group = TaskGroup():
        group.start_soon(slow)
        group.start_soon(bad)
    print("after the group")
```

```console
$ time aura run src/main.au
slow child finished
error[AU4001]: bad child
 --> src/main.au:6:5
  |
6 |     assert false, "bad child"
  |     ^
  = note: Aura call chain (innermost first): bad at 5:1
  = note: Aura task entry: bad at 5:1
  = note: Aura task ancestry (youngest first): bad spawned from main at 11:15

real	0m2.046s
user	0m0.294s
sys	0m0.022s
```

`bad` traps almost immediately, but the program takes two seconds: the group
let `slow` run to completion and then reported the failure. In Python,
`asyncio.TaskGroup` cancels the remaining tasks as soon as one raises. Aura's
group does not cancel on its own. If you want "one failure stops everyone", you
observe the failure and call `group.cancel()` yourself, which is what
[Section 15.3](/book/ch15-03-cancellation-and-shutdown) is about. The upside is
that cancellation in Aura always comes from a line of code you can point to.

## What can cross into a task

Tasks in Aura really do run in parallel. The runtime starts one scheduler worker
per core the host reports (you can set the count with the `AURA_WORKERS`
environment variable), and each task is pinned to one worker for its whole life.
There is no global interpreter lock, so two CPU-bound tasks can use two cores at
once, unlike two Python threads.

Parallel execution is exactly when shared mutable data becomes dangerous, so
Aura doesn't allow it. Everything passed to a task, and everything a task
returns, must be `Transfer`: a value that can be moved to another worker and
used there without anyone else holding on to it. The compiler works out which
types are `Transfer` from their structure. Numbers, strings, lists and
dictionaries of transferable values, and your own classes and enums built from
them all qualify. A live host resource doesn't, because an open file handle
belongs to the worker that opened it:

```aura check-fail:AU3008
import fs

def read_it(file: own fs.File):
    print("reading")

def main():
    match own fs.open("notes.txt"):
        case Result.Ok(file):
            with group = TaskGroup():
                group.start_soon(read_it, file)
        case Result.Err(error):
            print(f"{error}")
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU3008]: task argument `file` cannot cross a task boundary because `fs.File` is a host resource and is not Transfer
 --> src/main.au:10:43
   |
10 |                 group.start_soon(read_it, file)
   |                                           ^
  = related src/main.au:3:13: task parameter `file` is declared here
  = help: send owned data made only from Transfer components; keep capabilities and host resources on their owning worker
```

The fix is to send the task what it needs to open the resource itself, such as
the path, or to read the data first and send the text. Other things that can't
cross include `random.Rng`, a `TaskGroup`, and views. You can't declare a type
`Transfer` yourself; it is always derived, so there's no way to claim a type is
safe when it isn't.

Two kinds of handle are the exception that makes communication possible. A
`Queue` handle and a `Task` handle can be passed to any task, because their
internal state is synchronized by the runtime. Everything else moves as owned,
unshared data. That's the whole model: tasks share nothing except the channels
between them.

### A result can be observed once

One consequence of moving values is that a task's result can be taken out only
once when it's an owned value. `count_words` returns an `int64`, a copy value,
so we could ask for it repeatedly. A task that returns a `str` is different:

```aura check-fail:AU3001
def shout(text: str) -> str:
    return text.upper()

def main():
    with group = TaskGroup():
        task = group.start(shout, "hello")
        print(task.poll(timeout=1s))
        print(task.poll(timeout=1s))
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU3001]: use of moved value `task`
 --> src/main.au:8:15
   |
8 |         print(task.poll(timeout=1s))
   |               ^
  = related src/main.au:7:15: value moved here
  = help: pass shared access when ownership is not needed, or transfer this non-cloneable value only once
```

`poll` is the short form of `result`: it gives back `Poll.Ready(value)` or
`Poll.Unavailable`, folding failure, timeout, and cancellation into one case.
The first `poll` consumed the handle. That holds even if the first attempt had
timed out: the right to observe the result is used up by the attempt, not by
success. If you need to retry a wait, use a copy value as the result, or have the
task send its result through a queue instead.

So far, each task gets all its input when it starts and hands back one value
when it ends. That's enough for splitting up a fixed batch of work. For work that
arrives over time, or for tasks that talk to each other while they run, we need
queues.

## Source: docs/book/ch15-02-queues.md

# Passing work with queues

In the last section every task got all of its input when it started and handed
back one value when it finished. Plenty of concurrent programs don't fit that
shape. A producer reads lines from a file and wants to hand each one off as soon
as it has it. A logger receives messages from many tasks for as long as the
program runs. For work that flows between tasks while they run, Aura has
`Queue[T]`: a typed channel that one task puts values into and another takes
them out of.

Let's change the word counter so that a producer task feeds documents to the
main task one at a time:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
def produce(documents: own list[str], lines: Queue[str]):
    for text in own documents:
        lines.put(text)
    lines.close()

def main():
    documents = ["the quick brown fox", "jumps over", "the lazy dog again"]
    lines = Queue[str]()
    mut total = 0
    with group = TaskGroup():
        group.start_soon(produce, documents, lines)
        for line in lines:
            words = len(line.split(" "))
            print(f"{words} words: {line}")
            total += words
    print(f"total: {total}")
```

<span class="caption">Listing 15-3: A producer task feeding the main task through a queue</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
4 words: the quick brown fox
2 words: jumps over
4 words: the lazy dog again
total: 10
```

`Queue[str]()` creates an empty queue of strings. We pass it to `produce` along
with the documents. `produce` puts each document on the queue and then calls
`close()` to say that nothing more is coming. Meanwhile the main task runs a
`for` loop over the queue, which takes values out as they arrive and ends once
the queue has been closed and emptied.

Look at how `lines` is used. We passed it to `produce` with `start_soon`, which
moves its arguments, and then kept using it in the `for` loop. That works
because a queue handle is a copy value. Copying the handle doesn't copy the
queue: both copies refer to the same channel, the way two Python references to
one `queue.Queue` do. That's what makes a queue useful between tasks. The
documents list, by contrast, was moved into `produce`, and `main` can't touch it
any more.

The values going *through* the queue are moved, not shared. `put` moves its
argument into the queue, and each receive moves one value out to the receiver.
At every moment exactly one task owns each string: first the producer, then the
queue, then whoever took it. That's how two tasks on two cores can exchange data
with no locks in your code and no chance of both changing the same value.

## Closing is the signal

The `close()` call is part of the protocol between the two tasks. Without it,
how would the consumer know the producer was done? Python programmers will
recognize the problem: for most of Python's history, `queue.Queue` had no way to
close, and the usual idiom was to put a sentinel such as `None` on the queue
and have every consumer check for it. (Python 3.13 added `Queue.shutdown()` for
the same purpose.) A sentinel works, but it's a value that means "not a value",
and every consumer has to remember to test for it.

In Aura, closing is a state of the queue. After `close()`, `put` fails, and
receivers get every value that was already queued, then learn that the queue is
closed. A `for` loop over a queue ends when any of these happens:

- the queue is closed and empty
- the task running the loop is cancelled
- every task in the surrounding group that could still send to it has finished

The last condition is a safety net: even if a producer forgets to close, the
loop won't wait forever for a value no live task can send. Still, write the
`close()`. It says in one line, in the producer, that the stream is complete,
and it works no matter how the consumer is structured.

A queue loop is always written in the bare form, `for line in lines:`. Each
received value is already owned by the loop binding, and the handle is a copy
value, so the `own` and `mut` modifiers you use with lists have nothing to do
here. The compiler says so if you try:

```aura check-fail:AU3004
def main():
    jobs = Queue[str]()
    jobs.put("index")
    jobs.close()
    for job in own jobs:
        print(job)
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU3004]: Queue iteration receives values; each received item is already owned by the loop binding, and the Queue handle is a copy value, so ownership modifiers have nothing to modify; use the bare form `for item in queue:`
 --> src/main.au:5:5
  |
5 |     for job in own jobs:
  |     ^
```

## Bounded queues and backpressure

`Queue[str]()` is unbounded: `put` always succeeds immediately, and the queue
grows as needed. That's convenient until the producer is faster than the
consumer. Then the queue grows without limit, and a program that reads a large
file can end up with the whole file in memory, waiting in a queue.

A bounded queue fixes the problem by setting how many values may wait at once.
When it's full, `put` waits until a consumer makes room. This is called
*backpressure*: a slow consumer automatically slows the producer down. Let's
watch it with a queue that holds one value:

```aura
def produce(jobs: Queue[int64]):
    for n in range(4):
        jobs.put(n)
        print(f"put {n}")
    jobs.close()

def main():
    jobs = Queue[int64](capacity=1)
    with group = TaskGroup():
        group.start_soon(produce, jobs)
        sleep(100ms)
        for job in jobs:
            print(f"got {job}")
            sleep(50ms)
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
put 0
got 0
put 1
got 1
put 2
got 2
put 3
got 3
```

The producer puts `0`, which fills the queue, and then its `put(1)` has to wait.
The main task sleeps for 100ms before it starts reading, and during that time
the producer is stuck: no `put 1` appears until `got 0` has made room. From
then on the two tasks move in lockstep. With an unbounded queue, all four `put`
lines would have printed at once.

A waiting `put` doesn't block the scheduler worker it runs on. The task is
parked, and other tasks on the same worker keep running until there's room.

### Sending without waiting

Sometimes waiting is the wrong response to a full queue. A task that polls for
work, or a request handler that should shed load rather than pile it up, wants
to know right away. `try_put` sends only if there is room now. It returns a
`Result`, and when the send fails, the error hands the value back:

```aura
def offer(jobs: Queue[str], job: own str):
    match jobs.try_put(job):
        case Result.Ok(_):
            print("queued")
        case Result.Err(SendError.Full(rejected)):
            print("full, kept " + rejected)
        case Result.Err(SendError.Closed(rejected)):
            print("closed, kept " + rejected)
        case Result.Err(SendError.TimedOut(rejected)):
            print("timed out, kept " + rejected)
        case Result.Err(SendError.Cancelled(rejected)):
            print("cancelled, kept " + rejected)

def main():
    jobs = Queue[str](capacity=2)
    offer(jobs, "index")
    offer(jobs, "render")
    offer(jobs, "upload")
    print(jobs.poll())
    offer(jobs, "upload")
    jobs.close()
    offer(jobs, "notify")
    for job in jobs:
        print("draining " + job)
```

<span class="caption">Listing 15-4: `try_put` on a full queue and a closed one</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
queued
queued
full, kept upload
Poll.Ready(index)
queued
closed, kept notify
draining render
draining upload
```

This listing runs on one task, which makes it easy to follow. The queue holds
two values, so the third `offer` finds it full. `jobs.poll()` takes one value
out without waiting, which is why there's room for `upload` the second time.
After `close()`, the `notify` offer fails with `SendError.Closed`, and the loop
drains the two values still in the queue before ending. Closing a queue doesn't
throw away what's already in it.

The detail to notice is `SendError.Full(rejected)`. Because `put` and `try_put`
take ownership of the value, a failed send would destroy it if the error didn't
give it back. Every `SendError` case carries the unsent value, so the caller can
retry, log it, or route it to another queue. `SendError` has four cases, one for
each way a send can fail: the queue was full, it was closed, the wait timed out,
or the task was cancelled while waiting. `try_put` never waits, so it only
produces the first two in practice, but the same type is used everywhere so one
`match` handles all sends.

## Waiting with a timeout

Both directions accept a timeout. A `put` with a timeout waits for room at most
that long, and a `get` waits for a value at most that long:

```aura
def main():
    jobs = Queue[str](capacity=1)
    jobs.put("index")
    match jobs.put("render", timeout=50ms):
        case Result.Ok(_):
            print("queued")
        case Result.Err(SendError.TimedOut(job)):
            print("no room for " + job + " after 50ms")
        case Result.Err(error):
            print("some other failure")
    match jobs.get(timeout=20ms):
        case QueueReceive.Item(job):
            print("got " + job)
        case QueueReceive.Closed:
            print("closed")
        case QueueReceive.TimedOut:
            print("nothing within 20ms")
        case QueueReceive.Cancelled:
            print("cancelled")
    match jobs.get(timeout=20ms):
        case QueueReceive.Item(job):
            print("got " + job)
        case QueueReceive.Closed:
            print("closed")
        case QueueReceive.TimedOut:
            print("nothing within 20ms")
        case QueueReceive.Cancelled:
            print("cancelled")
    print(jobs.get_or("nothing", timeout=20ms))
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
no room for render after 50ms
got index
nothing within 20ms
nothing
```

`get` returns a `QueueReceive[T]`, which has a case for each way a receive can
end: an item arrived, the queue is closed, the time ran out, or the task was
cancelled. Like `TaskResult`, it keeps "closed" and "timed out" apart, and that
matters. A closed queue means the stream is finished and you should stop. A
timeout means nothing arrived *yet*, and the right response depends on your
program: try again, report that a producer is slow, or give up.

For the common cases there are two shorter forms. `poll(timeout=...)` returns
`Poll.Ready(value)` or `Poll.Unavailable`, and `get_or(default, timeout=...)`
returns the value or the default you pass. Without a timeout, both check once and
return immediately, as `jobs.poll()` did in Listing 15-4.

One kind of wait is missing from that list: waiting with no timeout for a value
that can never come. We'll see in the next section that the group's exit is
careful about this case, but your own code isn't protected. If the main task
calls `jobs.get()` on a queue that no task will ever send to or close, it waits
forever. When there is any doubt about whether an answer will come, pass a
timeout.

## What can go through a queue

A queue moves values between tasks that may run on different workers, so its
payload type must be `Transfer`, the same rule as for task arguments. The
compiler checks it where the queue is created:

```aura check-fail:AU3008
import random

def main():
    generators = Queue[random.Rng]()
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
error[AU3008]: Queue payload `random.Rng` cannot cross a worker boundary because `random.Rng` is a stateful generator and is not Transfer
 --> src/main.au:4:18
  |
4 |     generators = Queue[random.Rng]()
  |                  ^
  = help: use a Queue payload made only from Transfer components; keep capabilities and host resources on their owning worker
```

A random number generator is mutable state that belongs to one task. If two
tasks could draw from the same generator, they would race on its internal state.
The fix is to give each task its own generator, seeded from a number you pass
it. Your own classes are fine as payloads as long as their fields are
transferable, and we'll send a `Job` class through a queue in
[Section 15.4](/book/ch15-04-worker-pool).

## When a producer fails

What happens to a consumer when the producer feeding it traps before it can
close the queue? This is where unstructured programs usually hang: the consumer
waits forever for a value that will never arrive.

```aura
def produce(jobs: Queue[int64]):
    jobs.put(1)
    jobs.put(2)
    assert false, "producer broke"
    jobs.close()

def consume(jobs: Queue[int64]):
    for job in jobs:
        print(f"got {job}")
    print("consumer done")

def main():
    jobs = Queue[int64]()
    with group = TaskGroup():
        group.start_soon(produce, jobs)
        group.start_soon(consume, jobs)
    print("after the group")
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
got 1
got 2
consumer done
error[AU4001]: producer broke
 --> src/main.au:4:5
  |
4 |     assert false, "producer broke"
  |     ^
  = note: Aura call chain (innermost first): produce at 1:1
  = note: Aura task entry: produce at 1:1
  = note: Aura task ancestry (youngest first): produce spawned from main at 15:15
```

The consumer received the two values that were sent, and then its loop ended,
because the only task that could have sent more is gone. The program didn't
hang. The group then raised the producer's unread failure, so the error is
reported with the line that caused it, and `after the group` never printed.
The queue and the group work together here: the group knows which tasks are
alive, so a queue loop inside it can tell "nothing yet" from "nothing ever".

We now have tasks that start, finish, fail, and talk to each other. What we
can't do yet is stop them. A slow producer, a stuck worker, an answer that
arrived from somewhere else first: all of these need a way to tell running
tasks that their work is no longer wanted, and that's cancellation.

## Source: docs/book/ch15-03-cancellation-and-shutdown.md

# Cancellation, timeouts, and shutdown

Starting work is the easy half of concurrency. The hard half is stopping it:
giving up on a task that's taking too long, shutting down a pool when the job
is done, and making sure that whatever was running gets to clean up on the way
out. This section is about that half. We'll see that a timeout and a
cancellation are different things, how a task notices that it's been
cancelled, and what a task group does at the end of its block when some of its
tasks are still waiting.

## A timeout stops the waiting, not the task

Let's make the word counter slow and wait for it with a short timeout:

```aura
def slow_count(text: str) -> int64:
    sleep(2s)
    return len(text.split(" "))

def main():
    with group = TaskGroup():
        task = group.start(slow_count, "a b c")
        match task.result(timeout=100ms):
            case TaskResult.Ready(count):
                print(f"words: {count}")
            case TaskResult.Error(message):
                print("failed: " + message)
            case TaskResult.TimedOut:
                print("gave up waiting")
            case TaskResult.Cancelled:
                print("cancelled")
    print("group closed")
```

```console
$ time aura run src/main.au
gave up waiting
group closed

real	0m2.054s
user	0m0.275s
sys	0m0.029s
```

`gave up waiting` printed after 100ms, as we asked. But the program still took
two seconds. The timeout ended *our wait* for the result. It didn't touch the
task, which went on sleeping, and when the block ended, the group's exit waited
for it, as it always does.

This is the behavior you want, even if it surprises you the first time. A
timeout is a decision about the waiter's patience, and only the waiter knows
whether giving up means "stop the work" or "check back later". If timeouts
killed tasks, you couldn't poll a task every 100ms to update a progress bar.
When you do want the work to stop, you say so separately.

## Cancelling a group

`group.cancel()` asks every task in the group to stop. Let's call it when we
give up, and have `slow_count` check whether it's been cancelled:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
def slow_count(text: str) -> int64:
    sleep(2s)
    if cancelled():
        print("slow_count saw the cancellation")
        return -1
    return len(text.split(" "))

def main():
    with group = TaskGroup():
        task = group.start(slow_count, "a b c")
        match task.result(timeout=100ms):
            case TaskResult.Ready(count):
                print(f"words: {count}")
            case TaskResult.Error(message):
                print("failed: " + message)
            case TaskResult.TimedOut:
                print("gave up waiting, cancelling")
                group.cancel()
            case TaskResult.Cancelled:
                print("cancelled")
    print("group closed")
```

<span class="caption">Listing 15-5: Cancelling a task after a timeout</span>

```console
$ time aura run src/main.au
gave up waiting, cancelling
slow_count saw the cancellation
group closed

real	0m0.148s
user	0m0.030s
sys	0m0.021s
```

Now the program finishes in a fraction of a second. Two things happened when
we called `group.cancel()`. The task was marked as cancelled, and its
`sleep(2s)` woke up early. `slow_count` then called `cancelled()`, which
returns `true` once the current task has been asked to stop, and returned
early.

Notice what *didn't* happen: nothing was thrown into `slow_count`. The `sleep`
returned normally, and the task ran its next line. Cancellation in Aura is
*cooperative*. It's a request that the task observes at well-defined points,
and the task decides how to wind down.

## Cooperative cancellation

To compare, think about Python again. A Python thread can't be cancelled at
all: there is no supported way to stop one from outside, so programs build their
own "stop" flags. `asyncio` can cancel a task, and it does so by raising
`CancelledError` inside the coroutine at whatever `await` it's suspended on.
That's closer to Aura, but the exception can surface from any `await`, and it
can be caught and swallowed by an over-broad `except`.

Aura's model has no exception. A cancelled task notices the request in two
ways. Any wait that the scheduler knows about wakes up and reports it: `sleep`
returns early, a queue `get` returns `QueueReceive.Cancelled`, a `put` returns
`SendError.Cancelled`, a task wait returns `TaskResult.Cancelled`, and so on for
`select`, `wait_any`, `wait_all`, and the network and process waits. And the
task can ask directly with `cancelled()`.

The `with` blocks in a cancelled task still run their exits. Here's a ticker
that runs until it's cancelled, inside a `Section` from the last chapter:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
class Section:
    name: str

    def __exit__(mut self) -> None:
        print("exit " + self.name)

def ticker(name: own str):
    with section = Section(name=name.clone()):
        mut ticks = 0
        while not cancelled():
            ticks += 1
            sleep(100ms)
        print(f"{name} stopped after {ticks} ticks")

def main():
    with group = TaskGroup():
        group.start_soon(ticker, "ticker")
        sleep(350ms)
        print("cancelling")
        group.cancel()
    print("group closed")
```

<span class="caption">Listing 15-6: A loop that stops when its task is cancelled</span>

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
cancelling
ticker stopped after 4 ticks
exit ticker
group closed
```

The ticker's fourth `sleep` is cut short by the cancellation, the loop
condition sees `cancelled()`, and the function leaves its `with` block, running
the exit on the way. The group then finishes joining and `main` carries on.

### The loop that never stops

The `while not cancelled()` in Listing 15-6 isn't decoration. Let's see what
happens without it:

```aura
def ticker():
    mut ticks = 0
    while true:
        ticks += 1
        sleep(100ms)
        print(f"tick {ticks}")

def main():
    with group = TaskGroup():
        group.start_soon(ticker)
        sleep(350ms)
        group.cancel()
    print("group closed")
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au | head -n 6
tick 1
tick 2
tick 3
tick 4
tick 5
tick 6
```

The first three ticks arrive 100ms apart. Then the group is cancelled, and
from then on every `sleep(100ms)` returns at once, because the task is
cancelled and a cancelled task's waits don't wait. Ticks 4, 5, 6 and millions
more pour out as fast as the machine can print, and `group closed` never
appears, because the group is waiting for a task that never returns. (We piped
the output through `head` to keep it short.)

So "cooperative" has a cost: a task that ignores cancellation won't stop. The
rule of thumb is that any loop that may run for a long time should either
receive from a queue (whose loop ends on cancellation by itself) or check
`cancelled()` in its condition.

The same applies to loops that do pure computation and never wait at all. The
compiler inserts a scheduling check at the end of every loop iteration so that a
busy task can't starve the other tasks on its worker forever, but that check
doesn't look at cancellation. A long calculation that should be stoppable has to
ask:

```aura
def crunch():
    mut total = 0
    mut i = 0
    while i < 20000:
        if cancelled():
            print(f"crunch stopped early at {i}")
            return
        total += i % 7
        i += 1
    print(f"crunch finished: {total}")

def main():
    with group = TaskGroup():
        group.start_soon(crunch)
        sleep(10ms)
        group.cancel()
    print("group closed")
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
crunch stopped early at 122
group closed
```

The number will differ from run to run. Without the `if cancelled()` check, the
same program prints `crunch finished: 59997` after running the whole loop,
cancellation or not. There's also a `yield_now()` builtin, which gives other
tasks on the same worker a chance to run, but it doesn't check cancellation
either.

Why make cancellation cooperative, when it means writing these checks? Because
the alternative, stopping a task at an arbitrary instruction, would leave its
data half-updated and its resources in an unknown state. An Aura task is only
ever cancelled at a point where it was waiting, or where it asked. Everything
between those points runs to completion, so you can reason about it as ordinary
sequential code, and cleanup always starts from a consistent state.

### Cancelling a queue loop

A `for` loop over a queue is one of those waiting points. Here a worker is
cancelled while it's in the middle of a long job:

```aura
def worker(jobs: Queue[int64]):
    for job in jobs:
        print(f"handling {job}")
        sleep(10s)
        if cancelled():
            print(f"cancelled in the middle of job {job}")
            return
    print("worker drained the queue")

def main():
    jobs = Queue[int64]()
    with group = TaskGroup():
        group.start_soon(worker, jobs)
        jobs.put(1)
        jobs.put(2)
        sleep(50ms)
        group.cancel()
    print("group closed")
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
handling 1
cancelled in the middle of job 1
group closed
```

The cancellation woke the ten-second `sleep`, the worker saw it and returned,
and job 2 was never started. If the worker had been waiting on the queue
instead, the loop itself would have ended.

## Computing durations

Timeouts and sleeps take a `Duration`. Literals like `10ms`, `2s`, and `1m` are
enough for fixed values. For delays computed at runtime, such as a retry
backoff that grows with each attempt, a `Duration` can be multiplied by an
integer, added, and compared, and there are constructors like `Duration.ms(n)`
and `Duration.seconds(n)`:

```aura
def main():
    base = 10ms
    for attempt in range(1, 4):
        delay = base * attempt
        print(f"attempt {attempt}: waiting {delay}")
        sleep(delay)
    print(Duration.seconds(2) > 1500ms)
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
attempt 1: waiting 10ms
attempt 2: waiting 20ms
attempt 3: waiting 30ms
true
```

A negative duration is never a way to say "wait forever". Passing one to
`sleep` traps with `sleep(...) must be non-negative`, and a negative timeout is
rejected the same way. The only way to wait without a limit is to leave the
timeout out.

## Waiting on more than one thing

Sometimes the next event could come from several places: a queue, a task, or a
deadline. `select` waits for whichever comes first. Here a producer sends one
result quickly and then goes quiet, and the main task gives up after 200ms of
silence:

```aura
def produce(results: Queue[str]):
    sleep(30ms)
    results.put("first result")
    sleep(500ms)
    results.put("late result")
    results.close()

def main():
    results = Queue[str]()
    with group = TaskGroup():
        group.start_soon(produce, results)
        mut waiting = true
        while waiting:
            match own select(results, 200ms):
                case SelectOutcome.Queue(index, received):
                    match own received:
                        case QueueReceive.Item(text):
                            print("got " + text)
                        case _:
                            waiting = false
                case SelectOutcome.Task(index, result):
                    pass
                case SelectOutcome.Deadline(index):
                    print("nothing for 200ms, cancelling")
                    group.cancel()
                    waiting = false
                case SelectOutcome.Cancelled:
                    waiting = false
    print("group closed")
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
got first result
nothing for 200ms, cancelling
group closed
```

`select` takes any mix of queues, task handles, and durations as arguments, and
returns a `SelectOutcome` saying which one won and its position in the argument
list. Our call has no task arguments, so the `Task` case can't happen here, but
`match` still asks us to write it. If several sources are ready at once, the
one with the lowest position wins, and cancellation of the current task beats
all of them. Only the winner is consumed: a queue that lost keeps its value for
the next receive. With one queue and one deadline, this is the same as
`results.get(timeout=200ms)`; `select` earns its place when you're waiting on,
say, a results queue *and* a supervisor task at the same time. The Manual's
[Concurrency](/manual/concurrency) chapter has the full rules.

## What the group does at the end of its block

We've said many times that a group's exit waits for its tasks. Now we can be
precise about what happens to a task that is still *waiting* when the block
ends.

If the task is making progress, or is waiting for something another live task
can provide, the group waits. A producer blocked on a full queue that a consumer
is draining is fine, however long it takes. The group never decides a wait is
stuck because it has gone on for a long time or the machine is busy.

But if a task is waiting with no timeout for something that no live task can
ever provide, waiting for it would hang the program. The group recognizes that
case and cancels the stuck task:

```aura
def consume(jobs: Queue[int64]):
    match jobs.get():
        case QueueReceive.Item(job):
            print(f"got {job}")
        case QueueReceive.Closed:
            print("closed")
        case QueueReceive.TimedOut:
            print("timed out")
        case QueueReceive.Cancelled:
            print("consumer cancelled: nobody can ever send")

def main():
    jobs = Queue[int64]()
    with group = TaskGroup():
        group.start_soon(consume, jobs)
        print("leaving the block")
    print("group closed")
```

```console
$ aura run src/main.au
leaving the block
consumer cancelled: nobody can ever send
group closed
```

The consumer is waiting on `jobs`, and when `main` reaches the end of the block,
no task is left that could put a value on `jobs` or close it. (The task doing
the joining doesn't count, because it's busy joining.) So the group cancels the
consumer, its `get` returns `QueueReceive.Cancelled`, and shutdown completes.

This protection applies to a group's children at the end of its block. It
doesn't cover a wait in your own code. If `main` itself calls `jobs.get()` on a
queue nobody will ever send to, it waits forever:

```aura
def main():
    jobs = Queue[int64]()
    with group = TaskGroup():
        match jobs.get():
            case QueueReceive.Item(job):
                print(f"got {job}")
            case QueueReceive.Closed:
                print("closed")
            case QueueReceive.TimedOut:
                print("timed out")
            case QueueReceive.Cancelled:
                print("cancelled")
    print("group closed")
```

```console
$ timeout 3 aura run src/main.au
$ echo $?
124
```

Nothing prints, and `timeout` has to kill the program after three seconds
(exit status 124 is `timeout` reporting that it did). The fix is the one from
the previous section: give a wait a timeout when there's any doubt that an
answer will come.

## Shutdown, in order

Putting the pieces together, here is what happens when control reaches the end
of a `with group = TaskGroup():` block, or leaves it early:
