## Source: docs/book/appendix-01-keywords.md

# Appendix A: Keywords

This appendix lists the words Aura's lexer treats specially. Most of them are
*reserved*: you cannot use them as the name of a binding, a parameter, a
function, or a field. A handful more are *contextual*: they are ordinary
identifiers almost everywhere, and take on a special meaning only in one
position. The [Lexical structure](/manual/lexical-structure) page of the
Manual has the exact rules.

## Reserved keywords

If you try to use one of these as a name, the parser stops you. It does not
know you meant a name, so the message describes the token it found instead:

```aura check-fail:AU1101
def area(class: str) -> str:
    return class
```

```console
$ aura check kw.au
error[AU1101]: expected identifier
 --> kw.au:1:10
  |
1 | def area(class: str) -> str:
  |          ^
```

When you see `expected identifier` pointing at a perfectly reasonable word,
check this list. The usual fix is a slightly longer name: `kind` or
`class_name` for `class`, or `is_match` for `match`.

Here are the reserved words, grouped by what they do.

Declarations:

- `def` declares a function or method.
- `class` declares a class. Put `copy` right before it (`copy class Point:`)
  to make a class whose values copy instead of moving.
- `enum` declares an enum with variants.
- `trait` declares a trait, a named set of methods that types can implement.
- `impl` implements a trait for a type: `impl Display for Account:`.
- `public` marks a declaration as visible to modules that import this one.
- `import` brings a module into scope: `import fs`, `import process as p`.
- `extern` and `opaque` declare C functions and C handle types for the FFI
  (Chapter 18).
- `indirect` marks a class field that is stored indirectly, which lets a
  class refer to itself: `next: indirect Node | None = None`.

Ownership and access:

- `mut` declares a mutable binding (`mut total = 0`), a parameter the callee
  may change (`items: mut list[str]`), or a receiver that changes its object
  (`def push(mut self, ...)`). It also appears in `for ... in mut ...` and
  `match mut`.
- `own` declares a parameter the callee takes ownership of (`job: own Job`), a
  consuming receiver (`own self`), and consuming loops and matches
  (`for job in own jobs`, `match own result`).

Control flow:

- `if`, `elif`, and `else` choose between branches. `else` also appears in
  the conditional expression `a if condition else b`.
- `while` loops while a condition holds.
- `for` and `in` loop over a collection, a range, or a queue. `in` is also the
  membership operator: `"a" in counts`.
- `break` leaves the innermost loop; `continue` starts its next iteration.
- `return` leaves a function, with or without a value.
- `match` and `case` choose a branch by pattern.
- `pass` does nothing, for a block that must contain a statement.
- `assert` checks a condition and traps if it is false:
  `assert total > 0, "no items"`.

Values, operators, and other forms:

- `true` and `false` are the two `bool` literals. They are lowercase.
- `and`, `or`, and `not` are the boolean operators.
- `try` passes an `Err` up to the caller: `text = try fs.read_to_string(path)`.
- `with` opens a scope that owns a resource and cleans it up on exit:
  `with group = TaskGroup():`.
- `as` names the value a pattern matched (`case str as line:`), renames an
  import (`import process as p`), and casts numbers (`count as int64`).
- `from` starts an import of specific names: `from fs import exists`.

`from` is a special case worth knowing. It is only a keyword at the start of
a module-level import, so it remains usable as a parameter name, a field name,
or a named argument. This is legal:

```aura
class Message:
    from: str
    to: str

def main():
    note = Message(from="ada", to="grace")
    print(note.from + " -> " + note.to)
```

## Contextual words

These words are ordinary identifiers to the lexer. They mean something special
only in a particular position, and you can use them as names elsewhere,
although doing so tends to confuse readers.

- `self` names the receiver in a method.
- `Self` refers to the current type inside a trait or an `impl`.
- `copy` makes a class a copy class when it appears directly before `class`.
- `None` is the unit value, and the "nothing here" member of a `T | None`
  union.
- `is` appears only in `value is None` and `value is not None`. Aura has no
  identity comparison between arbitrary values, so `a is b` is a syntax error.
- `lambda` starts an anonymous function: `lambda n: n + 1`.
- `view` creates a named alias for a place without moving or copying it:
  `view first = names[0]`, or `view mut` for a writable alias.
- `type` declares a type alias at module level:
  `type Reader = Callable[def() -> int64]`.
- `set` names the builtin set type.
- `_` is the wildcard in a pattern (`case _:`), and a conventional name for a
  value you do not use (`for _ in range(3):`).

## Words Aura does not reserve

If you come from Python, you may reach for words that Aura does not treat as
keywords at all: `null`, `yield`, `async`, `await`, `del`, `global`,
`nonlocal`, `raise`, `except`, and `finally`. They are plain identifiers, so
the error you get depends on how you used them. `x = null` is reported as an
unknown name (`AU2001`). `raise ValueError("x")` and `yield 1` read to the
parser as a name followed by more tokens than a statement can hold, so you get
`AU1101: expected Newline` pointing right after the word. `try:` followed by
`except` gets a targeted `AU2005` message that points you at `Result` and
`match`. Appendix C has the Aura way to express each of these ideas.

## Source: docs/book/appendix-02-operators.md

# Appendix B: Operators and symbols

This appendix collects Aura's operators and the punctuation that carries
meaning in its syntax. If you know Python, almost all of it will look
familiar, and the differences are deliberate: Aura has no implicit numeric
conversion, no truthiness, and no integer `/`, because each of those is a
place where Python quietly picks an answer for you. The
[Expressions](/manual/expressions) page of the Manual has the full typing and
evaluation rules.

## Arithmetic

| Operator | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `+` | addition, string concatenation, `Duration` sum | `total + 1`, `"ab" + "cd"`, `2s + 500ms` |
| `-` | subtraction, and unary negation | `end - start`, `-offset` |
| `*` | multiplication, `Duration` times `int64` | `width * height`, `100ms * 3` |
| `/` | true division, floating-point types only | `7.0 / 2.0` |
| `//` | floor division | `7 // 2` |
| `%` | remainder paired with `//` | `-7 % 2` |
| `**` | power | `2 ** 10` |

Both operands of a binary arithmetic operator must have the same type. An
`int32` plus an `int64` is an error, not a widening:

```aura check-fail:AU2999
def main():
    a: int32 = 1
    b: int64 = 2
    print(a + b)
```

```console
$ aura check mix.au
error[AU2999]: binary operator operands must match, found `int32` and `int64`
 --> mix.au:4:11
  |
4 |     print(a + b)
  |           ^
```

Convert one side explicitly with `as`, for example `a as int64 + b`. Unsuffixed
literals adapt to the type they are combined with, so `a + 1` is fine.

Integer `/` is rejected with `AU2003`, and the message tells you which of the
two operations you probably meant: `//` for floor division, or `.to_float()`
on both operands for true division. Floor division rounds toward negative
infinity, as in Python, so `-7 // 2` is `-4` and `-7 % 2` is `1`. Dividing by
zero traps with `AU4004`.

Integer arithmetic is checked. A result that does not fit its type traps
with `AU4002` instead of wrapping around:

```console
$ aura run ov.au
error[AU4002]: integer value `2147483648` does not fit in `int32`
 --> ov.au:3:11
  |
3 |     print(big + 1)
  |           ^
  = note: Aura call chain (innermost first): main at 1:1
```

When wrapping is what you want, every integer type has explicit methods such
as `wrapping_add` and `saturating_mul`.

Aura has no unary `+`. Writing `+3` is a syntax error.

## Comparison and membership

| Operator | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `==`, `!=` | equality and inequality |
| `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` | ordering, for numbers, `Duration`, and `str` |
| `in`, `not in` | membership in a list, dict, set, or substring in a `str` |
| `is None`, `is not None` | test a `T \| None` value, and narrow it |

Comparisons chain the way they do in Python: `1 < x < 10` means
`1 < x and x < 10`, with `x` evaluated once. String ordering compares the
underlying bytes, so `"Zebra" < "apple"` is true; there is no locale-aware
ordering built in.

`is` is not a general identity test. It only appears in `is None` and
`is not None`, and after the test the compiler treats the value as narrowed to
the non-`None` type in the branch where that is known.

## Boolean operators

`and`, `or`, and `not` work on `bool` and nothing else. `and` and `or`
short-circuit: the right side is only evaluated when it can change the
answer. Because there is no truthiness, `if values:` is an error; write
`if len(values) > 0:` instead.

The conditional expression `value if condition else other` picks one of two
values and has the lowest precedence of all.

## Bitwise and shift operators

| Operator | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `&` | bitwise and |
| `\|` | bitwise or; also the union type operator, as in `str \| None` |
| `^` | bitwise exclusive or |
| `~` | bitwise not (unary) |
| `<<`, `>>` | shift left, shift right |

These work on integers of one exact type. A shift count must be at least zero
and less than the width of the type, and `<<` traps with `AU4002` if bits
would be lost off the top.

## Assignment

`=` binds or assigns. Every arithmetic and bitwise operator has a compound
form that updates a mutable binding in place: `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `//=`,
`%=`, `**=`, `&=`, `|=`, `^=`, `<<=`, and `>>=`. Assignment is a statement,
never an expression, so there is no walrus operator and no `a = b = 0`.

## Precedence

From loosest to tightest binding:

1. `value if condition else other`
2. `or`
3. `and`
4. `not`
5. comparisons, `in`, `not in` (all one level, chained)
6. `|`
7. `^`
8. `&`
9. `<<`, `>>`
10. `+`, `-`
11. `*`, `/`, `//`, `%`
12. unary `-`, unary `~`, and the prefix forms `try` and `match`
13. `**`
14. calls, indexing, member access, specialization, and `as` casts

Two results surprise people. `**` binds tighter than unary minus, so `-2 ** 2`
is `-4`. And `**` groups to the right, so `2 ** 3 ** 2` is `2 ** 9`, which is
`512`. Parentheses are always allowed and often kinder to readers.

This program exercises most of the table:

```aura
def main():
    print(-7 // 2)
    print(2 ** 3 ** 2)
    print(-2 ** 2)
    x = 5
    print(1 < x < 10)
    print(6 & 3)
    print(1 << 4)
    print(2s + 500ms)
    print(3 in [1, 2, 3])
    print("big" if x > 3 else "small")
```

```console
$ aura run ops.au
-4
512
-4
true
2
16
2500ms
true
big
```

## Symbols

| Symbol | Where it appears |
| --- | --- |
| `:` | ends a block header (`def`, `if`, `for`, `class`, `case`, `with`); separates a name from its type (`count: int64`); separates keys from values in dict literals; separates slice bounds (`text[1:4]`) |
| `->` | introduces a function's return type |
| `.` | member access and method calls, and module paths (`process.run`) |
| `,` | separates arguments, elements, and tuple parts; a trailing comma before a closing bracket is allowed |
| `( )` | calls, grouping, tuples; `(x,)` is a one-element tuple |
| `[ ]` | list literals, indexing, slicing, and type arguments (`list[str]`, `Queue[Job]`) |
| `{ }` | dict and set literals, and interpolation inside f-strings |
| `=` | binding and assignment; also named arguments and defaults (`timeout=1s`) |
| `@` | a decorator line above a function, or `@property` in a class |
| `#` | starts a comment that runs to the end of the line |
| `f"..."` | an f-string with `{expression}` interpolation |
| `"""..."""` | a triple-quoted string, also used for docstrings |
| `ms`, `s`, `m` | suffixes on integer literals that make a `Duration`: `10ms`, `2s`, `1m` |
| `_` | the wildcard pattern, and digit separators in numbers (`1_000_000`) |
| `*name` | a rest pattern in tuple or sequence matching |

Aura has no semicolons: each statement gets its own line, and `x = 1; y = 2`
is rejected with `AU1001` at the `;`. There are no block comments either; use
a `#` on each line.

## Source: docs/book/appendix-03-from-python.md

# Appendix C: Aura for Python developers

Aura was designed so that Python programmers would feel at home in it, and on
the surface they do. Blocks are indented, functions start with `def`, classes
with `class`, strings with f-strings work the way you expect, and so do
comprehensions, keyword arguments, `for x in items`, `with`, and chained
comparisons. That familiarity is useful, but it also means the differences
arrive as surprises: code that looks right and does not compile. This
appendix collects those differences in one place, with the reason for each,
so that the first week with Aura is less of a negotiation with the compiler.

If you have read the book from the start, you have already met all of these.
Treat this as the cheat sheet you hand a Python colleague.

## Scripts and `main`

A file of top-level statements is a script, and runs from top to bottom with
no ceremony:

```aura
langs = ["python", "aura"]

for lang in langs:
    print(f"hello, {lang}")
```

There is no `if __name__ == "__main__":`. When you want an entry point,
usually because you want an exit status or a compiled binary, you write a
`main` function. Its `int32` result becomes the process exit status:

```aura
def main() -> int32:
    print("hello")
    return 0
```

A file chooses one style or the other. Mixing top-level statements with a
`main` is an error (`AU2999`: "files cannot mix top-level statements ... with
an explicit `main` function"). Declarations such as `class` and `def` are
fine in both.

One small thing trips people up on the first day: `print` takes exactly one
argument. `print(a, b)` is `AU2004`. Use an f-string, `print(f"{a} {b}")`.

## Bindings are immutable by default

In Python every name can be rebound. In Aura a binding is fixed unless you
say otherwise, and this is usually the first error a Python programmer sees:

```aura check-fail:AU3003
def main():
    total = 0
    total = total + 1
```

```console
$ aura check immut.au
error[AU3003]: cannot assign to immutable binding `total`; declare it with `mut` to rebind it
 --> immut.au:3:5
  |
3 |     total = total + 1
  |     ^
```

The fix is one word:

```aura
def main():
    mut total = 0
    total = total + 1
    print(total)
```

The same rule covers mutating a collection. `names.append("b")` needs
`mut names = [...]`, because appending changes the list. Aura asks you to
mark mutation because then you can read a function and see at a glance which
values it changes. It also lets the ownership checker reason about who can
see a change, which is the next topic.

## Values have one owner

This is the biggest difference, and the one worth the most patience.
Python passes references to objects and lets a garbage collector decide when
nobody needs them. Aura has no garbage collector. Every value has exactly one
owner, and a function signature says what the function does with what you
pass it:

| Parameter | The function may | Afterwards, the caller |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name: str` | read it | still owns it |
| `name: mut str` | change it | still owns it, changed |
| `name: own str` | keep it, change it, drop it | no longer has it |

Call sites look like Python: no `&`, no sigils. The compiler reads the
signature and does the right thing. When you give a value away with `own`, it
holds you to that:

```aura check-fail:AU3001
def consume(name: own str) -> int64:
    return len(name)

def main():
    label = "aura"
    n = consume(label)
    print(label)
```

```console
$ aura check owner.au
error[AU3001]: use of moved value `label`
 --> owner.au:7:11
  |
7 |     print(label)
  |           ^
  = related owner.au:6:17: value moved here
  = help: pass shared access when ownership is not needed, or call `.clone()` at the move site when an independent value is required
  = fix: replace owner.au:6:22-6:22 with `.clone()`
```

Read an error like this as a question: did you mean to hand `label` over, or
only to let `consume` look at it? If the function only reads, drop the `own`.
If you really need two independent values, make a copy at the call. Strings
copy with `.clone()`, and lists, dicts, and sets copy with `.copy()`.
Classes have neither method, deliberately: if you want a second instance,
build one.

Numbers, `bool`, `Duration`, and copy classes (declared `copy class`) copy
automatically, so you can pass them around freely. Strings, collections,
ordinary class instances, and resources such as files move. Chapter 4 covers
all of this in depth.

A related surprise: indexing a list of non-copy values does not give you an
independent value, because that would quietly copy or move it out of a list
you still own. `first = names[0]` on a `list[str]` is `AU3005`, and the
message names the alternatives: `view first = names[0]` for an alias,
`names[0].clone()` for a copy, or `names.pop(0)` to take it out.

## Types are static, locals are inferred

Parameters and return types must be annotated. Everything else is inferred:

```aura
def total(prices: list[float64]) -> float64:
    mut sum = 0.0
    for price in prices:
        sum += price
    return sum
```

Three consequences catch people. First, `def f(x):` does not parse, because
an untyped parameter is not a thing Aura has. Second, a function without
`->` returns `None`, and Aura does not infer a return type from the body:

```aura check-fail:AU2002
def double(n: int64):
    return n * 2
```

The compiler reports `return type mismatch: expected None, found int64`; add
`-> int64`. Third, numbers never convert implicitly. An unsuffixed integer
literal is `int64` and a float literal is `float64`. Passing an `int32` where
an `int64` is expected, or adding the two, is an error. Convert with
`value as int64`, or `.to_float()` for a float.

## No truthiness, no integer `/`

`if values:` is an error, because conditions must be `bool`. Write what you
mean: `if len(values) > 0:` or `if value is not None:`. Python's rule that
empty things are false is convenient until the day `0` or `""` turns out to be
a valid value, and Aura would rather you spell out which case you are
testing.

Integer `/` is rejected with `AU2003`. Python 3 made `7 / 2` produce `3.5`,
while most other languages produce `3`. Rather than pick one and surprise half
its users, Aura makes you choose: `//` for floor division, or `.to_float()`
on both sides for true division. `//` and `%` round the same way as in
Python.

## Failure is a return value

Aura has no exceptions, so there is no `raise`, `try`/`except`, or
`finally`. A function that can fail says so in its return type with
`Result[T, E]`, and the caller has to deal with both outcomes:

```aura
def parse_port(text: str) -> Result[int64, str]:
    port = try parse_int64(text)
    if port < 1 or port > 65535:
        return Result.Err(f"port out of range: {port}")
    return Result.Ok(port)

def main():
    match parse_port("8080"):
        case Result.Ok(port):
            print(f"listening on {port}")
        case Result.Err(message):
            print(f"bad config: {message}")
```

`try` in Aura is an expression, not a block: `try parse_int64(text)` returns
the `Ok` value, or returns the `Err` from the enclosing function at once. It
does the job that letting an exception propagate does in Python, but you can
see every place it happens.

"A value or nothing" is `T | None`, such as `str | None`, tested with
`is None` and `is not None`. The compiler narrows the type after the test, so
there is no `Optional` unwrapping to do by hand.

Some failures are not recoverable values: an index out of range, a failed
`assert`, integer overflow, division by zero. Those *trap*, stopping the task
with an `AU40xx` diagnostic and an Aura call chain, much like an uncaught
exception would. The difference is that you cannot catch a trap, so it is
reserved for bugs, not for conditions a program should handle.

## Classes, without inheritance

A class is a set of fields and methods. Without an `__init__`, you construct
it by naming its fields, and fields may have defaults:

```aura
class Account:
    owner: str
    balance: float64
    currency: str = "USD"

    def new(owner: own str) -> Account:
        return Account(owner=owner, balance=0.0)

    def deposit(mut self, amount: float64):
        self.balance += amount

    @property
    def summary(self) -> str:
        return f"{self.owner}: {self.balance} {self.currency}"

impl Display for Account:
    def display(self) -> str:
        return f"<account {self.owner}>"

def main():
    mut account = Account.new("ada")
    account.deposit(25.0)
    print(account.summary)
    print(account)
```

A few things in that listing replace Python habits:

- `new` has no `self`, which makes it an associated function, called as
  `Account.new(...)`. It is the Aura answer to `@classmethod` constructors,
  and a class can have as many as it likes.
- The receiver says what a method does to its object, with the same words as
  parameters: `self` reads, `mut self` changes, `own self` consumes. Writing
  `self.balance += amount` in a method declared with plain `self` is
  `AU3003`, and the help line tells you to write `mut self`.
- `@property` works much as in Python, for read-only computed values. It is
  one of the few decorators allowed on a method.
- `__str__` becomes an implementation of the `Display` trait. After that,
  `print(account)`, `str(account)`, and `f"{account}"` all use it.

`__init__` exists too, when construction needs logic, and `with` works with
classes that define `__exit__(mut self)` (Chapter 14).

`class Dog(Animal):` does not parse. Aura has no inheritance. Shared behavior
is a trait that several types implement (Chapter 10), and shared data is a
field holding another class. If you have spent time untangling deep class
hierarchies in Python, you may not miss it.

## Strings

`str` is Unicode, and `len(text)` counts Unicode scalar values. Strings are
not indexable: `text[0]` is an error, but slices such as `text[1:4]` work and
return a new string. Most methods have the names you expect, and a few have
Aura names:

| Python | Aura |
| --- | --- |
| `s.strip()`, `s.lstrip()`, `s.rstrip()` | `s.trim()`, `s.trim_start()`, `s.trim_end()` |
| `s.upper()`, `s.lower()` | `s.to_upper()`, `s.to_lower()` |
| `s.split()` | `s.split_whitespace()` |
| `s.splitlines()` | `s.lines()` |
| `s.partition(sep)` | `s.split_once(sep)`, which returns `(str, str) \| None` |
| `s.find(sub)` | `s.find(sub)`, which returns `int64 \| None` instead of `-1` |
| `s * 3` | `s.repeat(3)` |
| `int(s)` | `parse_int64(s)`, which returns a `Result` |

The pattern in the last three rows is the theme of the whole language: where
Python returns a sentinel or raises, Aura returns a type that makes the
missing case impossible to ignore.

## `is` means `is None`

`value is None` and `value is not None` are the only uses of `is`. There is
no identity comparison between arbitrary objects, and `a is b` is a syntax
error. Use `==` for equality.

## Concurrency and processes

Python offers threads, `asyncio`, and `multiprocessing`, each with its own
rules. Aura has one model: tasks started inside a `with group = TaskGroup():`
block, values passed between them through `Queue[T]`, and cancellation that
tasks observe at well-defined waiting points. There is no `async` or `await`
to color your functions, and no global lock: tasks really do run on several
cores. The price is that values crossing between tasks must move, never be
shared, which the compiler checks (Chapter 15).

`process.run` takes a list of arguments and never runs a shell, unlike
`subprocess.run(..., shell=True)`. If you want shell syntax, say so with
`["/bin/sh", "-c", command]`, as the job runner in Chapter 19 does.

## Module state

Top-level bindings in a file with `main` are immutable module storage. A
`mut` binding at the top level is rejected with `AU3003`, and moving a value
out of one is `AU3001`. Mutable state belongs to an owner, which is usually `main`
or an object it creates. This rules out the module-level caches and counters
that Python code tends to accumulate, and with them a whole class of
"who changed this?" bugs.

## Where to go next

Chapter 4 is the one to read slowly, because ownership is the idea that does
not map onto anything in Python. After that, the
[Manual](/manual/) is the reference for exact rules, and the diagnostics in
[Appendix E](/book/appendix-05-common-diagnostics) are the ones you will meet most as you
make the switch.

## Source: docs/book/appendix-04-tools.md

# Appendix D: Useful tools

The `aura` command does more than compile and run programs. It formats code,
runs tests, generates API documentation, and powers the editor support in VS
Code. This appendix is a tour of those tools, in roughly the order you will
want them. The [CLI and tooling](/manual/cli-and-tooling) page of the Manual
lists every command and flag.

## The everyday commands

You have used these throughout the book, so this is only a reminder of how
they divide the work:

- `aura check file.au` parses and type-checks without running anything. It is
  the fastest way to find out whether a change compiles, and it prints `ok`
  when it does.
- `aura run file.au` checks and then runs the program. Arguments after `--`
  reach the program through `sys.args()`.
- `aura build -o path file.au` produces a standalone native executable.
  Add `--debug` for a build a debugger can step through.
- `aura new name` creates a project directory with `Aura.toml`,
  `src/main.au`, `tests/smoke.au`, and a `.gitignore`.
- `aura version` prints the build channel and source commit, which is the
  first thing to include in a bug report:

```console
$ aura version
aura 0.11.0-dev (9e279b31f356)
```

`aura check` and `aura run` also accept `--format json`, which prints
diagnostics as a JSON document instead of the human-readable form. That is
what you want when another program is reading the output, such as a CI script
that turns diagnostics into annotations:

```console
$ aura check --format json src/err.au
{"diagnostics":[{"call_frames":[],"code":"AU2001","edits":[],"help":[],"message":"unknown name `missing`","notes":[],"primary_span":{"end":{"column":12,"line":2},"path":"src/err.au","start":{"column":11,"line":2}},"secondary_spans":[],"severity":"error","task_ancestry":[]}],"schema_version":1}
```

The fields are the same ones the human form shows: the stable code, the
message, the primary span, related spans, notes, help, and machine-applicable
edits.

## Formatting with `aura fmt`

Aura has one formatting style, and `aura fmt` applies it. There are no
options to configure, on purpose: if every Aura project is formatted the same
way, nobody has to argue about it in code review, and code you read in
someone else's project looks like code you wrote.

Let's see it at work. Here is a file written in a hurry:

*Filename: src/main.au*

```aura
import sys
def label(count:int64,unit:str="job")->str:
  if count==1:
    return f"{count} {unit}"
  return f"{count} {unit}s"
def main()->int32:
  print(label(len(sys.args()),
      unit = "argument"))
  return 0
```

It compiles, since Aura only cares that indentation is consistent, but it is
hard on the eyes. `aura fmt --check` reports which files would change, writes
nothing, and exits with status 1 if any would:

```console
$ aura fmt --check .
would format `./src/main.au`
$ echo $?
1
```

That makes `aura fmt --check .` a good step for CI. Running `aura fmt` with a
path rewrites the files in place:

```console
$ aura fmt src
$ cat src/main.au
import sys

def label(count: int64, unit: str = "job") -> str:
    if count == 1:
        return f"{count} {unit}"
    return f"{count} {unit}s"

def main() -> int32:
    print(label(len(sys.args()), unit="argument"))
    return 0
```

The formatter set four-space indentation, put single spaces around operators
and after colons and commas, removed the spaces around `=` in the keyword
argument (but kept them around the parameter default `= "job"`, where a type
annotation comes first), and put two blank lines between top-level
declarations. It also joined the call that was split over two lines, because
the whole statement fits in 88 columns. A statement that does not fit is
broken at its outermost bracket, one element per line, with a trailing comma.
You can see that style in the longer `Report(...)` constructor calls in
Chapter 19, which are formatter output.

If you want a list to stay one element per line even when it would fit,
write it with a trailing comma, and the formatter will respect that. Comments
stay on the lines where you wrote them, and string literals, including
docstrings, are never changed.

The formatter only touches code that parses. If a file has a syntax error,
`aura fmt` reports the usual diagnostic and leaves the file alone:

```console
$ aura fmt src/bad.au
error[AU1001]: unclosed delimiter `(`; expected `)` before end of file
 --> src/bad.au:2:1
  = related src/bad.au:1:9: opening delimiter `(` is here
```

After formatting, it parses its own output and checks that the tokens are
unchanged, so a formatter bug cannot silently change what your program means.
`aura fmt --stdin` reads source from standard input and writes the formatted
result to standard output, for editors and scripts that want to format a
buffer without a file.

## Testing with `aura test`

`aura test` finds the test programs under `tests/` and runs each one. A test
passes when it compiles, runs within its timeout (30 seconds by default), and
returns 0 from `main`. The project `aura new` creates has one placeholder
test:

```console
$ aura test
ok tests/smoke.au
1 passed; 0 failed
```

A failing assertion shows the values on each side, which saves a round of
adding `print` calls:

```console
$ aura test
FAILED tests/fail.au
error[AU4001]: math is broken
 --> tests/fail.au:2:5
  |
2 |     assert 1 + 1 == 3, "math is broken"
  |     ^
  = note: left = 2
  = note: right = 3
  = note: Aura call chain (innermost first): main at 1:1
ok tests/smoke.au
1 passed; 1 failed
```

`-k substring` runs only the tests whose names match, and `--timeout-ms`
changes the per-test limit. Chapter 11 covers testing properly, including
test functions, setup and teardown, and parameterized cases.

## API documentation with `aura doc`

A triple-quoted string as the first statement of a module, class, or function
is a docstring. Parameters are documented under an `Args:` heading:

*Filename: src/units.au*

```aura
"""Helpers for printing counts."""

public def label(count: int64, unit: str) -> str:
    """Return `count` followed by `unit`, pluralised when needed.

    Args:
        count: How many things there are.
        unit: The singular name of one thing.
    """
    if count == 1:
        return f"{count} {unit}"
    return f"{count} {unit}s"
```

`aura doc src/units.au` prints a Markdown page for the module: a
`# Module units` heading, the module docstring, and a section for each public
function with its signature, its docstring, and a parameter list built from
the `Args:` entries, with each parameter's type filled in from the signature.
With `--out`, it writes one file per module instead:

```console
$ aura doc --out api src/units.au
wrote api/units.md
```

`--json` produces the same information as JSON, for tools that render their
own documentation sites. The same docstrings also show up in the editor, on
hover and in completions.

## The VS Code extension

The **Aura Programming Language** extension for VS Code gives you syntax
highlighting, diagnostics as you type, completion, hover with types and
docstrings, signature help, go-to-definition (including into other modules),
find references, rename, document symbols, formatting, and debugging. It is
published by **JohnOlafenwa** on both the Visual Studio Marketplace and Open
VSX, so it works in VS Code and in editors such as VSCodium. Install it from
the Extensions view, or from a terminal:

```bash
code --install-extension JohnOlafenwa.vscode-aura-lang
```

The extension does not contain its own copy of the language. All of its
understanding of your code comes from the `aura` compiler you installed,
which it starts in the background with `aura lsp`. That command runs a
persistent compiler service that the extension's language server talks to;
it is not something you run by hand. Because of this design, the editor and
the command line can never disagree: a red squiggle in VS Code is exactly the
diagnostic `aura check` would print, with the same code.

That also means the extension needs to find `aura`. It looks on your `PATH`.
If you keep several builds of the compiler around, or `aura` is not on the
`PATH` that VS Code sees, start VS Code with `AURA_LSP_AURA_PATH` set to the
binary you want:

```bash
AURA_LSP_AURA_PATH="$HOME/tools/aura/bin/aura" code .
```

On Windows with WSL, install both the `aura` CLI and the extension inside
WSL. Open the project from the WSL terminal with `code .`, and install the
extension with **Install in WSL** in that remote window. An extension running
on the Windows side cannot reliably reach a compiler inside Linux.

To check that everything is connected, open any `.au` file and look at the
language mode in the lower-right corner: it should say **Aura**. Then type
something invalid and wait for an `AU` diagnostic to appear, and hover over a
binding to see its type. If you get colours but no diagnostics or hover, the
extension cannot start the compiler. Run `aura --version` in VS Code's
integrated terminal to see what the editor's environment finds, and open
**View → Output**, then **Aura Language Server**, to read the startup log.

Formatting in the editor uses the same rules as `aura fmt`. Run **Format
Document**, or set `"editor.formatOnSave": true` to format every time you
save. A buffer with a syntax error is left as it is.

For debugging, the extension adds a **Debug** link above `def main` and an
**Aura: Debug File** command. Both build the file with `aura build --debug`
and launch it under LLVM's `lldb-dap`, so breakpoints, stepping, the call
stack, and local variables work as in any other VS Code debugger. You need
`lldb-dap` installed; the extension looks for it in the `aura.lldbDapPath`
setting, then through `xcrun` on macOS, then on your `PATH`. Chapter 17 walks
through a debugging session.

## Source: docs/book/appendix-05-common-diagnostics.md

# Appendix E: Diagnostics you will meet often

Every message `aura` prints starts with a stable code such as `AU3001`. The
first digit after `AU` tells you which part of the compiler is talking: `1`
for reading the text of your program, `2` for names and types, `3` for
ownership and borrowing, and `4` for traps at run time. The code stays the
same from release to release even when the wording improves, so it is the
thing to search for.

A diagnostic has the same parts every time. The first line is the code and a
one-line message. The `-->` line gives the file, line, and column, and the
excerpt underneath marks the exact spot with `^`. Then come optional records:
`related` points at a second place that explains the first (where a value
moved, where a borrow started), `note` adds context, `help` suggests what to
do, and `fix` is an exact replacement that an editor can apply for you. When
there is a `related` line, read it; it is usually the half of the story you
were missing.

This appendix collects the diagnostics that people learning Aura run into
most, each with a minimal program that triggers it, the real output, and the
usual fix. The [Diagnostics](/manual/diagnostics) page of the Manual has the
complete table of codes.

## Reading your source

### `AU1001`: tabs and unclosed delimiters

`AU1001` means the compiler could not even split your file into tokens. The
two common causes are tab characters used for indentation and a bracket that
is never closed. Aura requires spaces for indentation, because a file that
mixes tabs and spaces can look correctly indented in one editor and wrongly
indented in another:

```console
$ aura check tabs.au
error[AU1001]: tabs are not supported for indentation; use spaces
 --> tabs.au:2:1
  |
2 | 	print(1)
  | ^
```

Configure your editor to insert spaces for `.au` files, or run `aura fmt`
once the file parses. An unclosed bracket is reported at the end of the file,
with a `related` line pointing at the bracket that was opened:

```aura check-fail:AU1001
def main():
    print("a"
```

```console
$ aura check unclosed.au
error[AU1001]: unclosed delimiter `(`; expected `)` before end of file
 --> unclosed.au:3:1
  = related unclosed.au:2:10: opening delimiter `(` is here
```

### `AU1101`: a missing parameter type

`AU1101` is the general syntax error. The one Python programmers hit first is
a parameter without a type:

```aura check-fail:AU1101
def double(x):
    return x * 2
```

```console
$ aura check untyped.au
error[AU1101]: expected Colon, found RParen
 --> untyped.au:1:13
  |
1 | def double(x):
  |             ^
```

The parser expected the `:` that starts a type annotation and found `)`
instead. Every parameter needs a type: `def double(x: int64) -> int64:`.
The same code appears when you use a keyword such as `class` or `match` as a
name; Appendix A lists them.

## Names and types

### `AU2001`: unknown name

```aura check-fail:AU2001
def main():
    count = 3
    print(cuont)
```

```console
$ aura check unknown.au
error[AU2001]: unknown name `cuont`
 --> unknown.au:3:11
  |
3 |     print(cuont)
  |           ^
```

Usually a typo, or a name from a module you have not imported. Remember that
module members are qualified: after `import fs`, the function is
`fs.read_to_string`, not `read_to_string`, unless you wrote
`from fs import read_to_string`.

### `AU2002`: type mismatch

`AU2002` covers any value of the wrong type in a position that requires a
specific one. Two versions come up constantly. The first is mixing integer
widths, because Aura never converts numbers implicitly:

```aura check-fail:AU2002
def wait_for(seconds: int64):
    print(seconds)

def main():
    n: int32 = 5
    wait_for(n)
```

```console
$ aura check argtype.au
error[AU2002]: argument type mismatch for function `wait_for`: expected `int64`, found `int32`
 --> argtype.au:6:14
  |
6 |     wait_for(n)
  |              ^
```

Convert at the call with `wait_for(n as int64)`, or change one of the types
so they agree. The second is a function that returns a value but forgot to
say so. A missing `->` means the function returns `None`:

```aura check-fail:AU2002
def double(n: int64):
    return n * 2
```

```console
$ aura check retmismatch.au
error[AU2002]: return type mismatch: expected `None`, found `int64`
 --> retmismatch.au:2:5
  |
2 |     return n * 2
  |     ^
```

Add the return type: `def double(n: int64) -> int64:`. You will also see
`AU2002` when you use a `T | None` value as if it were a `T`. The fix there is
to test it with `is None` first, which narrows the type.

### `AU2003`: integer division with `/`

```aura check-fail:AU2003
def average(total: int64, count: int64) -> int64:
    return total / count
```

```console
$ aura check intdiv.au
error[AU2003]: integer `/` is not supported; use `//` for floor division, or call `.to_float()` on both operands for true division
 --> intdiv.au:2:12
  |
2 |     return total / count
  |            ^
```

The message names both fixes. Use `total // count` when you want an integer
result rounded down, and `total.to_float() / count.to_float()` with a
`float64` return type when you want the exact quotient. Aura makes you pick
because the two meanings differ between languages, and guessing wrong
produces numbers that are subtly off.

### `AU2004`: arguments that do not fit the parameters

```aura check-fail:AU2004
def main():
    name = "ada"
    print("hello", name)
```

```console
$ aura check args.au
error[AU2004]: `print` expects 1 argument, found 2
 --> args.au:3:5
  |
3 |     print("hello", name)
  |     ^
```

`AU2004` means the arguments at a call do not bind to the callee's parameter
list: too many, too few, or a named argument that does not exist. With
`print`, the fix is an f-string: `print(f"hello {name}")`.

### `AU2005`: Python spellings

When you write something that is valid Python but not Aura, the compiler
often recognizes it and says what to write instead:

```aura check-fail:AU2005
def main():
    done = True
```

```console
$ aura check pyshape.au
error[AU2005]: unknown name `True`; did you mean `true`?
 --> pyshape.au:2:12
  |
2 |     done = True
  |            ^
```

The same code gives targeted advice for `try:`/`except:` (use `Result` and
`match`), for `str(...)`-style constructors, and for other habits that carry
over from Python.

### `AU2999`: a match that misses a case

Every `match` must handle every possible value. Leave out an enum variant and
the compiler names it:

```aura check-fail:AU2999
enum Light:
    Red
    Amber
    Green

def action(light: Light) -> str:
    match light:
        case Light.Red:
            return "stop"
        case Light.Green:
            return "go"
```

```console
$ aura check missingarm.au
error[AU2999]: non-exhaustive match over `Light`: missing `Amber`
 --> missingarm.au:7:5
  |
7 |     match light:
  |     ^
```

Add the missing arm, or a `case _:` when the remaining variants really do
share one answer. Prefer naming them: when someone adds a fourth variant
later, a match without a wildcard sends them to every place that needs a
decision. Matching on a union type such as `int64 | str` has its own code,
`AU2013`, with a message like `match does not cover str`; the fix is the
same.

### `AU2999`: a function that is missing a return

```aura check-fail:AU2999
def sign(n: int64) -> str:
    if n < 0:
        return "negative"
    elif n > 0:
        return "positive"
```

```console
$ aura check noreturn.au
error[AU2999]: function `sign` is missing a return
 --> noreturn.au:1:1
  |
1 | def sign(n: int64) -> str:
  | ^
```

Some path through the body reaches the end without returning, here when `n`
is zero. The compiler does not reason about which conditions are possible,
and it does not treat `while true:` as a loop that never ends, so a loop that
only exits through `return` gets this error too. Return on the last path, or
restructure so the loop exits with `break` and the function returns after it,
as Chapter 19 does in `run_job`.

## Ownership and borrowing

### `AU3003`: changing something that is not mutable

```aura check-fail:AU3003
def main():
    count = 0
    count += 1
```

```console
$ aura check immutable.au
error[AU3003]: cannot assign to immutable binding `count`; declare it with `mut` to rebind it
 --> immutable.au:3:5
  |
3 |     count += 1
  |     ^
```

Declare the binding with `mut count = 0`. The same code appears when you call
a mutating method such as `append` on a binding or parameter that is not
`mut`, and when a method changes `self` without declaring `mut self`:

```aura check-fail:AU3003
def add(items: list[str]):
    items.append("x")
```

```console
$ aura check mutparam.au
error[AU3003]: method `append` requires a mutable receiver
 --> mutparam.au:2:11
  |
2 |     items.append("x")
  |           ^
  = help: declare the receiver place with `mut` before calling a mutating method
```

Here the fix is `items: mut list[str]`, which also tells every caller that
`add` changes the list they pass in.

### `AU3001`: use of a moved value

```aura check-fail:AU3001
def consume(name: own str):
    print(name)

def main():
    name = "ada"
    consume(name)
    print(name)
```

```console
$ aura check moved.au
error[AU3001]: use of moved value `name`
 --> moved.au:7:11
  |
7 |     print(name)
  |           ^
  = related moved.au:6:13: value moved here
  = help: pass shared access when ownership is not needed, or call `.clone()` at the move site when an independent value is required
  = fix: replace moved.au:6:17-6:17 with `.clone()`
```

`consume` takes `own str`, so the call gave the string away, and the last
line tries to use it. Decide which side is wrong. If `consume` only needs to
read, change its parameter to `name: str`. If it really needs to keep the
value, and you need one too, pass a copy: `.clone()` for a `str`, `.copy()`
for a list, dict, or set. Starting a task with `group.start_soon(f, value)`
also moves `value`, which surprises people the first time; read anything you
need from it before the call, as the job runner in Chapter 19 does with
`total = len(jobs)`.

### `AU2999`: a move inside a loop

The same mistake inside a loop gets a different code, because the problem is
not a later use but the next iteration:

```aura check-fail:AU2999
def consume(name: own str):
    print(name)

def main():
    name = "ada"
    for _ in range(3):
        consume(name)
```

```console
$ aura check loopmove.au
error[AU2999]: `for` loop body moves `name` and may execute more than once
 --> loopmove.au:6:5
  |
6 |     for _ in range(3):
  |     ^
```

The first iteration moves `name` into `consume`, and the second would have
nothing to pass. Clone inside the loop with `consume(name.clone())`, or
change `consume` to borrow.

### `AU3002`: moving out of something you only borrowed

`AU3002` is the borrow checker's general complaint: you tried to take
ownership of something that is only lent to you. Two forms come up again and
again. The first is moving a field out of a borrowed object:

```aura check-fail:AU3002
class Job:
    name: str

def keep(name: own str):
    print(name)

def report(job: Job):
    keep(job.name)
```

```console
$ aura check fieldmove.au
error[AU3002]: cannot move non-copy field `name` out of borrowed value `job`
 --> fieldmove.au:8:14
  |
8 |     keep(job.name)
  |              ^
  = related fieldmove.au:7:12: `job` is borrowed here
  = help: take `job` as `own Job` when the field should be moved, or call `.clone()` on the field to return an independent value
  = fix: replace fieldmove.au:8:18-8:18 with `.clone()`
```

`report` has shared access to `job`, so it cannot hand a piece of it to
`keep`. Clone the field, or take `job: own Job` if `report` is meant to use
the job up.

The second is moving a value out of a plain `match`, which only borrows the
value it inspects:

```aura check-fail:AU3002
def first_word(text: str) -> Result[str, str]:
    words = text.split_whitespace()
    if len(words) == 0:
        return Result.Err("empty")
    return Result.Ok(words[0].clone())

def keep(word: own str):
    print(word)

def main():
    match first_word("hello world"):
        case Result.Ok(word):
            keep(word)
        case Result.Err(message):
            print(message)
```

```console
$ aura check sharedmatch.au
error[AU3002]: cannot move `word` out of a shared match on `first_word(...)`
 --> sharedmatch.au:13:18
   |
13 |             keep(word)
   |                  ^
  = related sharedmatch.au:12:24: value is borrowed here
  = help: write `match own first_word(...)` to consume the scrutinee, or call `.clone()` to consume an independent copy
  = fix: replace sharedmatch.au:13:22-13:22 with `.clone()`
```

When the matched value is a temporary that nothing else needs, as here, write
`match own first_word("hello world"):` and the arm owns `word`. A `for` loop
over a list has the same rule: `for job in jobs:` lends each element, and
`for job in own jobs:` hands them over.

### `AU3005`: taking an element out of a list by index

```aura check-fail:AU3005
def main():
    names = ["ada", "grace"]
    first = names[0]
    print(first)
```

```console
$ aura check index.au
error[AU3005]: cannot implicitly copy `str` out of a list index; use `view value = items[index]` for shared access, `items[index].clone()` for an explicit cloned owner, or `pop(index)` or `set(index, value)` to transfer ownership
 --> index.au:3:13
  |
3 |     first = names[0]
  |             ^
```

`first = names[0]` would either copy the string or move it out of a list that
still owns it, and Aura does neither silently. The message lists your
choices. For reading, `view first = names[0]` gives a name to the element in
place. For an independent value, `names[0].clone()`. To take it out of the
list, `pop(0)` on a `mut` list. Indexing a list of copy values, such as
`list[int64]`, works as you would expect.

### `AU3008`: a value that cannot cross into a task

```aura check-fail:AU3008
import random

def roll(rng: own random.Rng) -> int64:
    return 1

def main():
    rng = random.Rng(seed=1)
    with group = TaskGroup():
        task = group.start(roll, rng)
```

```console
$ aura check transfer.au
error[AU3008]: task argument `rng` cannot cross a task boundary because `random.Rng` is a stateful generator and is not Transfer
 --> transfer.au:9:34
  |
9 |         task = group.start(roll, rng)
  |                                  ^
  = related transfer.au:3:10: task parameter `rng` is declared here
  = help: send owned data made only from Transfer components; keep capabilities and host resources on their owning worker
```

Values passed to a task, returned from one, or sent through a `Queue` must be
plain owned data: numbers, strings, collections, and classes built from
those, plus queue and task handles. Live resources (open files, child
processes, sockets), random generators, and task groups stay on the task that
created them. The fix is to send the data instead of the resource: a seed
instead of a generator, a path instead of an open file.

## Traps at run time

Traps are failures the compiler cannot rule out in advance, so they appear
when you `aura run` a program that `aura check` accepted. They stop the task,
print an `AU40xx` diagnostic with an `Aura call chain` note showing how the
program got there, and make `aura run` exit with status 1. Output the program
printed before the trap is kept.

### `AU4003`: index out of bounds

```aura
def main():
    names = ["ada", "grace"]
    view third = names[2]
    print(third)
```

```console
$ aura run bounds.au
error[AU4003]: list index `2` is out of bounds for length `2`
 --> bounds.au:3:24
  |
3 |     view third = names[2]
  |                        ^
  = note: Aura call chain (innermost first): main at 1:1
```

Check the length first, or use `names.get(2)`, which returns
`Lookup.Found(value)` or `Lookup.Missing` instead of trapping. `AU4003` also
covers slice endpoints outside the string or list, and an empty separator
passed to `split_once`.

### `AU4002`: integer overflow

```aura
def main():
    mut small: int8 = 120
    small += 10
    print(small)
```

```console
$ aura run overflow.au
error[AU4002]: integer value `130` does not fit in `int8`
 --> overflow.au:3:5
  |
3 |     small += 10
  |     ^
  = note: Aura call chain (innermost first): main at 1:1
```

Integer arithmetic is checked in Aura, so a result outside the type's range
traps rather than wrapping around to a wrong number. Use a wider type, or the
explicit `wrapping_add` and `saturating_add` family when wrapping is what you
want.

### `AU4001`: failed assertions and other invalid states

`AU4001` is the general runtime trap. You will see it most often from a
failed `assert`, where the message is the text you supplied and notes show
the values on each side of a comparison (Appendix D has an example from
`aura test`). It also reports invalid values passed to the runtime, such as a
negative timeout: Chapter 19 runs into exactly that with
`get(timeout=...) must be non-negative`, and fixes it by clamping the value
to zero.

## Source: docs/learn/index.md

# Learn Aura

This book teaches Aura through short programs that do something real. Each
chapter extends them until the pieces fit together.

Every chapter introduces one part of the language through a program worth
running. By the end you will have built command-style tools, domain models,
text parsers, concurrent worker pools, subprocess runners, and small network
services. Along the way you will meet the language rules that keep those
programs correct.

## The Three Questions Aura Wants You To Ask

Aura programs are easier to read when the code answers three questions close
to where it matters.

**Who owns this value?**
Small values copy: numbers, booleans, durations, and queue handles. Binding
one to a new name is cheap, and both names keep working. Everything else
moves: strings, collections, class instances, files, processes, task groups,
and network resources. Assignment hands ownership over. A task handle sits in
between. It copies when its result can be read more than once. At a call
boundary, the signature tells you which applies. A bare parameter shares, and
`own` transfers.

**Can this call fail?**
Failure that a caller might reasonably handle lives in the return type.
`Result[T, E]`, `T | None`, `Lookup[T]`, `QueueReceive[T]`, `TaskResult[T]`,
and the I/O and process error enums let a program handle each failure at the
line where it matters.

**What closes this resource?**
Files, network sockets, subprocess pipes, supervisors, and task groups should
normally live inside a `with` block. The block runs cleanup on normal exit and
on runtime errors that unwind through it. With `with`, "remember to close
this" becomes "this closes itself."

## The Shape Of An Aura Program

A complete script:

```aura
class Point:
    x: float64
    y: float64

def distance(point: Point) -> float64:
    return sqrt((point.x * point.x) + (point.y * point.y))

point = Point(x=3.0, y=4.0)
print(distance(point))
```

Several ideas already show:

- `Point` is a class with named fields.
- `distance` only reads its argument. The bare parameter grants shared
  access, so the caller keeps the point.
- `print` renders a value and adds a newline.
- The script runs top to bottom. It needs no `main`.

Run it with:

```bash
aura run examples/classes/point_distance.au
```

## What This Track Covers

The chapters are ordered so that each idea has a practical reason to exist
before its formal rules arrive.

1. [Getting Aura Running](/learn/install-and-run): install the CLI, run your first program, and build your first binary.
2. [Aura For Python Developers](/learn/from-python): the fast track. What
   carries over from Python, and what will surprise you.
3. [The First Program](/learn/small-programs): bindings, functions, control flow, and small decisions made with `match`.
4. [Shaping Data](/learn/data-modeling): classes, enums, methods, and the patterns that keep domain data consistent.
5. [Working With Collections](/learn/collections): `list[T]`, `dict[K, V]`,
   `set[T]`, eager owned comprehensions, owned list and str slices, and
   fixed-shape numeric `Array[T]` values.
6. [Converting Between Types](/learn/casting): `as`, `.to_float()`, parsing
   text, and why nothing converts implicitly.
7. [Values, Moves, And Borrows](/learn/ownership-and-borrowing): the ownership model, explained through the programs that benefit from it.
8. [Results And Optional Values](/learn/results-and-options): how Aura represents absence and recoverable failure without hiding control flow.
9. [Testing](/learn/testing): writing tests, reading a failed assertion, parameterized cases, and CI output.

Three case studies put the pieces together:

- [Queue Worker Pool](/learn/case-studies/queue-worker-pool): a structured-concurrency pattern that shuts down cleanly.
- [Supervised Process Runner](/learn/case-studies/process-supervisor): a small service supervisor with a restart policy and an event stream.
- [Typed Tool Agent](/learn/case-studies/tool-agent): a tool-calling agent with derived JSON codecs, schemas, and a tracing decorator.
